  • Scope of revalidation: container closure integrity (CCI), stoppering force, visible particulates, E&L, simulated shipping tests

Cost impact: COC syringes cost about 2-3 times as much as standard glass syringes; the equipment investment for a vacuum stoppering system is typically several hundred thousand dollars or more; full validation may take 6-12 months.

Discussion Questions

  1. Your production line already has a conventional vent-tube stoppering system, but the new product needs silicone-free stoppers. Can you keep the existing stoppering mechanism and only change the stopper type? Explain why or why not, and propose an alternative.
  2. COC syringes do not need silicone oil, but could their polymer material itself have other adverse interactions with protein drugs? How would you evaluate this? (Hint: consider E&L studies and protein adsorption testing.)
  3. "Vacuum filling" solves the splashing problem at the luer tip, but does it bring new challenges or limitations of its own? (Hint: consider the tendency of the solution to foam and the problem of entrained bubbles.)
1.1.3 Physicochemical Properties

Original Text

Properties such as viscosity, surface tension, or foaming tendencies for liquids, or products that are suspensions, quick-drying, flammable, or explosive may require specialized filling technologies, special filling needles, or specific filling-process conditions for optimal, safe filling. Compatibility of the materials in contact with product should also be evaluated to ensure maintenance of the physicochemical properties of the product.

Powder characteristics that will influence powder filling-system selection and process control are flowability, particle size, particle morphology, bulk and tapped density, angle of repose, and surface area, among others (see Section 17.0).

The following are examples of physicochemical properties that may need to be taken into consideration:

High Viscosity: High viscosity products, which must be filled air-bubble-free, often need to be filled under vacuum. Depending on the surface tension and break-away behavior (e.g., likelihood to drip) during filling, a fluted filling needle (or, in some cases, a closing needle) may be considered (see Section 3.0 for additional detail on needle types).

Low Surface Tension: Products with a surface tension that is less than water must be filled with a smaller internal diameter cylindrical needle, or a needle with a crimped outlet or basketed outlet to prevent dripping (see Section 3.0 for more details on needle types).

Foaming: Products with a tendency to foam during handling often create a foam or froth when agitation occurs at the air-liquid interface. The fluid pathway and vessels must be carefully designed to minimize the opportunities for foaming, which may include but are not limited to:

  • Controlling the methods of introduction to the bulk or intermediate vessel (e.g., through a J-tube or tube that extends to the bottom of the vessel)
  • Limiting the pressure applied to the product
  • Controlling the fill-curve for the liquid dispensing (i.e., controlled velocity, acceleration, deceleration)
  • Use of diving needles (i.e., synchronized movement of the filling needle correlated to the liquid dispensing)
  • Or several of these techniques together (see Section 4.0 for more details)

Suspension: Suspension products are a heterogeneous mixture of a liquid and finely distributed solids (particles). To ensure that there is no settling of the particles and to ensure uniform filling, the solids must be continuously suspended in the liquid. This can be accomplished by agitating the suspension using agitators and/or recirculation. In addition, it will be very important to control filling-stoppage times (see Section 4.6 for diagrams of possible designs for both agitation and recirculation). Care must be taken to ensure that the selected suspension mechanism does not impact the biological or physicochemical characteristics of the product. Another consideration for suspensions is that the solids content in the suspension can have an abrasive effect, which may influence the selection of the materials of construction of the filling equipment (e.g., using ceramic instead of chrome-plated stainless steel).

Quick-Drying: Quick-drying products or those that have a tendency to crystallize can accumulate at the points where they are exposed to air such as at the tips of filling needles. The exact characteristics of the formulation will determine the appropriate engineering solution. Therefore, it is important to evaluate the composition of the product to determine which ingredient(s) is(are) responsible for any visible residue and, when possible, formulate to limit their impact (some excipients have a tendency to form very visible residues even when the solid quantities are negligible). Data should be available on the impact of dried residue ending up within a dosage unit in order to determine risk to patients (e.g., what are the quality implications for potency? stability? particulate?). When reformulation is not possible, the filling needle design must be selected to prevent dripping or accumulation; basket needle designs may be helpful. The implementation of jacketed needles (i.e., gassing needles) may help with some products (see Section 3.0 for additional details on needle selection). Suck back may also be helpful to avoid accumulation of product at the tip of the needle.

The fill curve is the primary method to control splashing and accumulation of product on the outside of the needle. The fill curve should avoid any sudden acceleration or excessive velocity, the filling should be conducted from bottom up, and the needle motion should avoid touching the surface of the liquid at any point during the fill curve. Smooth flow throughout the filling cycle should be the goal.

With regard to the dosing system, the product-lubricated rotary piston pump (RPP) may experience drying at the interface where the piston enters. Therefore, a better choice in filling system might incorporate closed system technology such as PP, TP, or DP. Environmental conditions such as low humidity may also exacerbate rapid drying. During prolonged operation or prolonged periods of line stoppage, drying may become inevitable and may require interventions such as flushing needles and discarding units upon restart, or disabling or replacing filling stations in the worst cases. From a quality control perspective if the residue affects dosing accuracy 100% IPC may be required (see Section 5.0 for additional details on IPC for dose control).

Flammable or Explosive: Flammable or explosive products will require that influencing factors be evaluated prior to determining the appropriate filling technology, such as:

  • Material properties (e.g., flash point, ignition temperature, maximum content of the flammable constituent in the formulation)
  • Maximum volume to be filled in each container and headspace for volatile constituents
  • Zone classification, temperature class, and explosion group
  • Identification of external influences and ambient temperature
  • Safety data sheet

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy: Filling Problems Are Like Challenges in the Kitchen

Think of the filling system as a "kitchen", with drug solutions of different properties as different ingredients:

High viscosity = pouring honey into a small jar: pour too fast and there are bubbles in the container; pour too slowly and it clings to the rim every time. Solution: heat to lower the viscosity (or use vacuum to remove bubbles).

Low surface tension = pouring alcohol into a glass: it "drips" more easily than water, because with low surface tension the droplets slide easily off the edge of the vessel. Solution: use a finer nozzle to control flow rate, or design a "suck-back structure" at the outlet.

Foaming = pouring beer into a glass: pour from a height and the foam surges out; pour slowly down the side of the glass and there is less foam. The "fill curve" is the program that controls "the speed and angle of the pour".

Suspensions = orange juice with pulp: without shaking, the pulp sinks to the bottom, so the first few glasses are all water and the last few all pulp. Continuous agitation is required before and during filling.

Crystallizing products = evaporating salt water: crystals form at the edges exposed to air. The same happens at the needle outlet: on contact with air the drug crystallizes and, over time, blocks the outlet.

Key Point: The Importance of the Fill Curve

The "fill curve" describes how the flow rate of the drug solution changes over time during filling, including three phases: acceleration, steady flow and deceleration.

A well-designed fill curve should:

  • avoid sudden acceleration (to prevent turbulence → foaming/splashing)
  • start filling from the bottom of the container (bottom-up, avoiding free-fall impact)
  • keep the filling needle out of contact with the liquid surface throughout (to prevent the needle being contaminated by the liquid and the surface being disturbed)
  • decelerate smoothly at the end (to prevent the last surplus drops from falling)

The fill curve is the parameter in filling process development that most needs to be tailored to the actual product characteristics; the curve of another product cannot simply be borrowed.

Key Point: A Special Risk of Suspensions: Abrasiveness

Many people know that suspensions need agitation to remain uniform, but they easily overlook another issue: abrasion of the filling equipment by solid particles.

Hard particles in a suspension (such as some inorganic salt crystals and mineral components) gradually wear metal surfaces like sandpaper as they flow through the pump and needle. The worn metal fragments become visible/sub-visible particles that enter the drug solution directly, which is a serious quality risk.

This is why filling pumps made of ceramic (hard, chemically inert and wear-resistant), rather than conventional chrome-plated stainless steel, are generally preferred for filling suspensions.

Decision Framework: Engineering Countermeasures for Products That Dry Out Easily

Assessing filling challenges for products that dry out/crystallize easily:
      │
      ├─ Step 1: Formulation assessment
      │     Identify which component causes crystallization/drying
      │     Can the formulation be adjusted to reduce the effect?
      │
      ├─ Step 2: Needle design selection
      │     - Basket needle: reduces the area where product can build up
      │     - Jacketed needle/gas-flushed needle: inert gas surrounds the needle outlet
      │     - Suck-back function: after the needle withdraws,
      │       residual liquid is actively drawn back so that
      │       it does not hang from the needle
      │
      ├─ Step 3: Fill curve optimization
      │     Avoid abrupt acceleration and deceleration
      │     Fill bottom-up
      │     Keep the needle out of the liquid surface throughout
      │
      ├─ Step 4: Filling pump selection
      │     The piston of an RPP (rotary piston pump) may dry at its inlet
      │     → Give priority to sealed designs: PP, TP, DP pumps
      │
      └─ Step 5: Line stoppage management procedure
            Stoppage → preset flush cycle
            Restart → discard the first few units, then resume filling
            Long stoppage → deactivate the filling station or change the needle
            If dose accuracy is affected → start 100% IPC

Key Point: The Regulatory Framework for Flammable/Explosive Products

Flammable/explosive drugs (such as ethanol-containing injections and some volatile organic solvents) must be filled in compliance with electrical explosion protection requirements. This is not a GMP issue but an industrial safety regulation issue, involving several sets of standards:

  • ATEX Directive (EU): the directive on equipment and protective systems for use in explosive atmospheres
  • NEC (US): the National Electrical Code, which defines hazardous location classification
  • IEC 60079 series: the international standards for explosion-protected electrical equipment

Key parameters: the flash point and ignition temperature determine the hazardous area classification (Zone 0/1/2 or Class I Div 1/2), which in turn determines the level of explosion protection certification the filling equipment must have (Ex d, Ex e, Ex i, etc.).

This means that all electrical equipment in the filling room (motors, switches, sensors, computer control systems) must meet the corresponding explosion protection certification, which has a major impact on equipment procurement and facility design.

Discussion Questions

  1. You are evaluating a contract to fill a vaccine suspension. The client says: "All we need is filling equipment that can stir the suspension." Why is this requirement far from sufficient? What other key questions do you need to ask to ensure filling quality?
  2. An injection containing 20% ethanol (flash point about 16°C) is to be filled, with a filling room ambient temperature of 20°C. From a safety standpoint, what special facility and equipment requirements does this filling operation need?
  3. The fill curve follows the principle of "bottom-up filling". Explain why filling from the bottom of the container is better than dripping from the top, from the perspectives of "sterility" and "fill accuracy".
  4. An RPP (rotary piston pump) is particularly unfavorable for crystallizing drugs, whereas a PP (peristaltic pump) is more suitable. What is the reasoning behind this statement? Explain how the structural differences between the two pump types determine their suitability for products that dry out easily.

Core Concept: Six Filling Challenges from Physicochemical Properties

This section lists the six most common special physicochemical properties, each corresponding to a different engineering challenge:

Practical Application: The CDMO Business Process for Evaluating Physicochemical Properties

Before a CDMO takes on a new filling project, the technical assessment stage should include a "Product Characteristics Questionnaire" covering the following questions:

The answers to this questionnaire directly determine whether additional investment in existing equipment is needed, or whether the project is simply unsuitable for production on the existing filling line. Clarifying these questions before quoting avoids costly late-stage modifications and project delays.

Section Summary — Section 1A

  • Bullseye design philosophy: SA (sterility assurance) is always the first priority; CQAs (critical quality attributes) come second; commercial flexibility comes last. When the three conflict, the upper level always prevails, a principle that runs through the whole of PDA Guide No. 1.
  • Irreversibility of design decisions: the design of an aseptic filling line locks in the technical architecture and business capability for the next 10-15 years; thorough product characterization up front is far more economical than later modification.
  • Highly pharmacologically active products: OEB 4-5 products mandatorily require a cRABS or isolator; the dual design objectives of "protecting the product" (positive pressure) and "protecting personnel" (containment/negative pressure) must both be considered.
  • Five product sensitivities: temperature (active temperature control/time limitation), oxygen (inert gas overlay, with gassing at stoppering the most effective), light (minimal protection after characterization studies, mindful of the visual inspection trade-off), metal (ceramic/SU systems, E&L assessment), silicone oil (COC container → silicone-free stopper → vacuum stoppering → possibly vacuum filling, a chain of design effects).
  • Six physicochemical properties: high viscosity (vacuum filling/special needles), low surface tension (narrowed orifice/basket needle), foaming (J-tube/dive needle/fill curve control), suspensions (continuous agitation/ceramic equipment against wear), products that dry out or crystallize (basket needle/suck-back/sealed pumps/100% IPC), flammability/explosiveness (explosion-protected electrical certification/area classification).
  • Integration of engineering and operation: the success of aseptic filling requires "equipment design" and "operator behavior" to work together; a gap on either side can compromise sterility, so the feasibility of operating procedures must be considered at the same time when selecting equipment.
