1.4

Filling Speed and Volume Driving Selection and Design

Filling Speed and Throughput Drive Equipment Selection and Design

1.4.1 Capacity Model Inputs — Shutdown Allowances & Core Factors
Original Text (English)

Only after creating a capacity model that takes the above factors into consideration can a filling speed target be set. The key inputs to the capacity model include:

  • Shutdown Allowances – How many days per year will the line be operated, accounting for such factors as shutdowns, aseptic process simulations (APS), testing, technical studies, recapitalization, and changes?
  • Campaign Strategy – Will multiple batches be campaigned to reduce changeover time? (See Section 1.5 for additional considerations for campaigning.)
  • Changeover Time – What amount of time is required between campaigns and between batches within a campaign, measured from the last good container (current batch) to the first good container (next batch)?
  • % Yield – How much scrap can be tolerated?
  • % Line Efficiency – When filling, what is the expected line efficiency (i.e., the tolerance level for stoppages/downtime)?
  • % Facility Efficiency – Of the available hours in a year, what percentage of these will the line operate (i.e., how much allowance for unforeseen events will be built into the production plan)?
  • Capacity Flexibility – Should the initial capacity plan be established for low filling-line utilization so there is ample time to make changes, if needed (e.g., plan for staffing more shifts than needed to meet the capacity plan, select a faster line than needed to meet the plan)?
  • Facility Suitability – In an existing facility, does the facility design (e.g., footprint, cleanroom classifications, utilities) support the selected filling line?

Only after creating a capacity model that takes the above factors into consideration can a filling speed target be set.

Commentary

The Eight Input Parameters of the Capacity Model

Before setting a filling speed target, a complete capacity model must be established. These eight parameters form the core inputs of the model:

  • Shutdown Allowances: non-production time such as APS runs, PM and regulatory inspections, typically 30–60 days deducted per year
  • Campaign Strategy: running multiple consecutive batches vs. single-batch mode; affects changeover cost and SA risk
  • Changeover Time: the time from the "last good container" of the previous batch to the "first good container" of the next batch
  • % Yield: the acceptable proportion of rejects; affects raw material consumption and cost
  • % Line Efficiency: actual efficiency during filling, including losses from short stoppages
  • % Facility Efficiency: the proportion of available annual working hours during which the facility actually operates
  • Capacity Flexibility: headroom reserved for growth; low utilization at the start makes later adjustments easier
  • Facility Suitability: whether the existing building's cleanroom grades and utilities can support the selected filling line

Capacity Model Calculation Logic

Annual effective hours = 365 days × 24 hr × % Facility Efficiency
          − Shutdown Days
Actual filling time = Annual effective hours × % Line Efficiency
Annual container output = Filling speed (containers/hr)
             × Actual filling time
             × % Yield

Only after these eight parameters are fixed can the required filling speed target be worked out backwards. For example, with an annual demand of 5 million units, 98% yield, 85% line efficiency and 70% facility efficiency, the corresponding filling speed (containers/hour) can be calculated.

Analogy: Restaurant Seat Utilization

Think of the filling line as a restaurant kitchen:

  • Shutdown allowances = the kitchen's days off each year plus equipment cleaning days
  • Changeover time = the time to re-prepare ingredients when the menu (product) changes
  • Line efficiency = the ratio of the chef's actual cooking time to time spent waiting for ingredients
  • Facility efficiency = the proportion of the 365 days the restaurant is actually open

Without a complete "restaurant scheduling model," you cannot know how many chefs (filling speed) you need to meet the sales target (annual output).

CDMO Application Scenario

David's CDMO receives an order from a new customer: 2 million units of 2 mL lyophilized powder vials per year. Before issuing the filling speed RFQ, the following must be confirmed:

  • APS once per quarter, with 2 days of line downtime each time → 8 days of shutdown per year
  • The product is an orphan drug with strict changeover cleaning validation → 16 hours of changeover time
  • Current line efficiency is about 78% and facility efficiency 65%

After plugging these into the model, if the required filling speed exceeds the limit of the existing equipment, adding shifts or upgrading the equipment must be considered. Decision order: SA assurance → product quality → commercial capacity.

1.4.2 Campaign Strategy Overview
Original Text (English)

Campaign Strategy — Will multiple batches be campaigned to reduce changeover time? The intent of campaigning is to minimize the number of interventions, fine-tune and stabilize the line, and improve the cost-and-capacity utilization of the line.

The changeover time is measured from the last good container of the current batch to the first good container of the next batch. This metric captures the full duration of teardown, cleaning, setup, and qualification activities between production runs.

The % yield reflects how much scrap can be tolerated. The % line efficiency captures the tolerance for stoppages and downtime during active filling. The % facility efficiency accounts for the proportion of available annual hours actually used in production, including allowances for unforeseen events.

The capacity flexibility question asks whether the initial plan should intentionally underutilize the line — for example, by staffing more shifts than needed or selecting a faster line — to preserve room for future adjustments. In an existing facility, facility suitability must be confirmed: the footprint, cleanroom classifications, and utilities must support the selected filling line.

Commentary

Precise Definition of Changeover Time

The start and end points of changeover time (Changeover Time) are critical:

  • Start point: filling of the last good container of the current batch is completed
  • End point: the first good container of the next batch passes quality inspection

This definition covers all activities including line teardown, cleaning, setup, sterilization, PUPSIT and APS (if required), and is one of the hardest variables to predict in the capacity model.

Reminder of SA Decision Priority

When considering Capacity Flexibility, the decision hierarchy must be kept in mind:

  • Choosing a "faster filling line" is a business decision (priority 3)
  • But a faster line speed may shorten operator reaction time and increase intervention frequency → affecting SA (priority 1)
  • Therefore, any speed increase must be assessed together with SA risk and cannot be judged on capacity alone

Comprehension Check

Consider this scenario: a filling line's annual line efficiency rises from 80% to 90%, while changeover time is cut from 8 hours to 4 hours (through quick-changeover technology). How much does each improvement affect annual output? Which improvement has the greater impact on SA risk, and why?

1.5

Aseptic Filling Campaign Requirements Driving Selection and Design

SA Requirements for Campaigning Drive Equipment Selection and Design

1.5.1 Definition and Applicable Scenarios of Campaigning
Original Text (English)

Campaigning is a filling strategy where multiple batches are produced back-to-back on a line without a complete teardown and setup between batches. Campaigning is most commonly encountered when the same product is filled at the same or differing fill volumes or into different primary containers and/or closures.

However, there may also be circumstances where different formulations are filled into the same container and closures within a campaign if the product-contact filling pathway is fully changed. This latter approach requires assurance that there is no risk of cross-contamination from spills or splashes with appropriate control strategies and risk assessments.

In either case, the intent is to minimize the number of interventions, fine-tune and stabilize the line, and improve the cost-and-capacity utilization of the line.

Campaigning is the preferred operating mode when managing a high-volume product on a filling isolator line that is set up and staffed to operate on a 24/7 basis. Lines that are required to fill multiple small-volume products, which may require different primary component types and sizes, are more suited to operate in batch mode.

Attributes that might differ under various campaign approaches include:

  • Changeover of fluid pathway
  • Changeover of format parts
  • Line clearance requirements
  • Changeover of containers and closures (e.g., hoppers, bowls, and/or tracks, provided these changes can be accomplished under fully closed barrier conditions)
  • Bulk changeover
  • Operator shift changes

The specific protection offered by a fully closed and decontaminated environment means that campaigning is commonly undertaken in isolators. In this case, the expectation for the campaign would be that the isolator is not opened for equipment changes between batches.

Campaigning is also possible in restricted access barrier systems (RABS) but in general the duration of the campaign is typically shorter than in isolators because of the increased risks due to the more "open" nature of RABS.

With the advent of more rapid changeover technology and, for isolators rapid decontamination (and aeration) processes, the time savings that originally drove much of the focus on campaigning is reduced. All variables that influence sterility assurance (SA) should be weighed carefully when making the decision on whether to campaign.

Commentary

Definition of Campaigning (Consecutive Batch Production)

Campaigning (consecutive batch production) is a strategy of producing multiple batches in succession on the same filling line without a full teardown and reassembly.

Common campaigning scenarios:

  • The same product with the same or different fill volumes (e.g., 1 mL, 2 mL, 5 mL series)
  • The same product in different primary containers (e.g., filling 2 mL glass vials first, then 1 mL syringes)
  • Different formulations using the same container, but the fluid pathway must be fully replaced and a strict cross-contamination control strategy applied

Core objectives: fewer interventions, a more stable line, and better cost and capacity utilization.

Analogy: Aircraft Turnaround vs. Heavy Maintenance

Campaigning is like an aircraft "quick turnaround":

  • Batch mode = a full C-check after every flight → safe but time-consuming
  • Campaigning = refuel and change passengers on arrival, then fly again → efficient, but pilot (operator) fatigue management and aircraft condition monitoring must be stricter

An isolator is like a fully sealed cabin: some maintenance can be done even while the engines keep running. RABS is like a semi-open hangar: maintenance must be done more carefully, and the maintenance time cannot be too long.

SA First Priority: Key Differences Between Isolator and RABS

In campaigning decisions, the choice of barrier technology directly affects SA risk:

  • Isolator: fully enclosed and capable of VHP biodecontamination → suited to long campaigns, with parts changed without opening the enclosure
  • RABS (Restricted Access Barrier System): relatively "open" by nature → campaign duration is usually shorter than with an isolator, and SA risk rises over time

As quick-changeover technology and rapid decontamination (fast VHP cycles) become widespread, the time advantage of campaigning has narrowed. The decision whether to campaign should return to SA risk assessment rather than simply considering time savings.

1.5.2 Variables Affecting SA Risk
Original Text (English)

The variables that impact sterility assurance (SA) risk include, but are not limited to:

  • Technology in use for barrier protection of the process (i.e., isolator or RABS, open or closed) and the overall expected quality of the environment throughout the intended use period
  • Length of processing times and the risks associated with the higher numbers of manipulations and interventions (routine and non-routine) in prolonged processing
  • Frequency and types of disinfection and/or biodecontamination
  • Waste accumulation (including packaging/wrap waste and any spills, breakage or dropped components) within the operating environment over prolonged processing times
  • Duration of use of sterilizing filter and/or sterile bulk hold conditions and times
  • Simplicity or complexity of changeover and setup including the number and complexity of the required interventions and frequency of the required changeover or setup events

A careful risk-benefit analysis is recommended based upon the specific technologies in use and the risks to SA. Controls should be designed to mitigate sterility assurance risks regardless of the selected mode of operation.

Commentary

The Six SA Risk Variables

When deciding on a campaigning strategy, the following six SA risk dimensions must be evaluated systematically:

  • Barrier technology: isolator > cRABS > oRABS; the higher the degree of enclosure, the longer the campaign can be
  • Length of processing time: the longer the operation, the more interventions accumulate → SA risk increases linearly; non-routine interventions carry especially high risk
  • Disinfection/decontamination frequency: if VHP biodecontamination is not frequent enough, the microbial load accumulates during the campaign
  • Waste accumulation: broken glass, packaging waste, liquid spills and the like build up over a long campaign and become contamination sources
  • Sterilizing filter use time: the duration of continuous filter use is linked to integrity; exceeding the validated time limit is an SA risk
  • Changeover complexity: the more intervention steps and the more complex the changeover, the higher the probability of introducing contamination with each operation

Core Principle: Risk-Benefit Analysis Cannot Be Skipped

The PDA Guide states clearly: regardless of the operating mode chosen (campaign or batch), the control measures must be designed to effectively reduce SA risk.

This means that "we use an isolator so it is safer" cannot be used as a reason to skip risk assessment. Every campaign strategy must be supported by a documented risk-benefit analysis.

SA is always the first priority — even under heavy capacity pressure, commercial interests cannot be used as a reason to avoid SA risk assessment.

1.5.3 Campaign SA Risk Control Measures
Original Text (English)

To mitigate risks associated with prolonged processing, the intended operational approach should consider:

  • Partial or total clean-in-place/sterilize-in-place (CIP/SIP) of fluid pathway or replacement between batches
  • Biodecontamination of all, or of high-risk, parts of the environment between batches
  • Glove integrity-testing intermittently (but regularly) throughout the processing
  • Inclusion of new filter setups with new pre-use post-sterilization integrity-testing (PUPSIT) test results for each batch

When campaigning is selected, the aseptic process should be validated under the conditions associated with the campaign, to ensure that conditions and activities that may pose a risk to producing a sterile product are challenged in the APS. For example, the maximum time between biodecontamination events, while conducting the maximum number of interventions representing a routine campaign, should be evaluated.

The concept of a "piggy-back" APS — where one APS run is conducted at the beginning of the campaign and another at the end, with production batches in between — is used to validate the full duration of campaigning.

If designed and executed properly, campaigning should not introduce additional SA risk when compared to conventional batch-based models.

Commentary

Four Key Campaign SA Control Measures

To address the SA risk of long consecutive-batch production, the Guide proposes four specific control measures:

  • CIP/SIP (clean-in-place/sterilize-in-place): partial or full CIP/SIP of the fluid pathway between batches, or direct replacement of fluid pathway components. Applicable to high-risk products or formulation changes.
  • Biodecontamination: VHP (vaporized hydrogen peroxide) or other biodecontamination of all or high-risk areas between batches, resetting the environmental bioburden.
  • Glove Integrity Testing: regular (uninterrupted) testing of isolator glove integrity during the campaign, to prevent glove pinholes from causing environmental contamination.
  • PUPSIT for every batch: a new sterilizing filter is used for every batch, and a new pre-use post-sterilization integrity test (PUPSIT) result is submitted, ensuring the reliability of sterile filtration.

APS Validation Design: The Piggy-Back Concept

Campaign APS validation structure:

[APS Run 1] → [Batch 1] → [Batch 2] → ... → [Batch N] → [APS Run 2]
    |                                                          |
  Campaign start                                        Campaign end
  (worst-case condition:                          (worst-case conditions:
   maximum number of                               longest processing time,
   interventions)                                  most waste accumulation)

Piggy-Back APS: one APS simulation at the start and one at the end, bracketing all production batches of the campaign, to verify the full SA protection capability from the beginning to the end of the campaign.

The APS must challenge the worst-case conditions of the campaign: the longest decontamination interval and the greatest number of routine interventions.

CDMO Application: Campaign Decision Checklist

In a CDMO environment, whenever the feasibility of campaigning is assessed, the following should be confirmed:

  • Is the barrier technology an isolator (preferred) or RABS? If RABS, what is the upper limit of campaign duration?
  • Are CIP/SIP or fluid pathway replacement performed between batches?
  • Has the biodecontamination frequency been validated as sufficient? (Has the longest interval been challenged in the APS?)
  • Is the glove integrity testing frequency written into the batch record?
  • Are the PUPSIT results for each batch recorded independently?
  • Does the campaign APS use a Piggy-Back design?

Important: if any item cannot be met, fix it first rather than lowering the control standard. SA takes priority over commercial considerations.

Comprehension Check

Why is campaigning more common in isolators than in RABS, and why can campaigns run longer there? Explain from the SA risk perspective, and describe how the spread of fast VHP technology has changed the strategic value of campaigning.

1.6

Aseptic Filling Line Future-Proofing Requirements Driving Selection and Design

Future-Proofing Requirements Drive Equipment Selection and Design

Original Text (English)

Flexibility for the future is, of course, desirable and has a long history in manufacturing. Engineers and technical services staff will seek many options and design choices to plan for future changes. Project managers and financial staff may wish to avoid overly ambitious future-proofing a new filling line due to the increased project timelines and the potential additional costs.

A thorough understanding of the most likely future products, capacity flexibility, and alignment of risk (including current GMP compliance risk such as the need for increased barrier protections, the greater prevalence of biodecontamination, higher degrees of automation and/or robotics that comply with First Air principles) with strategic planning and finance is the surest path to incorporating flexibility successfully.

Commentary

The Core Tension of Future-Proofing

Future-Proofing means building into the filling line design, in advance, functions or flexibility that may be needed in the future, in order to extend the equipment's service life and adaptability.

A typical business tension exists here:

  • Engineers/technical team: want maximum flexibility reserved → favor multi-function, modular designs → higher initial investment
  • Project managers/finance team: want to control cost and timeline → favor a lean design → lower initial investment but possibly limited future options

The PDA Guide's recommendation: find the balance by understanding the "most likely future product mix" in depth, rather than pursuing flexibility without limit.

Risk Alignment: The SA Dimension of Future-Proofing

Future-proofing is not just a business decision; it also involves forward planning for GMP compliance risk:

  • Upgrading barrier protection: regulatory trends call for higher-grade barriers (e.g., moving from RABS to isolator)
  • Wider use of biodecontamination: VHP and other biodecontamination technologies are becoming standard, so space and interfaces must be reserved in the design
  • Automation/robotics: automated intervention systems consistent with the First Air principle can reduce the SA risk from human operations

First Air principle: ensures that the first air (coming directly from the HEPA filter) flows straight over the product-exposed area without being blocked by personnel or equipment, maintaining optimal environmental protection in the aseptic filling area.

Analogy: Pre-Laying Conduits When Building a House

Future-proofing is like deciding whether to pre-lay electrical and water conduits when building a house:

  • Spend 5% more now on pre-laid conduits → installing new equipment later only needs wire pulling, saving 80% of the cost
  • Skip it now → retrofitting later requires breaking into walls, at 5-10 times the original cost

The filling line analogy: reserving VHP connections, space for robotic intervention and utility capacity for capacity expansion — these "pre-laid conduits" are cheap at the design stage but extremely expensive to retrofit later.

CDMO Strategy Application

In a CDMO environment, the difficulty of future-proofing lies in the uncertainty of the customer product mix. The recommended strategy:

  • Analyze the existing customer pipeline: the most likely container types (vial/syringe/cartridge) and product types (protein/suspension/high-viscosity) over the next 5 years
  • Design modular filling heads that can switch filling technology without major changes to the main machine frame
  • Reserve installation space and interfaces for a VHP generator (even if it is not purchased initially)
  • Evaluate the space requirements of robotic intervention systems and reserve them in the RABS/isolator design

Key principle: future-proofing investment must align with the trend of SA compliance requirements, rather than simply pursuing commercial flexibility.

2.0

Aseptic Filling Technologies

Aseptic Filling Technology Overview

2.0 Introduction — The Four Major Filling Technologies
Original Text (English)

There are four commonly used filler technologies:

  • Peristaltic Pump (PP)
  • Rotary Piston Pump (RPP)
  • Time Pressure Filler (TP)
  • Rolling Diaphragm Pump (DP)

The selection criteria for the most appropriate filling technology should include:

  • Understanding and balancing the capabilities of each technology
  • Recognizing features and limitations related to primary components and product characteristics
  • Determining which filling system can support the required business objectives
Commentary

Overview of the Four Aseptic Filling Technologies

The choice of liquid aseptic filling technology directly affects product quality (CQAs) and SA risk, and is central to design decisions. The four mainstream technologies each have their own scope of application:

  • Peristaltic Pump (PP): generates flow by squeezing a tube; suited to single-use fluid pathways, but has poor compatibility with solvent-based products
  • Rotary Piston Pump (RPP): mechanical positive-displacement filling with high accuracy, suited to high-viscosity products, but not suitable for long-chain proteins (shear force issue)
  • Time Pressure Filler (TP): controls fill volume by pressure and time, with no moving parts contacting the product, but does not support single-use fluid pathways and has limitations for temperature-sensitive products (e.g., those needing a cold chain)
  • Rolling Diaphragm Pump (DP): a diaphragm isolates the product from the drive mechanism; suited to the medium-viscosity range, and some suppliers offer a single-use version

Three Dimensions of Selection Decisions

When selecting a filling technology, three dimensions must be considered together, and their order reflects the decision hierarchy:

  • First: product characteristics and container type (CQAs — patient safety) — shear sensitivity of the protein, viscosity range, compatibility of the product with pump materials
  • Second: SA compliance requirements (sterility assurance) — is CIP/SIP supported? Is campaigning supported? Can it be installed outside the RABS?
  • Third: business objectives (operational needs) — single-use fluid pathways reduce cross-contamination risk and changeover cost; does the fill range cover future products?
Table 2.0-1🔍: Comparison of Attributes of Four Major Filling Technologies🔍
Original Text (English) — Table 2.0-1🔍

The following table compares key technical attributes of the four filling technologies:

Commentary

Table 2.0-1🔍 Key Differences

The four technologies are similar in filling accuracy (all "Very accurate"); the key differences lie in:

  • Single-use (SU) fluid pathway: PP is best, while TP currently does not support it → affects the cross-contamination control strategy
  • Campaign compatibility: PP is limited by hose wear; long campaigns require monitoring hose life and regular replacement
  • Viscosity range: RPP is far higher than the other three (300,000 mPa·s) and is the only option for high-viscosity products (e.g., ophthalmic gels, suspensions)
  • Installation outside RABS: RPP cannot be installed outside the RABS (because of its complex mechanical structure), which affects First Air compliant design

SA Key Point: The Significance of Installation Outside the RABS

"Installation Outside RABS" is an important SA design consideration:

  • Filling pump installed outside the RABS → drive mechanism sits outside the controlled environment, with only the fluid pathway entering the aseptic area → less mechanical complexity inside the aseptic area → lower SA risk
  • RPP must be installed inside the RABS → more mechanical disturbance in the aseptic area → possibly more frequent interventions → additional SA control measures needed

This is a typical example of SA priority influencing technology selection.

Managing PP Hose Life During Campaigns

Hose wear risk assessment:

Monitoring indicators:
- Fill volume deviation trend (control chart)
- Hose usage hours (vs. validated life limit)
- Visual inspection (cracks, deformation)

Recommended practice for PP in campaigns:
- Set a maximum continuous usage time limit
- Mandatory hose replacement every N batches
- Perform fill accuracy verification after replacement
- Record in the batch record for traceability
Table 2.0-2🔍: Containers Used with Each Technology🔍
Original Text (English) — Table 2.0-2🔍

The following table shows which primary container types are compatible with each filling technology:

Commentary

Table 2.0-2🔍 Analysis: Container Compatibility

The four technologies differ little in container compatibility; all support all six mainstream container types. The key points of difference:

  • Cartridge: TP is the preferred technology. Cartridge filling requires precise pressure control, and the time-pressure mechanism of TP is particularly well suited to the narrow bore of cartridges, with less risk of air bubbles or liquid residue.
  • CDMO flexibility considerations: since all four technologies support the various container types, container type is usually not the deciding factor in technology selection; product characteristics (viscosity, protein sensitivity) are the key.

CDMO Application: Multi-Container Platform Strategy

For a CDMO, being able to switch flexibly between container types on the same filling line is a core competitive strength. As Table 2.0-2🔍 shows, all four technologies have broad container compatibility, so a CDMO's technology selection strategy should focus on:

  • The most common product types in the customer pipeline (proteins → exclude RPP; high viscosity → choose RPP)
  • Whether a single-use fluid pathway is needed to avoid cross-contamination risk (PP is preferred)
  • Future campaign needs (PP hose wear issue)
Table 2.0-3🔍: Comparison Based Upon Common Product Types🔍
Original Text (English) — Table 2.0-3🔍

The following table provides technology recommendations based on common pharmaceutical product types:

Commentary

Table 2.0-3🔍 Analysis: Product Type Determines Technology Choice

Product type is the CQA factor with the greatest influence on technology selection (priority 2):

  • Proteins: RPP is not suitable, because the shear force generated by the rotary piston can damage protein structure (e.g., mAbs, enzymes) and affect biological activity → a direct hazard to patient safety
  • Suspensions: PP is limited by its viscosity ceiling (60 mPa·s); DP has some limitations (suspended particle size must be checked for compatibility with the diaphragm gap); RPP and TP are suitable
  • High-Viscosity: only RPP is suitable (upper limit 300,000 mPa·s), e.g., ophthalmic gels and high-concentration antibody formulations
  • Low viscosity & SVP: all four technologies are suitable; selection returns to SA design (SU needs, campaign needs, installation outside the RABS)

RPP Shear Force Issue — The Intersection of SA and CQA

The reason RPP is unsuitable for long-chain proteins illustrates the core of CQA priority:

  • The rotary piston generates high shear force at the seams → damage to the higher-order structure (secondary/tertiary structure) of protein molecules → aggregation or degradation
  • Protein aggregates may trigger immunogenicity → a direct hazard to patient safety
  • This is a typical decision in which a CQA (protein integrity) outranks commercial convenience (RPP is simple to operate)

Decision principle restated: CQAs (patient safety) > business convenience.

Comprehension Check

A customer provides a product specification: a high-concentration mAb (150 mg/mL) with a viscosity of 45 mPa·s, filled into prefilled syringes, with an annual demand of 3 million units. Based on the information in Table 2.0-1🔍, 2.0-2 and 2.0-3, analyze which filling technology is most suitable and explain your reasoning. Which technology is definitely excluded, and why?

CDMO Quick Reference for Filling Technology Selection

Based on the three tables, a quick selection approach for a CDMO:

  • Step 1: Confirm the product type → protein? high viscosity? suspension? (Table 2.0-3🔍)
  • Step 2: Confirm whether a single-use fluid pathway (SU) is needed to control cross-contamination → PP preferred (Table 2.0-1🔍)
  • Step 3: Confirm whether campaigning is planned → PP hose life assessment; RPP/TP/DP are all compatible (Table 2.0-1🔍)
  • Step 4: Confirm the container type → all four technologies are broadly compatible (Table 2.0-2🔍)
  • Step 5: Confirm the fill volume range → RPP/DP have the widest range (0.1–250 mL) (Table 2.0-1🔍)

After excluding the unsuitable technologies, make the final choice among the remaining ones based on SA risk (installation outside the RABS, CIP/SIP capability).

Section 1B Summary — Key Takeaways

Review of Core Concepts

  • The capacity model must integrate eight input parameters to set the filling speed target scientifically, not by intuition
  • Campaigning works best in isolators and has shorter duration in RABS; fast VHP technology has reduced the time advantage of campaigning
  • The four pillars of campaign SA control: CIP/SIP, biodecontamination between batches, glove integrity testing, PUPSIT for every batch
  • Future-proofing must align with GMP compliance trends (higher-grade barriers, more automation), not just commercial flexibility
  • The four filling technologies are similar in filling accuracy; the key differences are viscosity range, SU support, campaign compatibility and protein compatibility

Reinforcing the Decision Hierarchy

1. Sterility Assurance (SA) — Always first

  • The shear risk of RPP to proteins excludes its suitability
  • Campaign duration is constrained by the grade of barrier technology
  • The APS must verify the worst-case conditions of the campaign

2. Product CQAs — Patient safety

  • Viscosity, protein structure and suspension uniformity determine technology selection
  • Protein aggregate risk > operating convenience

3. Business & Flexibility — Last consideration

  • The capacity model, future-proofing and campaign efficiency are optimized only after SA and CQAs are satisfied
2A

Section 2A: Peristaltic Pump

p26-p41

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p26 – p33

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the core operating principle of the peristaltic pump (PP): rotary squeezing, servo motor control, and the design logic of a closed fluid path
  • Distinguish the design differences between single-tube and double-tube PPs, and explain the trade-offs each makes between pulsation control and the number of connectors
  • Grasp the three-zone concept of tubing selection (upstream, within the rollers, downstream) and the mechanism by which wear causes dose drift, and so understand why 100% IPC control is strongly recommended for PPs
  • Understand the design considerations for PP system positioning: intermediate vessel height, bubble risk, and the major advantages and limitations of placing the PP outside the isolator
  • Understand, from a CDMO business perspective, the strategic significance of the PP as the filling pump of choice for biologics and single-use (SU) systems

In This Section

2.1 PP Overview 2.1.1 Design Configurations 2.1.2 System Setup 2.1.3 System Positioning Section Summary
2.1 Aseptic Filling Technologies: Peristaltic Pumps

Original Text

The principle of operation for the PP is the dynamic rotational squeezing of a flexible tube (in most cases, a silicone tube) placed between a backplate and rollers mounted on a rotor and driven by a servo motor to create positive displacement in the closed system (tube), thereby moving liquid products from product infeed side to product dispensing side. The pump tubes are fixed on the suction side to avoid the tubes travelling within the pump. The filling volume is governed by the number of revolutions executed by the rotor (degrees). The distance between the rollers and the backplate is called the occlusion-bed distance and is critical to minimize tubing wear for a given pump-tubing wall thickness.

Note: Linear peristaltic pumps are also available which provide the compressive force on the tubing at right angles to the direction of flow. These systems can provide excellent accuracy in filling with capabilities to fill microliter quantities (5). However, these systems are less common, therefore the focus in this section will be on peristaltic pumps with rotary heads.

The rotating motion of the rotor moves the dynamic squeezing point along the tube and moves the product along, at the same time, creating a vacuum at the inlet and drawing in the product (see Figure 2.1-1🔍). The product to be filled only comes into contact with the filling tube and the filling needle. The tube represents a closed system from the inlet of the product to the outlet through the filling needle.

[Figure 2.1-1🔍: Illustration of Progressive Rotary Motion of Rotor Along Backplate — shows how the rotor's rollers sequentially compress the silicone tube against the backplate, creating a traveling squeeze point that propels liquid forward while simultaneously drawing product from the inlet]

When the product is not viscous (typically less than 60 milliPascal-second (mPa-s); equivalent to 1 centipoise), the choice of using a PP is highly appropriate, as the cleaning and sterilization efforts needed are significantly less than with other technologies such as the RPP. PP systems are highly compatible with SU fluid pathways.

Figure 2.1-2🔍 provides a schematic of a possible PP fluid pathway. Notably, this image depicts the pumps within the aseptic boundary; however, it is possible to install the pumps outside of the aseptic boundary, thereby removing the primary mechanical components from the critical zone. As discussed in Section 2.1.5, there may be reasons that installation within the boundary is preferable for potent or toxic products.

[Figure 2.1-2🔍: Peristaltic Pump Fluid Pathway Configuration — schematic showing the overall PP fluid pathway from intermediate vessel, through pump assembly, to filling needle; illustrates both the option of pump inside the aseptic boundary and the alternative outside-isolator placement]

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: How a Peristaltic Pump Works

Peristaltic Pump (PP) takes its name from the biological concept of peristalsis. Just as intestinal muscles push food along, a PP uses rotating rollers to squeeze a silicone tube in sequence, pushing liquid from one end to the other.

Some key terms:

  • Servo motor: a motor that precisely controls speed and angle. Fill volume = angle of rotation, so the precision of angle control directly determines filling accuracy
  • Occlusion-bed distance: the gap between the rollers and the backing plate. Too small a gap means faster tubing wear; too large a gap lets liquid leak back, affecting accuracy
  • Closed system: the product contacts only the tubing and the filling needle, and no metal mechanical part of the pump

Analogy: A Masseur's Hands

Imagine a masseur pressing with their fingers along a water-filled tube from start to finish. Each press pushes the water forward a little, while negative pressure forms behind it and draws in more water automatically.

The PP rollers are those "fingers", the backing plate is the table, and the silicone tube is the hose. How many turns the servo motor makes determines how many milliliters of liquid are delivered.

Key difference: a real masseur's hands tire after a long session, and so does the tubing. Repeated squeezing causes material fatigue (tubing wear), which is the biggest management challenge of the PP.

Why can the PP be placed "outside" the isolator? What does this mean for sterility assurance (SA)?

This is one of the PP's most important engineering advantages. Because the product contacts only the inside of the closed tubing, the mechanical body of the pump (motor, rollers, backing plate) does not need to be in the sterile area. The whole pump mechanism can therefore be installed outside the isolator or RABS.

Benefits: less mechanical complexity inside the isolator → fewer particle generation sources → a simpler IQ/OQ/PQ scope → mechanical maintenance without breaching the sterile boundary.

Exception: for highly potent products such as ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates), if the tubing leaks, toxic material escaping outside the isolator creates an operator exposure risk. In this case, the pump may be placed inside the isolator to keep any leakage within the controlled area.

Viscosity Threshold: 60 mPa-s Is the Key Dividing Line

The PP suits low-viscosity products (< 60 mPa-s, roughly 60 times the viscosity of water). Beyond this range, roller squeezing efficiency drops and filling accuracy deteriorates. Shear-sensitive biologics (such as proteins) may also suffer structural damage as they pass through the pump.

By comparison, the RPP (rotary piston pump) is often more suitable at higher viscosities, but an RPP cannot be used in an SU fluid path (because the piston requires cleaning validation). This is the fundamental reason the PP + SU combination dominates in the biologics field.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the PP's fill volume determined by "degrees of rotation" rather than by time? How does this differ fundamentally from time-pressure (TP) filling?
  2. Suppose you are a process engineer at a CDMO, and the client's biologic has a viscosity of 45 mPa-s and requires a single-use system. Would you recommend a PP or an RPP? Explain your reasoning.
  3. What problems arise when the occlusion-bed distance is set too tight (too small) and too loose (too large), respectively?
2.1.1 Peristaltic Pump Design Configurations

Original Text

There are two different PP design configurations available: a single-tube PP and a double-tube PP.

Examples from one manufacturer of both roller configurations are depicted in Figure 2.1.1-1. In the roller set for the single-tube PP, in this particular design, the tube is threaded around the roller unit twice. In the offset rollers for double-tube PP, two separate tubes of the same diameter are wrapped around the upper and lower roller sets a single time. In the double tube configuration, the rollers on the top and on the bottom have an offset to minimize the pulsation of the system, such that the rollers in maximum compression are offset from the rollers in minimum compression. Different filling systems are equipped with more rollers than depicted below (up to six per rotor channel). The advantage of additional rollers is better control of pulsation and therefore additional filling accuracy.

[Figure 2.1.1-1🔍: Roller Configurations for Single- and Double-Tube Peristaltic Pump — shows side-by-side comparison of single-tube roller head (tube threaded twice around unit) versus double-tube roller head (two separate tubes on upper/lower offset roller sets); illustrates how offset positions of compression zones cancel out pulsation peaks]

Single-Tube PP

In a single-tube PP, one silicone tube must be placed in between the backplate and the rotor (although it may be wrapped around the rollers twice). Special care has to be taken to ensure that the pulsation of the system is minimized. Pulsation is usually impacted by the number of rollers and the available space for the tube to retract. The pulsation can have an impact on the filling accuracy and may generate pulsation at the sterilizing filter if there is no sterile intermediate vessel between the filter and the PP. In rare applications, if filling speeds are low and required accuracy is not demanding, an intermediate vessel may not be necessary.

Single-tube pump heads provide the ability to use one complete tube from intermediate vessel to filling needle without any connection pieces installed within the rotor. This gives three advantages:

  • Less handling, which means potentially less risk of contamination
  • Fewer parts to be delivered by tube suppliers, which means reduced costs
  • Less component integrity risk

While a single tube may be extended from the vessel through the pump to the filling needle, there are other designs for single-tube pump heads, such as that depicted in Figure 2.1.1-2🔍, where the tubing assembly is designed to support long campaign lengths. For example, the tubing inside the pump may be of a special wear-resistant design, and the tubing between the pump and the filling needle may be of a higher rigidity than the pump tubing to prevent axial pulsation expansion of the tubing at the outlet side of the pump. To support these features, the design will result in at least one (if not two) connectors in the tubing, as shown in Figure 2.1.1-2.

[Figure 2.1.1-2🔍: Schematic of a Single-Tube Sterile Fluid Pathway with Connectors — shows a single-tube PP fluid pathway design that incorporates 1-2 connectors to allow different tubing specifications in different zones: wear-resistant tubing within the rollers, higher-rigidity tubing downstream to the filling needle; each connector is a potential contamination/integrity risk that must be managed]

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy: Pulsation Is Like a Heartbeat

Imagine that each time your heart beats, your blood vessels feel a pressure wave. Each time a PP roller "leaves" a section of tubing, the tube rebounds elastically and produces a pressure pulse. This is "pulsation".

The clever design of the double-tube configuration: the upper and lower roller sets are positioned out of phase. When the upper roller is at "maximum squeeze", the lower roller is at "minimum squeeze", so the two pressure waves cancel each other and the overall flow becomes steadier, like two ventricles beating together but alternately to give a smoother blood flow.

Adding more rollers (up to 6) has the same effect. The more rollers, the smaller each pulse and the steadier the combined flow, like several small hearts working together in place of one big heart.

Key Point: The Impact of Pulsation on Downstream Equipment

Pulsation affects not only filling accuracy but can also put pressure shocks on the sterilizing filter. Each pulse applies one positive-negative pressure cycle to the membrane, which over time may accelerate membrane fatigue and even affect integrity test results.

This is why a sterile intermediate vessel is usually needed between the filter and the PP. It acts as a buffer that absorbs pulsation and protects the membrane, and also serves as a stable-pressure source for the fill volume.

Exception: the intermediate vessel may be omitted only where filling speed is very slow and accuracy requirements are low (such as small laboratory batches). Omitting it is almost never recommended in commercial-scale production.

CDMO Perspective: Are Connectors a "Necessary Evil"?

Long-campaign production (such as 3 weeks of continuous influenza vaccine production) places very demanding requirements on tubing wear. In this case, the tubing within the pump rollers must use a special wear-resistant material, while the downstream tubing must use a stiffer material to prevent axial pulsation expansion. Two tubing specifications therefore have to be joined with a connector.

Every additional connector is an additional potential sterility risk point. When designing the fluid path, the necessity of each connector must therefore be clearly justified, and the aseptic process simulation (APS) must verify that these connection points do not become contamination weak spots.

Design decision principle: the minimum necessary number of connectors → each connector has a functional justification → each connector is documented in the validation documents.

Practice Questions

  1. If your CDMO client requests a very short batch (500 mL) with very high filling accuracy requirements (±1%), would you recommend a single-tube or double-tube PP? Why?
  2. A single-tube PP can have as few as 0 connectors. In which situations is this truly feasible, and in which situations must connectors be added?
  3. When the number of rollers increases from 2 to 6, pulsation improves, but how do the complexity of equipment cleaning and tubing installation change? What quality management trade-off does this represent?

Core Concept: Design Logic of Single-Tube vs. Double-Tube PPs

There are two basic PP configurations, and choosing between them is essentially a trade-off between "simplicity" and "pulsation control":

2.1.2 Peristaltic Pump Setup

Original Text

Double-Tube PP Fluid Pathway Setup

The setup for the fluid pathway for a double-tube PP is shown in Figure 2.1.2-1. The suction tube is split by a Y-connector into two pump tubes, which are installed between the backplate and the rollers. Both pump tubes are joined by an identical Y-piece to one filling tube at the outlet and connected to the filling needle. The tubes may be of differing diameters (e.g., the two pump tubes may be half the volume of the upstream suction and downstream filling tubes).

[Figure 2.1.2-1🔍: Schematic for a Double-Tube Sterile Fluid Pathway — shows complete double-tube PP assembly: single suction tube from intermediate vessel → Y-connector splits into two equal pump tubes through upper and lower roller sets → second Y-connector rejoins → single filling tube to needle; tube diameter relationships shown]

Innovations are being made all the time to improve the capability of traditional technologies. For example, alternative PP designs exist that provide linear flow to reduce shear force and line losses. These designs are beyond the scope of this document, but keep in mind that any upgrades to technology should be proven and validated.

Tubing Selection — Three Distinct Sections

When selecting tubing for PP applications it is important to think about the required attributes of three distinct sections of tubing:

  1. Upstream of the pump
  2. Within the rollers of the pump
  3. Downstream of the pump

The factors to be considered when selecting the tubing for each section include, but are not limited to:

  • Functionality within the distinct position of the pumping system (e.g., effective transport without deformation, required level of flexibility)
  • Prevention of reactivity or harm to the product (e.g., adsorption of API or preservatives, shear forces, leachables)
  • Method of sterilization of the tubing (e.g., to avoid changes in texture, adsorption of sterilant, generation of free radicals)
  • Performance over time to prevent distortion (e.g., tubing integrity, wear and the formation of particulate, permanent changes in dimension)

In general, materials of construction upstream of the pump are less critical for the filling operation. Within the rollers, the tubing must be flexible to permit effective reaction to the rollers, but without distortion that can result in changes in the volume of transfer over the intended period of use. Downstream of the pump, the materials of construction should be less flexible as this section of tubing does not need to interact with the rollers. The lower flexibility will ensure that the tubing does not distort from the pressure of the transferred liquid. Distortion in the downstream section can result in changes in the delivered dose or dripping.

The interior diameter of the tubing and connectors throughout the entire fluid pathway should be designed to ensure that there is no back pressure or significant pressure drop along the fluid path. This includes any connectors such as the Y-connectors and the filling needle.

Tubing Wear and Dose Drift

Due to the softening of the pump tubing due to tubing wear (Figure 2.1.2-2🔍), the PP system will eventually show a drift in delivered dose over time, therefore, a correction value needs to be applied. The correction value (algorithm) is statistically based on the weight-check results of the inline process control scales. Therefore, using a statistical or 100% IPC check-weighing method when using PP filling systems is highly recommended (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4).

The usable life of PP tubing depends on fill volume, product characteristics (e.g., solvents, corrosives, abrasives), pump-tubing robustness, filling speed, and start/stop curves, as well as the general design of the pump. It is recommended to validate the filling time/filled-dose count of the tubes as, at some point, the wear and tear will generate particles that will contaminate the product.

The PP tubing will certainly wear on the exterior but, in extreme cases, factors such as a high number of doses or high pump acceleration or deceleration can lead to internal tubing wear, potentially releasing particles into the product. Figure 2.1.2-3🔍 includes microscopic images of tubing with external and internal wear.

[Figure 2.1.2-2🔍: Diagrams of External Tubing Wear — cross-section diagrams showing progressive deformation of tube wall at the point of roller contact: new tube (uniform round cross-section) → used tube (flattened, asymmetric cross-section) → worn tube (permanent deformation, thinned wall); illustrates how wall geometry change alters the swept volume per revolution]
[Figure 2.1.2-3🔍: Microscopic Examination of Worn Tubing — scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or optical microscopy images showing: (left) external surface wear — cracking, flaking, surface erosion of silicone; (right) internal surface wear — pitting, delamination, particle generation on inner lumen surface; demonstrates the contamination risk of particulate release into product]

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy: An Aging Rubber Band

Imagine folding a rubber band in half and releasing it over and over. After a few thousand times, the band becomes soft and loses its elasticity, fine cracks appear at the fold, and it may eventually break.

The wear mechanism of PP tubing is exactly the same. Each roller pass is one "fold and release". After tens of thousands of fills:

  • External wear: cracks and delamination appear on the outer wall in contact with the rollers → rubber particles may contaminate the production environment
  • Internal wear (more dangerous): if acceleration/deceleration is too rapid, friction and shear on the inner wall → tiny silicone particles enter the product directly → unacceptable for injectable products

This is why the service life (maximum number of fills) of every tube must be validated. Tubing cannot be "used until it fails".

Dose Drift Correction Mechanism

The core problem of the PP: the tubing gradually "deforms" with wear. A tube that delivered 1.05 mL per compression may, as the tube wall softens, deliver only 1.02 mL or 1.07 mL for the same compression. This is "dose drift".

Correction mechanism (schematic):

Fill volume = baseline volume × correction factor(t)

correction factor(t) = f(real-time weighing data)
             = continuously updated statistical model

Example: if the mean of 100 consecutive samples
    drifts from 1.000 mL to 0.995 mL
    → the system automatically compensates speed by +0.5%
    → target fill volume restored

This real-time feedback loop
is why 100% IPC weighing
is essential for PP systems.

By contrast, the RPP (rotary piston pump) has a fixed displacement (piston stroke) and no wear-induced volume change, so its dose stability is better and an RPP does not need IPC correction at the same frequency.

Key Point: Why Is 100% IPC Weighing Strongly Recommended for the PP?

Among the four filling technologies, the PP is the only pump type in which the physical degradation of its main consumable (the tubing) causes systematic dose drift. This is not a random error but a predictable systematic trend.

Regulatory perspective: EU GMP Annex 1 (2023) explicitly requires manufacturers to establish an appropriate IPC system to ensure fill volumes stay within specification. Statistical IPC (sampled weighing) is acceptable, but for a PP system, because drift is continuous, 100% IPC (weighing every container) is the best way to catch and correct drift in real time.

Commercial impact: 100% IPC requires a higher equipment investment (high-speed precision balances), but it can significantly reduce batch failure rates and rework costs. For high-value biologics (such as mAbs), the ROI on this investment can usually be recovered within one batch.

Key Point: The Four Tubing Selection Criteria (Item by Item)

  • Functionality: the roller section needs high elasticity while the downstream section needs low elasticity. These conflict, so different sections use different materials
  • Product reactivity: silicone may adsorb certain small-molecule APIs or preservatives (such as polysorbate 80), leading to low dose → extractables & leachables studies must be done beforehand
  • Sterilization method: gamma irradiation generates free radicals in silicone, changing its hardness and elasticity → the irradiation dose must balance "effective sterilization" against "no damage to the material"
  • Performance over time: the maximum number of uses must be validated, and the tube must be replaced once the limit is exceeded, with no compromise

Practical Application

Scenario: your CDMO is taking on a new mRNA vaccine client, with 500,000 injection vials filled per batch, a batch time of about 8 hours, and a single-use system.

Tubing life calculation considerations:

  • 500,000 fills → far exceeds the typical life of 50,000–100,000 fills for ordinary silicone tubing → tubing must be changed mid-batch
  • Tubing change = aseptic connection operation = contamination risk point → the validation must include sterility confirmation of the tubing change procedure
  • mRNA is extremely shear-sensitive → pay special attention to the pump acceleration/deceleration profile settings to avoid generating internal wear particles
  • 100% IPC is mandatory → fill volume may fluctuate briefly before and after a tubing change, so the correction algorithm needs to respond quickly

Practice Questions

  1. If the downstream tubing is not stiff enough (too soft), what specific filling defects result? Explain from the physical mechanism.
  2. If the inner diameter of a Y-connector is 10% smaller than the tubing inner diameter, what effect will this have on filling accuracy and product integrity?
  3. A product contains 5% ethanol (an organic solvent). What risks need special evaluation when selecting the tubing material for the roller section?
  4. Why does "high pump acceleration/deceleration" accelerate internal wear and not just external wear? Explain from a mechanical perspective.

Core Concept: The Three-Zone Tubing Selection Logic

The PP fluid path has three sections, each playing a different role, so the tubing requirements for each are completely different:

Key point: if the downstream tubing is too soft, it will balloon like a balloon under pulsation pressure, and each expansion discharges a little extra liquid → fill volume runs high, and "dripping" problems arise.

2.1.3 Peristaltic Pump System Positioning

Original Text

During the design phase of PP systems, the position of the intermediate vessel relative height to the filling needles should be evaluated in detail so air gaps in the tube are not created. If the pump has to work to pull product from a vessel positioned lower than the filling needle, air bubbles are a common result. Likewise, other parameters such as choosing the right tube diameters for the target fills and the length of the tubes between the PP and the needle should also be considered.

This consideration is due to the well-appreciated fact that a PP, being a closed system, can be placed outside of the isolator or RABS, which would position it farther away from the filling needles in some cases.

There are different methods to prime the pump to remove air from the system and to ensure the target fill volume is achieved without air gaps at the beginning of the batch. The approach to priming should be considered depending on the application, product characteristics, and the execution of the pump (see Section 12.2 for priming discard).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Balance Between Gravity and Pump Suction

The PP draws liquid in from upstream through the negative pressure (suction) produced by roller squeezing. But this negative pressure capacity is limited, and it must overcome:

  • Tubing resistance (length, diameter, bends)
  • Liquid column height difference (if the vessel is below the filling needle)
  • The weight of the liquid itself

When these resistances exceed the pump's suction capacity, the system cannot fully fill the tubing → bubbles enter → underfilling or empty-needle fills.

Design principle: the liquid level of the intermediate vessel should be as high as possible, at or above the position of the filling needle, so that gravity assists rather than hinders fluid transfer.

Analogy: A Hose Going Uphill

Imagine using a hose to pump water from a bucket at the foot of a hill to a nozzle at the top. If the bucket is at the foot (much lower than the nozzle), the pump must work very hard to "lift" the water up. Once the pump power is insufficient or the tubing has even a small air leak, bubbles appear in the tube and the flow breaks.

Conversely, if the bucket is at the top (higher than the nozzle), gravity naturally helps the water flow down, and the pump only needs to control the flow rate without fighting gravity.

The positioning of the PP intermediate vessel follows the same principle. In isolator design, the intermediate vessel is usually raised as high as possible, even placed on top of the isolator, so that gravity assists filling.

Key Point: The Distance Management Challenge of Placing the PP Outside the Isolator

One of the PP's biggest advantages is that it can be placed outside the isolator or RABS, but this raises a new problem: the filling needle is now farther from the pump.

The greater the distance, the more it means:

  • Longer downstream tubing → pulsation is attenuated along the tubing, but may also be amplified
  • Larger tubing volume → more product discarded at batch start/end (priming discard)
  • More complex liquid column height design → the hydrostatics of each segment of tubing must be calculated precisely

Therefore, although the PP can be placed outside the isolator, tubing length and height differences must be explicitly calculated at the design stage, and filling validation must confirm that no bubbles form under extreme conditions (such as low liquid level or the high-viscosity end).

CDMO Perspective: The Commercial Cost of Priming

Before the batch starts, the entire fluid path (from the intermediate vessel to the filling needle) is filled with air and must be "flushed" out with product. This process is called priming.

The product flushed out must be discarded and cannot be filled into containers for sale.

Commercial impact:

  • Longer tubing → more priming discard → higher cost (a significant impact for high-value biologics)
  • There is one discard at batch start and one at batch end → the effective yield per batch is reduced
  • Design optimization: shorten the tubing length and use the smallest permissible inner diameter → reduce priming discard volume

Section 12.2 gives more detailed guidance on managing priming discard, including how to minimize discard without compromising sterility.

Estimating Priming Discard Volume

Priming discard volume (approximation):

V_discard ≈ π × (d/2)² × L

where:
  d = tubing inner diameter (cm)
  L = total tubing length (cm)

Example:
  inner diameter 8 mm (0.8 cm), tubing length 200 cm
  V = π × (0.4)² × 200 ≈ 100 mL

If the fill volume is 1 mL/vial:
  → 100 mL ÷ 1 mL = equivalent to 100 vials discarded
  → if product cost is $5,000/mL, one priming = $500,000 discarded

This shows why a lean tubing design
is so important for high-value drugs.

Practice Questions

  1. In a PP system, the intermediate vessel is placed 30 cm below the filling needle. What problems may occur, and how would you solve them in the design?
  2. If the PP must be placed outside the isolator (1.5 meters from the filling needle) and the product is a high-value mAb ($3,000 per milliliter), what is your top priority when designing the tubing to reduce discard cost?
  3. The purpose of priming is to "purge gas", but the priming process itself also carries contamination risk (product flow, tubing contact). How would you verify the sterility of the priming procedure in an APS (aseptic process simulation)?
Appendix: PP Product Suitability Reference Table (from the source document, p26–p27)

Original Text — Product Suitability

The following table summarizes PP suitability across various product types, as referenced in the comparison table on doc pages 26–27:

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The PP Is Not a Universal Filling Pump

As the suitability table above shows, the main limitations of the PP are:

  • Solvent-based products: organic solvents (ethanol, DMSO) can swell or harden silicone and damage the tubing structure → the PP is not ideal
  • Long campaigns (such as 3-week influenza vaccine production): tubing needs frequent replacement → high operating cost and accumulating sterility risk
  • LVP (large-volume parenterals): large fill volumes → more pump revolutions per batch → tubing life is consumed quickly → tubing may need to be changed mid-batch

Key Point: Special Considerations for ADCs

ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates) are currently the hottest oncology drug platform and are extremely toxic (essentially a potent chemotherapy drug attached to an antibody). The PP is very well suited to ADCs in SU systems, but "whether to place it outside the isolator" needs special evaluation.

The usual PP advantage (pump outside the isolator) may actually need to be reconsidered for ADCs: if the tubing leaks, the environment outside the isolator has no sealed protection, and leakage of highly toxic material could endanger operators.

This is why the safety assessment must come before engineering decisions in the design of an ADC filling line. "Sterility assurance comes first", but toxin containment is an equally top-priority safety consideration.

CDMO Business Perspective: PP + SU Is the Golden Combination in the Biologics Market

From a market trend perspective, biologics (mAbs, gene therapies, mRNA vaccines) are growing at 10%+ per year, and these products almost all share the following characteristics:

  • Low viscosity (mostly 1–10 mPa-s) → PP technology is suitable
  • High shear sensitivity → the RPP raises concerns, while the PP has low shear
  • High value, small batches → the economics of single-use (SU) are favorable (no CIP/SIP time)
  • Strict sterility requirements → the closed PP system is fully compatible with SU fluid paths

Conclusion: for any CDMO that wants to take on biologics business, mastering the validation and operation of PP + SU systems is the basic technical entry ticket. European CDMOs such as White Raven have already invested ahead of others in AI-assisted filling management. That is the gap, and also the direction in which to catch up.

Synthesis Questions

  1. A client brings a small-molecule API solution containing 15% DMSO to be filled. Would you recommend a PP or another technology? Explain your evaluation framework.
  2. Comparing the PP and the RPP on the "necessity of 100% IPC", explain from the technical principles why the PP needs high-frequency weighing control more than the RPP does.
  3. Suppose your CDMO is evaluating a multi-purpose filling line that can accommodate both PP and RPP. Analyze the business logic of this decision along three dimensions: capital investment, operational flexibility and customer portfolio.

Section 2.1 Summary

  • How the PP works: rotating rollers squeeze the silicone tube, giving positive displacement; fill volume is controlled by rotation angle, and the closed system means the product contacts only the tubing and the filling needle.
  • Occlusion-bed distance: the gap between rollers and backing plate. Too tight accelerates wear and too loose causes backflow. Each tubing specification has an optimal setting that must be validated.
  • Single-tube vs. double-tube: single-tube is simple (fewer connection points, lower contamination risk), while double-tube suppresses pulsation effectively by offsetting the phase of the upper and lower rollers. Each has its own use cases, and the core trade-off is "flow path simplicity" vs. "filling accuracy stability".
  • Three-zone tubing selection: upstream is mainly about compatibility; within the rollers, high elasticity and wear resistance; downstream, high stiffness to prevent pulsation expansion. The four selection criteria are functionality, product reactivity, sterilization method and performance over time.
  • Tubing wear → dose drift → 100% IPC: a systematic drift mechanism unique to the PP. The correction algorithm depends on real-time weighing feedback, so 100% IPC weighing is strongly recommended (compared with the dose stability of the RPP, the PP places higher demands on IPC management).
  • System positioning: the intermediate vessel must be at or above the filling needle to avoid bubbles; the PP can be placed outside the isolator (an advantage), but this brings challenges of longer tubing, priming discard volume and hydrostatic design.
  • CDMO strategic positioning: PP + SU is the mainstream configuration for modern biologics filling. Low viscosity, high compatibility and low cleaning burden make it the first choice for high-growth products such as mAbs, mRNA and gene therapies; for ADCs, the risk of toxic leakage must additionally be considered when deciding pump location.

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the advantages and disadvantages of the peristaltic pump (PP), and make a technology selection judgement against RPP and TP technologies
  • Grasp the specific risks that PP tubing wear poses to sterility assurance (SA), and how they are controlled through 100% IPC and tubing use-time validation
  • Be able to perform a total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis: compare SU consumable costs with the lifecycle cost of reusable CIP/SIP systems
  • Understand how the EU GMP Annex 1 requirements for sterilize-in-place (SIP) drive technology selection
  • Assess the operational advantages of PP in a CDMO environment and the single-supplier risk, and build a balanced procurement and validation strategy
