2.1.4 Peristaltic Pump Advantages and Disadvantages

Original Text

Table 2.1.4-1🔍 identifies the advantages and disadvantages of PPs.

Table 2.1.4-1🔍 Advantages and Disadvantages of Peristaltic Pumps

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Full Picture of PP Technology

This advantages and disadvantages table is the basis for the selection decision. The core working principle of the peristaltic pump (PP) is "compression from outside the tube": the liquid never touches the metal parts of the pump, and the rollers on the pump head squeeze the silicone tubing from the outside to push the liquid forward.

This design brings two fundamental advantages:

  • Low shear: very gentle on protein drugs, liposomes and cell therapy products, causing almost no molecular damage
  • Inherently closed system: the pump body can sit outside the sterile barrier, greatly reducing sources of contamination in the Grade A area

It also has one fundamental limitation: the elastomer tubing is the only wear point, and all SA risks, cost issues and maintenance plans revolve around the tubing.

Analogy: The Sponge Rollers of a Car Wash

Picture the rotating sponge rollers in a car wash. They touch the car body (the tube wall), but the wash water (the liquid drug product) never touches the rollers themselves. PP works the same way: the rollers compress the outer wall of the tube, and the car (the drug solution) passes safely through inside the tube.

The catch is that after long hours of washing, the sponge rollers wear and shed fragments, and PP silicone tubing does the same. That is why "tubing use-life validation" is the core quality control activity of this system.

Key Point: High-Viscosity Products Are Excluded

PP is not suitable for high-viscosity products (such as some suspensions and gel formulations). High viscosity increases the compression resistance of the tubing, reducing dosing accuracy and accelerating tube wall wear.

Key question when taking on CDMO projects: when a client asks, "Can you fill a high-viscosity drug solution?", if the line has only PP, the answer may be "we need to do a feasibility assessment first". RPP or TP is usually more reliable for high-viscosity applications.

Practical Application: CDMO Multi-Product Flexibility

"Wide dose range" is the PP advantage with the greatest commercial value in a CDMO setting. By simply changing to SU tubing of a different diameter, the same pump head can fill a range of formats from 0.01 mL to 50 mL, without changing the pump drive unit.

By comparison with RPP: each dose format usually requires a dedicated piston/cylinder, so changing format amounts to a hardware change.

This gives the CDMO a competitive advantage: one PP line can serve more client products, with higher asset utilization.

Practice Questions

  1. How does the PP advantage that "the closed system can be placed outside the barrier" affect the sterility assurance decision hierarchy (SA > CQA > Business)? Why is this an SA advantage and not merely an operational convenience?
  2. When filling a liposomal nanoparticle formulation, which is more suitable, PP or RPP? What is the reason (hint: shear force)?
  3. The table says CIP/SIP is "rarely used" for PP in the "Sterilization" row. What do you think is the main reason? (The next section reveals the answer.)
2.1.5 Peristaltic Pump Sterility Assurance: Microbial and Total Particles

Original Text

A major driver in choosing a suitable dosing system is the risk of contamination that is posed during setup, handling, and production, as well as clean up or disassembly after the conclusion of the batch. Assuming there is absolute flexibility regarding the choice of the dosing system, PPs are always especially appreciated for the simplicity of the setup. Systems have minimal product contact parts (e.g., tubing and needles); this simplicity makes these systems especially suitable for SU applications. SU applications have the benefit of a reduced microbial contamination risk as the preassembled components are commonly gamma-irradiated. As a consequence, there are fewer required connections compared to other technologies. Connecting to the holding vessel or for recirculation purposes is also quite straightforward, and most of the connections can be executed outside of the Grade A area (e.g., using an RTP bag or intrinsic sterile connection device), which makes handling (including maintenance) easier.

Particulate in the sourced components may be identified by extractable and leachable testing as well as ongoing quality control of received components, but the disadvantage with a PP system is that the constant compression of the tubing by the rollers against the backplate will lead to further particle-generation as the tubes are subject to stretching and wear and tear. Therefore, it is crucial to always validate the use time of the tubes. This use time may need to be established in conjunction with the products being filled, as some products could potentially impact the speed of degradation (i.e., particle-generation).

The length of tubing used with PP is longer than with some other technologies, which can result in more product contact with elastomers. In addition, several types of tubing may be in use, as the different sections of tubing benefit from different stiffness, and there are substantial mechanical forces applied to the tubing (especially within the rollers). As a consequence, extractables and leachables testing is of particular importance for the range of materials and exposure conditions (e.g., times, temperature, friction forces).

Small cracks and breaks in the tube may not be immediately identified with PP technology. If a 100% IPC system is not in place for dose control, small breaks may go undetected for a period of time until the next statistical IPC (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4 for additional information on IPC strategies). The wear profile of the tubing within the rotors or the connectors that are employed for the fluid pathway can elevate this risk. As a consequence, leakage could result in contamination of this "closed system." In addition to the sterility risk, leakage will be problematic with potent or toxic products and may require reconsideration of the installation position to locate the mechanical components within the containment barrier.

There is no vertical movement on top of the machine table plate, therefore, machine-generated particles are minimized with PP systems. Since PPs can be placed outside of the barrier or isolator, the risk of particle-generation from the friction on the tubing can be reduced within the critical zone.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Where the PP SA Advantage Comes From

The advantage of PP in sterility assurance (SA) has two independent sources:

  • Gamma-irradiated pre-assembled SU: the tubing has already been sterilized by irradiation before it leaves the supplier, so no sterilize-in-place is needed before a batch starts, greatly reducing handling steps and the number of aseptic connections. This is the core advantage of the PP + SU combination.
  • Pump body outside the barrier: PP is one of very few filling technologies that can be placed entirely outside a Grade A isolator or RABS barrier. This means that particles generated by mechanical parts (metal wear debris, lubricants) never enter the critical zone; only the transparent silicone tubing passes through the barrier into the filling area. This is a structural SA advantage, not an operating technique.

Key Point: Tubing Wear Is the Core SA Risk of PP

The greatest SA risks of PP are concentrated at two levels:

1. Particle generation: the rollers continuously compress the silicone tubing, so rubber fragments shed from the tube wall and enter the drug solution. Key control measure: validate and set a maximum tubing use time, and consider in the validation the effect of different drug product matrices on the silicone degradation rate (for example, organic solvents may accelerate ageing).

2. Extractables & leachables (E&L): PP tubing is longer than in other technologies, uses more material types (tube sections of different hardness), and is under friction and stretching forces over a long period. E&L testing must therefore cover a matrix of all material types × all exposure conditions (time, temperature, friction); testing a single representative condition is not enough.

Key Point: The Hidden Risk of Small Cracks - Why PP Needs 100% IPC More Than RPP

This is an easily overlooked SA risk of PP: small cracks in the silicone tubing or minor leaks at connectors may not be visible, and the dose deviation is also very small (because the crack leaks only a few drops).

With statistical IPC (weighing one container every N containers), a tube that starts leaking right after the 1st container may not be detected until the Nth. Those N-1 containers could all be defective.

Conclusion: the recommendation for 100% IPC is stronger for PP than for RPP. The piston-cylinder mechanism of an RPP is a precision mechanical fit with very stable dosing, so the risk of error with statistical IPC is relatively low; with PP, because the tubing keeps ageing, "the fill volume of every container may differ from the previous one", and 100% weighing is the only way to make sure every container is within specification.

Analogy: The Invisible Leak at a Pipe Joint

Imagine a household water pipe leaking slightly inside the wall. You use water every day and the pressure gauge looks normal, but the wall has been quietly getting wet. By the time you notice, mold may have been growing for months.

A small crack in PP tubing is this kind of "invisible problem". Statistical IPC is like reading the pressure gauge once a day: it cannot detect a chronic leak. 100% IPC is like giving every container its own flow meter: any deviation is visible immediately.

Practice Questions

  1. You are validating a PP + SU system with a fill batch duration of 8 hours. How would you design the "tubing use-time validation" study? Which variables should be included (product type, temperature, pump speed)?
  2. A client asks: "Why is E&L testing for your PP line so much more expensive than for RPP?" Explain using the logic of this section.
  3. When filling a potent product, how does the SA risk change between placing the PP pump outside the isolator and inside it? Under what conditions does it need to be placed inside the isolator?
2.1.6 Peristaltic Pump Efficiency and Impact on Risk

Original Text

Once personnel have been properly trained in the installation and proper functioning of PP systems, the associated risk of contamination to product is relatively low, as no direct contact by personnel with the product or product-contact parts (tube) occurs. Visibility of the equipment is also superior to some of the other systems, as a group of PPs can also be set up either vertically or horizontally to enable easy handling (e.g., improving ergonomics) and to decrease error probability (e.g., incorrect tubing placement, incorrect mounting of the wrong tube, leakage/damage to tube). The selected mounting position should take into account gravitational forces between the pump and filling needles and between the intermediate vessel and pumps to ensure consistency of dosing accuracy for all of the pump heads. Because no aseptic connections to the pump itself have to be made, the risk is considerably lower than with a manually assembled RPP. However, when the RPP is CIP/SIP-capable, the technologies are more comparable.

Containment is also straightforward with highly potent products if the PPs are placed within the isolator, which is necessary due to the comparatively higher potential of leaks and breakage. Detection systems for leaks can be implemented to trigger an alert should there be a breach in tubing. However, if a tube breaks, the standard operating procedure (SOP) for system operation should define whether to continue without that dosing head or to replace the tube, in addition to addressing quality implications (i.e., deviation) associated with breach and required isolation of any associated product containers. Replacement of the tube can take place easily without breaching containment of neighboring product paths.

The pumps run with very high efficiency due to the direct translation of servo drive to pump head (e.g., no gears as with RPP), and the pump heads show minimal wear and tear over multiple years of use. Therefore, pump heads do not normally require regular replacement.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The PP Efficiency Advantage - Direct Servo Drive

The mechanical drive path of PP is very short: servo motor → rotor → roller → tube wall compression → liquid propulsion, with no gear set, no mechanical seal and no complex linkage in between.

By comparison, RPP: motor → gearbox → cam → piston reciprocation → inlet/outlet valve switching → liquid propulsion. The drive chain is longer, friction losses are greater, and there are more wear points.

The result for PP: the pump head has almost no mechanical wear, and its service life can reach several years. The only wear part that really needs managing is the silicone tubing.

Analogy: Direct-Drive Electric Vehicle vs Conventional Gearbox Car

An electric vehicle drives the wheels directly with a motor, with no gearbox, and the drive efficiency is close to 95%. In a conventional fuel car, the energy passes through engine → gearbox → drive shaft → wheels, with friction loss at every stage, and the overall efficiency is only 30-40%.

The servo direct drive of PP is like the electric vehicle: the rotor drives the tubing directly, with almost no intermediate loss. The gear drive of RPP is like a conventional gearbox: there are more conversion steps, and also more potential wear points and maintenance needs.

Key Point: Installation Position Decision for Highly Toxic Products

PP is normally placed outside the barrier, but highly potent products (HPAPI) are an exception: for these products, the PP must be placed inside the isolator.

The reason is that the logic is reversed. For ordinary drug products, we worry about external contamination entering the product; for highly potent products, we must also worry about the product leaking out and harming operators. PP tubing has a relatively high leak risk, and if a highly potent drug solution leaks outside the isolator, the occupational exposure risk is unacceptable.

Control measure: a PP for highly potent products should be equipped with a tubing leak detection system (flow anomaly, liquid sensors); once triggered, it stops immediately and a deviation procedure is initiated.

Practical Application: SOP Decision Tree for Tubing Rupture

When PP tubing ruptures during filling, the SOP must answer three questions in advance:

  • 1. Continue filling or not? Continue with the remaining healthy pump heads, or stop the line? (This depends on the multi-head configuration and the effect on batch size.)
  • 2. How are the affected containers handled? Trace back from the point of rupture to the last confirmed good IPC point, and quarantine all containers in between pending investigation
  • 3. What is the scope of the deviation report? Does the tubing rupture trigger batch rejection, or only local quarantine?

This decision tree must be clearly defined in the SOP and cannot be decided on the spot during a batch; otherwise it leads to inconsistent deviation handling and regulatory risk.

Practice Questions

  1. Your PP filling line has 8 pump heads, and the tubing on head no. 3 ruptures at 50% of the batch. A 100% IPC system is in place. Describe your decision steps and the range of containers that must be quarantined.
  2. Why is the visibility of PP an SA advantage? What operational risks come with equipment designs that are not visible (such as an RPP enclosed inside the machine)?
2.1.7 Peristaltic Pump Costs: Initial and Lifecycle

Original Text

Initial costs are comparable to initial investment costs for other systems for dedicated fill volumes. If multiple fill volumes are required, the PP becomes commercially superior, as the same pump head can cover a much higher dosing range in comparison to other technologies such as RPP. Lifecycle costs are negligible as pump heads seldom require replacement. Breakage of the servo motors can occur, but that is an infrequent failure mode. If single-use systems (SUS) are implemented, which is common with PP, the costs associated with the disposable components can be high. The total cost of ownership (TCO) calculations would take consumables into account; therefore, a TCO comparison might be made between the SU disposables and a reusable RPP system with CIP/SIP capability. Examples of considerations for the TCO calculations should be appropriate to the system design and may include, but are not limited to time, utilities, cleaning validation, maintenance, process know-how, training of operators, and downtime due to CIP/SIP cycles, and extended times in cases where parallel processing is not possible (such as not being able to run the biodecontamination cycles simultaneously with the CIP/SIP) (see Section 2.1.10 on SUS).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: TCO - the Complete View of Total Cost of Ownership

Total cost of ownership (TCO) is the correct framework for comparing different filling technologies, rather than looking only at the "equipment purchase price". The TCO calculation for a PP + SU system needs to cover:

  • Initial capital expenditure: the equipment itself (PP and RPP are similar)
  • SU consumable costs: tubing set, connectors and needles for every batch (recurring)
  • Validation costs: E&L testing, tubing use-time validation, IPC system validation
  • Operating costs: cleaning validation (required for RPP, not for PP SU), WFI consumption, clean steam
  • Downtime costs: time between batches taken up by CIP/SIP cycles (longer for RPP)
  • Personnel training: PP has low complexity, so training costs are lower

Analogy: Lifecycle Cost of Buying a Car

When buying a car you cannot look only at the "car price". An electric vehicle (EV) costs 20-30% more to buy than a comparable fuel car, but:

  • Electricity vs fuel (SU consumables vs utility costs)
  • No servicing vs regular oil/brake pad changes (low maintenance vs CIP/SIP maintenance costs)
  • Battery life vs engine overhaul (pump head service life vs piston/cylinder replacement)

PP + SU is like an electric vehicle: the purchase is cheap but the electricity (consumables) keeps costing money; RPP + CIP/SIP is like a fuel car: the purchase is cheap but fuel and repairs also keep costing money. Which is more economical depends on your usage intensity (batch volume) and fuel price (consumable unit price).

The purpose of TCO is to plot these two cost curves and find the "crossover point": below which batch volume SU is more economical, and above which RPP is more economical.

Formula: TCO Comparison Framework for PP vs RPP

PP (SU) annual TCO =
  Capital depreciation (equipment ÷ years)
+ SU tubing sets × batches/year
+ E&L validation (amortized)
+ Tubing use-time validation (amortized)
+ 100% IPC system maintenance
+ Operator training (low)
─────────────────────────
RPP (CIP/SIP) annual TCO =
  Capital depreciation (equipment ÷ years, including CIP/SIP system)
+ Cleaning validation (annual revalidation)
+ WFI consumption × batches/year
+ Clean steam × batches/year
+ Downtime cost (CIP/SIP cycles)
+ Periodic piston/cylinder replacement
+ Operator training (higher)

TCO decision point:
  Low batch count → SU PP usually wins (avoids fixed CIP/SIP costs)
  High batch count → RPP may reverse the result (accumulated SU consumables exceed fixed CIP/SIP costs)

Key Point: Special TCO Considerations for a CDMO

A CDMO is not a single-product manufacturer, so the TCO calculation has additional dimensions:

  • Changeover cleaning cost: with PP + SU the whole tubing path is discarded, so the cross-contamination risk is almost zero and no cleaning validation is needed; RPP needs cleaning validation at every product change, with high regulatory documentation costs
  • Single-supplier risk: PP SU tubing sets often come from a specific OEM, and a supply chain break (such as during COVID-19) can bring the whole production line to a halt. The TCO should include a "supply interruption insurance cost" (dual-supplier qualification, buffer stock)
  • Shared equipment for multiple products: a PP pump head can serve a wide dose range, giving the CDMO higher equipment utilization and lower allocated capital depreciation

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO fills 50 batches per year of a protein drug (2 mL/vial). Each SU tubing set costs €800, and the annual operating cost of an RPP + CIP/SIP system (excluding equipment depreciation) is estimated at €30,000. Question: roughly how many batches is the TCO crossover point between SU and RPP?
  2. The PP SU tubing set from one supplier is recalled. How does your production line respond? How can this "supply chain risk" be quantified in the TCO analysis?
2.1.8 Peristaltic Pump System Complexity: Setup, Handling, and Changeover

Original Text

System complexity is very low as the pump only consists of a rotor and a housing, which can cover a large filling range (e.g., 0.01 mL to 50 mL); therefore, the pump does not need to be changed to accommodate the filling of multiple product volumes. The setup of the pump is the installation of the housing, and the rotor. Neither requires sterile connections nor sterilization as the pump has no direct product contact; biodecontamination with hydrogen peroxide or another qualified SOP-driven disinfection procedure as appropriate for cleanroom use is sufficient. The tubes require proper handling, as they need to be mounted to the pump system either as a SU gamma-irradiated component or as an in-house autoclaved component.

With a two-tube PP, tube clips are commonly employed, which hold the two pump tubes going into and out of the pump heads (see Figure 2.1.8-1🔍). The tube clips are attached to the tubes, typically by pressing the tube into the corresponding slot on the clip. The tube clip is then mounted to the pump by simply clicking it into position, and the tubing that is internal to the rotary pump head is centered within the rollers. Special care must be taken so the fixed and loose sides of the clips are not confused; this is typically prevented by mistake-proofing the setup procedure (e.g., with appropriate photographs, marking of components, flow-direction indication). Tube clips are format-specific as the size of the slots within the clip are specific to the tubing outer diameter (OD) in use.

[Figure 2.1.8-1🔍: Diagram Showing the Positioning of Tube Clips used with Peristaltic Pump]

Because the pump is a closed system, it may be located outside the barrier, which would add further simplicity to the setup and handling. Changeover would be necessary if the filling volumes exceeded the limits covered by the pump head. The changeover is the same procedure as the setup, and only the housing and rotor would need to be changed if there were a large volume change on the line. It should be established whether an adapter or changeable plate will be required to accommodate the range of filling, and whether this will also require a different housing or rotor sizes.

There are some pumps that are designed to have small adjustment springs between the backplate and the rotor, which may be helpful in compensating for the stress effects on the tubes. However, the proper installation and adjustment of such springs typically requires expert setup knowledge.

Because different batches of tubes may have different geometry (e.g., inner diameter (ID), OD, thickness, length, elasticity), ensuring during setup that the fill volume is established to match the specific batch of tubing in use is important. A best practice is 100% IPC. Should a strategy for weight check other than 100% IPC be employed, maintaining a high monitoring frequency at the beginning of the batch is particularly critical, and there may be other points of criticality as well, particularly over long production durations when wear may start to affect performance. An appropriate risk assessment should be performed to justify the dose control approach if other than 100% IPC (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4 for additional content on weight-check strategies).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Two Dimensions of Very Low PP System Complexity

The low complexity of PP shows up in:

Mechanical complexity: the whole pump has only two main parts, the rotor and the housing. There are no valves, no seals and no pistons. A trained operator can complete the installation in a few minutes, without an engineer.

Sterile control complexity: the pump body itself does not contact the product, so no aseptic connection and no sterilize-in-place are needed. Vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP) biodecontamination or standard disinfection procedures are sufficient. The only item that needs sterile management is the tubing itself, but SU tubing is gamma-sterilized before it leaves the supplier and can be installed directly.

Key Point: Batch-to-Batch Variation in Tubing Geometry - Why the Fill Volume Must Be Reconfirmed Every Time

This is the most underestimated risk in PP operation: silicone tubing of the same brand and model may show small differences in ID, OD, wall thickness and elasticity between batches.

The dosing accuracy of PP comes directly from the inner diameter of the tubing (volume delivered per revolution = tube cross-sectional area × length compressed by the roller). If the ID of a new batch of tubing is 0.1 mm larger than the previous batch, every fill volume will be systematically high.

Best practice: every time a new batch of tubing is introduced (a new tubing lot, not just a new product batch), re-run the fill volume setup (gravimetric calibration) and confirm that the actual fill volume with the new tubing meets the target before starting production.

Key Point: The Importance of Mistake-Proofing

Installing the tube clip is the only high-risk manual step in PP setup. If the fixed side and the loose side are reversed, the tubing may come off during filling or cause dose deviations.

Practical standards for mistake-proofing:

  • Different colors on the two ends of the tube clip (visual identification)
  • Photos in the SOP (diagram of correct installation)
  • Flow direction arrows marked on the tubing (to prevent reversed installation)
  • A second person must verify after installation (two-person check)

This is a typical application of the poka-yoke (mistake-proofing) design principle in GMP.

Analogy: F1 Pit Stop vs an Ordinary Tire Shop

Changing PP tubing can be like an F1 pit stop (well designed, clear steps, complete mistake-proofing) and take only 2-3 minutes. Without good mistake-proofing (tube clip direction marking, SOP photos), the same operation becomes like an ordinary tire shop: it relies on the individual experience of the technician, and the result differs every time.

The CDMO challenge: operators may change tubing of several different formats in one day, so the consistency of mistake-proofing directly affects batch success rate.

The Logic Behind the Need for 100% IPC

There are three sources of PP dose deviation:
  1. Tubing geometry variation between lots (once per lot)
  2. Tubing wear within a batch (progressive over time)
  3. Sudden leakage from small cracks in the tubing (random)

The first two are "progressive" deviations that statistical IPC can partly capture;
the third is a "sudden" deviation, and only 100% IPC can ensure
that every container is within the acceptable range.

Conclusion:
  Recommended IPC strategy for PP = 100% weighing (gravimetric check)
  If statistical IPC is used, the following are needed:
    - High-frequency monitoring at batch start
    - Mid-batch monitoring for long batches (to capture the effect of wear)
    - Detailed risk assessment documentation

Practice Questions

  1. Your PP filling line changed to a new lot of tubing today (same model, but a new lot). Which steps should the SOP require the operator to complete before formal production can start?
  2. An operator claims: "We used 100% IPC last batch and we are continuing with the same tubing, so can we switch to statistical IPC?" How do you assess the reasonableness of this request?
2.1.9 Peristaltic Pump Maintenance and Aging

Original Text

As described in the preceding sections, the focus for this system must be on the aging and replacement of tubing.

The pump system itself is essentially maintenance-free, although the original equipment manufacturer's recommendations for checking the operation of the roller bearings should be observed.

The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) should provide a replacement strategy for the servo motors (although infrequent), to avoid unnecessary downtimes or potential loss of batches.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Shift in Maintenance Focus

The maintenance philosophy for PP systems is completely different from that for RPP. RPP requires regular maintenance of many mechanical parts such as pistons, cylinders, valves and seals; the maintenance of PP is concentrated almost entirely in one place: the tubing.

This characteristic has practical significance for CDMO equipment management:

  • Simplified preventive maintenance (PM) plan: the main PM items are confirming the tubing replacement interval and checking the condition of the roller bearings
  • Simplified spare parts inventory: there is no need to stock many mechanical parts, and the main spare is the tubing set (already bought in bulk as SU)
  • Lower technical requirements: maintenance does not require a specialist mechanical engineer, and trained operators can perform most routine maintenance

Key Point: OEM Replacement Strategy for Servo Motors

Although servo motor failures are very rare, a failure in the middle of a batch has serious consequences:

  • Batch interruption → possible rejection (especially for high-value products)
  • Uncertain repair time → affects delivery dates
  • OEM parts lead time (especially for imported equipment) may be several weeks

Best practice: ask the OEM for the "servo motor preventive replacement interval" (usually in operating hours), and track the cumulative hours of each motor in the equipment history. Replace proactively during planned downtime before the replacement interval is reached, to avoid unplanned downtime.

For high-volume CDMO production lines: it is recommended to stock 1-2 spare servo motors, so that a replacement can be made within 24 hours.

Analogy: The Maintenance Philosophy of a Printer

The hardware of an inkjet printer (print head, motor, rollers) is designed for long-term use and almost never needs replacement; what needs continual replenishment and management is the ink cartridge (the consumable).

A PP system is like a high-end inkjet printer: the machine itself is almost maintenance-free, but management of the ink cartridge (the silicone tubing) is the core of the operation: reorder in time, confirm the specification and lot, and validate the service life.

Practice Questions

  1. Outline an annual maintenance plan for a PP filling system, listing the items it should include (tubing-related, pump head-related, motor-related), and indicate the basis for the frequency of each item (OEM recommendation, operating time, number of batches).
  2. For a PP that fills 100 batches per year, how would you decide the purchasing strategy on "whether a spare servo motor should be stocked"?
2.1.10 Peristaltic Pump Single-Use Versus Reusable Strategy

Original Text

Use of the SU strategy is much more common than the reusable strategy with PP due to the simplicity of the installation of presterilized components without any need for aseptic connections. The reusable strategy brings added risks to the process, for example, offline sterilization gives added complexity to the process, and cleaning for the tubing and filling needles requires validation and monitoring.

Regulatory guidance (e.g., European Commission Annex 1: Manufacture of Sterile Medicinal Products, EudraLex-Volume 4-EU Guidelines for Good Manufacturing Practice for Medicinal Products for Human and Veterinary Use (2022)) clearly states that any aseptic connections made for parts that come into direct product contact should be sterilized in place whenever possible (3). It is generally always possible to sterilize in place if a CIP/SIP system is designed for the filler, so the cost for reuse (and the increased costs associated with engineering and initial capital) should be weighed against the costs of SU.

For example, when the PPs use SU tubing (and connectors, where necessary), there are consumable costs associated with the system. These are additional ongoing costs as compared to a RPP or TP filler that might have more fixed piping, which is a greater initial capital investment. PPs are commonly used in a full SUS (e.g., disposable SU bags) due to the ease of setup. A comparison of expense between a fully disposable SU PP system and a conventional filling system with fixed piping that is CIP/SIP capable must take into account not only the initial installation and validation costs, but also the ongoing cost of utilities, manpower, time of changeover, maintenance of the validated state, and calibration, as well as the associated consumables.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The SIP Requirement of EU GMP Annex 1 Is a Regulatory Mandate

The core requirement of EU GMP Annex 1 (2022): any part in direct contact with the product must be sterilized in place (SIP) wherever this is technically feasible.

This requirement has a very large impact on PP with reusable tubing:

  • To use reusable tubing, a CIP/SIP system must be designed
  • The design, installation and validation of a CIP/SIP system are expensive
  • For PP tubing, as described later in this chapter, CIP/SIP presents many engineering challenges

The result of the regulatory mandate: choosing reusable tubing "without SIP" is almost unacceptable in the EU regulatory environment. This makes PP + SU (no SIP needed) the easiest route to regulatory compliance.

Analogy: Disposable Tableware vs Porcelain That Needs a Dishwasher

An office canteen has two options:

  • Disposable tableware (SU tubing): throw it away after each use, no dishwasher and no validated cleaning procedure, but the cost of consumables has to be paid every day
  • Porcelain tableware (reusable tubing): expensive to buy initially, and it needs an industrial dishwasher (CIP) + a high-temperature disinfection program (SIP) + regular validation that the tableware is really clean (cleaning validation)

In the world of Annex 1, the porcelain canteen is also required to ensure that "the dishwasher reaches a specific temperature and cycle standard (the SIP requirement)", and if it cannot, it can only use disposable tableware.

The CDMO need for frequent product changes (perhaps 3-4 products per week) makes the "zero cleaning validation" advantage of disposable tableware even more significant.

Key Point: Supply Chain Dependency Risk of SU

The SU strategy looks perfect but carries a major commercial risk: high dependence on a single supplier.

PP SU tubing sets usually have to be compatible with a specific pump (tube diameter, connector specifications, tube clip size), and often only one or two OEM suppliers offer compatible products. If the supplier:

  • Runs out of stock (raw material shortage)
  • Discontinues a model
  • Has a quality problem leading to a recall
  • Raises prices (market monopoly)

the CDMO production plan may be hit immediately.

Risk control: require the OEM in the commercial agreement to give 12-18 months of advance notice (change notification), and assess whether an alternative supplier needs to be qualified or a buffer stock strategy established.

Practice Questions

  1. A new client asks: "Is the tubing on your PP line single-use or reusable, and why?" Give a complete answer that combines the Annex 1 requirements, TCO considerations and operational complexity.
  2. The sole supplier of your PP SU tubing announces that it will suspend supply for 3 months because of a raw material shortage. How do you respond? Which options are feasible, and which would raise regulatory problems?
2.1.11 Peristaltic Pump Clean-In-Place/Sterilize-In-Place Feasibility and Pitfalls

Original Text

CIP/SIP may be restricted to cleaning and sterilizing the intermediate vessel, tubes, and dosing needles. Because of this, the decision to implement a CIP/SIP system on a PP, and the practicality and the benefits thereof, will usually be considered to see if use of a SUS will not outweigh the CIP/SIP approach in terms of complexity.

In the case where CIP/SIP is applied, two main considerations apply:

  • Initial CIP/SIP of the interior surfaces
  • Subsequent biodecontamination of the exterior surfaces prior to the start of operations

For the initial CIP/SIP, the tubes cannot be mounted within the pump, as the pump rotor and rollers would restrict CIP/SIP media flow (e.g., cleaning fluid, steam). For the biodecontamination, tubes cannot be mounted within the clips or the pump as it will restrict biodecontamination (e.g., vapor phase access to surfaces that are in contact with each other). If the tubing biodecontamination is performed prior to SIP, the SIP will reduce the risk of residual absorbed biodecontamination agent (e.g., vaporized hydrogen peroxide absorbed in silicone tubing). Alternatively, after biodecontamination, a WFI flush or CIP might be applied to the tubing followed by SIP. The chosen sequence and process steps should be validated to be appropriate to ensure the residue-free, sterile condition of the tubing. During SIP the tube to needle, tube to Y-connectors, and vessel to tube connections must be fixed with a connector to ensure that the tube does not disconnect from the needle when under pressure for SIP. After SIP, manual assembly must take place, which again poses risks as a result of aseptic manipulation.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The CIP/SIP Engineering Challenges of PP

This section explains why "CIP/SIP rarely used for PP" (mentioned in the advantages and disadvantages table earlier). The root cause is a fundamental conflict between the physical structure of PP and the CIP/SIP process:

Conflict 1: The tubing must be removed for CIP/SIP

CIP/SIP requires cleaning liquid or steam to flow freely through the whole tubing lumen. But in the normal state the PP rollers are compressed against the tube wall. This compression is exactly how the pump works, but it also blocks the passage of fluid. The result: before CIP/SIP is performed, the tubing must be removed from the pump head.

Conflict 2: Reinstallation after removal is a manual aseptic operation

After CIP/SIP, the tubing must be fitted back onto the pump head. This is a manual step that introduces aseptic handling risk. The purpose of SIP (to provide sterile tubing) is partly undone by the "manual installation after SIP".

The PP CIP/SIP Operating Sequence

If the CIP/SIP route is chosen, the operating sequence is as follows:

Step 1: Remove tubing from pump head (necessary, to keep the fluid path clear)
   ↓
Step 2: CIP of tubing lumen (circulation of cleaning solution)
   ↓
Step 3: Biodecontamination of isolator/RABS outer surfaces (VHP fogging)
   ↓ (tubing must be removed from the clamps so that VHP reaches all surfaces)
Step 4: WFI rinse or go directly to SIP
   (if VHP biodecontamination was done first: SIP can break down residual VHP in the silicone tubing)
   ↓
Step 5: SIP (steam sterilization, tubing lumen reaches the required SAL)
   ↓
Step 6: Manually reinstall tubing onto the pump head (high-risk step!)
   ↓
Step 7: Confirm fill volume with 100% IPC, then start production

Risk concentration point: Step 6 (manual aseptic installation)
→ This is exactly the core advantage of the SU route: Step 6 is eliminated entirely

Key Point: VHP Absorption by Silicone Tubing

This is a subtle but important chemical issue: silicone is a porous material, and VHP (vaporized hydrogen peroxide) is easily absorbed into the silicone tube wall. If the absorbed VHP is not completely removed, during subsequent product filling it may:

  • Slowly release H₂O₂ into the drug solution (a leachables issue)
  • Cause oxidative degradation of protein drugs

Solution: after VHP biodecontamination, SIP (steam) can effectively break down residual VHP and reduce the risk. However, the effectiveness of this removal must be confirmed through validation (measuring the residual H₂O₂ concentration after SIP).

Analogy: Drying the Dishes by Hand After Washing

An industrial dishwasher (CIP) can get porcelain spotless, and high-temperature disinfection (SIP) can kill all bacteria, but if after disinfection the cook has to take the dishes out by hand to assemble and plate them, bacteria from those hands may contaminate them again.

This is the paradox of PP CIP/SIP: great effort goes into making the tubing sterile, but the last step needs manual installation, and this manual step turns all the earlier effort into an uncertainty. The advantage of SU is that tubing sterilized at the supplier is installed directly, skipping this manual step entirely.

Practice Questions

  1. A client insists on reusable tubing for environmental reasons (to avoid SU waste). As technical lead, how would you explain the challenges of CIP/SIP on PP and propose alternatives or supplementary measures?
  2. Outline a PP CIP/SIP validation plan: which critical parameters need to be validated? What are the acceptance criteria?
2.1.12 Peristaltic Pump Benefits and Risks

Original Text

Table 2.1.12-1🔍 highlights the common benefits-and-risks analysis that is pertinent to the use of PP systems.

Table 2.1.12-1🔍 Benefits and Risks of Peristaltic Pump Systems

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Reading the Benefit and Risk Matrix

This table is the structural summary of the whole PP chapter. Look at the patterns in the table:

Common theme on the benefit side: "simplicity"

  • Simple assembly, simple maintenance, low technical requirements, low operating costs
  • These simple characteristics all come from the same root: the closed system design of PP combined with the SU strategy

Common theme on the risk side: "fragility of the tubing"

  • Supply chain dependency, wear, rupture, viscosity limits: all are related to the tubing
  • These risks also share the same root: silicone tubing is the only component in the whole system that is both a wear part and a critical safety barrier

Key Point: PP Is Not Suitable for Sensor-Filling

"Sensor-filling" is a fill control method that relies on a level sensor or weight sensor to send a stop signal in real time once the target fill volume is reached. It is often used where container capacity is limited (such as small vials and ophthalmic products) or in foam-sensitive applications.

The problem with PP: the elasticity of the flexible tubing creates a certain fluid inertia in the line (after the tubing is compressed it takes a short time for flow to stop completely), so there is a delay between the sensor triggering the stop signal and the flow actually stopping, which leads to overfilling.

TP (time-pressure filling) has a more responsive sensor reaction and suits container types that need precise level control. When a CDMO receives such container specifications, TP should be evaluated before PP.

Practical Application: Summary of CDMO Use Cases for PP Technology

Ideal scenarios for PP:

  • Multiple dose formats on one line (the wide dose range advantage is maximized)
  • Low- to medium-viscosity injectables (buffers, biologics, aqueous small molecule solutions)
  • Frequent product changeovers (the no-cleaning-validation advantage of SU is maximized)
  • Biologics (the low-shear advantage matters most)
  • Preclinical/early clinical small batches (low capital investment, quick start-up)

Scenarios where PP should be assessed carefully or avoided:

  • High-viscosity formulations (suspensions, high-viscosity versions of lipid formulations)
  • Small-volume, high-precision containers that need sensor-filling
  • Formulations containing organic solvents (which accelerate tubing degradation)
  • Ultra-potent HPAPI (which must be placed inside the isolator, adding design complexity)
  • Cost structures with very high batch volumes where the continuing cost of SU consumables is unacceptable

PP Technology Selection Quick Decision Framework

Question 1: Is the product viscosity high?
  Yes → consider RPP or TP first; PP not recommended
  No → continue assessment

Question 2: Is sensor-filling (level-triggered stop) required?
  Yes → TP preferred; PP not recommended
  No → continue assessment

Question 3: Is it a biologic/cell therapy (low-shear requirement)?
  Yes → PP is the preferred choice
  No → continue assessment

Question 4: Does the CDMO run multiple products on one line with frequent changeovers?
  Yes → the advantages of PP + SU are significant (lowest cleaning validation cost)
  No → consider whether the fixed cost of RPP + CIP/SIP is justified

Question 5: Is it an HPAPI (highly potent product)?
  Yes → PP can still be used, but design for installation inside the isolator + leak detection
  No → PP can be placed outside the barrier, with the simplest operation

Analogy: Overall Technology Selection Is Like Choosing Kitchen Equipment

When choosing kitchen equipment you do not buy only one kind; you choose different tools according to the type of cooking:

  • PP = silicone spatula: gentle, versatile, hygienic single use, no tedious washing; but not suitable for stirring thick batter
  • RPP = stainless steel mixer: durable, precise, suitable for many viscosities; but it needs thorough cleaning after every use
  • TP = measuring cup + timed valve: metering by pressure and time, best for situations that need precise sensor-based stopping

A mature CDMO kitchen should have all three, and choose the right tool according to the client's "cooking needs" (product characteristics), rather than filling every client's product with the same tool.

Practice Questions

  1. Using the benefit/risk framework learned in this chapter, choose a filling technology for each of the following three new clients and explain the reasons:
    • Client A: monoclonal antibody, 2 mL, 5,000 vials per batch, 12 batches per year, low viscosity
    • Client B: ophthalmic formulation, 0.5 mL, requires sensor-based stop filling, 50 batches per year
    • Client C: highly potent anti-tumor small molecule, containing DMSO solvent, 1 mL/vial, 3 batches per year (clinical)
  2. Looking back over all sub-sections of this chapter (2.1.4 to 2.1.12), which aspect of PP technology has the greatest impact on the day-to-day operation of a CDMO? Why?

Section Summary (2.1.4–2.1.12)

  • Technical characteristics: PP is a low-shear filling technology with a wide dose range and low system complexity. Its core advantage is that "the closed system can be placed outside the sterile barrier"; its core limitation is that "the silicone tubing is the only wear point and the concentration point of all SA risks"
  • SA control: tubing use-time validation + E&L testing matrix + 100% IPC are the three SA pillars of PP; the recommendation for 100% IPC is stronger for PP than for RPP, because PP dosing is more affected by tubing wear and batch-to-batch geometric variation
  • Cost structure: the TCO advantages of PP + SU are no cleaning validation, low maintenance costs, and a wide dose range that improves equipment utilization; the disadvantages are the continuing cost of SU consumables and the supply chain dependency risk
  • Regulatory driver: the SIP requirement of EU GMP Annex 1 means reusable tubing must be equipped with a CIP/SIP system, which is a major engineering challenge; this is the key regulatory background for PP + SU becoming the mainstream choice
  • CIP/SIP pitfall: CIP/SIP for PP has a fundamental engineering contradiction (the tubing must be removed for cleaning, but must be manually reinstalled after SIP); in practice PP rarely uses CIP/SIP, and SU is the preferred strategy for almost all PP installations
  • Selection decision: PP suits CDMO scenarios with low viscosity, multiple formats, biologics and frequent changeovers; it does not suit high viscosity, sensor-filling and solvent-containing formulations; using PP for HPAPI requires additional leak containment design
2B

Section 2B: Rotary Piston Pump

p42-p53
