Learning Objectives

  • Understand how the RPP works: the piston-cylinder structure, the product-lubrication mechanism and the four-phase dosing cycle
  • Master the key differences between RPP and PP: the RPP must be located inside an isolator/RABS; the RPP has no dose drift, so statistical IPC is technically feasible
  • Understand the CIP/SIP design requirements: two additional connections, the cleaning/sterilization position requirement, and why this is more complex than for a TP
  • Evaluate the TCO (total cost of ownership) of the RPP: the most expensive filling system, but the best choice for high-viscosity protein formulations
  • Be able to judge in a CDMO setting when to choose an RPP and when to choose a PP, and on what basis
  • Understand the importance of serialized piston-cylinder pairs and the applications for which a ceramic pump is suitable
2.2

Rotary Piston Pump — Overview & Operating Principle

Rotary Piston Pump Overview and Working Principle

Original Text

The Rotary Piston Pump (RPP) is one of the oldest and most established filling technologies for aseptic liquid filling. It operates on the principle of a piston moving within a cylinder, where the product itself acts as the lubricant between the piston and cylinder surfaces — a concept known as product-lubricated operation.

The RPP dosing cycle proceeds through four distinct phases:

  1. Suction phase: The piston retracts, drawing product from the intermediate vessel into the cylinder chamber through the inlet port.
  2. Rotation phase: The cylinder (or piston) rotates to align the outlet port with the filling needle pathway, closing the inlet.
  3. Dispensing phase: The piston advances, pushing the precisely measured volume of product out through the filling needle into the container.
  4. Return phase: The cylinder rotates back to the inlet position, ready for the next suction cycle.

Because the piston-cylinder interface is open to the surrounding environment at the point where the piston inserts into the cylinder, the RPP must always be positioned inside the containment — either inside an isolator or a Restricted Access Barrier System (RABS). This is a fundamental constraint that distinguishes RPP from peristaltic pumps (PP), time-pressure (TP), and rolling diaphragm pumps (DP), some elements of which may be installed outside the aseptic barrier.

[Figure 2.2-3🔍: Rotary Piston Pump Filler Fluid Pathway]

The dosing volume is determined purely by the stroke length of the piston within the cylinder — making it a true positive displacement device. Unlike the peristaltic pump, there is no dose drift over time, as the mechanical stroke remains constant regardless of product viscosity changes or tubing wear. This stability is a defining strength of RPP technology.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: How the RPP Works - Positive Displacement Filling

The rotary piston pump (RPP) is a positive displacement pump, which means that the volume of liquid delivered by each piston stroke is fixed and is not affected by inlet pressure or product viscosity.

Four-phase dosing cycle:

  • Suction: the piston retracts and product is drawn into the cylinder
  • Rotation: the cylinder rotates, switching the flow path from inlet to outlet
  • Dispensing: the piston advances and pushes out a precisely metered dose of product
  • Return: the cylinder rotates back, ready for the next cycle

Product-lubricated: there is no rubber seal between the piston and the cylinder; the product liquid itself forms the lubricating film. This eliminates particle contamination caused by seal wear, but it also means that the piston-cylinder interface is "open".

Analogy: RPP = a giant syringe plunger

Think of a medical syringe: you pull the plunger back and liquid is drawn in; you push it forward and the liquid is delivered precisely. The RPP works in almost exactly the same way.

The key difference: a syringe has a rubber gasket sealing the plunger to the barrel, whereas the RPP has no seal - the piston slides directly inside the cylinder, using "the product itself" as the lubricant. This is why the RPP must operate inside a sterile barrier: the syringe's rubber gasket is the seal protection, but the RPP interface is open, so any particle or microorganism in the environment could enter the fluid path at this point.

Key Constraint: the RPP Must Be Inside an Isolator/RABS

This is the most important design limitation of the RPP and the point most often tested in exams:

  • PP (peristaltic pump): the pump head can be outside the isolator; only the silicone tubing passes into the sterile area
  • TP (time-pressure): the pressure vessel and pinch valves can be outside the barrier
  • DP (rolling diaphragm pump): the diaphragm completely isolates the mechanical parts, so this is a closed system
  • RPP: the piston-cylinder interface is "open to the environment" at the point of insertion → the entire pump must be inside the sterile barrier

This constraint has an unexpected advantage: when handling highly potent or toxic active pharmaceutical ingredients (HPAPI), the entire fluid path is inside the isolator, which further protects operators from product exposure.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the RPP have no seal, while the silicone tubing of a PP is equivalent to a sealing mechanism? How does this difference affect the system positioning decision for each?
  2. What is the fundamental difference in accuracy mechanism between "positive displacement" filling and "time-pressure" filling? In which situations is the positive displacement characteristic of the RPP especially important?
2.2.1

Rotary Piston Pump Design Configurations

Design Configuration: CIP/SIP Capability and Dose Stability

Original Text

For inline CIP/SIP, a special design is necessary that allows the pump to be cleaned around the full circumference of the piston and cylinder. Therefore, two additional connections are required: one in the lower position and one in the upper position of the pump (see Figure 2.2.1-1🔍). In addition, the pump is required to move to a cleaning and sterilization position to ensure that all surfaces are opened to the greatest extent for exposure to both cleaning fluids and steam, allowing more space between piston and cylinder.

Due to the challenges in accommodating all the connections, the CIP/SIP of RPP is much more challenging than TP. However, although RPP is more technically complex, the focus on reducing aseptic assembly operations has made CIP/SIP more common with RPP.

[Figure 2.2.1-1🔍: Rotary Piston Pump with Clean-in-Place/Sterilize-in-Place Capability]

In contrast to the PP, the RPP has no drift in delivered dose over time and fills the same amount of volume at the beginning and at the end of the aseptic filling operation. This means that a statistical IPC is technically appropriate (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Two Additional Connections for CIP/SIP

The CIP/SIP design of the RPP is more complex than that of a TP because of the cylinder geometry: cleaning liquid and steam must be able to reach the full circumference of the piston-cylinder interface, both above and below.

This therefore requires:

  • Upper connection: lets steam enter from the top and fully contact the upper half of the cylinder
  • Lower connection: drains cleaning liquid and condensate, ensuring there are no dead legs at the bottom
  • CIP/SIP position (cleaning position): the pump must move to a special position that maximizes the gap between the piston and the cylinder, so that cleaning liquid and steam can fully surround the contact surfaces

This is why an RPP usually needs a third drive (third axis) dedicated to moving to the CIP/SIP position.

Analogy: CIP/SIP position = the tilt adjustment of a dentist's chair

Think of a dentist's chair: so that the dentist can clean every one of your teeth thoroughly, the chair must adjust its angle so that your mouth is exposed in the best possible posture.

The CIP/SIP position of the RPP works on the same principle: the pump must move into a special posture so that cleaning liquid and steam can "see" and contact every cylinder wall surface, including the hardest-to-reach piston-cylinder interface. This movement requires a dedicated mechanical drive, which in turn adds equipment complexity and validation burden.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is CIP/SIP of an RPP "more challenging" than of a TP? Analyze from the two angles of geometry and number of connections.
  2. If you were the QA manager and needed to validate the SIP effectiveness of an RPP, how would you design the steam penetration challenge points? What type of monitor would you place at the upper connection and at the lower connection?

Key Comparison: RPP vs PP - Dose Drift and IPC Strategy

This is the most important regulatory point in this section:

Important reminder: even though statistical IPC is technically permitted for an RPP, in practice periodic IPC is still recommended, mainly to detect air bubbles in the tubing. This is the focus of Section 2.2.6.

2.2.2

Rotary Piston Pump Setup

Installation and Setup: Serialized Pairing, Material Selection and Priming

Original Text

The tight mechanical tolerances of the piston and cylinder often require that the two parts of each pump be scribed with serial numbers (by the OEM), which will ensure that the matching parts are always assembled together to avoid binding, seizing, or having a large tolerance range that can result in changes in dosing accuracy, dripping at the needles, or leaking.

There may be exceptions for some materials of construction, such as ceramic, that enable the piston and cylinders to be interchangeable. Product characteristics should be considered carefully when selecting technology, as the tight mechanical tolerances cannot withstand the formation of crystals during operation that may result in blocking of the piston and cylinder. In these cases, ceramic pumps may be called for, or larger tolerances may suffice, if there is no dripping concern with the specific product.

The pump stroke is adjusted depending on the fill volume but, for priming, it is advantageous to use the complete stroke to exhaust the air out of the system. There are different methods to prime the pump to remove air from the system and ensure reaching target fills without air gaps at the beginning of the batch. The approach to priming should be considered depending on the application, product characteristics, and execution of the pump.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Serialized Piston-Cylinder Pairs

The pistons and cylinders of an RPP are precision-machined at the OEM factory and then pair-tested before shipment. Each piston-cylinder pair is engraved with a unique serial number, indicating that the two parts are a dedicated, matched pair.

Why can parts not be mixed and matched?

  • The piston-cylinder clearance is typically accurate to the micrometer (µm) level
  • If the mismatched clearance is too large → product leaks past the piston and the dose is inaccurate
  • If the mismatched clearance is too small → the piston binds or seizes, causing mechanical damage
  • Either case can lead to dripping from the filling needle, contaminating the sterile environment

Exception: because ceramic material is more uniform, some manufacturers allow interchangeable use, but the supplier's specification must still be confirmed.

Analogy: serialized pairing = wedding rings

A piston and cylinder are like a pair of wedding rings: they are a dedicated match, made for each other. You would never mix rings from different pairs, because they either would not fit at all or would fit loosely.

In a pharmaceutical plant, mixing piston-cylinder pairs with non-matching serial numbers is like forcing rings from different pairs together: at best the fill dose is inaccurate, at worst the equipment is destroyed, and the most serious consequence is needle dripping that contaminates the sterile area, leading to rejection of the whole batch and a deviation investigation.

Practical rule: every time the RPP is dismantled for cleaning or maintenance, the serial numbers must be checked at reassembly. This is a mandatory verification step in the SOP and must not be skipped.

Key Point: When to Use a Ceramic Pump

The tight tolerance of a stainless steel RPP is a risk for some products:

  • Crystallizing products: crystals may lodge in the piston-cylinder gap, causing the pump to seize or generating particle contamination
  • Abrasive suspensions: solid particles wear the stainless steel surface, gradually enlarging the gap and generating metal debris

Advantages of a ceramic pump:

  • Higher hardness and better wear resistance
  • Chemically inert; does not react with the vast majority of drug products
  • The tolerance uniformity of some ceramic materials is better, so they can be used interchangeably

Weakness of ceramic: it is brittle and can easily crack from sudden temperature change (thermal shock) or impact. Special care is needed in handling and in the rate of temperature change during CIP/SIP.

The Importance of Priming

Priming is the process, before a filling batch starts, of expelling air from the tubing and pump and filling them with product.

Why prime with a complete stroke? Using a complete stroke maximizes the amount of product moved in and out per cycle and expels residual air from the cylinder more efficiently. If priming is done with a stroke that is too short, air may remain at the top of the cylinder, causing underfill at the start of the batch.

Note: during priming the pump runs "dry" (dry-start) and the piston-cylinder interface temporarily has no product lubrication; friction is highest and wear risk is greatest during this time. This is an important particle risk control point in Section 2.2.5 Sterility Assurance.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO is filling a highly saturated solution (prone to crystallization). The filling speed is slow (the product stays in the cylinder for a long time) and the filling temperature is low. Would you choose a stainless steel pump or a ceramic pump? Explain your reasoning.
  2. If an operator forgets to check the serial numbers when assembling the RPP, resulting in a mismatched piston-cylinder pair, what observable filling abnormalities are most likely to occur? How could this problem be found in the batch production record (BPR)?
2.2.3

Rotary Piston Pump System Positioning

System Positioning: Intermediate Container Level Control and Head Pressure Consistency

Original Text

To prevent too much pressure on the product, thereby preventing product release from between the piston and cylinder, the intermediate vessel must be ventilated and should be maintained at a consistent fill-level to maintain constant head pressure. This is especially important for low-viscosity products.

For higher-viscosity products, the intermediate vessel is commonly used with overpressure and might not be ventilated.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Effect of Head Pressure on the RPP

Head pressure is the gravitational pressure produced by the height of a liquid column. Formula: P = ρgh (density × gravitational acceleration × column height).

For an RPP, the consequence of excessive head pressure is that product is pushed out through the tiny gap between the piston and cylinder (product release from between piston and cylinder). This is similar to a burst water pipe: the higher the water pressure, the faster the leak.

Control strategy:

  • Low-viscosity products: ventilate the intermediate container to avoid overpressure and keep the fill level consistent to stabilize head pressure
  • High-viscosity products: because of the high flow resistance, a moderate positive pressure (overpressure) is needed to help product enter the cylinder, and the intermediate container may be left unvented

Analogy: level control = the pressure-stabilizing design of a water tower

A water tower in a city supply system maintains a constant level so that every household has the same water pressure. If the tower level kept rising and falling, the pressure at your home would be sometimes strong and sometimes weak, and your shower would be unpleasant.

Level control of the RPP intermediate container follows the same principle: constant level → constant head pressure → the same resistance on every piston suction stroke → better dose consistency. Especially for low-viscosity products (such as water for injection or low-concentration buffers), even a level difference of 5 cm can produce an observable fill difference.

Key Point: Different Strategies for Low vs High Viscosity

This is a design choice, not an operating error, and reflects a deep understanding of product characteristics:

  • Low viscosity (e.g. physiological saline, buffers): the product flows readily, so even small changes in head pressure affect filling accuracy. The container must be vented (not pressurized) and the level tightly controlled.
  • High viscosity (e.g. concentrated protein, on the order of 300,000 mPa-s): flow resistance is high and gravity cannot effectively drive fluid into the pump. Positive pressure is needed, and the intermediate container can be sealed and pressurized.

The RPP is the preferred technology for filling high-viscosity biologics (such as high-concentration mAbs for subcutaneous injection), precisely because its positive displacement mechanism can meter accurately under moderate applied pressure, regardless of viscosity.

Practice Questions

  1. You are filling a protein solution of 100 mPa-s. Midway through the batch, because of an operator error, the intermediate container level drops from 70% to 30%. Based on the head pressure principle, how do you expect the fill weight to change (increase / decrease / no change)? Explain why.
  2. What is the risk of using a positively pressurized intermediate container for a high-viscosity product? How would you control this risk in the design (hint: think of overpressure protection devices and set points)?
2.2.4

Rotary Piston Pump Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages and Disadvantages of the Rotary Piston Pump (Table 2.2.4-1🔍)

Original Text

Table 2.2.4-1🔍 identifies the advantages and disadvantages of RPP systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: How to Read This Table

This table of advantages and disadvantages is a frequently tested PDA topic. The key is not to memorize it but to understand the physical mechanisms behind it:

  • Viscosity compatibility: the positive displacement mechanism does not depend on fluid flowability → high viscosity is fine
  • Shear force: compressing the liquid with the piston generates high local shear → risk for shear-sensitive proteins
  • Dose stability: the mechanical stroke is fixed → consistent dose from the start to the end of the batch
  • 10-fold filling range: the piston stroke is adjustable but the cylinder volume has an upper limit → a wide range requires changing the pump

Key Point: Shear Force - the RPP's Biggest Product Risk

During filling, the RPP applies significant shear force to the product, which is its main product quality risk:

  • When the piston compresses the liquid in the cylinder, the liquid is forced hard through a narrow space
  • The tiny gap at the piston-cylinder interface creates a region of high shear rate
  • High-risk products: monoclonal antibodies (mAb), aggregation-prone proteins, liposomes

Decision logic (selection principles from Table 2.0-1🔍):

  • High viscosity + not shear-sensitive → the RPP is the first choice
  • High viscosity + shear-sensitive → requires more careful process evaluation; a low-pressure TP system may be selected
  • Low viscosity + shear-sensitive → PP or a low-pressure TP system

Analogy: 10-fold filling range = the same engine with different displacements

The engine in a given car series can deliver 1.5 L to 2.5 L of displacement by changing the cylinder stroke. But if you want a 5 L displacement, you need a completely different engine.

The same applies to the RPP: one pump model can usually cover a 10-fold filling range (for example 0.5 mL to 5 mL), but if your products include both a 0.1 mL and a 50 mL presentation, you need several pump head sizes. This matters a great deal in a CDMO: multiple pump sets must be kept, which increases inventory and changeover cost.

Practical Application: CDMO Scenario

Your CDMO client has a high-concentration mAb for subcutaneous injection (180 mg/mL) with a viscosity of about 80 mPa-s, but with high aggregation sensitivity (high shear causes protein aggregation). The client requires a fill volume of 1 mL (fixed presentation).

Your recommended technology choice:

  • Viscosity of 80 mPa-s → exceeds the PP upper limit (about 40-60 mPa-s), so PP is not suitable
  • Aggregation sensitivity + high shear risk → the RPP needs careful evaluation
  • Final recommendation: conduct a shear compatibility study to test the effect of the RPP on aggregation of this protein. At the same time, consider a low-pressure TP system as a backup option.

This is exactly why, in Table 2.0-1🔍, the RPP is marked as the best choice for "high-viscosity, non-shear-sensitive products".

2.2.5

Rotary Piston Pump Sterility Assurance: Microbial and Total Particles

Sterility Assurance: Microbial and Total Particle Control

Original Text

The RPP, one of the oldest filling technologies for aseptic filling, is a system where the product has some exposure to the filling environment (even though that area is small at the point where the piston inserts in the cylinder). Therefore, the system must be inside the containment (i.e., isolator or RABS) at all times to maintain sterility, unlike TP or PP where some elements may be installed outside of the environment. This positioning is helpful when handling potent or toxic products, as all vulnerable fluid pathway components are within the containment, thereby protecting the operators and the external environment from product exposure.

Due to the complexity and expense of the system, RPP is rarely employed as a SUS. Consequently, to avoid product residues being carried over between batches, the RPP must be thoroughly cleaned before use, followed by sterilization and aseptic installation (when not subject to CIP/SIP). RPP systems are capable of CIP/SIP, thereby avoiding aseptic installation. Maintenance of aseptic conditions requires a validated cleaning, sterilization, and setup process as required in EU GMP Annex 1; therefore, new systems should be designed with CIP/SIP in mind.

Since it is a seal-free system and product-lubricated, there is limited friction of the piston and pump to form particles. However, care must be taken during priming, when the pump is first empty and then becomes lubricated with product, so that excessive friction does not occur. Shear-sensitive products may experience localized shear due to the product lubrication of the piston and pump and should be evaluated for compatibility with the technology.

Due to the tight mechanical tolerance of the piston and cylinder, it is essential to maintain the serialized pairings to prevent friction (unless otherwise specified by the supplier). If the product itself is abrasive (e.g., suspensions, products that tend to crystallize), a ceramic pump can be used instead of a stainless-steel pump. If damage is suspected of any pump, evaluation by the supplier is recommended to ensure that the mechanical tolerances have been maintained and the damage will not continue. Damage to the pumps could result in a loss of accuracy, leaks or drips in severe cases, and/or the formation of particulate.

Attention should be given to the airflow above and around the pumps. The mechanical assembly for the drive and pump stroke should be designed to prevent particulate from becoming entrained in the air that flows over the piston and cylinder to avoid it from entering the product stream.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Three Pillars of RPP Sterility Assurance

The SA design logic of the RPP rests on three interrelated pillars:

  • 1. The entire system is inside the sterile barrier: because the piston-cylinder interface is open to the environment, the whole RPP must work inside an isolator or RABS, so that all vulnerable fluid paths are protected by the sterile barrier
  • 2. CIP/SIP is the design standard for new systems: EU GMP Annex 1 emphasizes reducing manual operations in the sterile environment, and CIP/SIP capability is key to the RPP meeting modern regulatory expectations
  • 3. No seals = low particle risk (but the priming phase must be controlled): in steady-state operation the product lubricating film reduces friction; but the priming phase (dry-start) is the time window of highest particle risk

Key Point: The Priming Phase Is the Highest-Risk Moment

During normal filling, the product acts as lubricant, friction between piston and cylinder is low, and particle generation is limited.

The priming phase is completely different:

  • The tubing is full of air and the piston moves without lubrication (dry-start)
  • Dry stainless steel-on-stainless steel friction → highest risk of metal particles
  • Abnormally high friction → may also damage the precision inner surface of the cylinder

Control measures:

  • Before priming, confirm that product has flowed smoothly from the intermediate container to the pump inlet
  • Consider slow priming (lower piston speed to reduce frictional heat and particles)
  • After priming, discard the priming waste (not counted in the batch) so that particles from the priming phase do not enter the product

Analogy: priming phase = a cold start of a car

When a car is cold-started in cold weather, the oil has not yet circulated fully to lubricate the engine, and this is when engine wear is worst. Experienced drivers wait until the engine has warmed up before driving at full speed.

The RPP priming phase is exactly analogous: when the pump has a "cold start" there is no product lubrication, which is a high-risk period for wear and particle generation. A good SOP design should: (1) minimize the number of cycles needed for priming, (2) specify how priming waste is handled, and (3) avoid priming at excessive speed.

Airflow Design: Preventing Mechanical Particles from Contaminating the Product Stream

The RPP drive mechanism (gearbox, push rod, connecting arm) moves directly above the piston-cylinder and is an easily overlooked source of particles.

Design requirement: the design of the drive mechanism must ensure that any particles generated by mechanical wear are not carried by the HEPA unidirectional airflow into the open piston-cylinder interface and into the product stream.

This is usually achieved by: a sealed drive housing, positive-pressure inert gas protection, and airflow direction design (ensuring that the drive components are "upstream" of the unidirectional flow, so that particles are carried away from the product area).

Practice Questions

  1. EU GMP Annex 1 emphasizes "reducing manual interventions in the sterile environment". Compare an RPP with CIP/SIP and one without: what manual operating steps are required in the sterile environment in each case? Which design is more consistent with the spirit of Annex 1?
  2. Suppose that during an APS (aseptic process simulation) you find that the particle count in the RPP priming waste exceeds the limit. As an engineer, what investigation and improvement actions would you take?
2.2.6

Rotary Piston Pump Efficiency and Impact on Risk

Efficiency and Risk Impact: Justification for Statistical IPC

Original Text

The RPP is a high-precision dosing system for which the accuracy remains stable throughout the filling process. Even though the system is highly accurate, a periodic IPC is recommended to detect any underfills due to possible air bubbles within the tubing over time (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4).

As a consequence, an appropriate rationale should be developed for the timing and frequency of the IPC that reflects the attributes of the product being filled and real-world data, when available.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Why Does an RPP Still Need Periodic IPC?

Even though the RPP has no dose drift, periodic IPC should be retained, for these reasons:

  • Air bubbles: an occasional bubble in the tubing causes one or a few containers to be underfilled. Bubbles can come from: gas dissolved in the product itself, foam introduced by mixing or recirculation, and tiny leaks at tubing connections
  • Occasional mechanical problems: piston-cylinder damage or seal failure is rare but has serious consequences
  • Design principle for IPC frequency: the frequency should be based on product characteristics (foaming tendency, gas solubility) and actual production data, not a one-size-fits-all approach

Regulatory position: even where statistical IPC is technically permitted, the company must still provide a sound scientific rationale to support the design of the sampling frequency, and continue to monitor trends.

Analogy: statistical IPC vs 100% IPC = traffic enforcement strategy

Imagine the speed enforcement system on a highway:

  • 100% IPC (PP) = every car is photographed and its speed measured, because you do not know which car will speed (dose drift is unpredictable)
  • Statistical IPC (RPP) = random spot checks, because you know that most drivers on this road obey the rules (fixed mechanical stroke), and occasional violations (bubbles) will be caught by the spot checks

The key: statistical IPC is justified only on the premise of "inherent system stability". As soon as there are signs of mechanical damage to the RPP, the IPC strategy should be re-evaluated immediately.

Practice Questions

  1. You are drawing up an IPC plan for a new RPP filling line. The product is a highly foaming protein solution (prone to entraining air bubbles during mixing and transfer). How would you adjust the IPC frequency compared with a typical low-foaming product?
  2. The statistical IPC sampling plan for an RPP filling line requires 10 samples every 30 minutes. Midway through the batch there is a brief tubing bubble event (the operator sees bubbles spurting from the filling needle for about 2 minutes). What investigation and handling does this event need to trigger?

Core Concept: Why Does the RPP Allow Statistical IPC?

The fill weight check in IPC (in-process control) has different frequency requirements for different filling technologies:

Statistical IPC means that not every container is weighed; instead, samples are taken according to a statistical sampling plan (such as AQL or fixed intervals). This greatly reduces the operating burden on a high-speed filling line.

2.2.7

Rotary Piston Pump Costs: Initial and Lifecycle

Cost Analysis: Initial Investment and Lifecycle Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)

Original Text

An RPP filler, together with CIP/SIP, is the most expensive dosing system. The CIP/SIP components drive much of the increase in cost. CIP/SIP-capable pumps have additional connections for the flow of the cleaning and sterilization media, with or without valves on each pump, depending upon the system design. There is commonly an additional mechanical drive to bring the pump into the CIP/SIP position.

When multiple fill volumes are required, additional pump sizes are commonly necessary, which can add to the system cost. For firms that intend to dedicate equipment to a single product, additional pumps will be required for each product, not just the tubing. Spare pumps are typically maintained to avoid downtime from pump damage.

Lifecycle costs are negligible as the pumps have a long lifespan, provided they are protected from damage (e.g., dropping, assembly and setup accidents, mismatch of piston and cylinder, scratching due to abrasive products).

Periodic revalidation of SIP will require access to difficult-to-reach locations for temperature-mapping and bioindicator placement, making the revalidation time consuming to complete.

TCO calculations would need to include setup, operation, and CIP/SIP as appropriate to the specific system design. Examples of considerations for the TCO calculations may include, but are not limited to, time, utilities, cleaning validation, maintenance, process know-how, training of operators, downtime due to CIP/SIP cycles, and extended times in cases where parallel processing is not possible (such as not being able to run the biodecontamination cycles simultaneously with the CIP/SIP).

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Why Is the RPP the "Most Expensive Filling System"?

The high cost of the RPP comes from several stacked factors:

  • The equipment itself: precision-machined stainless steel or ceramic piston-cylinder sets are costly to manufacture
  • CIP/SIP accessories: two additional connections, possibly additional valves, and a third mechanical drive (the CIP/SIP position drive)
  • Need for multiple pump sets: different fill volumes require different pump head sizes; if different products require dedicated equipment, each product needs its own separate pump set
  • Spare pump inventory: to avoid line stoppages due to pump damage, additional pump sets must be held as backup
  • SIP revalidation: temperature mapping and bioindicator placement are difficult, making validation time-consuming

Analogy: RPP cost = Porsche vs Toyota

Buying an RPP filling system is like choosing a Porsche rather than a Toyota:

  • Purchase price (Porsche): the initial investment is far higher than for comparable competitors (PP, TP)
  • Maintenance cost (Porsche): specialist technicians, high-end parts, more frequent in-depth servicing
  • Performance (Porsche): far ahead of the competition for specific uses (high-viscosity products, long-run stability, precise metering)
  • TCO thinking: if you only need a car for commuting (low viscosity, short batches, small scale), the Porsche is not worth it; but if you need track performance (high-viscosity proteins, long runs, strict accuracy), the Porsche is the right investment

Conclusion: the cost of an RPP is justified only when the product characteristics genuinely require its capabilities. A CDMO's TCO analysis must consider whether an RPP is truly needed or whether a PP or TP is already sufficient.

TCO Calculation Framework: RPP Total Cost of Ownership

RPP TCO = initial capital expenditure + lifecycle operating cost

Initial capital expenditure:
  + pump unit (multiple sizes) × quantity
  + CIP/SIP system (connections, valves, third drive)
  + spare pump inventory
  + installation and commissioning (FAT + SAT)
  + initial validation (IQ/OQ/PQ + SIP validation)

Lifecycle operating cost (annualized):
  + time occupied by CIP/SIP cycles (line downtime cost)
  + utilities (steam, WFI, compressed air)
  + cleaning validation maintenance cost
  + periodic SIP revalidation (temperature mapping, bioindicators)
  + operator training cost
  + parts replacement (valve seats, gaskets, servo motors)
  + if they cannot run in parallel: time lost from serial decontamination + CIP/SIP

Note: when isolator decontamination (VHP) and CIP/SIP
cannot be performed at the same time, they must be scheduled
in series, which significantly increases batch preparation
time. In a high-changeover CDMO environment this is an
important scheduling bottleneck.

Key Point: The Challenge of SIP Revalidation

SIP revalidation of the RPP is the most time-consuming of all filling technologies, because:

  • It is difficult to place thermocouples inside the cylinder, at the piston-cylinder interface, and at the upper and lower connections
  • The steam penetration of each pump head must be validated independently (multi-pump filling line = N times the workload)
  • The placement of bioindicators (such as Bacillus subtilis spores) is limited by the pump structure
  • Validation frequency: usually annually or after major equipment modification

CDMO practical advice: before purchasing equipment, confirm that the supplier can provide detailed SIP validation support documentation, and assess whether enough time can be reserved in the line validation schedule.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO is evaluating whether to buy an RPP filling line for a new high-viscosity protein client. The client's expected annual output is 50,000 vials, with 5,000 vials per batch and 10 batches per year. Which major cost items should you consider in the TCO analysis? Is a PP feasible in this scenario?
  2. If the VHP decontamination cycle of the isolator takes 4 hours and the CIP/SIP cycle of the RPP takes 3 hours, and the two cannot run in parallel, what is the minimum total batch preparation time? What does this mean for the CDMO's daily capacity scheduling?
2.2.8

Rotary Piston Pump System Complexity: Setup, Handling, and Changeover

System Complexity: Two-Drive or Three-Drive Design and Changeover Challenges

Original Text

The RPP is a two- or three-drive system — hub and rotation (two drives) with CIP/SIP positioning (common third drive) — which increases the complexity compared to TP and PP single-drive systems.

Setup associated with CIP/SIP for the RPP is more complex due to the number of connections required to ensure flow through all portions of the cylinder chamber. Additional points on setup, operation, and changeover are described in Sections 2.2.2–2.2.7.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: RPP Drive System Architecture

The mechanical complexity of the RPP stems from its need for several independent axes of motion:

  • Axis 1 - Hub drive: controls the vertical movement of the whole pump assembly (the vertical movement of the piston stroke) and determines the fill volume
  • Axis 2 - Rotation drive: controls the rotation of the cylinder, switching the inlet and outlet paths (suction → dispensing)
  • Axis 3 - CIP/SIP positioning drive (optional): moves the pump to the cleaning/sterilization position, maximizing the piston-cylinder gap to ensure CIP/SIP effectiveness

Comparison: PP and TP basically need only one drive (a motor compressing the tubing, or a solenoid valve opening and closing), so the three-axis design of the RPP is far more complex than competing technologies.

Analogy: three-drive system = a three-axis CNC machine

A CNC machine in a factory needs the X, Y and Z axes controlled in synchrony to machine a complex part. One more axis = one more degree of freedom = one more system to calibrate and maintain.

The three-drive design of the RPP is similar: every additional drive axis adds a subsystem that must be commissioned, validated, maintained and troubleshot. This shows up directly as: longer IQ/OQ/PQ validation time, more preventive maintenance items, higher technician training requirements, and more complex root cause analysis when a fault occurs.

Key Point: The Impact of Complexity on a CDMO

In a CDMO environment, the impact of system complexity is especially significant:

  • Changeover time: changing over an RPP requires dismantling more connections and verifying more components, so changeover takes significantly longer than for a PP
  • Training cost: operators and engineers need more in-depth technical training to operate an RPP independently
  • Fault diagnosis: if any one of the three drive systems has a problem, each must be checked in turn, so downtime is longer
  • Documentation requirements: calibration records, maintenance logs and abnormality records for multiple drive axes must each be managed independently

These complexity factors should all be included in the TCO calculation (the "process know-how" and "training of operators" costs).

Practice Questions

  1. An RPP filling line has 10 pump heads, each with three independent drives. In the IQ/OQ phase, how many drives do you need to verify for function? What does this mean for the validation timeline?
  2. If your CDMO needs 3 changeovers per week (3 different client products), would you lean toward an RPP or a PP? Analyze from the three angles of changeover time, cross-contamination control and operator training.
2.2.9

Rotary Piston Pump Maintenance and Aging

Maintenance and Aging: Preventive Maintenance Program and Material Management

Original Text

The additional valves that are needed as part of the CIP/SIP system will require that the valve seats be replaced periodically, along with the gaskets at the CIP/SIP connection points. Lubrication of gear boxes for drivers will be required. The arm(s) that depress(es) and withdraw(s) the pistons will also require lubrication. The pumps have a long life, but they will eventually require replacement.

Servo motors should be tested routinely to ensure proper operation and to avoid catastrophic failures that disrupt operations; replacement should be anticipated when servo motors have reached their prescribed run-time limits.

There are three main types of materials used for the RPPs: stainless steel with chromium surface treatment, ceramic and glass. If the product is reactive to stainless steel, ceramic or glass pumps can be used. Independent of the type of material of the pumps, if any defect is observed on the surface of the piston, it must be thoroughly analyzed to determine if the entire pump assembly should be taken out of service for repair or replacement.

The replacement strategy for servo motors should be provided by the OEM, with appropriate spares kept on hand to avoid unnecessary downtime.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Point: Servo Motor Management - Prevention Is Better Than Cure

The servo motor is the power source of each RPP drive axis and is also the critical part most likely to fail suddenly:

  • Planned replacement: the OEM's prescribed run-time limits for the motor are the trigger for replacement; do not wait until the motor fails
  • Spare parts inventory: keep at least one spare for each servo motor model, to avoid the long wait of emergency procurement
  • Periodic testing: at PM, test the motor's torque output, positioning accuracy and temperature, and build trend data

Why is servo motor failure "catastrophic"? A servo motor failing in the middle of filling → the filling line stops immediately → product is exposed in the sterile environment → the whole batch may have to be rejected → major financial and customer impact.

Analogy: managing piston surface defects = inspecting aircraft engine blades

At every maintenance, aviation engineers carefully inspect every scratch on the engine turbine blades, because they know that a small crack today may be the start of an engine failure tomorrow.

The management of RPP piston surfaces is exactly the same: if any defect is found (scratch, corrosion spot, deformation), the piston must not continue in use and must be sent back to the OEM for assessment. The reasoning: piston surface damage → clearance change → particle generation → reduced filling accuracy → ultimately a possible patient safety risk. In the pharmaceutical industry, the cost of "flying safely" is always worth paying.

Practice Questions

  1. Your RPP filling line has 8 pump heads, each with 3 servo motors (hub, rotation, CIP/SIP positioning), and the OEM specifies a replacement interval of 5,000 hours for each motor. Your filling line runs 2,000 hours per year. Build a 5-year motor replacement plan and state how many spare motors you need to hold.
  2. The filling line maintenance team reports a fine scratch on the piston surface of one pump head (about 2 mm long, with depth that cannot be judged visually). As the production manager, how would you make the decision? Which departments need to be involved?

Core Concept: The RPP Preventive Maintenance (PM) Checklist

The RPP has greater maintenance needs than PP and TP, but the pump body itself has a very long life:

2.2.10

Rotary Piston Pump Single-Use Versus Reusable Strategy

Single-Use vs Reusable Strategy

Original Text

RPP is not typically operated as a SUS due to system complexity and cost. Instead, pistons and cylinders may be dedicated to given products, when required.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Why Is Single-Use Almost Never Used for the RPP?

Compared with the PP (peristaltic pump, with almost 100% single-use tubing), the proportion of RPPs using a single-use strategy is extremely low, for two reasons:

  • Cost: the precision-machined piston-cylinder set costs far more to manufacture than silicone tubing. Single use would mean discarding these expensive metal parts after every batch, which is economically unfeasible.
  • Complexity: SUS requires a sterile connection interface to the drive mechanism, and the complex geometry of the RPP makes such a design extremely difficult.

Exception: some manufacturers (OEMs) do offer an SUS RPP option, but usage is very low and it is usually considered only for very special highly toxic or high-value product scenarios.

"Product-Dedicated" as an Alternative Strategy

When there is a risk of cross-contamination between products (for example highly potent biologics or highly toxic molecules) and a company does not want to perform cleaning validation of the equipment, a CDMO or pharmaceutical manufacturer can choose to:

  • Prepare a dedicated piston-cylinder set for each product (product-dedicated pistons and cylinders)
  • This set is not shared with other products, avoiding the cleaning validation burden of cross-contamination
  • Note: even with "product-dedicated" parts, CIP/SIP or thorough cleaning is still needed; only the cross-product cleaning validation is not required

Comparison with PP: "product-dedicated" for a PP only requires changing a length of silicone tubing (very low cost), whereas "product-dedicated" for an RPP requires a whole piston-cylinder set to be kept, at significantly higher cost.

Key Point: Decision Framework for SUS Selection

When evaluating whether SUS is needed, ask the following questions:

  • Does the cost of cleaning validation exceed the cost of SUS consumables? → almost never the case for an RPP
  • Is changeover time a bottleneck? Can SUS significantly shorten changeover time?
  • Does the product have extremely high residue sensitivity, such that conventional cleaning cannot reach an acceptable standard?

For most RPP application scenarios, the answer points to a strategy of "reuse + CIP/SIP + product-dedicated (when necessary)" rather than SUS.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO receives a filling order for a highly potent mAb (OEL < 1 μg/m³, high occupational exposure risk), and the client requires zero cross-contamination risk. How would you design the piston-cylinder usage strategy (SUS / product-dedicated / shared + cleaning validation)? What is your reasoning?
  2. An OEM claims that its RPP supports a single-use mode, but each piston-cylinder set costs about NT$50,000. Your batch size is 10,000 vials and you use 8 pump heads. Under a single-use strategy, what is the pump head consumable cost per batch? How would you decide compared with the cleaning validation strategy?
2.2.11

Rotary Piston Pump CIP/SIP Feasibility and Pitfalls

CIP/SIP Feasibility and Considerations: Regulatory Compliance and Multi-Product Flexibility

Original Text

CIP/SIP is feasible for an RPP that is prepared with two additional connections and the ability to flush the piston (see Figure 2.2.1-1🔍). For the two additional connections, additional valves may be required, making the CIP/SIP system more complex.

The advantage of the CIP/SIP is a multiuse dosing system over a wide range of product viscosities and less handling inside the containment barrier when the system is equipped with CIP/SIP capability, in compliance with EU regulatory guidance.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: The Three Value Propositions of CIP/SIP

An RPP equipped with CIP/SIP capability brings three key advantages:

  • 1. Multiuse: after thorough cleaning, different products can be filled, so product-dedicated equipment is no longer needed (unless there are special requirements), improving equipment utilization
  • 2. Compatibility with a wide viscosity range: the positive displacement mechanism of the RPP itself allows a broad range of applications, from low-viscosity aqueous solutions to high-viscosity concentrated proteins; together with CIP/SIP capability, it becomes the most versatile reusable filling system
  • 3. Reduced manual operations inside the sterile barrier: one of the core principles of EU GMP Annex 1 is to minimize human interventions in the sterile environment. Having CIP/SIP means operators do not need to enter the isolator or open the RABS to dismantle, clean and reinstall the pump assembly

Key Point: The EU GMP Annex 1 Compliance Perspective

EU GMP Annex 1 (2022 revision) explicitly emphasizes:

  • Sterile manufacturing should minimize human intervention as far as possible
  • Equipment design should support the implementation of the CCS (contamination control strategy)
  • Equipment designs capable of cleaning-in-place and sterilization-in-place should be preferred

Therefore, an RPP without CIP/SIP capability is difficult to defend under the EU GMP Annex 1 framework (see the Disadvantages column of Table 2.2.4-1🔍: "aseptic installation requires extensive training and is not an approach that easily fulfills EU GMP Annex 1 objectives").

For new equipment purchases, CIP/SIP capability has in effect become a regulatory requirement rather than an option.

Analogy: CIP/SIP RPP = a hospital's automated surgical instrument washer-disinfector

Modern hospitals no longer require nurses to wash and disinfect every surgical instrument by hand (which is both time-consuming and prone to human error). They use an automated washer-disinfector (CSSD): the instruments go into the machine, run through the program, and come out clean and sterile.

An RPP with CIP/SIP follows the same logic: after filling is complete, the pump does not need to be dismantled and cleaned by hand; cleaning liquid and steam pass through the designed piping and "automatically" complete the cleaning and sterilization. This greatly reduces the risk of human operating error and is consistent with the modern GMP spirit of "reducing human intervention".

CIP/SIP Design Requirements Checklist

RPP CIP/SIP design requirements:

Required:
  ✓ upper connection
  ✓ lower connection
  ✓ CIP/SIP positioning drive (third axis)
  ✓ a design that allows the piston to be flushed

May be needed (depending on design):
  ± additional valves for each pump head
  ± separate CIP liquid supply line
  ± separate SIP steam supply line

Validation requirements:
  ✓ proof of steam penetration to all surfaces
  ✓ cleaning effectiveness validation (TOC / residue analysis)
  ✓ periodic SIP revalidation (temperature mapping + BI)
  ✓ sterility assurance (microbial challenge data)

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO is replacing an old RPP filling machine (without CIP/SIP capability), and a new client's EU marketing application requires compliance with EU GMP Annex 1. Without CIP/SIP, how would you defend the current aseptic installation strategy to the regulator? Is this realistic and feasible?
  2. CIP/SIP validation needs to "prove steam penetration to all surfaces". For the upper and lower connection design of the RPP, where would you place thermocouples and bioindicators? List at least 5 challenge points.
2.2.12

Rotary Piston Pump Benefits and Risks

Benefits and Risks Summary Table (Table 2.2.12-1🔍)

Original Text

Table 2.2.12-1🔍 highlights the common benefits and risks analysis that is pertinent to the use of RPP systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concept: Interpreting the Benefits and Risks Table

This table is the distilled essence of the whole of Section 2.2, using four benefits and four risks to summarize the core characteristics of the RPP:

Benefit side:

  • "Volumetric accuracy": positive displacement → the mechanical stroke determines the volume → not affected by viscosity/temperature/pressure → high consistency from the start to the end of the batch
  • "Broad product adaptability": covers products from low viscosity to ultra-high viscosity (hundreds of thousands of mPa-s)
  • "Low maintenance": no seal wear (vs the silicone tubing of a PP), and the pump body has a long life

Risk side:

  • "Requires multiple pump sizes": the 10-fold range limit → a wide range of fill volume needs → investment in multiple sets of equipment
  • "Metal sensitivity/crystallization risk": product compatibility must be evaluated; a ceramic or glass pump may be needed
  • "High training requirements": serialized pairing, priming procedures and CIP/SIP operation all require in-depth training
  • "Complex validation": CIP/SIP validation is more time-consuming and labor-intensive than for TP and PP

Practical Application: CDMO Technology Selection Decision Tree

Based on the whole of Section 2.2, the following is the core decision logic for a CDMO selecting a filling technology for a new product:

  1. Viscosity > 60 mPa-s?
    • Yes → continue below
    • No → PP or TP may be sufficient
  2. Is the product shear-sensitive (e.g. an aggregation-prone protein)?
    • Yes → conduct a shear compatibility study and choose an RPP with caution
    • No → the RPP is the first choice for high-viscosity products
  3. Is long-run stability needed (multiple batches without resetting the dose)?
    • Yes → RPP is better than PP (no dose drift)
  4. Does the CDMO have sufficient capital investment and technical capability to support an RPP?
    • Yes → choose an RPP equipped with CIP/SIP and carry out a full TCO analysis
    • No → re-evaluate the product portfolio or consider a technology partnership

Key Point: "Low Maintenance" Needs to Be Understood Correctly

Table 2.2.12-1🔍 lists "Low maintenance" as a benefit, and this statement needs to be understood correctly:

  • Maintenance of the pump body is indeed low: with correct use the piston-cylinder set has a very long life and does not need frequent replacement like silicone tubing
  • But maintenance of the CIP/SIP system is not low: valve seats, gaskets and servo motors all have periodic replacement needs
  • "Low maintenance" is a relative concept: compared with the consumable cost of replacing the silicone tubing of a PP every batch, the parts replacement frequency of an RPP is indeed lower

This "low maintenance" should not be misread as meaning that an RPP needs almost no maintenance; in fact, an RPP needs a high-standard preventive maintenance program and a well-trained engineering team.

Practice Questions

  1. Based on Table 2.2.12-1🔍, consider the RPP advantage of "low maintenance" and the PP advantage of "low initial cost" in a CDMO scenario with 4 changeovers per month and 3 products of different viscosities filled (2 mPa-s, 50 mPa-s, 300 mPa-s). Which technology is likely to have the lower TCO? Explain your analytical logic.
  2. Table 2.2.12-1🔍 mentions "a flexible system for a wide range of product attributes". Where are the boundaries of RPP flexibility (that is, which product characteristics make the RPP no longer flexible)?

Section Summary: Section 2.2 Summary - Rotary Piston Pump

  • Working principle: positive displacement pump, piston-cylinder structure, product-lubricated, four-phase dosing cycle (suction → rotation → dispensing → return)
  • Most critical constraint: the piston-cylinder interface is "open" to the environment → the RPP must be 100% inside an isolator or RABS (unlike PP/TP/DP)
  • No dose drift: fixed mechanical stroke and no silicone tubing wear problem → statistical IPC is technically feasible (but periodic IPC is still recommended to detect bubbles)
  • CIP/SIP design: requires two additional upper and lower connections + a CIP/SIP position drive; more complex than a TP; key to EU GMP Annex 1 compliance
  • Serialized pairing: pistons and cylinders must be assembled by serial number and never mixed (ceramic is an exception); the "wedding ring principle"
  • Most expensive system: RPP + CIP/SIP has the highest TCO of all filling systems; a full TCO analysis is needed to judge whether the investment is justified
  • Three-drive system: hub + rotation + CIP/SIP positioning (2 or 3 drives), far more complex than the single-drive design of PP/TP
  • Material selection: stainless steel (standard), ceramic (abrasive/crystallizing products), glass (metal-sensitive products); ceramic is brittle and must be protected from thermal shock
  • When a CDMO should choose it: high viscosity (>60 mPa-s) + not shear-sensitive + need for long-run batch stability → the RPP is the clear choice
  • Priming-phase risk: dry-start is the moment of highest particle risk and requires a carefully designed priming SOP and waste handling

Key Comparison Table: RPP vs PP vs TP - Selection Decision Summary

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the operating principle of Time Pressure (TP) filling: how fill volume is controlled by pressure and time, its CIP/SIP advantages, and why temperature compensation is necessary
  • Master the unique closed design of the Rolling Diaphragm Pump (DP), and understand how the diaphragm isolates mechanical parts from the sterile liquid path
  • Compare TP and DP in terms of viscosity, shear, SU options, maintenance complexity and TCO, and apply the comparison to CDMO equipment selection
  • Identify the filling needle designs (open, jacketed, closing) and the product characteristics and SA considerations each suits, and understand how needle installation affects sterility assurance

2.3 Aseptic Filling Technologies: Time Pressure

Original Text

TP filling systems get their name because a slight overpressure is applied to the bulk or intermediate product vessel and a pinch valve is opened and closed for a specified time to control the flow of the product to the filling needle. The "pressure" that is applied to the bulk vessel makes use of air, inert gas, or gravity.

There are high-pressure systems where product flows through an orifice plate placed along the fluid pathway to achieve the intended accuracy. There are also low-pressure systems that operate without an orifice plate and are designed for a gentler product flow (e.g., lower shear force, lower foaming, slower). The selection of the system is best achieved through knowledge of the product attributes and the desired filling speed.

The TP dosing system has an independent control (typically a high-speed programmable logic controller (PLC)), that calculates the actual time required for filling from the current pressure and temperature. Without this independent control, a pure time control would lead to deviations in the filling accuracy when the pressure or temperature changes. Temperature fluctuation influences are greater with low-pressure systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Time Pressure: Instead of pushing the liquid with a mechanical pump, a slight positive pressure is applied to the product vessel and a pinch valve opens and closes to control the flow time precisely; dose is controlled by time × pressure = fill volume.

Orifice plate: In high-pressure systems, a flow-restricting orifice placed in the liquid path. Its precise bore ensures consistent flow rate and is one of the core components behind TP accuracy.

PLC (programmable logic controller): The "brain" of the TP system. Because fill volume is affected by temperature and pressure, the PLC senses both in real time and adjusts the fill time dynamically to compensate for any deviation.

Analogy

TP filling is like a coffee machine fed by a water tower: the tower holds a constant water pressure, you press the dispense button (open the pinch valve) and time it, and closing after a fixed time gives a fixed amount of coffee. A high-pressure system with an orifice plate is like fitting a precision nozzle at the outlet so the flow is more consistent; a low-pressure system is like removing the nozzle and letting the water out more slowly.

The PLC is the smart control module that knows "the water is a bit denser on a cold day than on yesterday's warmer one" and adjusts the dispense time automatically.

Key Notes

The biggest weakness of a TP system is its sensitivity to temperature fluctuation: long fill runs or mid-run stoppages can cause temperature drift that affects accuracy. This is why the PLC temperature compensation curve must be established during the product assessment stage.

Of the four filling technologies, TP is the one that integrates CIP/SIP most easily, and the only one that can be designed as an almost fully closed system (no direct contact between product and mechanical parts). This is critical for sterility assurance.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does a TP system need real-time PLC calculation instead of controlling fill volume with a fixed time alone?
  2. What product characteristics suit high-pressure TP and low-pressure TP respectively? How do you decide between them?
2.3.1 Time Pressure Design Configuration, Setup, and Positioning

Original Text

Figure 2.3.1-1🔍 depicts a TP filling system from the intermediate vessel to the filling needle. The TP filler may be equipped with an intermediate vessel and manifold if desired. Not shown is the proportional pressure control valve and optional orifice plate.

Note that the pressure vessel and pinch valve may be located outside of the aseptic barrier, but the risk of leaks at the pinch valves may make placement within the aseptic barrier advantageous.

Figure 2.3.1-1🔍: Diagram of a Time Pressure Filling System
[Intermediate vessel → manifold → proportional pressure valve → orifice plate → pinch valve → filling needle]

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Intermediate vessel: A buffer vessel between the bulk vessel and the filling needles. In a TP system it is held under positive pressure and distributes liquid to the filling stations through a manifold. Not every TP system needs an intermediate vessel.

Pinch valve position inside or outside the barrier: Although the pinch valve can be outside the barrier (reducing complexity in the aseptic area), the leakage risk makes installation inside the barrier better for SA. This is a classic application of "sterility assurance > operating convenience".

Key Notes

Another advantage of TP systems is system flexibility: simply changing the orifice plate, tubing and needles (few change parts) covers a very wide range of fill volumes, whereas an RPP requires replacing the whole pump set. This is very valuable for multi-product CDMO production.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: if your customer needs 0.5 mL to 50 mL of different formulations filled on the same line, a TP system only needs a different orifice plate and needles to cover the whole range, while an RPP may need the whole set of pump heads replaced. The changeover cost of TP is much lower than that of RPP.

2.3.2 Time Pressure Advantages and Disadvantages

Original Text

Table 2.3.2-1🔍 identifies the advantages and disadvantages of TP filling systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Suck back: At the end of filling, the needle quickly draws back the liquid droplet at its tip to prevent dripping. TP suck back capability is limited (simulated by closing the pinch valve rapidly), and rapid closing accelerates tubing aging; this is an inherent limitation of TP.

Why SU is not suited to TP: The pressure vessel (intermediate vessel) of a TP system must withstand positive pressure; single-use pressure-rated bags are costly and structurally more complex. PP and DP are the main SU options.

Key Notes

The core limitation of TP: low viscosity only. High-viscosity products have high flow resistance, and a TP system that relies on pressure and time cannot control them accurately. Such products should be considered first for RPP or DP.

The wear cycle of the pinch valve tubing (silicone tubing) must be risk assessed and validated, with a clear replacement schedule established; otherwise the risk of particulate contamination accumulates.

Conceptual Formula

Fill volume ≈ pressure × time × orifice factor
(Volume ∝ Pressure × Time × Orifice factor)

PLC compensation logic:
  Measure actual temperature T and pressure P
  Calculate the corrected valve opening time t_adj
  So that fill volume = target volume

Practice Questions

  1. Why are TP systems generally not suitable for SUS (Single-Use Systems)?
  2. If the temperature rises during filling (for example, an air-conditioning failure in the room), how will the TP system respond? What would the result be without PLC compensation?
2.3.3 Time Pressure Sterility Assurance: Microbial and Total Particles

Original Text

TP filling systems are typically designed for CIP/SIP. The system is fully closed, therefore, there is no risk of extraneous microbial or particulate contamination; however, exercising the pinch valve during filling may generate particles in the tubing. As a consequence, knowing the wear profile of the tubing is important to ensure the replacement of the tubing before particulate-generation can occur. Regular visual inspection is required and should be based on a risk assessment.

Small breaks in the hose, especially at the point of the pinch valve, may not be immediately identified with TP technology, although this risk is less than PP systems because there is less mechanical stress and fewer tubing connections overall. If a 100% IPC system is not in place for dose control, small breaks may go undetected for a period of time until the next statistical IPC. As a consequence, leakage could result in contamination of this "closed system." This may be problematic with potent or toxic products and may require reconsideration of the installation position to locate the mechanical components within the containment barrier.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Wear profile: A tubing life assessment curve built from actual usage data (number of fills, number of cleanings). It must be established during validation, with a mandatory replacement interval set to prevent particulate generation.

The two-sided nature of a closed system: TP is a relatively closed system, and sterility assurance is good under normal operation; but once the tubing fails, the leak itself is a contamination risk, and the system gives no warning before the failure.

Key Notes

SA decision point: When TP is used for potent/toxic products, the pinch valve must be placed inside the isolator or RABS barrier, to avoid harming operators or contaminating the environment in the event of a leak. This is a regulatory expectation, not an option.

Regular visual inspection of the tubing is a mandatory SOP item for TP systems; the inspection frequency should be determined by risk assessment and recorded in GDocP documentation.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: when a customer brings a highly potent drug (HPAPI) filling project, the first question in your TP system design assessment should be: "Is the pinch valve inside or outside the isolator?" If outside, you need to assess whether equipment modification is required before the contract is signed, as this directly affects the quotation and lead time. Sterility assurance always comes first.

2.3.4 Time Pressure Efficiency and Impact on Risk

Original Text

The TP filling system is a high-precision dosing system that depends on the flow behavior. The flow is influenced by temperature and pressure inside the intermediate vessel, which is the reason for the high-speed PLC controller. Changes in temperature, such as during long fill operations or during interruptions in filling, should be avoided.

Even though the system is highly accurate, a periodic IPC is recommended to detect underfills due to possible air bubbles within the tubing over time (which can be exacerbated by the mandatory use of over pressure to control filling) (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4). Therefore, an appropriate rationale should be developed for the timing and frequency of the IPC that reflects the attributes of the product being filled and real-world data, when available.

TP systems are routinely CIP/SIP-capable, as a result there is a limited risk of contamination impacting the filling operation during the setup of the system. Containment is also simplified with TP filler for highly potent products if the pinch valves are placed within the isolator. Hose breakage with TP fillers is a greater risk than with other filling systems due to the stressors placed on the hoses within the pinch valves, though the stressors on the tubing are less than with PPs. Detection systems for leaks can be placed within the isolator to alert if a breach in tubing occurs.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Notes

Air bubbles are the hidden killer of TP accuracy: A positive-pressure system may carry trace air into the tubing, and a bubble passing through the filling needle causes an underfill. This is the fundamental reason why, even with high accuracy, TP still requires periodic IPC (statistical weight checks).

The temperature recovery period after long fill runs or production interruptions is a high-risk window for TP accuracy, and should be controlled by SOP in the process design (for example, after an interruption, wait for the temperature to stabilize and confirm with an IPC).

Key Concepts

Risk assessment of IPC frequency: The IPC frequency of a TP system should be set according to the product's flow characteristics (viscosity, surface tension) and historical filling data, with the rationale documented. Too frequent increases cost; too sparse increases the risk of missed underfills. This is a typical application of QRM (quality risk management).

Practice Questions

  1. Why might using positive pressure (overpressure) in a TP system actually aggravate the air bubble problem? How can the system design reduce this risk?
  2. How should the IPC frequency of a TP system be determined? What are the key factors affecting the decision?
2.3.5 Time Pressure Costs: Initial and Lifecycle

Original Text

The initial cost of a TP dosing system is similar to a PP or RPP for the system itself (excluding CIP/SIP that may or may not be present). The initial capital cost of a CIP/SIP is high, but comparable to the lifecycle costs associated with the SUS, such as recurring expense of the disposables with the PP.

TCO calculations would need to include setup, operation, and CIP/SIP as appropriate to the system design. Examples of considerations for the TCO calculations may include, but are not limited to, time, utilities, cleaning validation, maintenance, process know-how, training of operators, downtime due to CIP/SIP cycles, and extended times in cases where parallel processing is not possible (such as not being able to run the biodecontamination cycle simultaneously with the CIP/SIP).

If multiple fill-volumes are required, additional filling-size parts consisting of orifice, tubing, and a filling needle are necessary.

Lifecycle costs are negligible because the drives have a long lifespan. If dedicated equipment is necessary, for example, at a contract manufacturing organization, changing the intermediate vessel and piping may be difficult, but would be required in addition to the format-size parts (e.g., orifice, tubing, needles).

Tutorial Commentary

Formula and Calculation: TCO Framework

TP system TCO =
  Initial capital cost (equipment + CIP/SIP)
  + Validation cost (cleaning validation, SIP validation)
  + Annual operating cost (tubing consumables, calibration)
  + CIP/SIP downtime cost (cycle time per run × batch opportunity cost)
  + Changeover time (orifice + needle replacement)
  + Personnel training cost

vs. PP + SUS:
  Low initial cost + high ongoing consumable cost (per batch)

Conclusion: for high volume / many batches, TP CIP/SIP is more economical

Key Notes

The changeover cost of TP is very low: only the orifice plate, tubing and needles need replacing, usually completed within a few tens of minutes. This is an important advantage for multi-product, small-batch CDMO production, as it shortens equipment occupation time and raises line utilization.

Note that biodecontamination and CIP/SIP cannot be carried out at the same time: in an isolator environment the two cycles must run one after the other, which significantly increases batch-to-batch turnaround time and must be built into the production plan.

2.3.6–2.3.10 TP System Complexity, Maintenance, SU, CIP/SIP & Benefits/Risks

Original Text

2.3.6 Time Pressure System Complexity: Setup, Handling, and Changeover

The system design and fluid pathway are simple and straightforward with the TP; however, a fast PLC must calculate the temperature and pressure in real time as provided by sensors. The temperature compensation requires a curve for filling each product at different product temperatures. This product-dependent fill-curve must be established during product evaluation so that the system is able to fill with high accuracy.

Setup is simple; such format parts as the orifice, tubing, and needle must be changed, but they are typically assembled prior to CIP/SIP.

2.3.7 Time Pressure Maintenance and Aging

The pinch valves represent the only moving part of the dosing system requiring routine maintenance. A replacement strategy of pinch-valve motors should be provided by the OEM to avoid unnecessary downtimes or potential loss of batches. Sensors for temperature and pressure must be calibrated.

The system has limited wear-parts, other than the tubing. Sensors for temperature and pressure may require replacement over time. Because the system is subjected to overpressure, the gaskets and pressure relief valve will require periodic replacement.

2.3.8 Time Pressure Single-Use Versus Reusable Strategy

Usually, a TP dosing system is not suitable as a SUS due to the expense of the pressure-rated intermediate vessel and fluid path. As a consequence, most systems are reusable and will require cleaning as well as sterilization validation.

2.3.9 Time Pressure Clean-In-Place/Sterilize-In-Place Feasibility and Pitfalls

The TP dosing system is well suited for CIP/SIP, which is the typical design standard. There is limited changeover required between different filling volumes and products. When performing CIP/SIP, there is a small risk that the orifice will become obstructed, especially after the silicone tubing has been replaced. Typically, prior to the start of the CIP/SIP, a leak test will be performed, but this test will not confirm that the orifice is not obstructed. Therefore, the CIP/SIP process should be monitored to ensure no obstruction, as the sensor for conductivity and temperature are located at the combined exit flow from the needles.

2.3.10 Time Pressure Benefits and Risks

Table 2.3.10-1🔍 highlights the common benefits and risks analysis that is pertinent to the use of TP filling systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Temperature compensation curve: For each product, fill volumes are tested in advance at different temperatures and a correction factor curve is built. This is one of the key deliverables of a TP system at tech transfer and must be completed during the product assessment stage.

Orifice obstruction: After silicone tubing is replaced, a cut end that is not aligned may partially block the orifice. This small detail can make an entire CIP/SIP cycle ineffective, because the cleaning fluid cannot flow through adequately and the monitoring sensor is on the outlet side (so it cannot tell which orifice is blocked). An additional verification step is needed after tubing replacement.

Key Notes

The maintenance simplicity of TP systems is one of their biggest commercial advantages: the only moving part is the pinch valve. The gasket and pressure relief valve of the pressure vessel also need regular replacement, but these are standard consumables, low in cost and predictable.

For low-temperature filling products that need active cooling (such as protein biologics), any uncooled exposed section of the TP liquid path can cause a local temperature rise and affect fill accuracy. This is a CPP that must be considered in system design.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the TP system the one that integrates CIP/SIP "most easily" of the four filling technologies? Which structural feature makes it superior to RPP?
  2. If you were building a new TP filling line at a CDMO, what preventive maintenance plan would you ask the OEM to provide? List at least 3 key items.
2.4 Aseptic Filling Technologies: Rolling Diaphragm Pump

Original Text

The rolling diaphragm pump (DP) is a positive displacement pump, which generally incorporates a piston-driven pump unit that includes a piston, a fluid chamber, and a body (see Figure 2.4-1🔍). The pump unit is used, in combination with timed pinch valves, to direct fluid travel through the pump chamber and the tubing.

In the case of the rolling diaphragm pump, a rolling diaphragm is used to separate the piston drive unit from the fluid chamber. This is to eliminate small but undesirable particulate contamination generated by piston and cylinder friction. In addition, the diaphragm totally separates the mechanical action of the piston and cylinder from the fluid pathway, making it a closed system.

Figure 2.4-1🔍: External and Cut-Away Views of a Rolling Diaphragm Pump
[Piston drive unit | Rolling diaphragm (separator) | Fluid chamber | Pinch valves at inlet/outlet]

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Positive displacement pump: Delivers a fixed volume of liquid per stroke, relatively independent of flow pressure, giving high dosing accuracy. The DP pushes a rolling diaphragm with a piston to deliver a precise volume, and belongs to this category.

Rolling diaphragm: The core innovation of the DP. The diaphragm rolls like a glove being turned inside out, fully isolating the piston mechanics from the liquid-contact surface, so there is no metal friction in the liquid path, particulate risk is very low, and the system stays closed.

Role of the pinch valve: The DP uses pinch valves to control inlet and outlet flow direction (unlike the RPP, which switches inlet and outlet by piston position). This makes the DP structurally simpler and easier to clean.

Analogy

Think of squeezing toothpaste: your hand (the piston) pushes the toothpaste (the liquid), and the tube (the rolling diaphragm) fully isolates your hand from the contents. However dirty your hand is, the toothpaste stays clean. This is the design philosophy of the DP: mechanical force is transmitted through the diaphragm, but the mechanical parts never touch the product.

By contrast, an RPP is like pushing a piston straight into the liquid to stir it: accurate, but with concerns about friction particles and shear.

Key Notes

The core SA advantage of the DP: a fully closed fluid path, so mechanical friction particles cannot enter the product. It is the positive displacement system with the lowest particulate risk of the four filling technologies. This is critical for compliance with particulate matter requirements for injectables.

2.4.1 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Design Configuration

Original Text

The use of a rolling diaphragm provides a number of advantages when used in a positive displacement pump. The rolling diaphragm provides a leak-proof seal for the fluid within the pump, separating the fluid pathway from the mechanical components. It also ensures gentle handling of the fluid to be delivered by minimizing the shearing of molecules within the pump head that may otherwise occur using a product-contact piston drive unit to drive the liquid.

The pump includes a pneumatic port, providing an outlet for a vacuum connection that controls withdrawal of the piston drive unit, leading to high dosing accuracy. This vacuum source accomplishes the additional function of placing proper differential pressure across the diaphragm to hold it firmly in position.
