This feature makes the mechanical pump actuation system extremely repeatable by not using a push-pull linkage.

Figure 2.4.1-1🔍 depicts the cut-away image of a DP stroke from suction to discharge. The DP suction and discharge are controlled by pinch valves (unlike the RPP, which makes use of the configuration of the piston to alternately block and expose the respective ports).

Figure 2.4.1-1🔍: Progression Images of a Rolling Diaphragm Pump Stroke
[Suction phase: inlet pinch open, outlet pinch closed, diaphragm expands → Discharge phase: inlet pinch closed, outlet pinch open, diaphragm compresses]

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The dual function of vacuum control:

  • Function 1: It controls the piston return stroke (suction phase); vacuum pulls the piston back rather than a mechanical push-pull, giving very high repeatability.
  • Function 2: It maintains a suitable differential pressure across the diaphragm to prevent diaphragm displacement or wrinkling, ensuring the diaphragm stays in close contact with the piston.

These two functions together explain why the DP cannot be operated without a vacuum supply: without vacuum, the diaphragm loses its positioning, fill accuracy is immediately compromised, and the diaphragm may even be damaged.

Key Notes

Key operating warning: If the piston moves accidentally while the DP is installed but not yet connected to vacuum (for example, while being carried from the preparation area to the filling line), the diaphragm will wrinkle, leading to inconsistent stroke and reduced fill accuracy.

This means training and SOPs must explicitly specify the piston protection measures during DP transport, and the verification step after installation and before connecting vacuum.

Practice Questions

  1. Why must the piston of a DP not be moved without a vacuum connection? What two roles does vacuum play in a DP?
  2. What is the fundamental difference between the DP and the RPP in the mechanism that controls the suction/discharge direction?
2.4.2 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Setup and System Positioning

Original Text

With the DP system, product can be fed directly from a pressurized supply vessel via manifold to the rolling diaphragm pumps. Alternatively, the pressurized supply vessel may feed an intermediate vessel or bag that uses gravity feed to supply the product to the manifold and then to the rolling DPs.

Figure 2.4.2-1🔍 depicts a possible configuration for the DP fluid pathway. Notably, the pumps are depicted within the aseptic barrier, but installation outside of the barrier is possible and may be preferable.

Figure 2.4.2-1🔍: Fluid Pathway for Rolling Diaphragm Pump Systems
[Bulk vessel → (pressurized) → manifold → rolling DP pumps → filling needles. Pumps shown inside aseptic barrier; external installation also feasible.]

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The SA logic of installing the pump outside the barrier: The DP liquid path is fully closed (closed fluid path) and the mechanical parts are on the outer side of the diaphragm, so the pump body can be installed outside the isolator, leaving only the filling needles and the last section of the liquid path in the aseptic area. This is an important SA advantage of the DP over the RPP: moving mechanical parts outside reduces complexity and sources of disturbance in the aseptic area.

Practical Application

CDMO design consideration: installing the DP pump body outside the isolator significantly reduces maintenance complexity in the aseptic area (pump servicing does not require entering the aseptic area) without affecting SA (because the liquid path is closed). It also makes routine pump maintenance and PM (preventive maintenance) easier to perform and reduces the need for operators to enter the aseptic area, in line with the spirit of minimizing personnel interventions in EU GMP Annex 1.

2.4.3 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Advantages and Disadvantages

Original Text

Table 2.4.3-1🔍 identifies the advantages and disadvantages of rolling DPs.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Temperature insensitivity of the DP vs temperature sensitivity of TP: As a positive displacement system, the DP delivers a fixed physical volume per stroke, unaffected by liquid temperature (the effect of small density changes is negligible). This contrasts sharply with TP, whose flow is directly affected by temperature and must be compensated by the PLC in real time. For long fill runs or products with a risk of temperature fluctuation, DP accuracy is more stable.

10-fold range: The stroke of each DP pump is adjustable, usually covering 1/10 to 10 times the target volume. Beyond this range a pump of a different size is needed, unlike TP, where only the orifice plate needs replacing.

Key Notes

SU feasibility is an important difference of the DP versus the RPP: some vendors offer an SU DP in which the whole liquid path (from connector to filling needle) is pre-assembled and pre-sterilized, greatly reducing the complexity of aseptic installation and the training needed. This makes the DP one of the few positive displacement pump technologies that support both the traditional CIP/SIP and SU strategies.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the fill accuracy of the DP "highly insensitive" to temperature change while TP is the opposite? Explain from the physical principle.
  2. When a customer requires several formats from 1 mL to 20 mL, how does the changeover procedure of a DP system differ from that of a TP system? What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?
2.4.4 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Sterility Assurance: Microbial and Total Particles

Original Text

Due to the rolling diaphragm separating the fluid chamber from the piston drive, product is contained within a leak-proof chamber without risk of particle contamination from friction wear of the piston or microbial contamination from extraneous sources. Several methods are available to ensure SA following use. Rolling DPs are designed to be easily cleanable and are easy to assemble prior to sterilization. CIP/SIP designs, as well as presterilized, aseptically installed options are available, as are SU presterilized designs.

Small breaks in the diaphragm or tubing could result in a breach of the "closed" sterile fluid pathway, although the system will remain under negative pressure (vacuum), which minimizes the risk of microbial and particulate ingress. In order to detect any potential leak, best practice is to add a moisture-sensor on the vacuum line to detect such a breach so that it can be addressed immediately.

Even with the sensor in place, should the closed system be breached, this condition may be problematic for highly potent or toxic products, which require containment. As a consequence, the installation position of the pump should be reconsidered to locate the mechanical components within the containment barrier. Since the diaphragm is a wear-part, this risk of a breach reinforces the importance of monitoring the number of use-cycles for the diaphragm and replacing it before the point of failure.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Negative pressure as a passive protective barrier: A DP system runs under vacuum, so if the diaphragm or tubing is slightly damaged, outside air may be drawn in (rather than liquid leaking out). This actually reduces the risk of the product contaminating the environment, but introduces the risk of outside air (carrying microorganisms and particles) entering the liquid path, so a moisture sensor is needed for monitoring.

Moisture sensor on the vacuum line: When the diaphragm ruptures, liquid enters the vacuum line, and the moisture sensor detects this change and alarms immediately. This is the best practice for SA monitoring of DP systems.

Key Notes

Diaphragm life management is key to SA: The diaphragm is a wear part; its use-cycles must be tracked and it must be replaced before the vendor's recommended limit is reached. This is not optional but an SA requirement. It is recommended to set up a diaphragm cycle counter in the electronic batch record (eBR) with automatic alerts.

For highly toxic/potent products: the pump body should be installed in a sealed container or containment enclosure; even with a moisture sensor, product contact with the outside environment on diaphragm failure still needs to be controlled. This is an operator protection (OEB/OEL) compliance requirement.

Practice Questions

  1. A DP system runs under vacuum; if the diaphragm fails, in which direction does the risk run (liquid leaking out, or outside contamination entering the liquid)? What are the consequences of each case?
  2. How would you design a diaphragm life management procedure in an SOP? What key tracking elements should it include?
2.4.5 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Efficiency and Impact on Risk

Original Text

The rolling DP is a high-precision dosing system with stable accuracy throughout the filling process. Even with high accuracy, an IPC is recommended when using rolling DPs to detect any underfills. However, as a volumetric dosing system, 100% IPC is not commonly employed; instead, a statistical IPC is performed (see Sections 5.1–5.1.4).

Once properly trained in assembly and installation of rolling DPs, the associated risk is low, as no direct contact with the product or product-contacts parts occurs during production. However, aseptic assembly requires training and represents the highest risk when using the pump. To significantly reduce this risk, CIP/SIP or SU execution should be implemented.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

"The highest risk occurs outside production, not during it": During actual filling, the risk of a DP system is very low (closed system, no personnel intervention needed). But aseptic assembly, the step of connecting the sterilized components in a clean environment, is the highest-risk point in the whole process. CIP/SIP or SU designs exist precisely to eliminate or reduce this high-risk step.

Key Notes

The rationale for choosing statistical IPC rather than 100% IPC for the DP: a positive displacement pump delivers a highly consistent volume per stroke with minimal batch-to-batch drift, so statistical sampling is sufficient to ensure dose compliance. Even so, IPC is still necessary: even with a highly accurate system, abnormalities such as equipment failure and air bubbles still need to be detected by IPC.

2.4.6 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Costs: Initial and Lifecycle

Original Text

Initial costs are comparable to initial investment costs for other systems for dedicated fill volumes. When multiple fill-volumes are required, additional pump sizes are commonly necessary, which can add to system cost. Lifecycle costs can be negligible because the pumps have a long lifespan, provided they are well maintained and protected from damage. Diaphragms can be cleaned or replaced between batches, based on user requirements defined in site SOPs.

Rolling DPs equipped with CIP/SIP have added costs. The CIP/SIP infrastructure systems drive much of the increase in costs; however, CIP/SIP-capable pumps have additional configurations and connections for the cleaning and sterilization media-flow as well as proper media-draining.

If SUS that use disposable rolling DPs are implemented, the costs for SU are high and can be compared to initial and ongoing costs of a CIP/SIP system operation and maintenance. This is often driven by total costs of ownership (TCO) calculations. TCO calculations for a CIP/SIP-capable system would need to include setup, operation, and CIP/SIP as appropriate to the system design. Examples of considerations for the TCO calculations may include, but are not limited to, time, utilities, cleaning validation, maintenance, process know-how, training of operators, downtime due to CIP/SIP cycles, and extended times in cases where parallel processing is not possible.

Tutorial Commentary

Formula and Calculation: TCO Comparison Framework

Reusable DP + CIP/SIP TCO:
  High initial cost (pump body + CIP/SIP infrastructure)
  + Validation cost (cleaning + SIP validation)
  + Low consumable cost (only tubing, diaphragms, seals)
  + CIP/SIP cycle downtime cost
  → Most economical at high batch volumes

DP SU TCO:
  Low initial cost (no CIP/SIP infrastructure)
  + High ongoing consumable cost (whole liquid path per batch)
  + Low downtime cost (swap the set and run)
  → Advantageous for low batch volumes / high flexibility needs

Decision trigger: annual batch number is the key variable
Typically >50 batches/year → CIP/SIP more economical
<20 batches/year → SU may be more economical

Key Notes

For a CDMO, the advantage of a DP SU system is fast product changeover (dispose and replace) and a greatly reduced cleaning validation workload, which is very attractive for the small-batch, multi-product CDMO business model. However, the per-batch consumable cost must be clearly communicated to the customer and built into the quotation model.

2.4.7–2.4.11 DP Complexity, Maintenance, SU, CIP/SIP & Benefits/Risks

Original Text

2.4.7 Rolling Diaphragm Pump System Complexity: Setup, Handling, and Changeover

DP is a two-drive system for piston actuation and actuation of the pinch valve. The system design and fluid pathway are simple and straightforward; however, it requires proper training for pump assembly and aseptic installation (when not CIP/SIP-capable). When assembled and not connected to vacuum supply (e.g., during transport to the line, during setup), any inadvertent movement of the piston without vacuum could result in diaphragm displacement (wrinkling) that can alter piston movement and affect dosing accuracy.

For CIP/SIP-configured rolling DPs, installation is different, but not significantly more complex. Rather, the primary difference is that pumps, which are normally installed vertically, are required to be installed horizontally to ensure proper draining after CIP/SIP.

2.4.8 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Maintenance and Aging

Rolling DPs are precisely machined to critical tolerances and must be handled gently to prevent damage and ensure accurate fills. Reusable rolling DPs are constructed of stainless steel; if any defect is observed on the pump, it must be thoroughly inspected to determine if a repair or replacement action is required to the entire pump assembly.

Diaphragms can be cleaned and reused or replaced after each batch, depending on user requirements. Vacuum seal and diaphragms are wear-parts that can be expected to be replaced regularly. A replacement strategy for servo motors should be provided by the OEM to avoid unnecessary downtimes or potential loss of batches.

2.4.9 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Single-Use Versus Reusable Strategy

The SU application of rolling DPs is gaining adoption and is available from some OEMs. All elements of the fluid path (from aseptic connector to the product vessel through intermediate product bag, manifold, pump, tubing, and filling needle) are preassembled, disposable, and easy to set up and change over, but they need to be considered as consumable costs associated with the system.

Reusable systems bring added risks to the process as offline cleaning and sterilization introduces added complexity since the validation for pumps and needles requires additional time, costs, and paperwork. Aseptic connections made for parts that come into direct contact with product should be sterilized in place, if possible; therefore, a rolling DP configured for CIP/SIP (or SU-presterilized) is recommended for future system designs (3, 6).

TCO calculations for both applications need to be evaluated according to user protocols prior to selecting a configuration.

2.4.10 Rolling Diaphragm Pump CIP/SIP Feasibility and Pitfalls

CIP/SIP is well-suited for rolling DPs, with an established design standard for tubing attachment (compression fitting vs. barbed fitting) and a horizontal setup for proper draining of the cleaning media. Due to the altered orientation of the CIP/SIP pump within the filler, proper care should be taken to design with cleanroom or isolator airflow in mind. The advantage with the CIP/SIP configuration is less handling and reduced aseptic installation complexity (3, 6).

2.4.11 Rolling Diaphragm Pump Benefits and Risks

Table 2.4.11-1🔍 highlights the common benefits and risks analysis that is pertinent to the use of rolling DP systems.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Notes

The importance of horizontal orientation: A DP is normally installed vertically in use, but a CIP/SIP design requires horizontal installation to ensure cleaning fluid and steam drain completely (drainage). This seemingly minor engineering decision affects the feasibility of the entire cleaning validation, so it must be confirmed at the start of the design.

Decision matrix for the three configuration strategies:

  • Offline cleaning then installation (old approach): most burdensome validation, highest SA risk; suitable for small/early-stage sites
  • Reusable CIP/SIP (recommended standard): high initial cost, but best SA and lowest long-term TCO
  • Pre-sterilized SU (new trend): high consumable cost, but fastest changeover; suitable for small-batch, multi-product CDMOs
Regulatory trend: EU GMP Annex 1 explicitly encourages CIP/SIP or SU and discourages traditional offline aseptic assembly.

Key Concepts

Compression fitting vs. barbed fitting: Two ways of connecting tubing. A compression fitting seals better and suits the high-pressure CIP/SIP environment; a barbed fitting installs faster but has a lower sealing grade. The design standard for a CIP/SIP DP should specify which to use, as part of the equipment specification (URS/DQ).

Practical Application

Recommendation for a new CDMO line design: if the future customer portfolio is mainly biologics (low viscosity, shear sensitive), the low shear and SU option of the DP make it the first choice. If large batches and few products are expected, investing in a CIP/SIP DP gives the best TCO; if customers are diverse and batches small, the flexibility and changeover efficiency of an SU DP are more competitive.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the CIP/SIP version of the DP need horizontal rather than vertical installation? What effect does this change have on the airflow design of the aseptic area?
  2. A CDMO is evaluating whether to invest in a DP CIP/SIP system (vs continuing with a DP SU system). List at least 5 key cost items that should be included in the TCO calculation.
3.0 Filling Needle Designs

Original Text

Filling needles can be customized to specific applications. The intent of the various designs is to provide greater control over the filling (e.g., to prevent splashing, prevent foaming, control dripping, aid in filling highly viscous products). The major needle designs are described in Table 3.0-1🔍 and are depicted in the images that follow the table. Innovations in needle design continue to be made and variations are possible.

When selecting a filling needle design, consider that the:

  • Filling needle should be easy to install in the right position with a tight connection to prevent movement (and the potential for splashing); installation into the needle holder is often required to be performed either with automation or with sterilized implements (e.g., forceps). Regardless of the approach to installation the design should facilitate installation without risk of contamination.
  • Needle holders should be designed to affix needles in a manner that stabilizes needles with a tight fit and prevents risk of damage such as bending during operation.
  • Needle holders, and any fixtures between the source of first air and critical operations, should be as minimal as possible, not be a source of particle generation, facilitate easy cleaning, sterilization and/or decontamination, and be designed to minimize turbulence.
  • Flexible tubing used at the filling needle connection, directly above critical operations must be minimized due to the risk that flexible materials could release particles over time due to motion during the filling process.
  • Flexible tubing should be selected to permit any necessary equipment motion; the unsupported length should be minimized to prevent sagging, bending, pinching, or any restriction of flow.

Needles should be selected to be compatible with the filling curve (e.g., synchronized needle motion and fluid start, acceleration, stop, liquid retraction when available). The filling curve is selected for the specific formulation with consideration of the distance from the surface of the liquid (taking into account the meniscus that forms based on the diameter of the vial and the surface tension of the specific formulation). When an appropriate filling curve has been identified, there should be no (limited or reduced) splashing, foaming or dripping of the product, which can cause some types of filling rejects.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

First air: The clean airflow coming straight from the HEPA filter before it has touched any surface. Critical operations (such as the filling needle-container opening area) must always be exposed to first air coverage, and any obstruction (such as an oversized needle holder) interferes with this protection. Minimizing the needle holder design is based on exactly this principle.

Filling curve: Describes the synchronization of filling needle movement and liquid flow over time, including the precise timing of needle insertion speed, when liquid starts to flow, acceleration, deceleration, stop and liquid retraction. Different formulations (with different surface tension and viscosity) need different filling curves.

Meniscus: The curved liquid surface formed in a container by surface tension. During filling, the distance between the needle and the meniscus is key to avoiding splash: too high and the liquid splashes, too low and the needle may dip into the product.

Analogy

Choosing a filling needle is like choosing a milk-frothing nozzle for latte art: when pouring the foam (i.e. filling) you have to consider the milk viscosity, the cup size (container), and the pouring angle and speed (filling curve). Different nozzles (needle types) let you control where and how fast the foam lands: a wide nozzle is fast but may splash, a fine nozzle is slow but precise.

Key Notes

Needle installation from an SA perspective: Needles must be installed with sterilized tools (such as sterile forceps) or automated equipment, avoiding bare-hand contact; this is a basic requirement of aseptic operation. Needle installation is a typical high-risk intervention and should be included in the scope of the APS (aseptic process simulation) assessment.

The principle of minimizing the length of flexible tubing at the needle connection is not only a matter of mechanical stability but also of SA: tubing movement can generate particles, and particles may settle into open containers in the HEPA airflow.

3.0 Filling Needle Design Types — 🔍 Table 3.0-1🔍

Original Text

Open Needle Designs

Jacketed Needle Designs

Closing Needle Designs

Figures 3.0-1, 3.0-2, and 3.0-3
Figure 3.0-1🔍: Open Needle Designs (Cylindrical, Basket, Crimped, Cut/Fluted, Slotted)
Figure 3.0-2🔍: Jacketed Needle Configuration (inner filling needle + outer gas jacket)
Figure 3.0-3🔍: Inside Closing Needle Schematic and Cutaway

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts: Needle Selection Logic

The core driver of needle selection is product characteristics (decision hierarchy level 2: Product CQAs). In detail:

  • Low surface tension products (prone to dripping): → Basket, Slotted or Crimped needles (increase surface tension at the outlet to stop droplets detaching)
  • High viscosity products: → Closing needle (actively cuts off the liquid flow)
  • Oxygen-sensitive products requiring gas protection (such as protein biologics): → Jacketed gassing needle (fill + inert gas blanketing at the same time)
  • High-speed filling / large volume: → Cut/Fluted needle (larger outlet cross-section, lower impact velocity)
  • SU systems: → Cylindrical or Single-Use needles (simple structure, easy to sterilize)

Key Notes

The CIP/SIP limitation of the jacketed needle is an important SA consideration: Jacketed needles cannot be cleaned with standard CIP/SIP and must be disassembled and cleaned for every batch, increasing the complexity and SA risk of aseptic assembly. If the product needs oxygen protection, this validation workload must be planned at equipment selection.

Why the closing needle is rare in aseptic operations: The complex geometry of a pneumatic valve with a central plunger makes CIP/SIP validation extremely difficult: it is hard to demonstrate that steam reaches every dead leg. Under the SA-first principle, the risk of failing a complex CIP/SIP validation is unacceptable, so closing needles are seldom used in aseptic filling.

The design wisdom of "fail open": The closing needle defaults to open when there is no air pressure, ensuring cleaning fluid can flow freely during CIP/SIP rather than being stuck in a closed state and creating a cleaning blind spot. This is engineering design thinking that puts SA first.

Analogy

Needle design is like a bartender choosing how to pour:

  • Cylindrical → pour straight from the bottle mouth (simplest, suits most drinks)
  • Basket/Slotted → use a forked spout (prevents drips of precious spirits)
  • Crimped → use a fine-spout pitcher for precise thin streams (suits high-proof, low surface tension spirits)
  • Cut/Fluted → use a bevel-cut spout so the liquid slides down the glass wall (fast with low impact)
  • Jacketed → double-walled tube: the inner tube pours the wine while the outer tube simultaneously fills N₂ for protection (oxygen-sensitive premium wine)
  • Closing → precision shut-off valve (extremely viscous honey or syrup)

Practice Questions

  1. A customer's formulation is a low surface tension protein solution (prone to foaming and dripping) that is also oxygen sensitive. Which needle design should be chosen? What is the rationale? What SA challenges are possible?
  2. Why is the closing needle so rare in aseptic filling? Explain the fundamental challenge of this design from the CIP/SIP validation perspective.
  3. From the perspective of first air coverage and SA, what are the important principles for the design of the needle holder?

Section Summary

  • Time Pressure (TP): Controls filling by pressure and time; best suited to CIP/SIP, with the simplest equipment (the only moving part is the pinch valve). Disadvantages: temperature sensitivity (needs real-time PLC compensation), unsuitability for high viscosity and SU, and limited suck back capability. Its wide range is achieved by changing the orifice plate rather than the pump, making it the preferred option for CDMO multi-product changeover.
  • Rolling Diaphragm Pump (DP): The rolling diaphragm fully isolates the mechanical parts from the liquid path, making it the positive displacement pump with the lowest particulate risk among closed systems; its accuracy is insensitive to temperature and it is friendly to shear-sensitive biologics. The three configurations (offline / CIP/SIP / SU) give maximum flexibility. Core risks: the diaphragm is a consumable whose use-cycles must be tracked, and the pump cannot run if the vacuum supply is interrupted.
  • Reinforcing the decision hierarchy: The needle installation method (forceps/automation), the position of the pinch valve inside or outside the barrier, and the location of the DP pump body: every design decision puts sterility assurance (SA) first, product CQAs second, and operating convenience last.
  • Needle design by product characteristic: low surface tension → Basket/Slotted/Crimped; high viscosity → Closing; O₂ sensitive → Jacketed; high speed and large volume → Cut/Fluted; SU systems → Cylindrical. Needle geometric complexity correlates positively with the difficulty of CIP/SIP validation: the more complex the design, the greater the SA validation workload.
  • TCO perspective: The consumable costs of TP and DP (tubing, diaphragms, orifice plates) are lower than the SU consumables of PP; but the infrastructure cost and downtime of CIP/SIP must be included in the TCO calculation and compared with the SU strategy, with the assessment completed under the user requirements framework before the decision is made.
4A

Section 4A: Functionality I

p71-p86

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p71 – p80

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the structure of Table 4.0-1🔍: how a "functionality requirements" matrix is used to evaluate the suitability of the four filling pump types
  • Understand what continuous/campaign filling demands of equipment design and of the number of aseptic connections
  • Compare the four pump types in terms of changeover speed and filling speed
  • Learn the engineering measures for foam prevention and drip control, and their impact on CQAs
  • Build a decision framework of "functionality → pump selection → sterility assurance"

Section Overview

4.0 Table Overview 4.1 Continuous/Campaign Filling 4.2 Speed of Setup/Changeover 4.3 Speed of Filling vs. Control 4.4 Foam Prevention 4.4 Drip Control
4.0 Table 4.0-1🔍: Functionality Requirements Overview 🔍

Original Text

Table 4.0-1🔍 presents the Functionality Requirements and their influence on liquid filling system selection. The table evaluates four pump technologies across a range of operational considerations:

  • Peristaltic Pump (PP)
  • Rotary Piston Pump (RPP)
  • Time Pressure (TP)
  • Diaphragm Pump (DP)

Each row in the table addresses a specific Consideration and lists the relevant Critical Attributes / Enablers — the measurable or design features that determine how well each pump technology meets the requirement.

The considerations evaluated across Sections 4.0–4.10 include:

  • Continuous Filling / Campaign Filling Operations vs. Batch Filling
  • Speed of Setup / Changeover
  • Speed of Filling vs. Control Aspects
  • Foam Prevention
  • Drip Control
  • Need to Maintain Homogeneity in Filling Loop and Filling Vessel
  • Need to Control Product Temperature During Filling
  • For Large Batches, Mechanisms to Supply the Product to the Filler
  • Head Space Management / Head Space Replacement
"Functionality requirements define the operational envelope within which a filling system must perform — they translate product and process needs into concrete engineering specifications."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Functionality Requirements Matrix: Table 4.0-1🔍 is essentially a "selection decision tool". It translates abstract process needs (such as "long continuous filling runs") into concrete engineering evaluation criteria, then compares the characteristics of the four pump types against each one. This structured comparison is an expression of Quality by Design (QbD) thinking.

Critical Attributes / Enablers: The "quantifiable characteristics" or "design features" listed under each consideration, for example "revolutions per minute", "number of aseptic connections" or "CIP/SIP support". They are the bridge language between a requirement and an equipment specification.

Analogy

Think of this table as the purchasing matrix a restaurant uses when selecting kitchen equipment: the rows are requirements (such as "can it cook at high temperature", "ease of cleaning", "capacity") and the columns are equipment from different brands, with each cell recording how that unit performs. Selection is not about which unit is the "strongest", but which best fits the specific menu of your restaurant.

Key Notes

Reconfirming the decision hierarchy: When using this matrix, keep the order of priority in mind:

  • Sterility assurance always comes first
  • Functionality (speed, flexibility, capacity) comes second
  • Commercial cost considerations come last

If a pump performs very well on "speed" in the matrix but increases the number of aseptic connections (aseptic risk points), the risk must be evaluated first, before the speed advantage is considered.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does PDA use a "functionality requirements matrix" rather than simply recommending one pump type? What does this mean for a CDMO?
  2. What role does the "Critical Attributes / Enablers" column play in actual validation? How does it relate to CPPs and CQAs?
4.1 Continuous Filling / Campaign Filling Operations vs. Batch Filling

Original Text

Consideration: Continuous Filling / Campaign Filling Operations vs. Batch Filling

Critical Attributes / Enablers:

  • Durability of setup — ability to process in a stable manner for a long time, as would be required for continuous/campaign filling
  • Location of fill pump vs. barrier system (inside vs. outside containment)
  • Minimal aseptic connections required between batches
  • Minimization of number of aseptic connections required for setup
  • Format parts (e.g., hoses, needles) accommodation for different filling volumes across individual batches within a campaign

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Continuous / Campaign Filling: Running the filling operation for an extended period without fully dismantling the equipment, possibly spanning multiple batches or multiple days. This contrasts with "batch filling", where the line is fully cleaned and set up again after each batch.

Aseptic Connections: Fluid-path connections made under aseptic protection. Every connection point that must be "opened and reconnected" is a potential contamination risk. The fewer the connections, the better the sterility assurance. This is exactly why the decision matrix places particular emphasis on minimizing aseptic connections.

Analogy

Imagine a multi-race Formula 1 season. The peristaltic pump (PP) is like the strategy of "changing tires every few laps": the tubing must be replaced when it reaches the end of its life, and this has to be done in an aseptic environment. The time-pressure system (TP) is like "keeping the pump body in the garage and only changing the needle on the track": most of the equipment never enters the aseptic area, greatly reducing the number of connections per intervention.

Key Notes

Continuous filling limitation of the DP: The main risk for the diaphragm pump (DP) is that the diaphragm wears and needs a "mid-run replacement". If the total duration of the campaign exceeds the design life of the diaphragm, a component change must be made in the middle of the process. This is a high-risk operation in aseptic processing, and the changeover procedure must be adequately validated.

Continuous filling advantage of the TP: In a TP system the filling pump (pressure vessel) sits outside the barrier system, so a campaign usually requires changing only the needle that enters the aseptic area, which greatly reduces the number of aseptic interventions. This is the core strength of the TP in continuous filling scenarios.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: Suppose you take on a large commercial batch order that requires 48 hours of continuous filling and 200,000 vials. Points to evaluate:

  • PP: Confirm that the validated tubing life covers the whole run; if a mid-run replacement is needed, validate the replacement SOP in advance
  • TP: Evaluate the stability of pressure control in the intermediate vessel; check whether pressure drift after prolonged operation remains within acceptable limits
  • DP: Confirm whether the diaphragm cycle life exceeds 200,000 dispenses; if not, resolve this before the campaign is planned

Practice Questions

  1. When evaluating suitability for continuous filling, why is "minimizing the number of aseptic connections" the top priority rather than "the fastest speed"?
  2. If your facility chooses a PP for continuous filling, at which process steps would you design "tubing change validation" to ensure sterility?
4.2 Speed of Setup / Changeover

Original Text

Consideration: Speed of Setup / Changeover

Critical Attributes / Enablers:

  • Number and type of format parts required (fewer parts or greater range of capability, or each part is faster)
  • SU fluid path is faster than CIP/SIP

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Changeover Speed: The total time from the end of one batch to the start of filling of the next, including dismantling, cleaning, sterilization, reassembly and connection verification. The shorter the changeover, the higher the equipment utilization (OEE) and the greater the capacity flexibility of the CDMO.

Format Parts: Parts that must be changed for different container formats (for example 2 mL vs. 20 mL vials), such as filling needles, needle spacing adjustment plates and tubing. The fewer the format parts, or the faster they can be changed, the more efficient the changeover.

Analogy

Changeover is the pit stop of a Formula 1 car. The single-use (SU) set-ups of the PP and DP are like "pre-prepared sets of tires": the entire tubing system arrives already sterilized and is simply fitted in the pit. The traditional stainless steel set-up of the RPP is like "having to sand down the old tires and re-vulcanize them first": the CIP/SIP cycle is long and changeover time increases markedly. The recommended CIP/SIP practice for the TP ensures cleanliness, but it also lengthens the "pit stop".

Key Notes

Changeover: SU vs. traditional stainless steel: One of the greatest commercial advantages of a single-use (SU) flow path is changeover speed. The SU configurations of the PP and DP virtually eliminate CIP/SIP waiting time, whereas the traditional configurations of the RPP and TP require a complete cleaning and sterilization cycle at each changeover, which significantly affects scheduling in a multi-product CDMO environment.

RPP/DP offline preassembly strategy: The RPP and DP can have the entire fluid path preassembled and sterilized offline, so that only a single aseptic connection is needed at changeover. This is an effective strategy for reducing line downtime.

Framework for Thinking About Changeover Efficiency

Changeover time =
  dismantling time + CIP time + SIP time + reassembly time + aseptic connection time + IPC verification time

SU configuration:
  CIP / SIP time can usually be eliminated (the largest single item)
  Typical changeover time: 1–3 hours

Traditional configuration (RPP/TP non-SU):
  Typical changeover time: 4–8 hours (including CIP/SIP)

Changeover time directly affects the number of batches
possible per day and is one of the key parameters
in CDMO quotation and scheduling.

Practice Questions

  1. A CDMO has to switch between 10 different filling products every month. In this scenario, how much weight should changeover speed carry in pump selection, and how should it be balanced against sterility assurance requirements?
  2. What risk points of the RPP's "offline preassembly then connect" strategy require particular validation from a sterility assurance standpoint?
4.3 Speed of Filling vs. Control Aspects

Original Text

Consideration: Speed of Filling vs. Control Aspects

Critical Attributes / Enablers:

  • Number of cycles per minute defines speed, including conveyance (e.g., walking rake servo motion), number of pump cycles required to hit volume, and weight check
  • Balance between required fill accuracy and speed
  • Product characteristics (e.g., foam, dripping) may drive maximum speed limits
  • Fill-curve profile may also influence speed (i.e., slower at the end of the cycle)
  • Acceleration and deceleration may influence maximum speed permissible
  • As long as fill-time is less than cycle-time, the speed is maximized

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Fill Curve: The profile of flow rate over time within a single fill cycle. A typical fill curve may include three phases, "slow start → high-speed main fill → slow finish", intended to balance speed and accuracy while also controlling foam and drips.

Cycle Time vs. Fill Time: Cycle time is the total time a container spends from entering the filling station to leaving it, while fill time is the time the pump is actually dispensing liquid. As long as fill time < cycle time, filling will not be the rate-limiting step (bottleneck).

Key Notes

Limited fill curve flexibility of the TP: A time-pressure (TP) system cannot adjust pressure dynamically during filling (that is, it cannot actively modify the "shape of the fill curve"); it can only make limited adjustments through the opening and closing time and distance of the pinch valve. This means that for products with a high foam tendency or high viscosity, the filling speed of a TP may be strictly limited by product characteristics.

Fill curve flexibility advantage of the PP: The PP can change the pump head speed in real time through a servo motor and adjust the flow rate dynamically within a single fill, achieving a flexible fill curve. This is an important advantage of the PP for complex formulations (such as high-foaming protein formulations).

Analogy

A fill curve is like the way you pour milk into a coffee cup: pouring quickly from a height creates foam, and the finish has to be slow so the liquid surface can settle. The PP is like a coffee machine with precise control: you can set a "slow-fast-slow" dispensing profile. The TP is like a traditional gravity-fed kettle: it relies on valve opening time and can only make a rough "fast or slow" adjustment, with no fine dynamic adjustment during the fill.

Practice Questions

  1. For a high-foaming biologic, how should fill curve flexibility influence the choice of filling pump? Is a TP suitable?
  2. The RPP and DP both use "dedicated-size pump heads" to match different fill volumes. What challenges does this create for equipment management in a multi-product CDMO?
4.4 Foam Prevention

Original Text

Consideration: Foam Prevention

Critical Attributes / Enablers:

  • Foam may be dependent on the product and, therefore, is unavoidable
  • Placing vessel a little higher than filling pumps (ideally with bottom outlet)
  • Optimal sizing of fill-path components to reduce overpressure
  • Adjustment of filling curve (rate of fill at start, midpoint, end of each container) will minimize foam
  • Minimizing distance from the outlet of filling needle to the liquid height

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Causes of foam: During filling, foam forms when the liquid-air interface is agitated at high speed or high pressure. The severity of foam depends on: (1) the surface tension and foaming tendency of the product itself (protein formulations are particularly sensitive); (2) the filling speed and flow rate; and (3) the drop height (the distance from the needle outlet to the liquid surface).

Diving-Needle Design: The filling needle first "dives" to the bottom of the container at the start of filling and rises gradually as the liquid level rises, so that the liquid flows out smoothly along the needle wall rather than dropping in from a height, greatly reducing foam. All four pump systems can be combined with a diving-needle design.

Analogy

Pouring beer is the best analogy for foam control: pouring straight down from a height into the bottom of the glass makes the foam overflow, whereas tilting the glass and pouring slowly down its side gives the least foam. The "diving-needle design" is the industrial version of the "tilted-glass pour": the liquid fills slowly along the container wall instead of free-falling from a height. "Slowing down at the end of the fill curve" is like "easing off gently at the finish", preventing the turbulent foaming caused by the last few milliliters.

Key Notes

Special foam risk of the TP: At the end of a filling operation in a TP system, if gas is entrained in the product, extra foam may form in the final stage of the fill. This is a risk specific to the TP and must be mitigated through the geometry of the pinch valve and its opening and closing speed.

Impact of foam on CQAs: Excessive foam directly affects fill accuracy (the fill volume CQA) and the integrity of the drug solution (risk of protein aggregation and oxidation). In terms of the decision hierarchy, foam control belongs to the "Product CQAs" level of requirements and must take precedence over pure speed optimization.

Practice Questions

  1. For a high-foaming monoclonal antibody (mAb) formulation, which pump combination (including diving-needle design) would you choose first? Explain your reasoning.
  2. There is a potential conflict between two PP strategies, "dual tubing to reduce pulsation" and "larger tubing diameter to reduce foam". How would you strike a balance in actual design?
4.4 (cont.) Drip Control

Original Text

Consideration: Drip Control

Critical Attributes / Enablers:

  • Matching fluid characteristics to the appropriate technical characteristics
  • Needle design is one of the most important features
  • Length and hardness of tubing is very critical

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Drip Control: After filling is complete, liquid remaining at the needle tip can form a drop that falls into the container or the environment. This directly affects: (1) fill accuracy (a drop causes overfill); (2) environmental contamination (a drop landing on the rim of the vial affects the seal); and (3) sterility assurance (a liquid bridge formed by a drop can become a contamination pathway).

Liquid Retraction / Suck Back: At the end of filling the pump makes a small "reverse movement" (the PP rotates slightly backward, the RPP/DP make a small reverse stroke) to draw the liquid at the needle tip back into the needle and prevent a drop from forming. This is an active control mechanism common to the PP, RPP and DP.

Key Notes

Drip control disadvantage of the TP: The TP system has no "reverse stroke" mechanism and cannot actively retract liquid. The only means of drip control is to increase the closing speed of the pinch valve, but this is a passive approach with limited precision. For low-viscosity products or those with high surface tension, the drip control capability of the TP is relatively weak and more compensation is needed in the needle design.

Importance of needle design: The source text specifically identifies needle design as "one of the most important features" for drip control. The needle material, tip geometry, inner diameter and tip cut angle all affect drop formation. Tubing length and stiffness are also critical: tubing that is too long or too soft may recover elastically after the end of the fill and cause additional drops.

Analogy

Drip control is like the "drip-free spout" on a fine wine bottle. A good drip-free spout lets the last drop fall precisely back into the bottle (similar to liquid retraction in the PP/RPP/DP), while a bottle without one can only reduce dripping by how fast you rotate the bottle (similar to the TP relying on pinch valve closing speed). The former is active control and the latter is passive coping. In pharmaceutical production where fill accuracy requirements are strict, active control is clearly more reliable.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: A high-value biologic with a target fill volume of 1.0 mL and a tolerance of ±1% (that is, ±10 µL). Drip control requirements are very high:

  • Give priority to pumps with an active liquid retraction mechanism (PP/RPP/DP)
  • Combine with an optimized needle design (appropriate tubing diameter, anti-drip tip geometry)
  • If the product has low viscosity (and so is more prone to dripping), consider a hydrophobic coating on the needle tip
  • If a TP is used for such a product, the dynamic characteristics of the pinch valve must be additionally validated and strict IPCs set

Practice Questions

  1. If drip control fails (a drop lands on the vial rim), what specific risks might this create from a sterility assurance standpoint? How would you address them in the Contamination Control Strategy (CCS)?
  2. If a customer insists on using a TP system to fill a low-viscosity formulation, how would you design the validation plan to confirm that drip control meets requirements?

Section Summary (4.0–4.4)

  • Table 4.0-1🔍 structure: The functionality requirements matrix is a structured decision tool leading from "process requirements" to "pump selection"; each consideration quantifies the suitability of the four pump types through "Critical Attributes / Enablers".
  • Continuous filling: Because the pump body of the TP sits outside the barrier, it needs the fewest aseptic connections and has the greatest advantage in continuous filling; for the DP, attention must be paid to whether diaphragm wear life covers the full campaign period; for the PP, tubing life management is at the core of continuous filling validation.
  • Changeover speed: SU configurations (PP / DP) greatly shorten changeover time and suit a multi-product CDMO environment; the offline preassembly strategy of the RPP and DP effectively reduces line downtime, but the reliability of the aseptic connection must be validated.
  • Fill curve flexibility: The PP has the highest capacity for dynamic fill curve adjustment (servo speed control); the TP has the lowest fill curve flexibility, and product characteristics (high foaming, high viscosity) may strictly limit its filling speed.
  • Foam control: The diving-needle design applies to all pump systems; fundamental foam management comes from optimizing the fill curve, the needle design and an appropriate container/liquid level height configuration; for the TP, particular attention must be paid to the risk of gas entrainment at the end of filling.
  • Drip control: The PP / RPP / DP all have an active liquid retraction mechanism (reverse stroke), which is a reliable means of drip control; the TP has only passive control through pinch valve closing speed and is clearly at a disadvantage with low-viscosity products; needle design is the common key to drip control in all pump systems.
  • Decision hierarchy: For all functionality considerations in this section, the order of priority is always: sterility assurance > product CQAs (accuracy, foam, drips) > commercial flexibility (speed, changeover efficiency).
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p81 - p86

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the difference between continuous filling and batch filling, and the central role of the isolator in extended production.
  • Grasp the key sterility assurance (SA) challenges in campaign filling design, including filter changes, RTP introduction and APS design.
  • Understand how changeover functionality directly affects overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) and cost per unit, and the limits of single-use (SU) technology.
  • Analyze what determines filling speed: the filling curve, the choice of IPC mode, and how product-conserving features trade off against speed for high-value products.
4.0 [cont.] — Robotics Functionality Comparison Across Pump Technologies (doc p81)

Original Text

Robotics — Technology Comparison (continued from p80)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Robotics integration: In aseptic filling, the first job of a robot is to replace human intervention, because every entry of personnel into the grade A environment is a contamination risk. The design must consider: CFD airflow simulation to ensure that robot arm movements do not create turbulence; and ergonomics to ensure that component weights are within the robot's load capacity.

Robotic advantage of the PP: The fluid path of a peristaltic pump (PP), a silicone tubing set, is a pre-assembled closed system, so the robot only needs to pick up the pre-assembled filling needle assembly and place it in grade A. The fluid paths of the RPP, TP and DP, by contrast, must be assembled in a complex way inside the aseptic environment, and a robot has difficulty performing such precise connections.

Analogy

Imagine a robot helping to prepare surgical instruments in an operating room. The PP is like supplying a sterilized, single-use surgical pack: the robot just carries it in and puts it in place. The RPP/TP/DP is like asking the robot to assemble complex surgical instruments on the spot in the operating room: the precision required is very high and the risk of failure is large.

Key Notes

CIP/SIP capability is a double-edged sword: for the RPP, TP and DP, CIP/SIP removes the need to disassemble and reassemble the fluid path for every batch, but if the pump has to be changed in the middle of a campaign, this advantage disappears. In that case the SU-PP, which has no CIP/SIP, comes out ahead because pre-assembled components can be introduced aseptically and quickly.

Decision principle: sterility assurance (SA) > commercial flexibility. A robot design cannot look only at whether it "can perform the movement"; it must also confirm that the movement will not compromise the airflow integrity of the grade A environment.

Practice Questions

  1. If your CDMO's new line plans to introduce a filling robot, which pump type would you choose first, and why?
  2. Why is CFD modeling so important at the robot design stage? What risks can it predict?
4.1 — Continuous Filling / Campaign Filling Versus Batch Filling (doc p82–p83)

Original Text

4.1 Continuous Filling/Campaign Filling Versus Batch Filling

In manufacturing, a batch is defined as the complete production procedure from compounding, product filtration, filling-line preparation, filling, and closing all the way up to final packaging (end-to-end). The batch size can typically be defined by the volume of product that is manufactured or by the number of units that are processed.

Some users will perform continuous filling operations where the definition of batch is volume or time-based (e.g., every ## of liters filled, one batch per ## operating shifts or ## days). As an example, continuous bulk drug substance to bulk drug product formulation systems will also make use of continuous aseptic filling. However, continuous formulation is not the only time that continuous filling may be employed. In these cases, large volumes of bulk product are filled into identical container–closure systems. The designation of a batch (or filling order or section) is primarily to facilitate quality control approval and release of the product, as well as to enable a clear initiation and conclusion of monitoring and sampling that are assigned to each batch.

In contrast, some users who happen to have a single bulk formulation that is filled with different fill volumes may choose to run the product in campaigns. Therefore, in a campaigned process, the same product is filled in two or more container–closure formats, where each format represents an individual batch, and the sum of batches would be considered the campaign. For example, a user may formulate a product batch of 1,000 liters, fill half of the bulk solution (500 liters) in 6R vials and, when that fill is complete, switch to fill the last 500 liters of the same product, with a different filling volume in 10R vials. Other campaign designs are also possible (e.g., production of two or more bulk solutions requiring a fluid pathway change, campaigns that require modest format part changes, etc.).

In the case of both continuous filling and campaign filling, the most common use case is that the user is filling the same active substance, as a different active substance would pose a risk of cross contamination. If different active substances are to be used, appropriate contamination control strategies should be employed to minimize the risk.

4.1.1 Environment for Filling

Isolators are the most common environment for manufacturers who intend to operate in a continuous filling or campaign mode for the production of a sterile product. The use of isolators for prolonged processing is the strongest option for SA, as the initial surface biodecontamination provides an extremely high-quality environment, and the ability to operate for long periods without opening the doors is assured by the design.

4.1.2 Sterility Assurance

When running a continuous or campaigned process, the major objective SA is to minimize the disruptions within the barrier between batches. Therefore, when designing filling systems for continuous/campaign production, it is crucial to plan them in a manner that allows batch completion and modest changeover (when required) to be made with closed doors. This requires that the introduction of tools, format parts, wipes, environmental monitoring supplies, and the like, are properly planned during the design phase (e.g., implementing RTPs and material transfer chambers to avoid the need to open the barrier). Careful thought should be given to whether a filter change will be needed during the prolonged production period.

Annex 1 indicates that a liquid sterilizing filter should not be used for longer than one working day unless such process has been validated. See filter use considerations under Annex 1, Section 8.95.

Design of the sterile fluid pathway will determine whether a presterilized SUS can be introduced easily or whether the sterile fluid pathway will require recleaning and resterilization, as this will influence equipment layout, design, controls, and environment. Risk analysis is recommended to determine the associated risks. In some cases, parallel filtration pathways are established at the outset so that the change-over activities (which may include PUPSIT of filters) are minimized at the time the new pathway is to be connected.

The length or duration of the production period should be established based on production needs and the process designed to meet those needs. The process should then be qualified based on equipment/process capability and limitations. Once established, that period and duration, as well as duration-related interventions and conditions, including those associated with equipment change-over, should be taken into consideration in the design of the APS. However, the APS should not be used as the primary means to establish or validate the duration of the aseptic process. Continuous manufacturing/campaigns may be able to last multiple weeks within an isolated environment if the process is properly designed and validated.

4.1.3 Benefits and Risks

The most significant benefit of continuous or campaign production modes is the total production-time to turnaround-time ratio. For example, every time a line is turned around, time is needed to clean, set up, perform integrity tests on filters, perform (isolator) leak tests and glove integrity tests and, of course, to decontaminate the isolator itself (e.g., using hydrogen peroxide). Continuous and campaigning filling processes save by reducing the number of times that these activities need to be performed. Other benefits might also be realized, such as a reduction in product losses, as a proportion of the total volume filled.

Despite the benefits, the feasibility of running in a continuous or campaigned mode is not always straightforward as the limitations of the filling technology and changeover requirements must be weighed in the decision-making. For continuous-filling operations, there may be little to no mechanical changeover required between batches as the containers and closures will typically remain identical from batch to batch. For campaigns, the primary limitation is the size difference of the formats that need to be processed. As an example, if a manufacturer intends to run the first batch with a 2R vial with a 13 mm stopper, and then run a second batch in the campaign, filling the same product in a 10R vial with a 20 mm stopper, the transport parts, star wheels, sorting systems, product fluid-path components, and everything needed for further batches must either be placed in the barrier before beginning the campaign, or should be aseptically introduced via RTP or material transfer chambers after finishing the first batch. Due to the size and handling of some of these components (e.g., sorting systems), it may not be feasible to carry out the campaign under these constraints. Batch-wise filling would be a better option to reduce risk rather than attempting a campaign.

4.1.4 Equipment Design Options

Some OEMs have technologies where format parts are reduced or even eliminated. For example, some manufacturers have constructed universal feeding bowls that will feed stoppers of relevant sizes to the sorting tracks where the orientation takes place. In these cases, the large bowls need not be exchanged, thereby reducing changeover and disruption of the campaign.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Comparison of the three production modes:

  • Batch filling: A full changeover after each batch; the most flexible, but with the longest downtime.
  • Continuous filling: Containers of the same format are produced continuously; the batch is defined by volume or time, and there is almost no changeover downtime.
  • Campaign filling: The same drug substance is filled into different container formats in sequence. It is a compromise: set-up time is shared, but changeover must be done in a closed state.

The core challenge of campaign filling: how to introduce the format parts needed for the next batch into the barrier in advance, without opening the door.

Analogy

Think of a Formula 1 pit stop:

  • Continuous filling = the same car runs many laps in a row, refueling but not changing tires along the way: the greatest time saving.
  • Campaign filling = the same engine fitted in sequence into two different car bodies: the spare parts for the second body must all be stocked in the pit beforehand, so that nobody has to open the pit door mid-race to fetch them.
  • Batch filling = a complete teardown and rebuild after every race: flexible but the most time-consuming.

The isolator's "closed door" is the glass partition of the pit: once it is opened, the integrity of the sterile barrier is at risk.

Key Notes

The core of the SA decision: The key to continuous/campaign mode is not "how efficient it is" but "whether changeover can be completed without breaching the barrier".

Annex 1 filter limit: Unless validated, a liquid sterilizing filter must not be used for longer than one working day. This is a major constraint for multi-day continuous batches: parallel filtration pathways or pre-sterilized single-use systems (SUS) must be planned at the design stage.

APS design note: The aseptic process simulation (APS) must include the changeover interventions that occur during continuous production, but the APS itself cannot be used to "validate" or "determine" the maximum production duration; that must be decided by the capability of the process itself and by validation data.

Benefit Calculation

Assume the downtime cost of each batch changeover is:
  Isolator vaporized hydrogen peroxide (HPV) decontamination: 4 hours
  Integrity test + glove test: 2 hours
  Equipment cleaning/set-up: 4 hours
  Total: ~10 hours per batch changeover

Campaign production (5 batches per campaign) vs batch production (5 independent batches):
  Downtime saved = 10 hours × (5-1) = 40 hours

If capacity is 3,000 vials/hour:
  Potential output saved = 40 hours × 3,000 = 120,000 vials

Practice Questions

  1. If a customer plans to split 500 L of the same drug substance into two formats, 2 mL and 10 mL, would you recommend batch filling or campaign filling? What factors would you evaluate?
  2. Why is an isolator better suited than RABS to continuous/campaign production? Analyze from the SA decision hierarchy.
4.1.4 (cont.) — Equipment Design for Campaign Flexibility (doc p84)

Original Text

4.1.4 Equipment Design Options (continued, doc p84)

For varied container sizes, OEMs have introduced technologies, such as universal or adjustable rake, walking-beam systems, or transport with prismatic (i.e., triangular) carrier pockets with an adjustable rail, that enable the transport of containers of different dimensions (e.g., diameter, height, neck) without having to replace or change the transport system. An adjustment is commonly required during changeover to the next size, but this adjustment is automated as part of the recipe to enable touchless adjustments. Vendors may also implement adjustable or universal star wheels, which contain pockets for each of the pertinent diameters in adjacent positions. The automation then ensures that the containers are held within the appropriate-sized pocket. The ultimate goal of the universal star wheel is to eliminate or reduce the needed interventions for changeover. While these universal technologies are designed to accommodate a wide variety of sizes, there are practical limitations to the number of sizes that the various transport mechanisms can accommodate. Therefore, when planning for campaign production, it is important to ensure that the required sizes are known in advance and included in the system design.

With regard to dosing systems, the same constraints on the feasibility of changeover would apply. For example, if RPPs are used and the intention of the campaign is to fill containers with two different fill volumes of 2 mL and 14 mL, this change in volume would typically necessitate exchanging the RPPs. This campaign would not be considered feasible if the barrier has to be opened in order to exchange the pumps. Breaching sterility by opening the barrier to accommodate the larger-format RPP would jeopardize the campaign. As a consequence, if the design requirement included the ability to campaign these two disparate fill volumes, a different filling technology might need to be selected to enable the intended range of fill.

Where a RPP's limitation is the filling range, other technologies have different limitations. For example, a PP can only run for so many revolutions until the hoses begin shedding particles. Therefore, if the duration of the continuous process or campaign is longer than the permissible use-time of the hoses, the hoses must either be repositioned or exchanged. This procedure has to be validated and qualified.

For continuous manufacturing or campaigns, manual interventions associated with batch changeover represent possible contamination-control risks that should be assessed and evaluated as part of the intended control strategy for the line.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three forms of universal transport technology:

  • Universal/Adjustable Rake: The spacing of the transport fingers can be adjusted to suit different container diameters.
  • Walking-Beam System: Containers move step by step on the beam, and the pitch can be adjusted through the recipe.
  • Prismatic Carrier Pockets: A triangular pocket design in which containers of different diameters naturally locate at different depths in the pocket, so one mechanism fits multiple sizes.
  • Universal Star Wheel: A single star wheel contains several pockets of different diameters and switches automatically to the target size.

The common goal of these technologies: to replace "physical changeover" with "recipe-driven automatic adjustment", so that changeover can be completed in a closed state.

Key Notes — Campaign Limitations of Each Pump Type

Filling range limit of the RPP: The piston stroke determines the fill volume. If a campaign needs to span beyond the range a piston can cover (for example 2 mL vs. 14 mL), a pump change is almost inevitable, which amounts to having to open the barrier, and the campaign plan collapses.

Tubing life limit of the PP: Peristaltic pump tubing degrades through repeated squeezing during continuous operation, which may lead to particle shedding. This service life must be validated, and the tubing must be replaced or repositioned before it is exceeded. This operation itself must also be performed under a validated procedure.

Key judgment: There is no "perfect" filling technology; each pump has its own limitations in campaign mode, so the full parameter range of the campaign requirements must be defined clearly before design.

Practical Application

A CDMO receives a campaign request: drug substance from the same customer, to be filled in the same production campaign into two formats, 2 mL (2R vial) and 14 mL (10R vial).

Assessment: An RPP cannot change pumps in a closed state, so that option is excluded. Consider a time-pressure pump or a PP with a wide filling range (if the tubing life covers the campaign period). Also confirm whether the transport system supports universal transport of 2R and 10R; if a universal star wheel is used, both sizes must be included in the equipment specification at the design stage.

4.2 — Changeover Functionality (doc p84–p85)

Original Text

4.2 Changeover Functionality

For any production line, the uptime-to-downtime ratio (e.g., overall equipment effectiveness) is a critical factor in the return on investment and profitability of the line. For facilities with the ability to fill in a continuous batch or campaign mode, the speed of setup/changeover may be less of an issue as there is a significant boost in uptime with the ability to make multiple batches in a row without (or with reduced) changeover. However, for companies that produce single batches, the speed of setup/changeover can have a significant influence on efficiency and, ultimately, cost per unit. The impact of setup/changeover time is especially severe for companies that may be capacity-limited.

The advent of SU technology in the industry has resulted in significant gains in efficiency in all phases of the manufacturing process, including the filling operation. SU technology can reduce or eliminate the need for offline or in-place cleaning and sterilization of many critical components. However, while this approach may be useful for filling systems that make use of PP fillers, for example, the same level of benefit will not be achieved for RPPs where pump cleaning and assembly will still be required even with SU tubing sets.

Lines that are designed to make use of fewer format parts, or that make use of format parts with a greater range of capability, have reduced time devoted to setup/changeover. The ergonomics of the line can also facilitate or hinder rapid setup/changeover. When all parts to be changed or adjusted are within easy reach from a limited number of positions on the line, setup/changeover can be performed with less time-investment. Similarly, lines that make use of features, such as "tool-less" adjustments for guides and conveyance parts, can simplify and speed setup/changeover.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) is the core indicator of the return on investment of a production line:

OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality

Changeover time directly compresses Availability
→ the longer the changeover, the lower the OEE and the higher the cost per vial

Boundary conditions of SU technology: Single-use (SU) offers the greatest benefit for the PP (no cleaning or sterilization at all) and limited benefit for the RPP (the piston/cylinder still has to be cleaned and assembled; only the tubing is SU). When selecting equipment, do not assume that "using SU solves every problem".

Analogy

Changeover functionality is like the table turnover of a restaurant. The secret of a restaurant with high turnover is not that the waiters run faster, but that tables and chairs are simple and easy to clean (few format parts), supplies are within arm's reach (ergonomics), and no tools are needed for dismantling and fitting (tool-less adjustment).

SU technology is like switching to disposable tableware: for the PP, the whole set is replaced and dishwashing time is saved; but the RPP's "cookware" (piston/cylinder) is stainless steel, so disposable tableware saves only the chopsticks and bowls, and the pots still have to be washed.

Key Notes

The crisis in capacity-constrained facilities: For a CDMO already at its capacity limit, every hour of changeover downtime represents not just "cost" but "lost customer orders". Rapid changeover capability is a direct competitive advantage in such facilities.

Three levers of changeover design:

  1. Reduce the number of format parts (universal design)
  2. Increase the size range covered by each format part (avoid changeover)
  3. Optimize ergonomics and tool-less operation (speed up changeover)

Practice Questions

  1. Your filling line needs 8 hours per batch changeover, with 60 batch changeovers per year. If design improvements could shorten this to 5 hours, how much effective capacity would be gained in a year (assuming a filling speed of 3,000 vials/hour)?
  2. Why might changeover speed matter more to a CDMO than to a pharmaceutical company's own plant?
4.3 — Functionality Affecting Line Speed (doc p85)

Original Text

4.3 Functionality Affecting Line Speed

When user requirements specifications designate the speed of filling, it is usually based on calculations that either directly or indirectly relate to production (throughput) requirements. Some examples of factors that determine (or limit) the speed of filling include:

  • Cycle-time limits (after priming)
    • Filling volume (e.g., number of pump cycles)
    • Number of cycles per minute of the conveyance system (e.g., walking rake servo motion, weight-check cycle-time/frequency of weigh checks)
    • Fill curve (e.g., end-to-end cycle-time for single-filling cycle)
  • Deceleration and acceleration limits
    • Product characteristics may affect fill curve (e.g., foaming, viscosity, flowability, dripping, temperature exposure)
    • Required dosing accuracy may affect fill curve (e.g., could be influenced by factors such as container type (e.g., vial vs. prefilled syringe), contents (i.e., single-dose vs. multi-dose), overage limits (cost of product, i.e., high-volume production vs. niche high-cost products))
  • Other factors that affect the overall duration of fill/readiness to fill
    • Priming time (e.g., filling any oversized sections of fluid path, eliminating air bubbles, standardizing fill)
    • Batch size
    • Shift length (the time allocated to filling a batch)
    • Turnaround time (the time needed to prepare the line for the next batch)

The first two categories will have an influence on the selected filling technology. The final category affects the acceptability of the speed of filling but has no significant influence on the selection of the filling technology.

4.3.1 Dosing Accuracy, Weight Verification, and Speed

With some high-volume applications, where dosing accuracy is only of moderate importance (e.g., conventional vaccines or heparins), the batches are typically large and the containers are usually slightly overfilled, as the product is not very expensive. In such applications, a 100% IPC, where the empty containers are weighed prior to filling and then check-weighed after filling to determine the filling volume in 100% of the containers, may not be opted for if the user decides that a statistical check is sufficient. The higher the output requirements of such lines, the bigger the possible influence the weight check would have on cycle-time. If statistical weight checking enables faster production with continuous transport machines, it would be the desired option for high-speed fills where slight over-filling is acceptable. 100% IPC weight checks, on the other hand, would typically require intermittent transport and, hence, lower filling-line speeds. In contrast, small batches of expensive products will commonly target 100% IPC (or net-weight filling) for accuracy and reduction in product losses through tighter fill-volume targets. For additional information, refer to dose control in Sections 5.1–5.1.4.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three layers of factors that determine filling speed:

Layer 1 (affects the choice of filling technology):

  • Cycle time: how long a single filling cycle takes. The larger the fill volume and the more pump cycles required, the slower the speed.
  • Fill curve: the dynamic profile of flow rate during filling: initial acceleration, steady phase and final deceleration. Product properties (foaming, viscosity) directly affect this curve.

Layer 2 (affects the choice of filling technology): Acceleration/deceleration limits: a high-viscosity or foam-prone product must be run slowly, however fast the machine can run mechanically.

Layer 3 (does not affect the choice of technology, but affects scheduling): Priming time, shift length and batch changeover preparation time. These are scheduling issues, not mechanical ones.

Core logic of IPC mode selection:

  • Statistical IPC: High-speed continuous transport, suited to high-volume, low-price products that can tolerate a slight overfill (vaccines, heparin).
  • 100% IPC with individual weighing: Intermittent transport (stop, weigh, then move on); lower speed but very high accuracy, suited to high-value, small-batch products.
  • Net-weight filling: An upgraded form of 100% IPC that does not merely check, but dynamically controls the fill amount from the actual weight, maximizing product retention.

Analogy

The trade-off between filling speed and IPC is like the design of supermarket checkout lanes:

  • Statistical IPC = the express lane: not every item is scanned, only a few are spot-checked. It is fast, and the occasional error is acceptable (the goods are cheap).
  • 100% IPC = the standard lane: every item is scanned and confirmed. It is slow, but nothing is missed (the goods are valuable).
  • Net-weight filling = the precision weighing of a high-end jeweler: every piece is measured accurately to three decimal places, which takes time but wastes nothing.

Key Notes

The filling curve is an incompressible physical limit: No matter how fast the machine is, if the product foams, the final deceleration phase of the filling curve cannot be omitted, otherwise foam causes inaccurate filling and directly affects the CQA. This is a "hard boundary" set by the product's properties.

The correct way to set a speed specification: The speed in the URS should be worked back from the "output requirement" (how many units per hour must be filled), then adjusted for the limits of the filling curve and the IPC mode, rather than specifying a "mechanical speed" figure directly.

Practice Questions

  1. A high-viscosity biologic, batch size 5,000 vials, selling price $5,000 USD per vial. Would you recommend 100% IPC or statistical IPC? Explain your reasoning from three angles: SA, CQA and commercial.
  2. Why can nested containers usually only be checked by statistical IPC and not by 100% IPC?
4.3.2 & 4.3.3 — Product-Conserving Features and Filling Curve (doc p86)

Original Text

4.3.2 Product-Conserving Features Which Can Affect Speed

Additional controls for high-cost, small-batch products that will conserve product include, but are not limited to:

  • Net-weight filling or filling on weighing scales at the beginning of the batch to ensure no product is discarded due to air bubbles during priming and batch initiation that might result in underfills.
  • Automatic correction of underfilled containers in order to avoid having to discard them due to not reaching the target fill.
  • Systematic emptying of the product vessel at end of the aseptic fill-unit operation by filling on load cells to ensure that the containers discarded due to underfills are kept to the minimum.
  • Automatic checks for stopper presence and raised stopper detection (see Section 7.0).
  • Automated re-stoppering capability in order to ensure that correctly filled containers are not discarded due to missing or raised stoppers while they are still under Grade A controls.
  • Force and rotation control during capping-and-crimp operations and quality inspection (e.g., vision system inspections for stopper height and correct crimp seal) to ensure the container is closed correctly before leaving the line.
  • Recapping in order to ensure that correctly filled and stoppered containers are not discarded due to missing or bad crimp seals.
