Evolution path to gloveless lines: The industry consensus is "progressive introduction" rather than doing it all at once. In practice:

  1. Phase 1: identify the highest-risk manual interventions (such as filling path installation) and robotize them first
  2. Phase 2: robotize the next-highest-risk interventions (such as container sampling and waste removal) step by step
  3. Phase 3: establish a complete APS (aseptic process simulation) covering all residual manual intervention points, and confirm that their frequency is acceptable over the annual batches

Every residual manual intervention must be documented in an SOP and verified in the APS design; there can be no gray areas.

Practical Application

A CDMO is evaluating introducing robots to an existing isolator filling line. Decision checklist:

  • Confirm the scope of the CFD study (it must cover every working posture of the robot)
  • Assess the resistance of the robot arm materials to VHP and IPA
  • Confirm the sealing design of the servos and cams (dual lip seal specification)
  • Update the APS design to include worst-case simulation of robot operations
  • Assess the additional training needs of operating and maintenance staff (robot programming, troubleshooting)
  • Confirm that line speed after robot introduction still meets commercial capacity requirements

Practice Questions

  1. This section notes that RPP and TP filling systems are harder to set up for robotic automation, while PP is relatively easy. If a CDMO plans to build a new robot-centered "near-gloveless" filling line, how should this information influence the choice of filling pump system?
  2. What is the advantage of a robotic particle monitoring sampler (viable and total particle monitoring) over manual sampling? Why can manual sampling produce "false positive" results?
  3. In a progressive robot introduction strategy, how do you decide which intervention point should be robotized first? Design a priority assessment matrix.

Section Summary

  • Double-loop recirculation (4.6.1 cont.): The three-way valve design keeps the dosing pump running when the machine stops, and product returns through the inner loop to the intermediate vessel, so high-value product is not scrapped because of a stoppage. This design is driven by commercial benefit, but it must be implemented without compromising sterility assurance
  • Temperature control (4.7, 4.7.1): The temperature budget is a cumulative account across the whole product life cycle, and the aim at filling is to consume as little of it as possible; condensation is a twofold threat to sterility assurance and product CQA, so relative humidity control is key; because viscosity in TP systems changes with temperature, poor temperature control directly affects filling accuracy
  • Large batch design (4.8): The intermediate vessel stabilizes head pressure, buffers liquid level fluctuation and ensures continuous supply; for large batches, fixed piping with CIP/SIP is preferred; the ability to switch to a redundant filter is an important design consideration for large-batch risk management
  • Oxygen control (4.9): Gassing at closing has been shown by studies to be the most effective way to reduce oxygen; the vacuum sequence (vacuum-inert-vacuum-close) suits ultra-sensitive products but is limited by low viscosity; the inert gas tunnel design must be verified by CFD to confirm it does not affect First Air; residual oxygen can be verified by 100% in-line monitoring (the choice is driven by CQA)
  • Robotics (4.10): People are the greatest contamination source, and robots are a strategic sterility assurance tool, not technology for show; CFD + smoke studies are essential tools for validating robot design; PP systems are the easiest to robotize, RPP/TP harder; the gloveless line represents the highest form of SA evolution, and progressive introduction is the mainstream industry path; every residual manual intervention must be included in the APS design
5

Section 5: Dose Control

p101-p114

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p101 – p107

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the central role of the dose control system in aseptic filling and its direct link to CQAs
  • Compare 100% weight checks with intermittent statistical weight checks, including their advantages, disadvantages and appropriate use cases
  • Master the four sources of uncertainty in gravimetric dose control: container holdup, scale bias, sMU and sFill
  • Understand how the k-factor system converts uncertainty into the adjustment limits and reject limits of the filling machine
5.0 Designs for Dose Control Systems

Original Text

To ensure that the delivered parenteral dose to the patient is highly accurate, the filled volume must be controlled during the filling process. Whether filling a SU container (e.g., a prefilled syringe in an autoinjector or a vial where all the contents are fully withdrawn for injection) or a multi-use container (e.g., a cartridge in a device or a multi-use vial), the amount of drug product filled into the container is of the utmost importance.

To ensure this CQA for each container, the system must be designed to accommodate either 100% weight checks or intermittent (statistical) weight-check for IPC of dosing accuracy. Sections 5.1–5.1.4 explore the benefits and risks of both approaches, design options, and factors that influence system stability.

Note: This section does not discuss Quality Control methods such as United States Pharmacopeia <697> Container Contents for Injections (harmonized with European and Japanese Pharmacopeia). Such methods are typically designed for off-line use, are destructive tests, and are not typically employed for in-process control purposes.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Dose control is one of the core CQAs (critical quality attributes) of the filling process. The amount of drug product filled into each container must be accurate, because it directly determines the therapeutic dose the patient actually receives.

The two main container types present different dose control challenges:

  • Single-use (SU) containers (e.g., prefilled syringes): the whole content is injected, so the fill volume is the administered dose
  • Multi-use containers (e.g., multi-dose vials, cartridges): the amount withdrawn each time varies, so the total fill must cover every dose taken

Analogy

Imagine a barista pulling an espresso: the customer orders a double shot and wants exactly 60 mL, because too much or too little changes the taste and caffeine content. A filling machine faces the same task with an even stricter accuracy requirement, typically within ±2%, and every single unit must be accurate. "It averages out about right" is not acceptable.

Key Notes

Pharmacopoeial methods such as USP <697> are off-line destructive tests and cannot replace in-process control (IPC). This section discusses only on-line control methods. Auditors often probe this distinction during inspections, so keep it firmly in mind.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the filling accuracy requirement for a single prefilled syringe (PFS) stricter than for a multi-dose vial?
  2. Is USP <697> an IPC? Why can it not replace on-line weight control?
5.1 Dose Control Systems Risks and Benefits

Original Text

Whenever possible, 100% of container doses should be checked as an integral part of the filling process, as long as line speed and line design permit this approach. If this is not possible, an intermittent statistical dose-check should be done automatically on-line. Both approaches have advantages and disadvantages that will be described in this section.

Quarantine buffers are required for all intermittent on-line weight check systems to ensure that the automation is accurately tracking any container between the last good weight check and a failing weight check. For filling systems that make use of nested components, part of the design approach for on-line intermittent weight checks should be to ensure the quarantine buffer enables the identification of entire nests between weight checks so that they can be easily segregated for further investigation or discard.

Typically, off-line IPC, which is not automated, has the disadvantage of introducing a high degree of human error either during the weight-check procedure or the documentation of the results. Off-line weight checks are commonly required to be destructively tested (e.g., emptying the product in the container for weighing on an external laboratory balance), which also makes this process undesirable.

Throughout the remainder of this section all check-weigh descriptors will describe on-line techniques unless specifically identified.

A thorough risk assessment, such as that described in the International Council for Harmonisation's Quality Guideline Q9(R1): Quality Risk Management, PDA's Technical Report No. 54: Implementation of Quality Risk Management for Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology Manufacturing Operations or PDA/ANSI Standard 03-2025, Standard Practice for Quality Risk Management of Aseptic Processes might be employed to assess the risks associated with the various weight-check approaches for a specific filling configuration (7–9). See TR 54-2 for applied examples of packaging risk assessments (10).

The benefits and risks of on-line intermittent and on-line 100% weight-check approaches are described in Sections 5.1.1–5.1.4.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

A quarantine buffer is a necessary companion to an intermittent sampling system. If a problem occurs between the last passing measurement and the next measurement, every container filled during that period must be tracked and held until it is confirmed acceptable for release.

This concept is especially important on nest filling lines: each nest holds multiple containers, and the system must be able to map the fill result precisely to each nest.

Analogy

A quarantine buffer works like an airport security holding area: every traveler (container) must be tracked in the holding area until cleared by security (weight verification). If a problem is found at a given point in time, everyone in the holding area must be re-examined and cannot be released. The longer the interval, the larger the holding area and the higher the management cost.

Key Notes

ICH Q9(R1) requires that the choice of dose control method be supported by formal quality risk management (QRM) documentation. Choosing intermittent sampling over 100% checking requires sound scientific and risk-based justification, not speed or cost alone. The documented rationale for this decision is a frequent inspection focus.

Practice Questions

  1. Your site uses a nest filling line with intermittent sampling. If the sampling rate is 1% and each nest holds 100 syringes, how many nests need to be quarantined?
  2. What are the two main drawbacks of off-line IPC? Why is it especially unsuitable for an aseptic filling environment?
5.1.1 Benefits of Intermittent Weight Checks

Original Text

The benefits of intermittent statistical weight-check approaches include:

  • For RTU primary packaging material, the containers can remain within the nest, and no denesting process is needed.
  • Filling lines can run at a higher speed as samples are only taken statistically, depending on the IPC rate.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

RTU (ready-to-use) components are usually supplied in nests, such as a full tray of syringes or vials. Intermittent sampling does not require containers to be removed from the nest (denesting). Filling and measurement can be completed directly in the nest, keeping the container arrangement unchanged and reducing the risk from mechanical handling.

Analogy

Imagine a restaurant serving dishes on a shared tray: the chef only needs to spot-check the portion of a few dishes, without taking every dish off the tray to weigh it. Service is fast, but if one dish has a problem, the whole table may need to be rechecked.

Key Notes

The "speed advantage" of intermittent sampling comes at a cost: your fill target must be set more conservatively (further from the lower limit) to compensate for the uncertainty of the unchecked containers. This means more overfill, i.e., each container is filled a little extra so that unsampled containers do not fall below the lower limit. For high-value products (e.g., mAbs, gene therapies), the overfill cost is considerable.

5.1.2 Constraints of Intermittent Weight Checks

Original Text

The risks of an intermittent (statistical) weight-check approach include:

  • Potential missing detection of underfills between the IPC sampling points
  • Quarantine handling between the IPC sampling points (e.g., with a 10-fill station RTU filling line running IPC at a 1% rate with 100 containers per nest, 1 row of 10 syringes in each of 10 nests will be weighed; in this case, 10 nests must be held in a quarantine buffer awaiting results of subsequent check-weigh results)
  • Filling control strategy must take bias between the measurements tare and gross into account, whether two scales or a single scale are used, potentially resulting in a smaller filling range to compensate (see Section 5.2 and Section 5.3 for additional details on dose control).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The three risks of intermittent sampling are interlinked:

  • Detection blind spot: problems that occur between sampling points (e.g., air bubbles, pump drift) cannot be detected immediately
  • Quarantine cost: sufficient physical buffer space and an automated tracking system are required, increasing equipment cost and line length
  • Compensation for measurement bias: tare and gross weights are not necessarily taken on the same scale, so the bias between the two scales must be included in the fill window calculation, which narrows the usable operating range

Formula and Calculation: Estimating the Number of Quarantined Nests

Example setup:
  Number of filling stations: 10
  IPC sampling rate: 1% (1 container per 100)
  Containers per nest: 100
  Each draw: 1 row from each of 10 nests (1×10 units)

Number of nests to quarantine = number of nests passing during the sampling interval
  = 1/1% = 100-container interval ÷ 10 stations = 10 nests

Conclusion: the system must hold 10 nests in the quarantine buffer
while waiting for the subsequent measurement result before release or rejection.

Practice Questions

  1. If the sampling rate increases from 1% to 5%, how does the number of quarantined nests change? What is the effect on line speed?
  2. How does scale bias affect the setting of the lower fill limit? Why does a larger bias leave a smaller usable operating window?
5.1.3 Benefits of 100% Weight Checks

Original Text

Typically, 100% IPC weight checks are accomplished using a tare scale (which weighs the empty container prior to filling) and a gross scale (which weighs the container after filling). Tare and gross scales are provided for each filling station so that each dosing path is verified for weight. (Configurations with a single scale per dosing path are also available for low-throughput applications, where the single scale is used for both tare and gross.)

The benefits of 100% weight checks include:

  • Possibility to dose-in, re-dose, and dose-out for maximizing product yield:
    • Dose-in means the filling set is primed, where air is expelled into the container until a constant flow of product is achieved, on the gross scales until the correct filling volume is achieved. After priming is accomplished for the initial setup of the filler, this dose-in process will generally not need to be repeated, unless there is downtime where prime is lost. Normal filling operations will follow the dose-in (priming) step.
    • Re-dosing means that there is the ability to add small increments of product to an individual container if the net weight is lower than the target to bring the container to volume before acceptance. When re-dosing is performed, it should be performed (or simulated) as a standard part of the APS, as the extended filling time has the potential to increase risk. Re-dosing is generally not practical for very small fill volumes.
    • Dose-out means the line will be run until the filling path to each needle is completely empty on the gross scales; underfilled containers will be rejected, but any containers that achieve target weight before reaching empty may be retained. For high-value products, the increase in time to execute the dose-out is compensated with the savings achieved by minimizing scrap. The dose-out process will typically start when the intermediate vessel is below the lower replenishment level and there is no further product to be supplied. For specialty products, like suspensions, dose-out may not be advisable as mixing may no longer be sufficient.
  • Constant final dosing is possible where two-step filling is performed; the first filling step fills more than 80–95% of the volume, with a second dose provided by the filler to provide a fine-tuned quantity of product. This conserves product by not requiring an excess fill, while providing a highly precise final volume within the container. The two-step filling approach is especially valuable for rare or expensive products, or for products where the dose must be very precise due to clinical effect.
  • Data is available for each container, and each container can be rejected directly after the net-weighing; as a consequence, there is no quarantine handling.
  • Detection of low or high doses due to undetected special-cause variation is possible at the filling process (e.g., an air bubble in the filling hose).
  • Constant feedback will be provided to the filling system, which may be beneficial to systems such as PP for correcting drift (see Section 2.0).
  • A 100% check-weigh enables the filling target to be closer to the lower limit, maximizing product yield.

Historically, mass flowmeters were used for some continuous motion, high-speed machines as a 100% IPC for dosing management; however, the mass flowmeters were poor options for low-volume fills, which resulted in the need for overfilling. Mass flowmeters are capable of withstanding CIP and SIP; however, it is difficult to verify their cleanliness and sterility, so the validation can be challenging. As a result, the gravimetric approach is by far the more common approach.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The three filling operation modes of 100% weight control are the greatest flexibility advantage of this system:

  • Dose-in: the priming operation at the start of a batch, ensuring the tubing is free of air bubbles and the flow is stable before formal filling begins. This step "wastes" a small amount of product but ensures that every subsequent unit is accurate.
  • Re-dosing: topping up individual containers that fall short, correcting a slight underfill and improving yield. However, it must be included in the APS (aseptic process simulation), because each additional needle intervention is an additional exposure risk.
  • Dose-out: at the end of the batch, filling as much of the residual product in the tubing as possible into containers to reduce waste. It is not suitable for suspensions, because mixing may be inadequate at that point.

Analogy

100% weight checking is like "every car having a reversing radar": each time the car parks (fills), the system gives real-time feedback on the distance (weight) and the driver (the filling machine controller) corrects immediately, with no need to wait for after-the-fact statistical analysis. Intermittent sampling is like "parking by eye": a skilled driver can park well, but there is no guarantee of accuracy every time and no real-time correction.

Key Notes

Two-step filling is a key technique for high-value products: the first step fills 80–95%, and the second step tops up precisely to the target. This allows the fill target to be set almost right at the lower limit, greatly reducing overfill. For products such as gene therapies and mAbs, where each milliliter can be worth tens of thousands of US dollars, overfill savings directly affect the batch COGS (cost of goods sold).

Although mass flowmeters can withstand CIP/SIP, cleaning validation is difficult and they are unsuitable for small fill volumes, so gravimetric filling has become the mainstream approach.

Practical Application

When a CDMO takes on high-value biologics (e.g., ancillary injectable solutions for CAR-T cell therapy), choosing 100% weight control combined with two-step filling allows the target to be set only 2–3% above the lower limit, rather than the 8–10% conservative offset that intermittent sampling requires. For a batch of 5,000 units, saving 0.1 mL of product per unit gives 5,000 × 0.1 mL × unit price; even at USD 1,000/mL, the saving is USD 500,000 per batch. This calculation is very persuasive in a business case presentation.

5.1.4 Constraints of 100% Weight Checks

Original Text

The risks of 100% weight checks include:

  • Limited filling speed
  • Denesting is typically required for RTU containers that are provided in nests
  • Filling control strategy must take bias into account between the two measurements, tare and gross, whether a single scale or two scales are used, potentially resulting in a smaller filling range in order to compensate (see Section 5.2 and Section 5.3 for additional details on dose control).
  • Depending upon system design, 100% weight checks can result in additional handling and/or exposure time prior to stoppering

Finally, concerning risks for both intermittent and 100% IPC, weight-check systems are much more robust than earlier generations of equipment, and therefore are much less likely to be damaged should mishandling of containers on the line occur. Nevertheless, care should be taken to ensure that the container transport and movement is aligned. To facilitate aligning these elements, ergonomic devices such as locating pins can be used. Confirming alignment during setup avoids incurring costly replacement or repairs or product-reject losses.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The cost of 100% control lies mainly in equipment complexity and operational risk:

  • Speed limitation: each container must dwell on the scale long enough to obtain a stable reading. This is a physical limit and cannot fully meet the demands of a high-speed line
  • Denesting requirement: RTU nested components require containers to be removed one by one before weighing and filling, adding mechanical handling steps and the associated particulate and contamination risks
  • Additional exposure time: while moving from the tare scale to filling to the gross scale, containers are exposed to the environment longer than with direct filling, and the impact on sterility assurance must be evaluated at the design stage

Key Notes

Practical application of the decision hierarchy: because denesting adds operating steps, 100% control may increase exposure time (affecting sterility assurance). The order of decision-making then becomes important:

Sterility assurance: top priority
▼
Dose accuracy (CQA): second priority
▼
Speed and throughput (business): last priority

If the denesting operation cannot ensure that the exposure risk is acceptable, sterility assurance takes priority over dose accuracy, and the system design must be reconsidered or intermittent sampling adopted.

Practice Questions

  1. How does the "speed limitation" of a 100% weight check system affect batch capacity? What are the implications for a CDMO's scheduling and customer commitments?
  2. If a customer requires high-speed filling (>300 vials/min) and uses RTU nested components, would you recommend 100% or intermittent checking? Why?
  3. What problem do locating pins solve? At which level of control do they operate?
5.2 Dose Control System Design Options: Statistical Overview

Original Text

For some filling lines with singularized containers, especially in filling rooms with limited size and required high throughput, a 100% check-weigh is not possible. In this case, a statistical dose-control model must be used. Statistical dose-control is also used on a majority of nested filling lines. In statistical check weighing, every container fill-weight is not known, and extra protection must be incorporated to protect for the filling variability for containers not checked for dose. Typically, this results in target-fills set farther away from the lower fill-reject limit, and filling reject-limits set farther away from the maximum and minimum filling limits. Practically, this results in a smaller operating window for products with both upper and lower filling limits and in more overfill for products with only a lower filling limit.

The greatest disadvantage of statistical dose-control is the handling of rejects. Should a dose-check for a filling pump or needle exceed the reject limits, all filled containers from the last good dose-check to the current failing dose-check must be discarded for that pump position. In a nested line, it is relatively simple to segregate underfilled containers based on position in the nest (which correlates to the filling needle); nevertheless, a quarantine system must be in place to ensure that the "faulty" containers can be rejected, whether the nests are fully held on the line or have exited the line. For a line that handles individual containers, such as a vial line, segregation is more difficult depending on container-handling and shift-register control, and it is often simpler to discard all units filled for all pump positions back to the last good dose, resulting in more rejects.

Figure 5.2-1🔍 provides an example of statistical dose-control in a nested filling-machine, where one row out of every six nests is tare-weighed, filled, and then gross-weighed. Figure 5.2-1🔍 shows the removal of the syringes from the nest, the filling of the units, and the dose numbering-system needed to associate the units in each tub to the last good dose-check. This association is critical for handling rejects.

Figure 5.2-1🔍

Statistical In-Process Control for Nested Containers – All Doses Within Limits

[Figure not available in text source — refer to original PDA Guide No.1 p104]

Figure 5.2-2🔍 depicts the same nested filling process but, this time, a dose-check fails either high or low reject-limits. In this case, the filler will reenter a dose "in process" to center and control the dose for each pump, and all containers back to the last passing IPC check will be discarded (either per pump position or for all, depending on the reject control strategy).

Figure 5.2-2🔍

Statistical In-Process Control for Nested Containers – Dose Outside of Limits

[Figure not available in text source — refer to original PDA Guide No.1 p105]

There are two main methods to control the dose in parenteral containers—gravimetric and volumetric fill—to a physical stopping point (e.g., laser-fill endpoint detection on a cartridge).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The core logic of statistical dose control: because not every container is measured, the fill target must be "conservative", set far enough from the lower limit that even the worst unmeasured container does not fall below it. The size of this "conservative offset" depends on the fill variability of the system (σFill) and the sampling design.

Two main dose measurement methods:

  • Gravimetric: weighing on a scale and calculating net weight. This is the mainstream method, with high accuracy, and is suitable for most liquid filling
  • Volumetric: counting physical limit points (e.g., laser detection of the liquid level in a cartridge), suitable for special container geometries

Figure Analysis

Figure 5.2-1 (normal condition): shows the operating flow of a nest filling line when all doses are within the control limits. One row is drawn for weight measurement every fixed number of nests, and only after the measurement passes can this group of nests be released to continue downstream processing.

Figure 5.2-2 (abnormal condition): shows the handling procedure when a measurement exceeds the reject limit. The system returns to the "in-process" state for readjustment, and all containers between the last passing measurement and this failing measurement are either all rejected or only those from the corresponding filling station are rejected, depending on the rejection strategy.

The core message of these two figures: the accuracy of the shift-register tracking system determines the scope of rejection. The more accurate the system, the less unnecessary rejection.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the "reject handling" of statistical dose control its biggest drawback? What is the impact on a CDMO's batch yield?
  2. Why is the rejection scope often larger on a vial filling line (non-nest) than on a nest filling line?
5.2.1 Method 1: Gravimetric Dose Control Process & 5.2.1.1 Considerations

Original Text

5.2.1 Method 1: Gravimetric Dose Control Process

The basics of gravimetric dose control are simple and well understood. An empty container is weighed on a load-cell to obtain tare weight; the container is filled, and then the filled container is weighed again on a load-cell to find gross weight. The net weight is calculated from those numbers.

The tare and gross load-cells can be the same, as is the case in many nested filling lines. However, on many bulk or singularized filling lines, two separate load-cells are used to measure tare and gross weight.

5.2.1.1 Gravimetric Dose Control Considerations

To ensure the dose delivered to the patient is correct, several sources of uncertainty need to be considered. These sources of uncertainty, when applied to the label claim and maximum- and minimum-fill weights, can be used to calculate the filling-machine's adjust and reject limits. However, some parenteral products do not have maximum-filling weight limits (e.g., a multi-use cartridge or a vial in which the patient uses a syringe to determine the dose delivered).

Below are the sources of uncertainty that must be taken into consideration when applying a gravimetric dose-control strategy:

  1. Container Holdup – Container holdup is the undelivered volume that cannot be dosed to the patient due to such features as container geometry, device limitations, or plunger compliance. Container holdup can be empirically determined with a Gage Repeatability and Reproducibility Study or using the relevant U.S. Pharmacopeia estimates. Because the label claim is the mandatory lowest volume (or weight) that can be delivered to the patient, protections must be built into the dose-control strategy to account for container holdup.
  2. Scale Bias – In filling machines with separate tare and gross scales, the bias between the two scales must be considered to protect the maximum and minimum fill-weight. In filling machines with only one scale for both tare and gross weights, an analogous calculation for the two measurements that are taken on the single scale is applicable. To ensure no units exceed the minimum or maximum fill-weight, the upper and lower filling-machine reject limits should be protected against scale (or measurement) bias by including guard-banding from the minimum and maximum fill-weight limits. A guard-band is an adjustment or offset to the pass/fail process limits that include known uncertainties (such as the potential bias between the two measurements).
  3. Scale Measurement Uncertainty (sMU) – Measurement uncertainty of the scale must be known in the range of the weights being considered. To ensure that no units exceed the minimum or maximum fill-weight, the upper and lower filling-machine reject limits should be protected against sMU by guard-banding in from the limits by a correction factor of k1, shown in Figure 5.2.1-1. The scale calibration should be checked periodically to ensure its uncertainty does not exceed the value used for the dose limit. Checking the scale calibration before and at the end of the batch, at a minimum, is also recommended. It is also common for machines equipped with IPC to periodically tare (i.e., zero) the weighing cells at defined intervals, especially for long fills. If this feature is not included, then the scale-calibration checks should be executed more frequently.
  4. Filling Standard Deviation (sFill) – The standard deviation of the fill process must be empirically determined for the dose and the container being filled. The filling standard deviation, when multiplied by correction factors k2 and k3, is used to set the target of the dose a distance away from the upper and lower reject limits. In Figure 5.2.1-1🔍, the target is centered between the upper and lower reject limits, when the target most often is closer to the lower reject limit to minimize overfills. The filling standard deviation is also multiplied by correction factor k4 to set the adjust limits for the filler. This adjustment is discussed further in Figure 5.2.1-1.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The four sources of uncertainty in gravimetric dose control: each must be quantified and included when designing the fill window:

  • Container holdup: after filling, part of the liquid still cannot be withdrawn by the patient because of the container geometry (e.g., the plunger space in a syringe). The label claim is the minimum amount that must be deliverable, so the fill amount must equal label claim + holdup
  • Scale bias: the difference between the systematic errors of the tare scale and the gross scale. Even if each scale is individually calibrated and within tolerance, a fixed bias may remain between the two and must be compensated with a guard band
  • sMU (scale measurement uncertainty): the random error of the scale within a given measurement range, expressed as a standard deviation and included in the reject limit calculation through the k₁ factor
  • sFill (fill standard deviation): the within-batch variability of the filling process itself, expressed as a standard deviation, which controls the target position and adjustment trigger points through the k₂, k₃ and k₄ factors

Analogy

Imagine you are baking and every cake must weigh exactly 500 g:

  • Container holdup = the baking tin absorbs some oil, so you must add a little more batter
  • Scale bias = the fixed difference between your kitchen scale and the factory scale, which needs a correction
  • sMU = the error range of each reading on the kitchen scale (±2 g), so you must operate within a safe margin
  • sFill = how shaky your hand is when pouring the batter, sometimes more and sometimes less. This variability determines how much "safety margin" you need to reserve

The core of filling machine design is to control all four sources of error at the same time, ensuring that the dose of every syringe delivered to the patient is within specification.

Formula and Calculation: Guard-band Concept

Logic for setting the lower fill limit (conceptual):

Minimum fill amount (label claim)
+ Container holdup (holdup compensation)
+ Guard band for scale bias
+ k₁ × sMU (measurement uncertainty protection)
+ k₂ × sFill (fill variability protection)
= Lower reject limit of the filling machine

Fill target (Target)
= Lower reject limit + k₂ × sFill

[See the Section 5.2.1-1 figure for the actual k-factor calculation]

Conclusion: each additional error source moves the lower fill limit upward,
meaning every container must be filled with more product (more overfill).

Key Notes

Scale calibration is a critical GMP operation and should be performed at least once before and once after each batch. In long batches, periodic zeroing (tare/zero) is also needed to prevent accumulated error from factors such as temperature drift. If the machine has no automatic zeroing function, the manual calibration frequency must increase, which directly affects production efficiency and must be considered during design evaluation.

Figure 5.2.1-1🔍: K Factors and Standard Deviation Explanation (doc p106–p107)

Original Text

Figure 5.2.1-1🔍

Gravimetric Dose-Control Range Determination Depicting K Factors and Standard Deviation

[Figure not available in text source — refer to original PDA Guide No.1 p107]

Key for Figure 5.2.1-1🔍:

  • k1 = Controls the risk that a container determined to have an acceptable weight is actually within the minimum- and maximum-fill weight requirements. Recommended that k1 is set to have a high statistical confidence of containers meeting the weight requirements.
  • k2 = Controls the number of containers that will fail the lower reject limit by controlling how close the average fill weight can be to the lower reject limit. The larger k2 is, the lower the risk of rejecting containers; also, a larger k2 raises the target and allows more product to be put into each container, which increases the cost. Rejection risk vs. overfill must be balanced to choose the appropriate k2.
  • k3 = Calculated value of the number of filler standard deviations between the target and the upper reject limit, it determines the number of containers that will fail the upper reject limit by determining how close the average fill weight is to the upper reject limit. The larger k3 is, the lower the risk of rejecting containers. If the difference between the maximum and minimum fill-weights is large compared to filler variability, then the target can be closer to the minimum fill weight requirement to minimize overfill. In this case, k3 will be larger than k2; otherwise, k3 will be equal to k2.
  • k4 = Controls the average container weight so it is near the target. The smaller k4 is, the more adjustment will occur to keep the filler on target; if adjustments are manual, it could slow down the line. If k4 is too large, the filler could drift significantly far from the target before an adjustment occurs.
  • σMU = Scale measurement uncertainty (standard deviation). (See k1 above.)
  • bias = Measurement bias between tare and gross. (See k1 above.)
  • σFill = Filling standard deviation. (See k2, k3, and k4 above.)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts: The k-Factor System Explained

The k-factor system is a tool for balancing risk and cost, and each factor controls a different failure mode:

  • k₁: protects against scale measurement error (sMU + bias). The larger k₁ is, the further the reject limit sits from the specification limit and the lower the risk of misjudgment, but the narrower the operating window
  • k₂: protects the fill target from falling into the lower reject limit. The larger k₂ is, the higher the target and the lower the rejection rate, but the greater the overfill (and the higher the cost)
  • k₃: protects the fill target from exceeding the upper reject limit. If the gap between the upper and lower limits is large, k₃ can be larger than k₂, letting the target sit closer to the lower limit to reduce overfill
  • k₄: controls the sensitivity of the adjustment trigger point. If k₄ is too small, adjustments are frequent and the line is slow; if k₄ is too large, excessive drift is tolerated and the yield risk rises

Formula and Calculation: The Business Meaning of the k Factors

Relationship between k factors and overfill:

Offset of the target above the lower limit
= k₂ × σFill + k₁ × (σMU + bias) + Holdup

If σFill is large (high process variability):
  → k₂ must be larger → higher target → more overfill

If σMU is large (poor scale accuracy):
  → k₁ must be larger → narrower operating window → more containers rejected

Key insight: investing in a more accurate scale (lower σMU)
can reduce overall overfill, with a significant return for high-value products.

Worked example:
  Product unit price = USD 10,000/mL
  Overfill per unit due to k factors = 0.05 mL
  Batch size = 10,000 units
  Overfill cost per batch = 0.05 × 10,000 × 10,000 = USD 5,000,000
  → The ROI of improving process accuracy (lowering σFill) is extremely high

Key Notes

Impact of k₄ design on automated vs. manual adjustment: if the filling machine relies on manual operator adjustment, setting k₄ too small leads to frequent operator interventions and increases the risk of human error (contrary to the principles of sterility assurance). An automated filling machine can use a smaller k₄ to achieve tighter target control without adding manual intervention. This is one of the important technical reasons for choosing automated equipment, and a CDMO should include it in the TCO (total cost of ownership) calculation during equipment evaluation.

Practice Questions

  1. If your filling process σFill improves from 0.05 mL to 0.02 mL with k₂ unchanged, how will the fill target move? What is the effect on batch overfill?
  2. What does it mean if k₄ is too large (e.g., k₄ = 5)? What is the long-term effect on filling quality?
  3. Why do high-value biologics (e.g., gene therapies) need more precise k-factor design? Explain with a calculation from a business perspective.

Section Summary (5.0–5.1.4 + 5.2 intro + 5.2.1)

  • Dose control is a CQA: the fill amount of each container directly determines the therapeutic dose the patient receives and is one of the most critical quality attributes in aseptic filling
  • 100% vs. intermittent sampling: 100% control offers high accuracy, needs no quarantine buffer and allows re-dosing and dose-out, but is speed-limited and requires denesting; intermittent sampling is fast and suits RTU nests, but needs a quarantine buffer and a more conservative overfill setting
  • Dose-in / re-dosing / dose-out: three operating modes unique to 100% control systems, corresponding to batch start-up, topping up underfilled containers and batch end respectively, maximizing recovery of high-value product
  • Four sources of uncertainty: gravimetric dose control must quantify container holdup, scale bias, sMU and sFill, and convert them into filling machine operating limits through guard-banding and the k-factor system
  • The business essence of k factors: each of k₁–k₄ is a balance point between risk (rejection rate) and cost (overfill); improving process accuracy (lowering σFill and σMU) translates directly into substantial product savings per batch
  • Putting the decision hierarchy into practice: even where the business advantages of 100% control are clear, if denesting introduces an unacceptable sterility exposure risk, sterility assurance must take first priority
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p108 - p114

Learning Objectives

  • Understand how volumetric filling works and how laser sensors control the dose
  • Understand the differences in automatic dose correction strategies across filling pump systems (RPP, DP, PP, TP)
  • Identify the three categories of external and machine-related factors that affect weighing system accuracy, and the corresponding design compensations
  • Understand IPC production limits and weighing error types, and how to define upper and lower limits that do not reject truly conforming units
  • Understand the calculation and industry standards for the process capability index Cpk, and interpret what the defect rate per million fills means
5.2.2 Method 2: Volumetric Filling Process

Original Text

In a volumetric filling process, the volume of product filled into the container is not controlled gravimetrically by scales, but instead relies on container geometry, plunger position (for cartridges), and residual air-bubble (air gap) size to determine sufficient filling. In the cartridge-filling example below (Figure 5.2.2-1🔍), a laser and sensor are used to detect the filling endpoint. As filling occurs, the laser light is deflected by the empty neck of the cartridge and does not reach the sensor. As the container is filled and the neck fills with product, the laser light is transmitted through the neck of the container, signaling the control system to stop dosing.

Figure 5.2.2-1🔍: Volumetric Dosing Triggered by Laser Sensor
[Figure: Cartridge filling — laser beam blocked during empty state, transmitted when neck is filled, triggering stop-dose signal to control system]

5.2.2.1 Volumetric Filling Dose-Control Considerations

For a volumetric filling process to deliver repeatable doses to the containers, the container geometry must be well understood. This includes both the length and the ID of the container and, for cartridges, the precise placement and installed height of the plunger. In addition, the setup of the laser and sensor must be precise, as must be the presentation height of the container to the laser. In practice, each laser-sensor fill station will have an individual adjustment for delay, allowing milliseconds of additional fill after the sensor detects the laser. Operators on the line must be well trained to fill the container with an appropriate residual air bubble, guaranteeing an adequate dose is in the container. Volumetric filling is most appropriate for containers that do not have maximum-fill weight limits (e.g., a multi-use cartridge or a vial in which the patient uses a syringe to determine the dose delivered).

5.2.2.2 Adjustment of Dosing

Stability differs across the various filling–pumping systems (see Section 2.0). Consequently, there are also differences in philosophy on whether filling machines should automatically correct doses based on feedback from the filler. For stable systems, such as RPPs or rolling DPs for liquid filling, the doses delivered at the end of the batch will show no drift relative to the doses delivered at the beginning of the batch. For this reason, many stable fillers will require manual adjustment of the dose to prevent autocorrecting of the dose based on common-cause variability, thereby preventing overcorrection and the potential oscillation of filling weights.

For PP filling, stress on the pump tubing can cause a reduction of dose given the same number of rotations from the beginning of the batch to the end of the batch. To compensate for this reduction in pumping efficiency, many fillers use automatic dose-correction to compensate. The algorithm used in that automatic dose-correction can be simple or sophisticated depending on the filling-machine supplier. Most are designed, however, to not overcorrect for small changes and use a time-averaged dose to make corrections more stable.

For TP filling, automatic dose-correction is standard, due to the need to perform constant calculations to adjust pinch-valve timing owing to the everchanging intermediate vessel or manifold pressures as they empty and fill.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Volumetric filling: Fill control is based not on weight but on container geometry, plunger position and the size of the residual air bubble to judge whether the fill is sufficient. The advantages are speed and simple equipment; the drawback is that accuracy depends on the consistency of the container geometry.

Laser sensor fill endpoint: While the container neck is empty, the laser beam is refracted and does not reach the sensor; once liquid fills the neck, the laser passes through and triggers the "stop filling" command. This is an optical feedback control mechanism.

Residual air bubble (air gap): Particularly in cartridge filling, an appropriate air bubble must remain after filling so that the plunger is not over-pressurized during insertion and the product volume is correct. The bubble size must be judged by a trained operator.

Analogy

Imagine measuring coffee beans with a measuring cup instead of weighing them. You control the portion by "the shape of the cup plus filling to a certain mark" rather than by a scale. That is the logic of volumetric filling: the geometry of the container itself is the "measuring instrument".

Laser endpoint detection works like the light curtain on an elevator door. When the beam gets through, the door can close (filling can stop).

Key Notes

Choosing between automatic and manual correction: This is an important fork in design philosophy:

  • RPP / DP (stable systems): The dose output is stable and does not drift. Automatic correction may overcorrect in response to common-cause variability and cause the fill weight to oscillate. Recommendation: manual adjustment.
  • PP (peristaltic pump): The tubing deforms under compression over time and its efficiency declines, so the dose drifts as the batch proceeds. Automatic correction is needed, using a time-weighted average to avoid overreaction.
  • TP (time-pressure): The pressure source changes continuously (as the vessel empties or is topped up), so the pinch valve opening and closing times must be calculated in real time. Automatic correction is standard.

Practical Application

When a CDMO accepts a new client project for cartridge filling, the validation protocol must cover container geometry measurements (length, inner diameter, and batch-to-batch consistency of plunger installation height). If the container supplier changes batch or supplier, the accuracy of volumetric filling must be re-evaluated. In addition, calibration of the laser sensor station must be included in the per-batch or periodic calibration program.

Practice Questions

  1. Why is volumetric filling particularly suited to containers with no maximum fill weight limit? What risks arise if it is used for injection vials that do have a weight limit?
  2. A CDMO operates both RPP and PP filling lines. Why does the dose correction logic differ between them? What would happen if an engineer mistakenly applied the PP settings to the RPP?
  3. Why does the pressure in TP filling "change continuously"? What challenges does this create for pinch valve control?
5.3 External and Internal Influences on Dose Control Systems

Original Text

On filling machines, the weighing cells are constantly being confronted with external and environmental factors that will ultimately negatively influence the ability of the weighing cells to provide accurate readings. This drives many manufacturers to cross-check the IPC readings during production using destructive methods (i.e., sampling). Therefore, in the design phase, it is crucial to ensure that good design is implemented, and risk-based methodology is used to define the steps of weighing and check-weighing.

Typically, these factors can be categorized into three groups:

  1. Statistical weighing sources of variability
    • Unidirectional airflow above weighing cells in the Grade A environment
    • Release mechanism, design, and speed thereof to ensure the objects being weighed set on the weighing cells are freestanding
    • "Time-settling" (the longer the time allocated for weighing, the more reliable the readings will be)
    • Vibrations of the building where the line is placed
    • Machine vibrations (e.g., vibratory sorting systems) can be reduced if the weighing scales are decoupled from the machine baseplate, which reduces the influence of vibrations on the accuracy of the weighing cells; alternatively, a vibration compensation system can be used (e.g., physical compensation or software compensation)
    • Static charges on objects (e.g., vials coming out of the dry heat depyrogenation tunnel) can also affect the weighing performance of the cells
  2. Constant weighing sources of variability
    • Unidirectional airflow offset
    • Vibrations, if constant
    • Load-cell offset (from the manufacturer)
  3. Machine- and product-related sources of variability
    • Filling-line setup, nest vs. bulk, multiple filling steps
    • Filling time allocated to filling individual containers
    • Filling volume (smaller volumes are more difficult to weigh with the same accuracy as higher volumes)
    • Product characteristics (e.g., foamy products)
    • Built-in taring
    • In-process calibration
    • Automated vs. manual setup and in-process calibration
    • Weighing cell "filters" to identify and cancel out vibrations

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three categories of weighing error sources:

  • Statistical: Random errors that follow a normal distribution, so each measurement differs slightly. Typical examples: airflow disturbance, vibration, static electricity, insufficient settling time. They can be averaged out statistically with longer settling times or more measurements.
  • Constant: Systematic errors that shift every measurement in the same direction, such as the load-cell offset from the factory or the fixed buoyancy effect caused by constant airflow. These errors can be compensated by calibration.
  • Machine- and product-related: Errors caused by filling line design, product characteristics (for example foaming) and mode of operation (automatic vs. manual calibration). They must be minimized through good design and process validation.

Destructive sampling: Filled containers are taken from the line and their actual fill weight is confirmed on an offline laboratory balance, as a cross-check of the IPC readings.

Analogy

Imagine selling fruit at a market with an old-style scale. Statistical error is like a breeze making the scale wobble slightly (the result differs each time); constant error is like the scale being pulled to one side by a magnet (it always under-reads); machine-related error is like placing the apple on the scale too quickly and reading it while it is still shaking.

The unidirectional airflow of a grade A cleanroom is central to sterility assurance, yet its velocity and direction disturb precision balances. This is the paradox of the aseptic filling environment: the measure that protects against microorganisms is also the enemy of weighing accuracy.

Key Notes

Static electricity is an easily overlooked error source: Vials leaving the dry heat depyrogenation tunnel can accumulate static charge as they cool from high temperature, affecting the balance reading. On a high-speed line this must be deliberately designed out (for example with ionized air).

The trade-off of time-settling: Letting the vial rest longer on the balance gives a more accurate reading, but directly reduces filling line speed (UPH). When designing the IPC, the trade-off between accuracy and speed must be made explicitly and the risk assessment documented.

The smaller the fill, the harder the weighing: For small-dose products below 1 mL, weighing error has a larger relative effect. This is exactly why such products need an especially rigorous IPC design and validation.

Practical Application

When performing qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) of a filling line at a CDMO, it is advisable to test each of the three error source categories separately: (1) Statistical: measure the distribution of the same reference weight under different airflow conditions and vibration states; (2) Constant: compare the IPC balance readings with the laboratory balance readings for systematic offset; (3) Machine/product-related: test dose accuracy at different filling speeds and with different container types. The results of these three tests determine how wide the IPC upper and lower limits should be set.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the unidirectional airflow in a grade A zone interfere with weighing accuracy? How is this balanced against its function of protecting sterility?
  2. What is the essential difference in management strategy between "statistical error" and "constant error"? What tools are needed to deal with each?
  3. How would a foamy product affect the weighing system of a filling line? What design countermeasures would you recommend?
5.3.1 In-Process Control Production Limits and Weighing Accuracy

Original Text

Weighing cells during production, if not equipped with a defined recipe and programmable correction-factor(s) as explained in Figure 5.3.1-1🔍, will deviate from the actual weight of the container (empty and filled or tare and gross). Therefore, it is not practical to use IPC values as parameters to depict the actual filling weight in a filled container.

The approach to compensate for weigh-scale measurement uncertainty compared to the actual weight of the empty and filled containers will vary slightly from end user to end user but, in principle, defining the IPC parameters will typically require an overall understanding of the deviations caused by the external factors. Some points to consider include:

  • Weighing accuracy always refers to the net weight; there is no separate accuracy considered for tare-weighing and gross-weighing
  • Weighing accuracy of the net weight consists of the sum of the two deviations (see Figure 5.3.1-1🔍):
    • Statistical weighing error (σ): Normally distributed scatter of the weighing process (multiple weighings of an identical weight on the same scale)
    • Constant weighing error: Constant offset of the net value due to the difference between the target weight and the achieved mean value of the test quantity per digit
Figure 5.3.1-1🔍: In-Process Control Production Limit
[Figure: Bell curve showing statistical weighing error (σ) as normally distributed scatter, plus constant weighing error as systematic offset. The IPC production limit must encompass both error types.]

A good way to analyze the influence from external factors is to check the actual readings of several fill weights against their readings of the IPC cell. Assuming only one IPC cell is being checked against one laboratory balance, using standard-deviation(s) methods, a bell curve can be plotted that would look something like Figure 5.3.1-2. Because a laboratory balance is not affected by typical external factors on a filling line such as unidirectional air flow, it will be more accurate, and the bell curve would be narrower.

Figure 5.3.1-2🔍: Actual Weight Versus In-Process Control Balance Reading
[Figure: Two bell curves plotted together — narrow curve = lab balance (accurate, unaffected by line conditions); wider/flatter curve = IPC cell reading (broader distribution due to external factors).]

Now, if constant offset deviations of the weigh cells to the left and the right of the IPC bell curve are added, a wider and flatter bell curve will result, as seen in Figure 5.3.1-3.

Figure 5.3.1-3🔍: Actual Weight Versus In-Process Control Balance Reading including Weighing Scale Offset
[Figure: The IPC bell curve becomes even wider and flatter when systematic offset deviations (constant errors) from individual weigh cells are included. Multiple cells with different offsets create a composite distribution significantly wider than the lab balance curve.]

If one of the weights in this example is taken, and the reading of the laboratory balance and the reading of the weight of the IPC cell are compared, two different readings would result that may be significantly different from each other (see Figure 5.3.1-4🔍).

Figure 5.3.1-4🔍: Significant Delta Between Actual Weight and In-Process Control Balance Reading
[Figure: Single data point example — lab balance reads 1.001 g (actual weight, within spec); IPC cell reads 1.005 g (appears out-of-specification if limits are set too tightly around lab scale values). Illustrates danger of defining IPC limits based solely on lab balance results.]

If the end user decides to define production limits according to lab-scale results, with the actual weight of 1.001 g, the fill weight would be acceptable since it lies in the bell curve of actual accepted weights. If, however, the end user interprets the weighing-cell reading of 1.005 g to be out-of-specification, then they would define this unit as a reject, although in reality, it fulfills the specifications.

A good approach would be to define the IPC limits (accepted minimum and maximum limits) according to the widest IPC bell curve (which will mean that the "true" weight of the filled container is assured to be within limits). This would represent an actual distribution if weighed on a laboratory balance of the narrow bell curve shown in Figure 5.3.1-1.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The IPC balance reading is not the actual fill weight: This is the most critical insight of this section. The in-line IPC balance is affected by airflow, vibration, static electricity and similar disturbances, so its reading distribution is wider and more shifted than that of a laboratory balance. IPC readings must never be treated as equal to the "true fill weight".

Superposition of two weighing errors:

  • Statistical error (σ): Random and normally distributed, described by the standard deviation. Weighing the same mass many times gives a bell-shaped distribution.
  • Constant error: A systematic offset that moves the whole curve to the left or right. Different balance sensors have different offsets.

Logic for setting IPC limits: Production limits should be based on the "widest IPC bell curve", so that any reading within the IPC limits is guaranteed to correspond to a true weight within specification. In other words, the IPC limits must be wide enough so that truly conforming product is not wrongly rejected.

Analogy

Imagine weighing a watermelon with an ordinary scale in a noisy, windy environment, while a laboratory next door weighs the same watermelon on a precision balance. The ordinary scale may show 10.2 kg (when it is actually 10.0 kg), but if your "acceptance standard" was set from the precision balance at 10.0 kg ± 0.1 kg, the reading of 10.2 kg would "wrongly reject" a watermelon that is in fact perfectly acceptable.

This is the danger of setting IPC limits too tight: you are not controlling quality, you are manufacturing false rejects, wasting expensive drug product and resources.

Key Notes

Business impact of false rejects: In a CDMO setting, false rejects are not just a yield problem but also a client satisfaction and compliance problem. If IPC limits are too tight, large numbers of conforming units are wrongly discarded; the client loses expensive material and a deviation must be investigated. Worse, if the investigation cannot find a root cause (because it is really a limit-setting problem), an unresolved deviation record is left in the quality system.

Net weight is the basis of accuracy: Note that the source text stresses that "weighing accuracy always refers to net weight", rather than evaluating the empty vial (tare) and the filled vial (gross) separately. This means the tare and gross errors add up and together affect the precision of the net weight.

Constant errors at different IPC stations may run in opposite directions: On a multi-station filling line, the constant offset of each weighing sensor differs in direction (some read high, some low), which widens the overall combined distribution curve. This is exactly why the limits must be set against the widest curve.

Formula

Net weighing accuracy = statistical error (σ) + constant error

Let the IPC reading range = [IPC_min, IPC_max]

Correct method:
  IPC_min = true minimum acceptable weight - (statistical σ + maximum constant offset)
  IPC_max = true maximum acceptable weight + (statistical σ + maximum constant offset)

Incorrect method (common mistake):
  Directly applying the specification limits of the
  laboratory balance as the IPC production limits
  → Consequence: large numbers of conforming units falsely rejected

Example (from the source text):
  Actual weight (lab balance) = 1.001 g → acceptable ✓
  IPC reading (weigh cell)    = 1.005 g → wrongly rejected if the limit is set too tight ✗

Practice Questions

  1. Why is the bell curve of a laboratory balance narrower than that of an IPC balance? Explain from the perspective of error sources.
  2. If a filling line has 8 weighing stations, and the direction and size of the constant offset differ at each station, what challenge does this pose for setting uniform IPC upper and lower limits?
  3. Suppose you are a CDMO quality engineer and the client asks you to tighten the IPC limits to be "closer to the specification limits". How would you use data to persuade the client that doing so is actually risky?
5.3.2 In-Process Control Production Limits in Relation to Process Capability Index

Original Text

Some manufacturers will define the robustness of their design in terms of the system's capability. This is an outcome based on upper- and lower-specification limits and the dosing accuracy of the pumps built into the filling machine. Equation 5.3.2-1 describes the inversely proportional relation of the capability index to relative standard deviation (σ).

Equation 5.3.2-1:

Cpk = min(x̄ − LSL, USL − x̄) / 3σ

Cpk checked with a test where:
x̄ = measured average by the test
σ = standard deviation calculated by the test

Given limits:
LSL = Lower specification limit
USL = Upper specification limit

A process capability index (Cpk) value between 1 and 1.33 is typically accepted as the industry standard (although the exact capability of any system will be dependent upon its design). A Cpk value of 1 to 1.33 translates to a calculation of ± 3 – 4σ on the bell curve. The higher the accuracy (higher σ) that an OEM can give, the tighter the upper and lower limit specifications that can be defined. Because this is a statistical calculation, it deals with how many rejects are allowed per number of filled containers due to bad fills. For example, in the case of Cpk = 1.33, the stable process would be expected to deliver no more than 66 fills, which are outside of the dose weight limits in every one-million filled units (see Table 5.3.2-1🔍).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Process capability index Cpk: Measures the ability of a process to run stably within the specification limits (LSL/USL). The higher the Cpk, the closer the process center is to the middle of the specification and the smaller the variation.

Reading the formula: Cpk = min(x̄ − LSL, USL − x̄) / 3σ, i.e. the distance from the mean to the nearer specification limit divided by 3 standard deviations. This calculates capability from the least favorable side of the process, which is conservative and reasonable.

Industry standard Cpk of 1.0 to 1.33:

  • Cpk = 1.00 → 2,699 out-of-limit units per million fills (±3σ)
  • Cpk = 1.33 → 66 out-of-limit units per million fills (±4σ)
  • Cpk ≥ 1.67 → 0 per million (±5σ, close to Six Sigma level)

Inverse relationship: Cpk is inversely proportional to σ (standard deviation). The smaller the σ (the more precise the process), the higher the Cpk and the tighter the specification can be set.

Analogy

Cpk is like the "marksman index" in an archery contest: LSL and USL are the edges of the target, σ is the spread of the archer's shots, and x̄ is the average landing point.

A Cpk = 1.0 means the archer's average landing point is exactly on the bullseye, but the spread is as wide as the target edges, so roughly 2 to 3 arrows in every 1,000 fly off the target. A Cpk = 1.33 is a more precise archer, with only 66 misses per million shots.

The "marksman level" of a filling line determines the competitiveness of the OEM equipment. The higher the Cpk, the tighter the specification (stricter dose tolerance) the client can use, which is especially important for high-value biologics.

Formula

Process capability index formula:

        min( x̄ - LSL,  USL - x̄ )
Cpk =  ───────────────────────────
                  3σ

Worked example:
  Target fill weight: 5.00 mL (density 1.0 g/mL → 5.00 g)
  Specification: 4.75 g ~ 5.25 g
  LSL = 4.75 g, USL = 5.25 g
  Measured x̄ = 5.02 g, σ = 0.03 g

  min(5.02 - 4.75, 5.25 - 5.02) = min(0.27, 0.23) = 0.23
  Cpk = 0.23 / (3 × 0.03) = 0.23 / 0.09 ≈ 2.56

  → Above the 6σ level, with almost no out-of-specification units per million!

Industry standard reference:
  Cpk 1.00 = 2,699 ppm  → generally the minimum acceptable standard
  Cpk 1.33 = 66 ppm     → industry standard
  Cpk 1.67 = 0 ppm      → Six Sigma level

Key Notes

Cpk is a quantitative tool for equipment acceptance: In the equipment purchase specification (URS), the OEM can be required to provide a guaranteed Cpk value. For example: "Fill accuracy requirement: Cpk ≥ 1.33 at a 5 mL fill target." This turns a qualitative requirement into a verifiable quantitative metric.

Cpk applies to stable processes: The source text specifically stresses a "stable process". If the process has a trending drift (such as PP tubing aging), even a small instantaneous σ will allow the accumulated drift to push the actual defect rate far above what Cpk predicts. This is the fundamental reason why PP needs automatic dose correction.

Decision hierarchy note: Equipment Cpk capability is a choice at the "business and flexibility" level, but it directly affects whether the dose accuracy requirement in the product CQAs can be met, and therefore patient safety. The decision hierarchy runs vertically through this point.

Practical Application

When a CDMO evaluates filling equipment for purchase, Cpk is one of the key purchasing metrics. It is advisable to state clearly in the URS: (1) Cpk commitment values at specific fill volumes (for example 0.5 mL, 1 mL, 5 mL, 10 mL); (2) Measured Cpk data from the OQ/PQ acceptance tests; (3) For high-value biologics (such as gene therapy), consider requiring Cpk ≥ 1.50 or even higher, because the unit cost can reach tens of thousands of dollars and the cost of false rejects is extremely high.

Practice Questions

  1. A filling machine achieves Cpk = 1.40 in acceptance testing, but in actual production it is used with PP filling and automatic correction is not enabled. How might the Cpk change, and why?
  2. The client requires a dose specification of target ± 2%, and the equipment supplier says a Cpk = 1.33 can be achieved. Calculate: how many units per million are expected to be out of specification? What does this number mean for a CDMO producing 5 million units a year?
  3. What is the significance of the "min" function in the Cpk formula? If the process mean is strongly shifted toward the USL side, how does Cpk reflect this risk?
6.0 Special Considerations for Advanced Container–Closure Design and Implementation (Transition — doc p114)

Original Text

Container–closure design is an area of intense research and development within the pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industries. As stated in Section 1.2, container–closure materials of construction and design will influence the design of the aseptic filling line and will also affect the selection of the closing system (see Section 7.3). When considering the use of a novel container and/or closure, it is essential to involve potential component suppliers as early as practicable with the design and selection of the equipment to ensure suitability and compatibility.

6.1 Container–Closure Design

Some recent examples of advanced container–closure systems in development and in the market include:

  • Multi-chamber vials
  • Multi-chamber syringes
  • Multi-barrel, single-plunger syringes
  • Multi-chamber cartridges
  • Autodisable (nonreusable) polymer-pouch intramuscular (IM) delivery system
  • Nested micro-vials
  • Multi-container-type association (e.g., vial connected to infusion bags)
  • Crush-proof vials
  • Silicone-free syringes
  • Needle-through-septum filling of presterilized, fully closed vials
  • Press-fit vial closures

The design objectives of the more advanced containers and closures can be varied, but often include:

  • Enhanced shelf life
  • Improved ruggedness in handling, transportation, storage (e.g., extreme low-temperature storage), and use
  • Enhanced SA at the point of filling or point of administration
  • Simplification and improvement of accuracy of patient administration
  • Reconstitution close to the time when the injection is to be administered
  • Reduction of waste in the extractable volume
  • Prevention of reuse or diversion of syringes
  • Reduction of components and reduction of waste during manufacturing and/or administration
  • Elimination of specific quality-attribute failures (e.g., silicone-induced protein agglomeration)
  • Simplification and improved quality of closing operations (e.g., elimination of vibratory feed systems, reduced risk of particle generation, reduction in closing steps, reduction in non-product contact parts, all closing operations completed under Grade A immediately after fill)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Advanced container-closure systems: Traditional injectable containers (glass vial + rubber stopper + aluminum cap) can no longer meet the needs of modern biologics, gene therapy and patient convenience. Advanced systems include innovative designs such as multi-chamber, auto-disable (to prevent reuse) and silicone-free.

Key design drivers:

  • Improved SA (sterility assurance): Needle-through-septum filling in a fully closed system maximizes the sterile barrier.
  • Silicone issue: Traditional syringes use silicone oil to lubricate the plunger, but silicone droplets in the drug solution can cause protein agglomeration, which led to the development of silicone-free syringes.
  • Extractable volume waste: Reducing dead volume is especially important for expensive biologics.

Analogy

A traditional injection vial is like ordinary tableware in a restaurant: fully functional but generic. An advanced container-closure system is like tableware that a Michelin-star restaurant customizes for a particular dish: the shape, material and sealing method are all optimized for a specific need, but the design complexity and the difficulty of supplier coordination also rise sharply.

This is also why Section 6.0 opens by stressing "engage suppliers early": a customized container cannot be considered after the filling line design is finished. It is like not being able to decide how big a pot to use after the kitchen has already been built.

Key Notes

The "early engagement" principle: Advanced containers/closure systems must involve the supplier at the early stage of equipment selection and filling line design. Container geometry affects filling needle design, IPC settings and capping equipment selection. If the container is changed after the equipment is purchased, full revalidation may be needed.

Decision hierarchy note: Among the design goals for advanced containers, "enhanced SA (sterility assurance)" is listed first, in line with the first priority of the decision hierarchy. Patient safety (CQAs such as dose accuracy and avoiding protein agglomeration) comes second. Convenience and commercial considerations (such as reuse prevention and waste reduction) come last.

Section 6 is a transition bridge: The discussion of dose control in Section 5 ends here, and Section 6 begins the in-depth discussion of container-closure systems (continuing through Section 7: closed system design). Container, filling and closure form an inseparable system engineering effort.

Practical Application

Implications for CDMO business development teams: when a client brings a new project with an advanced container system and asks about feasibility, the first question should be "What equipment compatibility data can your container supplier provide?" rather than quoting immediately. Advanced containers often require: (1) Special filling needle designs (such as needle-through-septum filling); (2) Modified or customized capping equipment; (3) A redesigned IPC system (for example, multi-chamber containers need multi-step fill verification); (4) Longer equipment acceptance and process validation timelines. These must all be made explicit in the technical feasibility assessment so that quotations and schedules are accurate.

Practice Questions

  1. What CQA problem do "silicone-free syringes" solve? Which type of drug (small molecule vs. biologic) is affected more by this problem, and why?
  2. How does needle-through-septum filling strengthen sterility assurance? Compared with conventional open filling, which critical contamination risk window does it address?
  3. If a client requires a multi-chamber cartridge, list at least 3 technical questions you would need to confirm at the early equipment design stage.

Section Summary (5B: doc p108-p114)

  • Volumetric filling (5.2.2): The endpoint is controlled by container geometry plus a laser sensor, without balance weighing. Accuracy depends on consistent container dimensions, and the method suits containers with no maximum fill weight limit (such as multi-dose cartridges).
  • Dose correction philosophy (5.2.2.2): Stable pumps (RPP/DP) use manual correction, PP uses automatic time-weighted correction, and TP requires automatic real-time correction, reflecting the inherent characteristics of each pump system.
  • Three weighing error types (5.3): Statistical (random errors from airflow, vibration, static electricity, etc.), constant (systematic errors such as sensor offset), and machine/product-related errors. Grade A airflow both protects sterility and challenges weighing accuracy.
  • Core principle for setting IPC limits (5.3.1): The IPC reading is not the actual weight. IPC upper and lower limits should be set against the "widest IPC bell curve", to avoid false rejects of actually conforming units caused by the inherent error of the IPC balance.
  • Process capability index Cpk (5.3.2): A Cpk of 1.0 to 1.33 is the industry standard (±3σ to ±4σ). At Cpk = 1.33, only 66 units per million fills are out of specification. Cpk is a key quantitative metric in the equipment purchase specification (URS).
  • Advanced container-closure systems (6.0 transition): Innovative containers such as multi-chamber, silicone-free and needle-through-septum filling require supplier involvement early in equipment design. The order of decision priority is always: sterility assurance > product CQAs > commercial flexibility.
6

Section 6: Container-Closure

p114-p118

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p114 - p118

Learning Objectives

  • Understand design trends and technical innovations in advanced container-closure systems, including multi-chamber, silicone-free and needle-through-septum filling designs.
  • Master the key factors for evaluating novel container-closure systems, from supply chain, handling and product compatibility to IPC complexity, and build a systematic risk assessment framework.
  • Understand how advanced container-closure designs balance sterility assurance, patient safety and commercial flexibility.
  • Be able to propose a sound technical evaluation process and early supplier involvement strategy when a CDMO client brings an innovative container-closure request.
6.0 Special Considerations for Advanced Container-Closure Design and Implementation

Original Text

Container-closure design is an area of intense research and development within the pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industries. As stated in Section 1.2, container-closure materials of construction and design will influence the design of the aseptic filling line and will also affect the selection of the closing system (see Section 7.3). When considering the use of a novel container and/or closure, it is essential to involve potential component suppliers as early as practicable with the design and selection of the equipment to ensure suitability and compatibility.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Container-Closure System: the overall system formed by the container body (e.g., vial, syringe, cartridge) and the closure components (e.g., rubber stopper, plunger, cap). The two must work together to protect product integrity, sterility and quality throughout shelf life.

Why are "design" and "materials" so important? The choice of container closure affects not only product protection but also the design of the filling line equipment itself, for example needle diameter, filling speed and sealing mechanism. It is a systemic decision in which one change ripples through everything else.

Analogy

Choosing a container-closure system is like an architect choosing building materials: you cannot build the house first and then decide which window frames to use. The container-closure design must be planned in step with the filling equipment, otherwise late changes are extremely costly.
