This is the fundamental reason this section stresses involving suppliers as early as possible.

Key Notes

Early supplier involvement: for novel container-closure systems, PDA explicitly recommends involving potential component suppliers as early as possible in equipment design and selection. In a CDMO setting, when a client brings an innovative container design, an equipment compatibility assessment must be started immediately, rather than discovering problems only after the filling line has been finalized.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the choice of container-closure materials affect filling line equipment design? Give a specific example.
  2. When a CDMO accepts a new client project in which the client requires an innovative container that has never been used before, at which project stage should supplier evaluation start?
6.1 Container-Closure Design - Advanced Examples & Design Objectives

Original Text

Some recent examples of advanced container-closure systems in development and in the market include:

  • Multi-chamber vials
  • Multi-chamber syringes
  • Multi-barrel, single-plunger syringes
  • Multi-chamber cartridges
  • Autodisable (nonreusable) polymer-pouch intramuscular (IM) delivery system
  • Nested micro-vials
  • Multi-container-type association (e.g., vial connected to infusion bags)
  • Crush-proof vials
  • Silicone-free syringes
  • Needle-through-septum filling of presterilized, fully closed vials
  • Press-fit vial closures

The design objectives of the more advanced containers and closures can be varied, but often include:

  • Enhanced shelf life
  • Improved ruggedness in handling, transportation, storage (e.g., extreme low-temperature storage), and use
  • Enhanced SA at the point of filling or point of administration
  • Simplification and improvement of accuracy of patient administration
  • Reconstitution close to the time when the injection is to be administered
  • Reduction of waste in the extractable volume
  • Prevention of reuse or diversion of syringes
  • Reduction of components and reduction of waste during manufacturing and/or administration
  • Elimination of specific quality-attribute failures (e.g., silicone-induced protein agglomeration)
  • Simplification and improved quality of closing operations (e.g., elimination of vibratory feed systems, reduced risk of particle generation, reduction in closing steps, reduction in non-product contact parts, all closing operations completed under Grade A immediately after fill)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three drivers of advanced container-closure design:

  • Enhanced sterility assurance: for example, needle-through-septum filling keeps the container fully closed during filling, greatly reducing exposure risk; it is the highest level of SA practice.
  • Product stability needs: for example, multi-chamber designs store the lyophilized drug and the diluent separately and mix them only just before administration, extending shelf life and ensuring efficacy.
  • Patient use safety: for example, autodisable systems eliminate the risk of syringe reuse at the container design level, providing technical support for public health policy.

SA (Sterility Assurance): SA sits at the top of the decision hierarchy. The ultimate purpose of every advanced design is to maintain or improve the level of SA.

Analogy

A multi-chamber container is like an instant coffee pack: the coffee powder and hot water are kept apart and mixed only before drinking, so every cup is at its best. A multi-chamber syringe lets the lyophilized drug and the diluent mix just before administration, both extending shelf life and ensuring efficacy.

Silicone-free syringe: like switching to non-stick coated tableware. Traditional silicone lubrication is convenient, but it can cause aggregation of protein drugs; a silicone-free design eliminates this CQA risk at its source.

Key Notes

Decision hierarchy reminder: note that in the list of design objectives, "Enhanced SA at the point of filling or point of administration" takes priority over all commercial convenience objectives. This is fully consistent with the decision hierarchy of this guide: SA always comes first.

Grade A closure requirement: the text states "all closing operations completed under Grade A immediately after fill", meaning all closing operations must be completed in a Grade A environment immediately after filling. This is a core discipline of aseptic filling, and no advanced design may lower this standard.

Practical Application

Suppose a CDMO client asks to use needle-through-septum filling for its lyophilized protein drug product. You need to assess:

  • Is the existing filling needle design compatible? Are needle diameter, material and puncture force within specification?
  • Is fusion-sealing equipment for the septum already available, or does it need to be purchased?
  • Does the APS (aseptic process simulation) design need to be updated to verify closure integrity after needle penetration?
  • Can the supplier provide pre-sterilized sealed vials that meet RTU (ready-to-use) specifications?

These questions should be settled at the feasibility study stage, rather than discovering equipment incompatibility only at the commercial batch.

6.1 (continued) - Design Attributes Achieving the Objectives

Original Text

These container-closure systems accomplish those significant objectives through such design attributes as:

  • Integrating filled containers with devices such as autoinjectors or bandoliers of autoinjectors to standardize and automate dosing
  • Providing SU, disposable-dose delivery systems, thereby reducing the stability requirements for multi-dose containers
  • Creating the ability to lyophilize active preparations and contain the lyophile separate from diluents, thereby enhancing shelf life
  • Creating the ability to freeze the vial to cryogenic temperatures without a loss of integrity
  • Fabricating vials, cartridges, and other systems with enhanced materials of construction or layers of different materials that assist the container in resisting crushing, cracking, or damage
  • Using multi-chamber cartridges or syringes that reduce the number and type of containers to be handled (e.g., lyophile and diluent can be combined in a single delivery device), so two products can be maintained separate for later combination and mixing at the time of dose administration
  • Reducing risk in contamination control by limiting the number of containers or devices subject to aseptic manipulation during manufacture
  • Reducing risk in infection control by reducing handling by the caregiver at the point of administration
  • Improving the dosing accuracy by filling the delivery device directly rather than requiring the caregiver to withdraw the dosage
  • Eliminating specific processing or treatment agents (e.g., silicone)
  • Filling through septum with small needle to enhance SA by keeping sterile container closed during filling with fusion-sealing of septums after through-septum filling to maintain integrity
  • Integrating stopper and overseal in a single closure applied simultaneously

Since the number and types of containers and closures available on the market is increasing, and development activities are providing continuous improvement, it would be impossible in a Manufacturing Technology Guide to address each in turn. Instead, when considering the topic of aseptic filling, there are some factors about the container-closure system and its intended handling that should be assessed. These factors include, but are not limited to:

  • Supply constraints
    • What are the available methods of supply from the supplier (e.g., RTU or to be prepared on site, bulk packs vs. nests, oriented vs. non-oriented)?
    • Are there multiple supplier sources for the chosen container (or equivalent)?
  • Handling requirements
    • What are the requirements for introduction (e.g., nesting or conveyance)?
    • As to conveyance, would they be conducive to back pressure or feed mechanisms?
  • Orienting risks
    • When designing systems for orienting components that are supplied non-oriented, what are the risks associated with the orientation process (e.g., particle generation during orientation processes, risks to deformation of the component during orienting, clumping, or improper flow due to high friction)?

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Strategic significance of SU (single-use): SU delivery systems eliminate the stability challenges of multi-dose containers (oxidation and contamination risk after opening) while simplifying patient use. From the CDMO perspective, SU also reduces the cleaning and validation burden on the filling line.

RTU (ready-to-use): components that the supplier has pre-washed, sterilized and packaged, and that go directly into the aseptic area. Compared with on-site preparation, RTU reduces process steps but depends on supply chain stability.

Fusion-sealing of septums: after needle-through filling, the puncture hole is fused closed with laser or thermal energy, restoring full container closure integrity. This is a key technical step in safeguarding SA.

Analogy

The concept of reducing aseptic manipulations in multi-chamber containers: like a top sushi restaurant, where the fewer times the chef touches the ingredients, the lower the risk of contamination. One core logic of advanced container design is to integrate several functions into a single container, reducing the number of steps in manufacturing that require aseptic manipulation. Every manipulation removed is one less opportunity for contamination.

Key Notes

Supply chain risk is an underestimated key factor: PDA specifically asks "Are there multiple supplier sources?" because advanced containers are often available from only a few specialized suppliers. With a single source, any supply interruption can stop the entire commercial filling line.

Trade-offs between RTU and on-site preparation: RTU reduces on-site workload, but costs more per vial and depends heavily on the supplier. On-site preparation (bulk packs) costs less but requires a full cleaning and sterilization validation infrastructure. This decision is directly tied to TCO (total cost of ownership).

Orienting risk: components supplied non-oriented require automatic orientation by the machine, which may generate particles or deform the components. For fragile containers (e.g., glass microvials) or surface-coated components, the orienting step is a major risk point.

Risk Quantification Framework

Supply chain risk score (conceptual model):

Supply risk =
  (share of single supplier) ×
  (annual demand) ×
  (inverse of buffer stock weeks)

Suggested targets:
- At least 2 qualified suppliers
- Buffer stock ≥ 12 weeks (innovative containers)
- Buffer stock ≥ 6 weeks (standard containers)

If there is only 1 supplier and buffer stock < 8 weeks,
the supply interruption risk is classified as "high risk",
and a backup supplier qualification plan should be started.

Practice Questions

  1. What are the advantages of RTU (ready-to-use) components over on-site prepared components in terms of sterility assurance? What are the potential risks?
  2. If a client asks to use a novel multi-chamber vial supplied non-oriented, what risk points would you focus on in the feasibility assessment?
6.1 (continued) - Comprehensive Risk Assessment Factors

Original Text

  • General handling risks
    • What are the risks associated with the selected handling mechanisms (e.g., risks to scuffing of preprinted surfaces during processing and handling, risks to cracking, breakage or scuffing with back-pressure conveyance, inconsistencies in flatness for bottoms or dimensions if conveyed or handled with robotics)?
  • Product risks
    • What are the risks to the product in contact with the container-closure system (e.g., extractables, leachables, particulate, adsorption, absorption, oxidation, free radicals)?
  • Product filling risks
    • What are the risks to the filling process (e.g., neck size and targeting risks, container-to-container consistency, loss of container integrity)?
  • Closure risks
    • What are the risks associated with the closing processes (e.g., need to draw vacuum to eliminate air bubbles in multiple-chamber devices, positioning-accuracy requirements, closure insertion challenges and risks, such as friction forces, likelihood of displacement, likelihood of a leak by allowing mixing in a multi-chamber device, laser septum-sealing integrity)?
  • Transport risks
    • What are the atypical risks during transport that are the result of the unique design or functional specifications of the container-closure system (e.g., wandering of stoppers due to lowered cabin pressure, residual air bubbles causing stopper movement during air shipment)?
  • Complexity of IPC sampling, testing, and associated reject management
    • What are the requirements for IPC to ensure that individual units/chambers within a unit are each filled to the correct volume and sealed properly (e.g., IPC inspection points may be required after each filling action and each closure placement, necessitating different strategies for segregation and rejection at multiple IPC points)?
  • Aseptic process simulation complexity
    • What will the APS design include to ensure that the appropriate surfaces are wetted and that each portion of a multi-stage fill process is evaluated (e.g., multi-chamber containers need to ensure that each portion of the container is appropriately challenged during APS)?
  • Post-fill inspection complexity
    • What will the inspection sequence require for machine and personnel training, qualification, and performance (e.g., numbers and types of defects, number of inspections required, different inspection conditions for different portions, different inspection conditions for different elastomer positions)?
"These factors, and more, should be carefully considered when looking to implement a novel container-closure system."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Extractables vs. Leachables:

  • Extractables: chemicals extracted from container materials under extreme laboratory conditions (e.g., high temperature, strong solvents); they represent the "worst case" list of potential contaminants.
  • Leachables: substances that migrate naturally into the product under actual storage and use conditions; they are the real quality risk affecting patient safety.
  • Relationship between the two: E/L studies are a standard regulatory expectation, and leachables are always a subset of extractables.

Complexity of IPC (in-process control) in multi-chamber containers: a traditional single-chamber vial needs only one weight or volume check after filling. In a multi-chamber container, each chamber needs independent verification of fill volume and closure integrity, so IPC sampling points multiply and the reject management strategy must be redesigned.

APS (aseptic process simulation): commonly called "media fill", it is the key tool for validating the entire aseptic process. For multi-chamber containers, the APS must ensure that every surface of every chamber is wetted by the media, which makes validation far more difficult than for conventional containers.

Analogy

Stopper drift during transport: imagine a bottle of sparkling water in an aircraft cargo hold: the low pressure at altitude may make the cap swell and loosen. Likewise, if air remains in a multi-chamber vial, the air bubble expands under the low-pressure conditions of air transport and can push the stopper out of position, causing container closure failure or premature mixing of the liquids in different chambers. Designers of advanced containers must solve this problem at the engineering level.

Complexity of post-fill inspection: like a quality inspector who must check a luxury suitcase with three compartments at the same time, confirming that each compartment is undamaged, free of foreign matter and has a working zipper. Each chamber of a multi-chamber container has different visual defect criteria and different optical conditions, so the training and qualification workload is a multiple of that for conventional containers.

Key Notes

These eight risk dimensions are the standard framework for evaluating advanced containers: the next time a client brings an "innovative container" request, use this eight-dimension framework to assess it systematically: supply, handling, orienting, general handling, product compatibility, filling, closing and transport, covering the full life cycle from component to shelf.

APS complexity is the core challenge: there is no ready-made template for APS design for multi-chamber containers. It must be customized to the container geometry and often needs longer duration and more batches to build sufficient statistical confidence. This directly affects the commercialization timeline and the validation cost budget.

Personnel qualification for post-fill inspection: stoppers in different chamber positions look different during visual inspection, so independent training and qualification procedures are needed for each defect pattern, greatly increasing QC resource demand.

Eight-Dimension Risk Framework for Evaluating Advanced Containers

Risk assessment matrix for novel container-closure systems:

Dimension         | Key question
-----------------|----------------------------------
1. Supply chain  | Number of suppliers, RTU vs on-site preparation
2. Handling      | Feeding method, conveying mechanism compatibility
3. Orienting     | Particle risk, deformation risk, friction
4. General handling | Surface scratching, breakage, robot gripping accuracy
5. Product compatibility | Extractables/Leachables, adsorption/absorption
6. Filling process | Container mouth positioning, consistency, integrity
7. Closing process | Vacuum requirement, friction, leakage risk
8. Transport     | Stopper drift caused by pressure changes

+ IPC sampling strategy design
+ APS design for multi-chamber validation
+ Post-fill inspection qualification plan

Practical Application

A biotech company commissions your CDMO to fill its dual-chamber autoinjector. The drug is a lyophilized powder and the diluent is water for injection; the two are stored separately in the chambers and mixed automatically at administration.

Your assessment plan should include:

  • Supply chain: confirm whether the autoinjector supplier offers an RTU format, and qualify a backup supplier.
  • Filling: the two chambers need separate filling stations, and the filling needle must be compatible with the chamber geometry.
  • Closing: the two ends use different closing mechanisms (a lyophilization stopper at the lyophilized end and a plunger at the diluent end), requiring two closing stations.
  • IPC: each chamber needs its own IPC sampling point after filling, and the reject segregation strategy must consider the results of both chambers together.
  • APS: media must be filled into the two chambers separately, and it must be verified that the mixing mechanism does not cause cross-contamination.
  • Transport: perform an air transport simulation test to confirm that the stoppers at both ends do not drift under low-pressure conditions.

Only if this assessment is started 18 months before commercialization is there enough time to resolve equipment compatibility issues and avoid delayed delivery of clinical trial material.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the difference between extractables and leachables? Why must both be studied rather than only one of them?
  2. Why is the APS design for multi-chamber containers more complex than for conventional single-chamber vials? List at least three additional considerations.
  3. What unique physical challenges does air transport pose for advanced container-closure systems? How can they be addressed at the engineering design level?

Section Summary

  • The core drivers of advanced container-closure design are "improving sterility assurance (SA)", "extending shelf life" and "improving patient use safety", not mere commercial convenience. This is fully consistent with the decision hierarchy of this guide: SA first, CQA second, commercial convenience third.
  • Early supplier involvement is a prerequisite for the successful introduction of novel container-closure systems. Equipment design and component design must proceed in parallel, and any late modification is costly.
  • The complexity of advanced container-closure systems is multiplicative: each additional chamber or function multiplies the complexity of IPC sampling points, APS validation design, post-fill inspection training and supply chain management, so the resource commitment must be fully considered at the start of project planning.
  • The eight-dimension risk assessment framework (supply, handling, orienting, general handling, product compatibility, filling, closing, transport), together with the three process aspects of IPC, APS and post-fill inspection, is a systematic tool for evaluating any novel container-closure system, applicable to CDMO feasibility assessments and client proposal scenarios.
  • Extractables/leachables (E/L) studies are a regulatory necessity and must be started early in product development, so that compatibility problems are not discovered only before the marketing application, causing major delays.

7.2

Elastomers — Selection Drivers & Stopper Types

Drivers of Elastomer Selection and Closure Styles (p118-p120)

7.2 Elastomers (Closures for Parenteral Containers)

The selection of an appropriate elastomer is primarily driven by:

  • Shape and size suitable to provide the necessary CCI (container closure integrity — e.g., egress or ingress of product or contaminants) for the selected container while also suitable for the process (e.g., lyophile stoppers)
  • Material of construction or coating (or absence of coatings) so the elastomer is chemically compatible with the product over its entire shelf life (i.e., stability), with minimal extractables or leachables
  • Low particle burden (upon supply, after processing including sterilization, and/or resistance to coring when penetrated by a syringe needle for multi-use vials or cartridges)
  • Suitable breakaway force and glide force for reproducible and smooth plunger actuation (syringes and cartridges only) to ensure trouble-free patient administration and, for multi-use containers, delivered dose accuracy

Analysis and Commentary

The Four Key Drivers of Elastomer Selection

When selecting a stopper, think in terms of the decision hierarchy:

  • CCI (Container Closure Integrity) - prevents microbial contamination from entering (sterility assurance #1)
  • Chemical compatibility - extractables and leachables affect product stability (CQAs #2)
  • Low particulate burden - especially for multi-dose vials, where repeated needle punctures create a risk of coring (rubber fragments)
  • Breakaway force / glide force - applies only to syringes and cartridges; affects dose accuracy and the patient's user experience (CQAs #2)

Terminology: Extractables vs. Leachables

  • Extractables: compounds released from the elastomer under extreme conditions (high temperature, strong solvents) - a controlled laboratory test
  • Leachables: substances that migrate into the product under actual storage conditions - directly affect patient safety

Regulatory expectation: leachables must stay below the safety threshold throughout the entire shelf life.

Coring Risk - A Threat to Sterility Assurance

Coring: when a needle pierces the rubber, a cut-out fragment of rubber falls into the drug solution. This directly threatens sterility assurance (#1) and the product CQAs (#2). For multi-dose vials, material selection needs particular attention to coring resistance.

Everyday Analogy: Breakaway Force vs. Glide Force

Imagine pulling a rubber plug that is stuck to a wall:

  • Breakaway force: the force needed for the first pull - static friction
  • Glide force: the force needed to keep it moving afterwards - dynamic friction

Both must be within the design range for an autoinjector to deliver the dose accurately.

7.2

Key Styles of Elastomer (Figure 7.2-1🔍) & Advanced Closures

Elastomer Styles A-F and Advanced Closure Systems (p119-p120)

Key Styles of Elastomer (Figure 7.2-1🔍)

Key styles of elastomer include (Figure 7.2-1🔍):

  • A: Serum stoppers (for SVPs — small volume parenterals)
  • B: Infusion stoppers (for LVPs — large volume parenterals)
  • C: Lyophilization stoppers — 2-legged with ribs to permit partial insertion and sublimation pathway
  • D: Cartridge stoppers (also called pistons) — sealing surface along the sides, no flange
  • E: Cartridge disc seals (also called CombiSeals) — elastomeric disc integrated with mechanical aluminum seal
  • F: Syringe stoppers (also called pistons or plungers) — threaded portion on upper surface for plunger rod or autoinjector mounting

Advanced container types may also have corresponding advanced closures (e.g., multi-chamber septa for in situ mixing, multi-chamber septa or plungers for separation of liquids and powders, press-fit or snap cap closures for low temperature applications).

Analysis and Commentary

Quick Comparison of the Six Elastomer Styles

  • A - Serum stopper: used for SVP (small-volume parenterals), e.g. 2 mL / 10 mL vials; the most common type
  • B - Infusion stopper: used for LVP (large-volume parenterals), e.g. 500 mL infusion bottles
  • C - Lyophilization stopper: has two legs + ribs; allows partial insertion so water vapor can escape, then is pressed fully home to seal after lyophilization
  • D - Cartridge stopper / piston: seals on the side, no flange; used in insulin pen injectors
  • E - Cartridge disc seal / CombiSeal: rubber disc and aluminum cap combined in one piece, at the delivery end of the cartridge
  • F - Syringe stopper / plunger: has a threaded recess on the top surface for attaching the plunger rod or autoinjector

Everyday Analogy: The Two-Stage Design of the Lyophilization Stopper

Imagine a cork that has not been pushed all the way into a bottle. The lyophilization stopper (Type C) works the same way: partially inserted = a channel is left so ice can sublime into water vapor and escape. When lyophilization is complete, the shelf presses the stopper fully home, and only then is the container actually sealed. This design directly serves sterility assurance (#1): sealing too early leaves residual moisture that ruins lyophilization quality and indirectly endangers product stability.

Comprehension Check Questions

1. Why does the cartridge stopper (Type D) have no flange, while the syringe stopper (Type F) has a threaded recess? What is the design purpose of each?

2. The CombiSeal (Type E) combines the rubber disc and the aluminum cap. From a sterility assurance standpoint, what are the advantages and disadvantages of this design?

CDMO Application Considerations

At an aseptic fill-finish CDMO, one line may handle vials + prefilled syringes + cartridges (multi-product shared line). When selecting elastomers, commercial flexibility (#3) must be considered at the same time: material SKU management, supplier qualification, and the effect of different stoppers on filling speed.

7.2

Press-fit Closures — Integrity by Design

Press-fit Closures: Integrity by Design (p120)

Press-fit Closures

Press-fit closures are a special closure system where the elastomer is integrated into a polymer cap. The polymer cap has tabs that snap around the vial neck. Claims "integrity by design" because only one process parameter needs to be achieved. Available as both serum and lyophile stoppers.

Lyophile press-fit closures have two seating positions:

  • High position — for sublimation channel (during lyophilization)
  • Fully sealed position — for final container-closure

Cartridge disc seals are a specialty closure for the delivery end of the cartridge; they include an elastomeric disc integrated with a mechanical aluminum seal.

Analysis and Commentary

What "Integrity by Design" Means

A traditional closure requires monitoring several process parameters (crimping force, crimp depth, neck finish dimensional tolerances, etc.), and a deviation in any one of them can lead to a CCI failure.

The design logic of a press-fit closure: polymer tabs snap onto the container neck, so the seal is essentially complete once the closure "clicks" into place, greatly reducing process complexity. This reduces the sterility assurance (#1) risk from "multi-parameter control" to "a single confirmation".

Key Caution: Where Press-fit Applies

Press-fit closures are particularly suited to low temperature applications, because a conventional aluminum crimp cap can lose its seal at very low temperatures as the material contracts. The polymer material of a press-fit closure performs more consistently at low temperatures.

Before use, confirm geometric compatibility with the target container and complete CCI validation (e.g. CCIT - Container Closure Integrity Testing).

Everyday Analogy: Press-fit vs. Conventional Crimping

A conventional aluminum crimp is like using pliers from a toolbox to roll and fix an aluminum cap: you have to adjust the torque, the angle and the jaw gap. A press-fit closure is like a Lego brick: line it up, press down, and a "click" tells you it is done. Process control moves from "tuning many tools" to "confirming a single action".

CDMO Application Considerations

If a customer's product requires low-temperature storage (e.g. an mRNA vaccine at -70°C), a press-fit closure is worth evaluating. But confirm: does the supplier offer a lyophilization version? Has the CCIT method been validated (especially headspace oxygen / helium leak test)? These decisions affect both CCI (#1) and lead time (#3).

7.2

Table 7.2-1🔍: Attributes Impacting Closing System Design

Key Attributes Affecting Closure System Design (p120)

Table 7.2-1🔍: Attributes Impacting Closing Design

Analysis and Commentary

Impact of the Five Key Attributes on CDMO Design

  • Size and shape: bowl parameters must be re-set for each stopper; "twinning" (two stoppers sticking together) is a common problem in volume production and directly affects yield
  • Material and coating: the coefficient of friction of siliconized vs. silicone-free stoppers differs greatly and affects insertion force - confirm this during equipment selection
  • Product requirements: nitrogen (inert gas) overlay vs. vacuum - the hardware requirements of the stoppering station are completely different
  • Batch/campaign details: larger batches = a larger stopper hopper; a high-speed line = a faster sorting system
  • RTU vs. self-processing: RTU stoppers eliminate the washing and sterilization steps (commercial flexibility #3) but cost more

The Twinning Problem - A Process Risk

Twinning: two stoppers lock together while being sorted in the vibratory bowl, interrupting feeding and stopping the machine. How often it occurs depends on the stopper's surface friction and geometry. It should be thoroughly evaluated before commercial process performance qualification (PPQ).

Decision Framework: RTU vs. Self-processing

RTU Stoppers:
  + No washing/siliconization/sterilization steps
  + Less operator intervention (sterility assurance #1)
  + Supplier holds the batch records
  - Higher cost
  - Supplier dependence (commercial flexibility #3)

In-house Processing:
  + Lower cost (large batches)
  + Own control of process parameters
  - Extra equipment and validation required
  - More process steps = more contamination risk
7.3.1

7.3.1 Elastomer Insertion in Vials and Bottles

Elastomer Insertion Technologies for Vials and Glass Bottles (p121-p122)

7.3.1 Elastomer Insertion in Vials and Bottles

The stoppering of vials, whether using serum stoppers or lyophilization stoppers, employs the same technique. After orienting the stopper with the finial or flange facing up and the shank facing down, the stopper is placed in the mouth of the container. This can be performed by vacuum transport, mechanical transport, or friction transfer. The elastomer is then depressed within the neck of the container (using a wheel or vacuum) to ensure a tight land seal.

The stopper insertion technology (mechanical or vacuum) is selected based on line speed, design of closure, and headspace. It is at the point of stopper insertion that evacuation commonly occurs to replace headspace with inert gas.

Automated re-stoppering capability can be added to ensure correctly filled containers are not discarded due to missing stoppers while still under Grade A controls. Raised stopper detection is a common sensor or vision-system integrated into filling lines to ensure correct insertion and no gap between stopper flange and vial landing seal.

For lyophilization stoppers, the shank has "legs" with ribs that enable partial, yet secure, insertion to allow for sublimation. At the conclusion of lyophilization, a vacuum is drawn, inert gas is flooded in, and shelves compress the stoppers.

Analysis and Commentary

The Three Steps of Vial Stoppering

  1. Orientation: finial/flange up, shank down - the vibratory bowl handles the orientation
  2. Placement: vacuum transfer / mechanical transfer / friction transfer places the stopper on the vial opening
  3. Insertion: rollers or vacuum press the stopper into the vial neck, forming the land seal

Land seal: the ring-shaped contact surface between the underside of the stopper flange and the top surface of the vial finish - this is the core of CCI.

Headspace Control - Where Sterility Assurance Meets CQAs

The stoppering station is the key point for headspace management:

  • Inert gas overlay (N₂ / Ar): prevents degradation of oxidation-sensitive products (CQA #2)
  • Vacuum: reduces residual air and improves visibility in subsequent visual inspection (commercial #3)
  • Lyophilization-specific: partial insertion → sublimation → final seating, a three-stage management of seal integrity

Raised Stopper Detection - Vision System Integration

Raised stopper: a stopper that is not fully pressed in, leaving a gap between the flange and the landing zone of the vial finish, which results in CCI failure.

Detection methods: sensors (height detection) or a machine vision system. With an automatic re-stoppering function, the stopper can be corrected in a Grade A environment, avoiding rejection of correctly filled units (commercial flexibility #3).

Everyday Analogy: The Three-Stage Seal of the Lyophilization Stopper

Imagine drying wet laundry outdoors (sublimation = moisture leaving). You first set up the drying rack but do not close it completely, so air can circulate. Once the clothes are dry, you fold the rack fully shut and lock it. The lyophilization stopper follows exactly the same logic: partial insertion (venting) → sublimation complete → vacuum and nitrogen backfill → shelf stoppering (full seal).

7.3.2

7.3.2 Elastomer Insertion in Prefilled Syringes and Cartridges

Elastomer Insertion Technologies for Prefilled Syringes and Cartridges (p122-p124)

7.3.2 Elastomer Insertion in Prefilled Syringes and Cartridges

Stoppers for prefilled syringes and cartridges serve dual roles: protection AND delivery (forced by plunger rod or autoinjector). These elastomers are often uniform in diameter with multiple ribs for leak protection and smooth gliding. Syringe plungers often have cone shape on product-facing side for full expulsion. Upper surface has threaded depression or retention-ring for plunger shaft or autoinjector mounting.

Three Primary Insertion Methods (Figure 7.3.2-1🔍)

  1. Vented (or unvented) mechanical insertion — stopper compressed through annular vent tube; central pin ensures consistent insertion depth using finger flange as reference; leaves minimal residual headspace helpful for swirling at visual inspection
  2. Vacuum insertion (vacuum bell) — placement pin with stopper lowered under vacuum; effectively removes bubble between product and stopper; less precise placement than vented; less precompression (important for coated stoppers); good for viscous products
  3. Vacuum-assisted vented insertion (short or long tube) — combination approach; lower vacuum level for products that cannot withstand deep vacuum; superior bubble removal with more precise elastomer placement

Silicone and fluoropolymers (e.g., Teflon®) are common coatings. Silicone may be prohibited for some protein products as it can induce aggregation. Silicone-free elastomers are commonly inserted using vacuum insertion or short-tube vacuum-assisted vented methods.

Analysis and Commentary

The Dual Role of the Syringe Stopper

A vial stopper only needs to "seal". The stopper of a prefilled syringe or cartridge is responsible for both of the following:

  • Protection: maintains CCI and prevents contamination (sterility assurance #1)
  • Delivery: moves smoothly under the plunger rod to deliver the dose accurately (CQA #2)

For this reason the multiple-rib design of a syringe stopper serves two purposes at once: sealing + low glide force.

The Three Insertion Methods at a Glance

  • Vented insertion: mechanical insertion; the fastest and lowest cost, but poor bubble removal and not suitable for silicone-free stoppers
  • Vacuum insertion (vacuum bell): the stopper is placed under vacuum; the best bubble removal, but lower accuracy, the highest cost and slower speed
  • Vacuum-assisted vented: combines the advantages of both; the short-tube version suits large fill volumes/shallow insertion, and the long-tube version suits small fill volumes/deep insertion

Siliconized vs. Silicone-free - A Key Decision for Protein Products

Silicone oil coatings can induce aggregation of protein drugs (e.g. antibodies, insulin), forming visible or subvisible particles that directly threaten patient safety (CQA #2).

For this reason, high-value biologics typically use:

  • Silicone-free elastomers + Teflon coating
  • Combined with vacuum insertion or short-tube vacuum-assisted vented insertion (vented insertion is not suitable)

Priority of this decision: CQA safety (#2) > commercial speed (#3).

Comprehension Check Questions

1. Why is vented insertion "not effective" for silicone-free stoppers? Explain in terms of friction and the insertion mechanism.

2. Why is the vacuum bell less effective at small fill volumes?

7.3.2

Table 7.3.2-1🔍: Comparison of Vent and Vacuum Insertion Techniques

Full Comparison of Vented vs. Vacuum Insertion Technologies (p124)

How to Select the Insertion Method

Selection is driven by the intersection of three key factors:

  • Stopper coating type — siliconized vs. silicone-free determines eligibility for vented method
  • Fill volume and insertion depth — small fill with deep insertion favors long-tube vacuum-assisted; large fill with shallow insertion favors short-tube or vacuum bell
  • Product characteristics — viscosity influences vacuum technique preference; protein sensitivity to silicone drives coating and method choices simultaneously

Line speed requirements (commercial demand) are a secondary filter applied after the primary technical constraints are satisfied.

Analysis and Decision Commentary

Decision Tree for Selecting the Insertion Method

Step 1: Is it a silicone-free stopper?
  YES → Exclude Vented and Long-tube VA
        → Choose Vacuum Bell or Short-tube VA

Step 2: What is the fill volume?
  Small fill volume (<0.5 mL) → Long-tube VA or Vacuum Bell
  Large fill volume (>1 mL) → Short-tube VA or Vacuum Bell

Step 3: Is the product viscosity high?
  YES → Vacuum Bell or the VA series (mechanical insertion has more difficulty giving uniform coverage)

Step 4: Speed / throughput requirement?
  High speed (>400 spm) → favor Vented or Short-tube VA
  Lower speed acceptable → Vacuum Bell can also be considered

The Bubble Problem - A Pain Point in Visual Inspection

If an air bubble remains after the syringe stopper is inserted:

  • It is easily mistaken for a foreign particle during visual inspection → higher false-reject rate
  • The bubble volume expands with temperature changes → affects dose accuracy (CQA #2)

The core value of the vacuum insertion family is to solve this problem (sterility assurance #1 benefits indirectly, CQA #2 benefits directly).

CDMO Application Considerations: Equipment Selection Strategy

In a CDMO environment that must serve PFS products from several customers at once (different fill volumes, different stopper types), consider the following when selecting equipment:

  • Give priority to Vacuum-Assisted Vented (short tube): it covers siliconized/some silicone-free stoppers, large fill volumes and medium speed, and is the most flexible
  • For a mAb product with a very small fill volume + a silicone-free requirement → evaluate adding a Vacuum Bell module
  • Equipment flexibility (#3) must not come at the expense of sterility assurance (#1): every change of insertion method requires revalidation
●

Section 7A Summary - Key Takeaways

Closing Systems: Elastomers & Insertion Methods

Key Takeaways

  • Elastomer selection is driven by CCI, chemical compatibility (extractables/leachables), particle burden (coring), and force profile (breakaway/glide)
  • Six stopper types (A–F) are each matched to specific container/delivery systems — lyophilization stoppers (C) uniquely require two-stage seating
  • Press-fit closures claim "integrity by design" by reducing multi-parameter sealing to a single snap mechanism — particularly suited to low-temperature applications
  • Three syringe insertion methods differ in cost, speed, vacuum level, and capability with silicone-free stoppers — selection must match stopper coating and fill volume
  • Silicone-free stoppers require vacuum-based insertion and are critical for protein biologics prone to silicone-induced aggregation

Review of the Decision Hierarchy

Applying the Decision Hierarchy in This Section

  • Sterility assurance (#1): CCI is the primary driver of stopper selection; raised stopper detection, the two-stage lyophilization seal, and bubble removal by vacuum insertion all serve this purpose
  • Product CQAs (#2): leachables, siliconization/aggregation issues, breakaway/glide force, and the effect of bubbles on dose - these directly affect patient safety
  • Commercial flexibility (#3): RTU vs. self-processing, insertion method speed, and multi-product equipment compatibility - optimize these only after the first two are secured

Integrated Review Questions

A customer brings a prefilled syringe product for a protein biologic, with a silicone-free stopper and a 0.3 mL fill volume. Consider the following:

  1. Which insertion method should be chosen, and why?
  2. If the customer also demands the highest throughput, how would you communicate the decision hierarchy to them?
  3. What key tests should the validation plan include?
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p126 - p133

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the special design requirements of the cartridge disc seal and why it must be located inside the aseptic boundary
  • Understand the common types of elastomer placement defects and their quality control significance
  • Understand the overall framework and considerations for container-closure integrity (CCI) validation
  • Evaluate closure system design choices using the decision hierarchy (sterility assurance > product CQAs > commercial flexibility)
7.3.2 (Cont.) Insertion Method Comparison & 7.3.3 Common Defects in Elastomer Placement

Original Text

Continuation of Table 7.3.2-1🔍 — Comparison of Insertion Methods (doc p126):

Mechanical insertion may be used for the insertion of stoppers into cartridges from the bottom prior to filling, as shown in Figure 7.3.2-2. In this case, the cartridge is then filled from the top. Whether from the bottom or top, stopper insertion has the same risks and required controls as those compared and contrasted in Table 7.3.2-1.

7.3.3 Common Defects in Elastomer Placement Operations

There are a number of defects that routinely occur with elastomer placement, among them:

  • Incomplete seating (vials) or inconsistent seating position (syringe/cartridge)
  • Disruption or smearing of silicone or fluoropolymer coating on elastomer
  • Wrinkling/distortion of ribs on syringe/cartridge elastomers during placement
  • Liquid in ribs of elastomer for syringes/cartridges, or product under the stopper flange on vials and bottles
  • Damage to plunger (e.g., bending, distortion of ribs)
  • Insufficient control of headspace (air or inert gas)

Many of these defects can be reduced through proper selection and design of the elastomer placement system. However, careful adherence to consistent, validated setup parameters of the insertion system is necessary to maintain quality control. Quality control is also important during the incoming inspection of elastomers to ensure that dimensional tolerances and quality of coatings is maintained.

As a final note, elastomers are subject to an array of testing for extractables and leachables (during initial qualification), as well as chemical and particulate contaminants (with each batch). Container-closure integrity is commonly tested on every batch, with careful adherence to the validated parameters for closing the containers (both with elastomer and mechanical seal) (see Section 7.7). Visual inspection of sterile products includes inspection of the elastomer for abnormal appearance or improper insertion. As a consequence, elastomer placement is an important part of the ongoing quality of the container-closure system and for the overall integrity of the sterile product.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The core trade-off in insertion methods: the four methods are in diagonal conflict across two dimensions:

  • Vented insertion: highly consistent placement, but high compression force makes wrinkling likely
  • Vacuum insertion: low wrinkling risk, but poor placement consistency (especially at deep placement positions)
  • Hybrid (short tube): a compromise, but still shows variability at deep positions
  • Hybrid (long tube): the most accurate placement, but compression risk comparable to vented insertion

Which method to choose depends on the geometry of the specific container and the elastomer specification; there is no one-size-fits-all best solution.

Analogy

Elastomer placement defects are like putting a cork in a bottle:
- Seated too shallow (incomplete seating): the slightest force from the corkscrew lets air leak
- Cork crooked (wrinkling/distortion): looks poor and may even seal incompletely
- Cork wet with wine (liquid in ribs): affects product purity
The difference is that a leaking wine bottle is only a waste, whereas a failed seal on a drug product can endanger a patient's life.

Key Notes

Three lines of defense ensure seal quality:

  1. Incoming inspection: confirm elastomer dimensional tolerances and coating quality
  2. In-process control (IPC): strictly apply the validated set parameters; they must not be adjusted at will
  3. Finished product inspection (visual inspection): screen out visual abnormalities or improper insertion

CCI testing is required for every batch. This is the direct embodiment of "sterility assurance" in the decision hierarchy.

Practice Questions

  1. If your prefilled syringes (PFS) show abnormal results in batch CCI testing, in which directions would you investigate the root cause?
  2. Which product CQA is directly affected by the defect "liquid in ribs of elastomer"?
7.4 Mechanical Seal Application and System Design

Original Text

Mechanical seals are inherent components in many container-closure systems. As with the primary packaging, the choice of mechanical seal will influence the design of the aseptic filling system. The use of more than one mechanical closure type on a line may require flexibility in the closing system design and use but, as with primary containers and closures, the objective is to ensure an integral seal on the container to protect its contents throughout its shelf life.

7.4.1 Mechanical Seal Application

There are specialty closures, such as press-fit caps or cartridge disc seals, that integrate both the elastomer and the mechanical seal in a single closure and, often, a single closing step. However, there are other processes where the mechanical seal is separate from the elastomer and is applied in a dedicated process step.

Mechanical seals for vials and bottles, often called overseals or crimp seals consist of a crimpable "skirt" with either a button, or dust cover (flip seal) over the top of the stopper. These mechanical seals are commonly produced of aluminum or aluminum with a polymer component.

Mechanical seals are specified to be slightly wider and longer than the combined dimensions of the flange or finial of the stopper plus the lip of the container. With these dimensions, they can be placed over top of the stopper, and the skirt of the seal can be folded under the lip of the container to secure them and supply sufficient downward pressure on the elastomer and glass to seal. A similar mechanical seal is commonly applied to cartridges.

Mechanical seals come in several common designs:

  • Flip-off – Has a removable button (often polymer) that can be detached to expose the stopper underneath during administration while leaving the aluminum skirt in place, which continues to secure the stopper on the container; this is the most common crimp seal for vials that are intended for syringe administration
  • Flip-up/tear-off – Has a button that, when flipped up, is used to help tear off the aluminum skirt so the stopper can be removed; not used for parenteral applications but may be used for ophthalmic solutions
  • Flip-off/tear-off – Offers the combination of features of the first two mechanical seal types, allowing access to the stopper only to remove the aluminum skirt; this is not used for parenteral applications, but may be used for sterile fluids that are used in testing settings
  • Center-tear seal – Usually all aluminum, these seals are most like the flip-off seal but, in this case, the center tab of aluminum is integrated with the aluminum skirt and can be lifted and removed for access to the center of the stopper flange while leaving the skirt in place; although intended for syringe administration, the risk of glove tears with the aluminum tab reduces the frequency that this design is used
  • Complete-tear crimp seal – Like the center-tear seal, these are all aluminum, however, when the center tab is lifted, it can be used to remove the entire crimp seal from the container; like the flip-up/tear-off seal, this is not used for parenteral applications

Mechanical seals are expected to be applied under Grade A air supply (at minimum) that is contiguous with the filling line. Some systems include the mechanical seal application within the Grade A cleanroom or isolator adjacent to the filling station. Whether within the cleanroom, isolator, or supplied with Grade A air supply the intent is to ensure the protection of fully stoppered vials where the mechanical seal has not yet been crimped. The mechanical seals are not required to be sterile, although in some applications they may be rendered sterile. The process of forming the aluminum around the lip of the container may generate significant particulate (as does the rapid spinning of the sealing machine). Therefore, the sealing equipment for vials is often separated from the rest of the filling line by having a physical barrier (often with a mousehole) in between the stoppering and seal placement sections of a filling machine within a RABS or isolator.

"Successful sealing station design will depend upon advanced knowledge of those elements described in Table 7.4.1-1."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Five designs of mechanical seals:

  • Flip-off: the most common and the mainstream for injectable vials. The plastic cap is removed to expose the stopper, and the aluminum skirt stays on to keep the stopper secured
  • Flip-up/tear-off: suitable for eye drops; not for injectables
  • Flip-off/tear-off (combination): for sterile test solutions; not for injectables
  • Center-tear: designed to be injectable, but with a high risk of aluminum tearing (risk of glove damage)
  • Complete-tear: the entire aluminum cap can be removed; not for injectables

Key judgment: for anything "parenteral", almost only the flip-off design is used.

Analogy

An aluminum seal is like the pull tab on a beverage can: different situations need different ways of opening.
- A nurse drawing up a drug with a syringe: flip-off (lift off the cap without removing the aluminum skirt, to prevent contamination)
- Pouring eye drops: tear-off (tear the cap off directly)
A design error is not just inconvenient; it can cause aluminum particle contamination and needle-stick injuries.

Key Notes

Particulate generation during crimping is a high-risk point:

During crimping, aluminum seals are spun at high speed, generating a large amount of aluminum particulates. This directly threatens the grade A cleanliness of the filling area. Solution: install a mousehole (a small physical partition) between the crimping station and the filling station, which lets vials pass through while blocking particulate spread. This is a typical case of the "sterility assurance > commercial efficiency" decision.

Note: the mechanical seal itself does not need to be sterilized, but if it is placed inside an isolator, it must be handled through the decontamination process.

Practice Questions

  1. Your customer asks for the same line to produce two different sizes of flip-off seals. What additional requirements does this place on the closure system design?
  2. If the crimping station is located inside a RABS, what factors must be considered in the design of the mousehole?
Table 7.4.1-1🔍 Attributes Impacting Sealing System Design (doc p130)🔍

Original Text

"The sealing station is considered to contribute to the CCI, which is a CQA; therefore, the equipment must be qualified, calibrated, and maintained in accordance with strict standards. Routine testing during setup should be performed to ensure that completed seals deliver integral units that are shown to be defect-free (e.g., no missing caps, no wrinkles in crimped skirt, no loose seals). Visual inspection of finished pharmaceuticals will also inspect the mechanical seals to check for, and cull, any sealing defects."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three main drivers of crimping station design:

  • Seal size and shape: determines the specification of the sorting bowl; "twinning" (one seal nesting inside another) is a common fault that requires special vibration or sensing design to eliminate
  • Batch size and line speed: the crimper is usually faster than the filler so that it does not become a production bottleneck; large batches need a large-capacity feed hopper to reduce the number of refills
  • Method of introduction: inside an isolator, the seals must be sterile; outside an isolator, only grade A airflow protection is needed

Formula

Crimping system speed planning:

Crimping system speed > filling speed
(typically 10-20% higher, so that filling never waits for crimping)

Sorting bowl capacity estimate:
Bowl capacity = target continuous run time (min) × filling speed (vials/min) × safety factor (1.2-1.5)

Example: filling speed 300 vials/min, target 30 minutes without refilling
→ bowl capacity ≥ 300 × 30 × 1.3 ≈ 11,700 seals

Key Notes

CCI is a CQA, and the crimping station is equipment, not an option: the text states explicitly that the "sealing station is considered to contribute to CCI, which is a CQA". This means:

  • The crimping equipment must undergo IQ/OQ/PQ qualification
  • Routine confirmation after setup (no missing caps, no wrinkles, no loose seals)
  • 100% screening of seal defects by finished product visual inspection

Any seal defect is a batch risk, not a cosmetic issue that can be ignored.

7.4.2 Mechanical Seals Applied to Nested Containers

Original Text

Nested containers may be de-nested for the application of mechanical seals. This is the traditional approach for closing nested containers.

Special systems are available where the mechanical sealing is conducted while the containers are within the nest. These systems can be used with press-fit caps or integrated stopper-seal combinations, which are also in a type of nest or plate that matches the configuration of the vial or syringe nest below. For these systems, the nest must remain separate from the tub to permit sufficient space between the tops of the containers, and a special sealing head descends to close all of the containers at once. The risk with this type of closure of a full nest of containers at one time is ensuring that each individual container has had sufficient force to fulfill the closing specifications, thereby assuring CCI.

Innovations continue to be made with both containers and closures, therefore, additional features and capabilities may also become available (see Section 6.0).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Two ways of sealing nested containers:

  • Conventional (de-nested): containers are first removed from the nest and then crimped. The process is clear and the equipment is mature
  • Whole-batch simultaneous crimping (in-nest): a special crimping head seals an entire tray at once (for example 6 × 4 = 24 containers). It is efficient, but it must be ensured that every container receives sufficient force

Challenge of in-nest crimping: if one container is at the low end of its height tolerance, the force of the crimping head is unevenly distributed, and some containers may be under-sealed (CCI failure). This is a worst case that process validation must evaluate.

Analogy

Whole-batch simultaneous crimping is like a factory press stamping a whole row of parts at once: efficiency multiplies, but if one part is too thin, the force is transferred to the neighboring parts, leaving some over-pressed and some under-pressed. "Uniform force application" is therefore the core engineering validation challenge.

Key Notes

CCI validation of the in-nest crimping method must consider the force uniformity at all positions in the nest (corner vs center). The validation samples must include containers from the worst-case positions (usually corners or edges) to ensure that the whole batch meets the seal specification.

7.5 Cartridge Disc Seal Application and System Design Considerations

Original Text

Cartridge disc seals (also called lined seals) consist of a flat elastomeric disc that is integrated with an aluminum seal (see item E of Figure 7.2-1🔍). These combination closures are applied in a single step.

As the elastomer is applied at the same time as the seal, these combination closures need to be fully sterilized before application, and the location of the sealing equipment will also need to be within the aseptic boundary; it should be close to the point of fill in order to reduce the duration of exposure of the open container to the environment.

Different crimping processes are used, depending on the system procured; however, all systems have a high risk of particulate near the critical filling station due to the particle-generation at the crimping station. As a result, some specific precautions should be considered:

  • Airflow should be designed to ensure that no air from the crimping station will move toward the filling station.
  • Crimping technology should be designed to minimize the generation of particles (e.g., minimizing the shear of blades over the metal seal, using seals that minimize particle-generation during crimping).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Special features of the cartridge disc seal (lined seal):

Unlike a standard seal, the cartridge disc seal integrates an elastomer disc with the aluminum cap, so a single crimping operation completes the seal. This has two key implications:

  • It must be pre-sterilized: the elastomer is part of the aseptic boundary, so the whole seal assembly must be sterilized before use (unlike a standard aluminum cap, which only needs grade A protection)
  • The equipment must be inside the aseptic boundary: the crimper itself must be placed inside the isolator or the aseptic zone of the filling station, as close to the filling point as possible

Analogy

A standard crimping process is like first placing the cork and then fastening it with a wire cage (two steps). The cartridge disc seal is like a "one-piece quick-close cap": the elastomer liner is already pressed into the metal cap, and one action completes the seal. This is convenient, but because the cap itself is part of the seal, it must be sterile.

Key Notes

Particle control is the core challenge of the cartridge disc seal: crimping generates particulates (aluminum shavings), and the crimper must be located near the filling station (or even inside the aseptic zone). Solutions:

  • Airflow design: ensure the airflow at the crimping station flows "away from the filling station" (unidirectional flow from the filling station toward the crimping station)
  • Low-particulate crimping technology: choose a crimper that minimizes blade shearing, and choose seal materials that shed little dust when crimped

This is a direct embodiment of the "sterility assurance > commercial convenience" decision hierarchy in hardware design.

Practice Questions

  1. If a customer asks you to add a cartridge disc seal crimper to an existing RABS filling line, which key environmental control modifications must you evaluate?
  2. What sterilization options are usually available for cartridge disc seals, and what are the limitations of each?
7.6 Container and Closure Defects

Original Text

PDA's Technical Report No. 76: Identification and Classification of Visible Nonconformities in Elastomeric Components and Aluminum Seals for Parenteral Packaging and Technical Report No. 43 (Revised 2023): Identification and Classification of Nonconformities in Molded and Tubular Glass Containers for Pharmaceutical Manufacturing: Covering Ampoules, Bottles, Cartridges, Syringes and Vials provide more detailed information on the most common quality defects for container-closures and for glass.

Defects or damage that occur on the line to either component can result in failed package integrity as discussed in Section 7.7.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

PDA defect classification technical reports:

  • TR76: classification of visible nonconformities of elastomeric components and aluminum seals
  • TR43 (revised 2023): classification of nonconformities of glass containers (ampoules, bottles, cartridges, syringes, vials)

These two technical reports are important external references for visual inspection standards. When establishing SOPs and preparing for audits, confirm that in-house standards are consistent with the PDA guidance.

Key Notes

"Defects or damage occurring on the line → may lead to package integrity failure": this causal relationship explains why every step in the process (denesting, transfer, stoppering, crimping) needs in-process control.
Any defect in a container or closure can be directly linked to the CCI failures discussed in Section 7.7. Defect management must not be dismissed as a "cosmetic issue".

7.7 Requirements for Effective Container-Closure Integrity and Validation

Original Text

The goal of CCI validation is to ensure that integrity can first be established in packaging development studies and, subsequently, can be tested and confirmed with the actual manufacturing equipment and intended process parameters to fully demonstrate process control, thereby providing integrity assurance.

When performing CCI assessments, the selection of manufacturing conditions should include worst-case factors impacting CCI characteristics. Additionally, variability in the manufacture of each of the primary components must be considered and represented in such assessments.

The following are common considerations that may impact component characteristics, and resultant closure integrity, that should be evaluated during development studies for each supplier (as applicable to the selected container-closure system):

  • Component fit for integrity — Stacked dimensional tolerances
  • Inherent-component CCI — Ensures a container system can provide the appropriate level of tightness for the intended application, for instance, maintaining a modified headspace or vacuum throughout the shelf life
  • Performance with intended capping force or residual seal force
  • Raised stopper threshold
  • Multi-puncture closures and limited microbial ingress and product leakage between doses
  • Plunger-insertion depth and critical bubble-size to support maintenance of sterility during shipment and transportation
  • Utilization with semiautomatic dosing pens that require minimal priming
  • Headspace maintenance for lyophilized and inert-gas overlay product
  • Cold-storage performance and maintenance of integrity under cold-storage conditions below the material properties (i.e., glass transition temperature) for elastomers
  • Freeze-thaw/thermal-cycling performance, for example:
    • Freeze-thaw impact on fragile containers (e.g., bags)
    • Impact to integrity of mechanical closures (e.g., threaded caps, snap caps) upon thermal-cycling
  • Carbon dioxide (CO2) ingress, if transported or stored with dry ice
  • Maintenance of closure over time and transport, including relaxation over time under the proposed storage conditions, and impact of transport (e.g., shock and vibration, pressure change in headspace due to altitude/temperature)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The two phases of container-closure integrity validation:

  1. Development studies: establish the integrity baseline during package development and explore various worst-case factors
  2. Process confirmation: use actual commercial-scale equipment and process parameters to confirm that production on the line can consistently meet integrity requirements

Both phases are indispensable. The development phase builds knowledge, and the process phase turns it into control.

Analogy

CCI validation is like safety testing for building a bridge:
- Development studies = in the laboratory, test a model bridge under various worst-case loads (simulated earthquakes, typhoons, overweight vehicles)
- Process confirmation = after the real bridge is built, run load tests on it to confirm that the construction process introduced no new defects
Together they ensure that the bridge (the drug package) will not collapse (lose its seal) throughout its entire service life.

Key Notes

Twelve development study considerations, with broad coverage:

Pay particular attention to the following items, which are easily overlooked:

  • Stacked dimensional tolerances: the container and the closure may each be within tolerance, but the "worst-case combination" can result in insufficient CCI
  • Cold storage / glass transition temperature: elastomers harden at low temperatures and sealing force drops; cold chain products must be verified for seal integrity at -80°C or lower
  • CO₂ ingress (dry ice shipping): CO₂ can permeate certain elastomers and affect the headspace composition of lyophilized products
  • Relaxation over time (elastomer relaxation): products with a long shelf life (5-10 years) require evaluation of the creep behavior of the elastomer under storage compression

Practice Questions

  1. You are developing a lyophilized protein product stored at -20°C with a target shelf life of 3 years. List the top five considerations that CCI development studies should evaluate first, and explain why.
  2. If a supplier provides two elastomer batches of the "same specification", does CCI validation still need to test them separately? Why?
7.7 (Cont.) General Considerations for CCI Evaluation (doc p132-p133)

Original Text

Once development work has been completed, the following are general considerations for inclusion in CCI evaluations:

  • Multiple primary component-batch combinations — To account for batch-to-batch component variability, validation samples should consider multiple (e.g., three) unique component-batch combinations from each supplier where each combination of components consists of a unique pairing (e.g., stopper batch "A" with vial batch "A," stopper batch "B" with vial batch "A," stopper batch "B" with vial batch "B").
  • Alternate component suppliers/sources — If multiple suppliers/sources are used for a single component, where an "identical" version of that component exists, CCI testing using components from each supplier/source should be considered. This approach is commonly applicable to components using identical dimensional specifications and material types. In these cases, the vendor must first affirm that they have qualified their fabrication processes. The supplier's qualification of components is a complex and separate exercise because, depending on the technology chosen, the supplier must be shown to qualify different fabrication lines on which they might produce the same component, for example:
    • Glass forming equipment
    • Needle insertion equipment
    • Open mills, mixers, molds, and presses for polymers
    • Crimp seals aluminum forming and assembly with either polymers or flip-off tops
  • Preparation — The impact of preparation processes that precede the filling operation (e.g., cleaning, sterilization) needs to be evaluated. These may be at the vendors, in the case of RTU components, at the filling site, or both, in the case of ready-to-sterilize (RTS) components.
  • Closing process — The aseptic filling line intended for routine production of the final package configuration should be used to generate the validation test samples. Process parameters impacting closure integrity should be identified prior to initiating CCI activities, with the intended production parameters used to generate validation test samples. Where a parameter is variable or has a range, the range should be supported by validation testing. For example, for vials, the capper testing should consider performing CCI testing at high, medium, and low application-force settings when variable forces may be applied during production setup and operation.
  • Manufacturing conditions — Test samples should represent the complete sequence of the final commercial process, including component cleaning and sterilization. In addition, terminally sterilized products would require test samples to be processed through the entire terminal-sterilization operation before testing.
  • Storage conditions and shelf life — CCI validation should consider the intended storage conditions of filled product containers, which are typically supported by development activities. All manufacturing conditions, including storage intervals where filled containers are held for a predefined period prior to final sealing operations, should be incorporated into the CCI validation study.
  • Packaging and secondary assembly — CCI and the impact of closure characteristics should be considered for additional processing steps following primary container-sealing and can include technical assessment or direct testing. Typically, the impact from the labeling and packaging of vials does not require additional CCI testing; however, the secondary assembly of plunger rod or safety devices and their incorporation into the final device delivery system can present risks requiring additional CCI evaluation.
  • Shipping and transport — Evidence that a container-closure system maintains integrity throughout shipping and distribution is expected. This can be achieved by either testing a container-closure system that has undergone actual or simulated shipping, or by providing robust evidence within a validation assessment that builds on the knowledge from development and CCI-validation activities and focuses on failure modes specific to shipping and transport. If shipping-and-transport CCI-testing is executed, it is typically a separate study from the filling-line CCI validation.
  • Vial-stopper and syringes — These do not typically benefit from additional CCI testing following shipping and transport if worst-case conditions have already been characterized in development and are demonstrated to be comparable or worse than the conditions experienced during shipment, for example:
    • Worst-case pressures via tests (e.g., helium leak, dye ingress, vacuum decay)
    • Plunger-movement characterization studies for syringes
    • Maintenance of headspace on cold storage
    • Resistance of CO2 ingress from dry-ice exposure

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Nine evaluation aspects of CCI validation:

  1. Multiple batch combinations: at least three unique batch pairings, covering batch-to-batch variability
  2. Multiple suppliers: "same specification" does not mean "same CCI"; each supplier must be tested separately
  3. Preparation: the cleaning and sterilization method of RTU vs RTS components affects CCI
  4. Sealing process: high/medium/low force settings must all be validated for CCI, covering the operating range
  5. Manufacturing conditions: the complete commercial process sequence must be replicated, including terminal sterilization
  6. Storage conditions and shelf life: include the time window of intermediate storage after filling
  7. Secondary assembly: assembly of plunger rods and safety devices may affect CCI
  8. Shipping: simulated or actual shipping tests, usually a separate study
  9. Vials/syringes: if the development studies already cover worst-case conditions, shipping CCI need not be repeated

Formula

CCI validation batch combination planning (vial + stopper as an example):

Minimum number of combinations = number of suppliers (stopper) × number of suppliers (vial) × 3 batches
Example: 2 stopper suppliers × 1 vial supplier × 3 batches
= 6 unique pairings

Crimping force test matrix (closing process CPP):
     Low force | Mid force | High force
Batch A  CCI  CCI   CCI
Batch B  CCI  CCI   CCI
Batch C  CCI  CCI   CCI
→ 9 test condition points

Key Notes

"Supplier qualification" and "CCI validation" are two separate things:

Even if the supplier has completed qualification of its manufacturing equipment (supplier qualification), the filler still needs to perform its own CCI validation. The reason: the supplier confirms that it "manufactures components that meet specification", whereas the filler verifies that "these components, combined with its own filling equipment and process, can maintain seal integrity". These are entirely different validation objectives.

Regulators (FDA, EMA) expect to see separate documentation for the two; they must not be merged.

Practical Application

CDMO scenario: your customer brings a new lyophilized antibody drug product (stored at -80°C, 3-year shelf life, with an injection safety device) and plans to use two vial suppliers (2 batches each) and one elastomer supplier (3 batches). Draft an initial CCI validation matrix:

  • Batch pairings: 2 vial suppliers × 3 stopper batches = 6 combinations
  • Crimping force: high/medium/low × 6 combinations = 18 process conditions
  • Additional evaluations: CCI at -80°C cold storage, shipping simulation (separate study), CCI after safety device assembly
  • Storage time points: initial, 6 months, 12 months, 24 months, 36 months (covering the full shelf life)

Although this matrix is large, missing any part of it may lead to supplementary studies being requested during FDA/EMA review, delaying the time to market.

Practice Questions

  1. What steps does the "complete sequence of the final commercial process" specifically include? For a lyophilized product, should CCI sampling time points be before lyophilization, after it, or both?
  2. If your PFS shows partial CCI failures after shipping simulation testing, but all on-line filling validation passed, what action would you take next?
  3. "For vials/syringes, shipping CCI testing may be omitted if the development studies already cover worst-case conditions." In what situations would the worst case of the development studies be insufficient to cover actual shipping conditions?

Section Summary (7.5+, doc p126-p133)

  • Three lines of defense for elastomer placement defects: incoming inspection (dimensional tolerances and coating), execution of validated parameters in process, and finished product visual inspection plus batch CCI testing; none of the three can be omitted
  • Mechanical seal design choice: injectable vials almost exclusively use the flip-off design; the crimping station generates a large amount of particulates, so a mousehole must physically isolate and protect the filling area, with grade A airflow as the minimum requirement
  • Dual requirements of the cartridge disc seal: elastomer and aluminum cap are integrated → the whole seal assembly must be pre-sterilized + the crimping equipment must be inside the aseptic boundary, and the airflow design must ensure particulates do not flow back to the filling station
  • Risk of whole-batch crimping of nested containers: verify that every container (especially at corner and edge positions) receives sufficient sealing force, to ensure CCI uniformity across the whole batch
  • Two-phase CCI validation framework: development studies (explore worst cases) → process confirmation (actual equipment and parameters); the nine evaluation aspects cover multiple batch combinations, multiple suppliers, preparation, sealing process, storage, shipping, and secondary assembly
  • The decision hierarchy runs through the whole section: sterility assurance (CCI = the core safeguard of sterility assurance) always takes priority over commercial flexibility, and no simplification of a closure system design may come at the expense of CCI
8

Section 8: Operational

p134-p152

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p134 - p140

Learning Objectives

  • Understand why microbial risk control is central to aseptic filling operations, and why every intervention must be approached with the goal of reducing contamination risk
  • Understand the key differences between RABS and isolators in the line setup process, including the sequencing logic for establishing the Grade A environment
  • Understand the significance of classifying parts as direct product contact, indirect product contact and non-contact, and how this affects the sterility protection strategy
  • Understand the general considerations for aseptic interventions in Section 8.2, including SOP requirements, personnel qualification and airflow visualization studies
  • Understand how filter changes are handled under different system designs and how they affect batch integrity
8.0 Microbiological Risks for System Operation

Original Text

Contamination control is the primary objective in aseptic filling. In Section 1.0, it was highlighted that the goal of producing a sterile product must remain the target in all design decisions and trade-offs. Successful operation of an aseptic filling system cannot be achieved without considering and mitigating microbiological risks and operating with good aseptic technique.

As a consequence, during design when looking ahead to the operation of any filling line, consideration should be given to the types of interventions that will be required to accomplish the fill. Interventions should be minimized or eliminated by proper design and effective risk assessments of the entire filling system including personnel and material flows, and changeover complexity.
