The aseptic system design should be adapted to ensure effective microbiological control during all phases of the operation for both inherent and corrective interventions that are required after the risk assessment and mitigation are successfully concluded.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Inherent Interventions: Interventions that are expected to occur during normal operation, such as routine adjustment of fill needle position or clearing of container jams. These can be anticipated at the design stage.

Corrective Interventions: Interventions that occur on an ad hoc basis because of equipment malfunction or operator deviation, such as opening a door to repair a sudden machine breakdown. These carry higher risk because they are not fully anticipated.

Aseptic Technique: A set of operating rules covering personnel behavior, manner of movement and interaction with the environment, intended to ensure that no contamination is introduced during operations. This is not only a technical matter but also a behavioral discipline.

Analogy

Think of an aseptic filling line as a surgical operation. Every action during surgery (disinfection before the incision, the way instruments are handed over, the checks before suturing) is an "intervention". The design of the operating room itself (traffic flow, airflow, lighting position) exists to keep the risk as low as possible when these interventions take place. The core message of Section 8.0 is: the purpose of design is to minimize the number and risk of future operational interventions.

Key Notes

This section states explicitly that "contamination control is the primary objective of aseptic filling", which is fully consistent with the decision hierarchy: sterility assurance always ranks first.

The best strategy for interventions is not to "deal with them when they happen" but to "design so that they do not happen". Regulators (FDA, EU GMP Annex 1) both emphasize identifying and reducing interventions at the design stage.

Practice Questions

  1. Why are inherent interventions easier to manage from a risk management standpoint than corrective interventions?
  2. If a line design requires very frequent interventions to complete filling, what does that say about the design?
8.1 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Associated with Line Setup

Original Text

Line setup (LSU) is an important part of the filling process because of the extent of operator interaction and potential to introduce contamination. Line setup can only occur after line clearance from the prior campaign or batch is complete. Parts to be sterilized out-of-place will have been removed at the conclusion of the campaign or batch. Those parts are subject to cleaning, pre-assembly (if any), and off-line sterilization in appropriate wraps and bags and are then staged for setup. The next step is preparation of the stationary parts of the filling line for setup.

Note: Since campaigns may also include setup during the campaign (between batches) this will be addressed in Section 8.1.2 as it has some additional considerations.

For isolators, preparation includes surface cleaning (and often manual disinfection) of the barrier and non-contact surfaces of the filling and closing machine prior to installation of the sterilized parts under unidirectional airflow within the barrier. This will be followed by closing the barrier and an automated 6-log sporicidal biodecontamination process (e.g., VPHP) that will be applied to establish Grade A conditions. Importantly, Grade A is established after the sterilized parts are installed and this approach is in variance to RABS.

For RABS, Grade A conditions need to be established via a combination of cleaning and sporicidal 6-log high-level disinfection before sterilized parts are installed. In RABS, following this preparation stage the filling line will be ready for starting the aseptic line setup ahead of aseptic filling operations.

The detailed steps for setup in both isolators and RABS are described below (see Section 8.1.1), however some definitions are required to ensure common understanding of the detailed steps. The parts to be installed during the setup stage can be divided into three groups:

  • Non-product contact parts include format parts such as feed screws, star wheels, container transport mechanisms that make no direct contact with sterile products to be filled.
  • Indirect product contact parts include parts such as vibratory feeders and feed bowls which touch the sterile primary packaging components and therefore represent a risk of indirectly transferring contamination to the sterile product.
  • Product contact parts include parts such as fluid pathway, filling needles and other surfaces which are in direct contact with the sterile product and any direct contact gas overlay parts.

Some non-product contact parts may be removed, cleaned, returned to the line and disinfected in place with the rest of the stationary parts of the equipment and the barrier rather than being sterilized off-line.

Both direct and indirect product contact parts have the potential to compromise product sterility, quality, and patient safety so precautions should always be taken to protect any part in these two groups from particle and microbial contamination. Therefore, when preparing these parts off-line prior to setup, care must be taken in their washing and sterilization. The parts must be dried and wrapped or bagged after cleaning before sterilization. The wraps must remain intact until the time of their installation as it is a vital part of their protection as they are transferred from the preparations area to the filling line.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Line Setup (LSU): The process of installing sterilized parts on the filling machine before the start of each batch or campaign. This is one of the highest-risk stages for introducing contamination because it involves the most personnel interaction.

VPHP (vaporized hydrogen peroxide): The standard method for biodecontamination of isolators. Achieving a 6-log spore reduction is the key criterion for establishing Grade A conditions.

Three part categories:

  • Non-contact parts: lowest risk, can be disinfected in place
  • Indirect contact parts: medium risk, touch sterilized wrapping materials
  • Direct contact parts: highest risk, come into direct contact with sterile product

Analogy

Imagine preparing surgical instruments for a patient. The scalpel (direct contact), the forceps used to pass the scalpel (indirect contact) and the metal frame of the operating table (non-contact) all need different levels of sterility protection. The scalpel's sterile packaging must stay closed "until the very last second", which is exactly the spirit of the original text: "wraps must remain intact until the time of their installation".

Key Notes: Key Sequencing Difference between RABS and Isolators

This is a key difference that is often asked about in exams and inspections:

  • RABS: Grade A is established first (cleaning + disinfection), and then the sterilized parts are installed
  • Isolator: The sterilized parts are installed first, and then the door is closed and VPHP is run; Grade A is established only after the parts have been installed

This sequencing difference determines which parts need to be protected at which stage. In an isolator, indirect contact parts can be installed during the open-door setup, but their protective covers must stay in place until VPHP is complete.

Practical Application

In real CDMO operations, line setup time directly affects line efficiency and scheduling. If a line needs complex setup between every batch, this is not only a microbiological risk issue but also a question of commercial competitiveness. Choosing a design with more pre-sterilized components (single-use systems) can shorten setup time, but VPHP compatibility must be considered (Section 8.1.3 discusses the issue of packaging impermeability).

Practice Questions

  1. Why do personnel need to wear higher-level protective garments than the Grade C background requires during the open-door setup stage of an isolator?
  2. If the protective packaging of an indirect contact part is damaged during handling, how should it be handled? Think about it from a sterility assurance perspective.
8.1.1 Detailed Steps of Line Setup in RABS and Isolators

Original Text

Depending on the barrier technology for aseptic processing, RABS or Isolators, the parts will be subject to different steps. All steps for line setup should be risk assessed in order to identify the risk mitigations and control measures that will best ensure the sterility of the critical components and should be included within the CCS. All setup activities (both open and closed door) should follow the general requirements for the performance of aseptic interventions (see Section 8.2).

The aseptic line setup in a RABS includes the following sequence of steps:

Open-door line setup (Grade B background):

  • Cleaning and disinfection of non-product contact parts, stationary filling machine parts, and barrier, to establish Grade A conditions
  • EM initiated for Grade A conditions
  • Installation of sterilized indirect product contact parts on the disinfected machine base
  • Installation of the sterilized direct product contact parts

To the extent possible, consideration should be given to protecting the direct product contact parts by transferring and installing them using closed transfer technologies (e.g., RTP) and closed-door interventions rather than open-door. At a minimum, protective sheaths may be used for critical parts such as needles, which can be left in place until the barrier door is closed.

The aseptic line setup in an isolator includes the following sequence of steps:

Open-door line setup (Grade C background) with isolator HVAC active:

  • Cleaning and disinfection of non-product contact parts, stationary filling machine parts, and barrier prior to establishing Grade A conditions
  • Installation of sterilized indirect product contact parts on the disinfected machine base leaving protective wraps in place over critical surfaces for as long as possible (even considering removal only after the door is closed)
  • Closure of the barrier door

Closed-door line setup:

  • Biodecontamination of the filling line (e.g., VPHP) to establish Grade A conditions
  • EM initiated for Grade A conditions
  • Installation of the sterilized direct product contact parts

Although the background classification for isolators is commonly Grade C, enhanced gowning is typically employed for those employees conducting the open-door setup. Including but not limited to goggles or face shield, hoods, sterile sleeves and sterile gloves.

To the extent possible, consideration should be given to protecting the indirect product contact parts by preventing their exposure to the background environment during open-door setup by making use of closed transfer systems or by retaining protective covers as long as possible. For this reason, the removal of final covers for these parts may occur immediately before door closure, immediately after door closure, or even after biodecontamination.

The approach to the removal of these covers will also affect how the biodecontamination cycle is validated (e.g., timing of cover removal if applicable, permissible bioburden on parts before VPHP exposure of indirect product contact parts to VPHP, aeration time for residuals with or without cover) and should be included as a standard procedure to be followed within APS (13).

Regulators have emphasized the importance of understanding the environmental conditions within the isolator and the cleanroom during open door activities. As a consequence, EM may be initiated during the open-door phases of setup. In addition, air flow visualization studies are commonly performed during the initial qualification of the isolator to ensure that there is no entrained air from the surrounding environment entering the isolator during the activities of setup.

Fully closed (during operation) isolators are permitted to be installed within Grade D backgrounds rather than Grade C. The risks associated with indirect product contact parts and the coordination of the removal of their covers becomes even more critical when considering the associated risks with a Grade D background environment.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

RTP (Rapid Transfer Port): A sealed transfer device that allows materials to be introduced into an isolator or RABS without compromising barrier integrity. Using an RTP allows sterilized parts to be introduced without opening a door, which is an important design measure for reducing intervention risk.

EM (Environmental Monitoring): Microbial and particle monitoring that begins once Grade A conditions are established. The monitoring results are direct evidence that environmental control is effective.

Airflow Visualization Study: The use of smoke or tracer particles to visualize airflow patterns and confirm that no air from a lower-grade environment flows into the higher-grade area during open-door operations.

Setup Step Comparison

RABS setup steps (Grade B background):
Step 1: Cleaning + disinfection (establish Grade A)
Step 2: EM start-up
Step 3: Install indirect contact parts
Step 4: Install direct contact parts
            ↓
Grade A is established first, then the parts are installed

Isolator setup steps (Grade C background):
Step 1: Cleaning + disinfection (basic treatment)
Step 2: Install indirect contact parts (protective covers left in place)
Step 3: Close the door
Step 4: VPHP biodecontamination (establishes Grade A)
Step 5: EM start-up
Step 6: Install direct contact parts
            ↓
The parts are installed first, then Grade A is established through VPHP

Key Notes

The timing of cover removal affects validation design: This is a detail, but a very important one. If the protective covers of indirect contact parts are removed before VPHP, VPHP must be shown to achieve a 6-log reduction on these exposed surfaces. If the covers are removed after VPHP, validation must confirm that VPHP can penetrate beneath the covers, or the design must ensure that the covers themselves do not prevent VPHP from reaching critical surfaces. This decision must be clearly specified in the SOP and reproduced in the APS.

Additional risk of a Grade D background: Allowing a fully enclosed isolator to be installed in a Grade D background offers flexibility, but it means a higher risk of contamination from the surrounding environment during open-door setup, and the protection requirements for indirect contact parts are therefore stricter.

Analogy

A RABS is like assembling a precision instrument in a disinfected cleanroom: the room is prepared first, and then the tools are brought in. An isolator is more like a spacewalk outside a space station: you first bring the parts into the airlock (open-door setup), close the hatch, complete the pressurization and decontamination (VPHP), and only then enter the core module to carry out installation (installing direct contact parts). Different systems have different airlock logic.

Practical Application

During CDMO customer audits, inspectors often ask: "Does your line setup SOP cover the protective measures for every part category? Is it reproduced in the APS?" Writing the protection logic for all three part categories fully into the SOP, and making sure the APS design covers worst-case setup activities, is therefore the key to inspection readiness.

Practice Questions

  1. If an isolator is installed in a Grade D background, what additional controls can reduce the risk of contaminating indirect contact parts during open-door setup?
  2. What role does the airflow visualization study (AVS) play in isolator line setup? At what point does it need to be performed?
8.1.2 Additional Considerations for Line Setup within a Campaign

Original Text

Within a campaign, limited line setup may occur between batches (i.e., to change container type, to establish a new fluid pathway, etc.) (see Section 4.1 for additional details on campaign requirements).

Care must be taken to ensure that Grade A conditions are maintained and that the interventions are limited to the essential activities, in order to preserve the aseptic environment. Risk assessments should be performed for all intended activities, and they should be included within the CCS to ensure that the appropriate controls are implemented.

Some general principles for line setup between batches within a campaign include:

  • All setup activities should follow the general requirements for the performance of aseptic interventions (see Section 8.2).
  • All setup activities must be included in an appropriately designed APS.
  • Where possible, any parts that are to be exchanged should be brought within the barrier using closed transfer mechanisms (e.g., RTP) or should be present within the barrier from the beginning of the campaign (e.g., second fluid pathway).
  • When using RABS, setup should be performed using closed door interventions.
  • When using RABS and open door interventions are unavoidable, consideration should be given to what disinfection or biodecontamination is appropriate prior to resumption of aseptic operations.
  • When extensive setup is required, consideration should be given to terminating the campaign; recent advances in technology including rapid biodecontamination within isolators, for example, make it possible to turn around a line within a shorter period of time.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Campaign: An operating mode in which multiple batches are produced consecutively under the same aseptic environmental conditions. Setup changes between batches (such as changing container format or fluid path) are among the highest-risk moments in a campaign.

Second Fluid Pathway: A spare fluid path is placed inside the barrier at the start of the campaign, so that changing the fluid path between batches does not require opening a door to introduce new parts. This reflects a design approach of preparing in advance to reduce interventions.

Rapid Biodecontamination: Advances in modern isolator technology allow shorter VPHP cycles, which lowers the time cost of terminating the campaign and carrying out a full re-setup, making this option more practical.

Key Notes

Terminating the campaign is sometimes safer than continuing setup: When a great deal of setup work is needed between batches, carrying it out within the existing campaign may carry a higher risk of microbial contamination. Terminating the campaign and performing a complete line setup again costs more time, but it provides more certain sterility assurance. This is a typical "sterility assurance > commercial efficiency" decision scenario.

Any between-batch setup activity must be included in the APS design, including worst-case simulation. If a setup activity is not covered by the APS, regulators will consider that the sterility assurance of that activity has not been adequately validated.

Analogy

Think of a tire change in an F1 pit stop: if it is only four tires, the stop takes 15 seconds; but if the suspension also has to be changed, you may need to consider withdrawing from the race and preparing again. Setup between batches works the same way: minor adjustments can be made within the campaign, but when major changes are involved, "starting over" is sometimes the safer and more efficient choice.

Practice Questions

  1. In a RABS, the container format needs to be changed between batches (from 1 mL vials to 5 mL vials). What options should be considered first to complete this setup while maintaining Grade A conditions?
  2. Under what conditions would you recommend terminating the campaign rather than continuing with between-batch setup? List at least three decision criteria.
8.1.3 Other Considerations for Line Setup

Original Text

When making use of Single Use Systems (SUS), and they are part of the load for the biodecontamination cycle, care should be taken to ensure that the packaging is impermeable to the biodecontamination agent (e.g., VPHP) to prevent absorption that might be harmful to products (14).

See PDA PtC No.12: Restricted Access Barrier Systems for additional information with regard to the design and operation of RABS (4). In particular, a UDAF should be present above doors to protect the environment during any open-door activity such as line setup.

CFD for airflow design within the barrier (both RABS and isolators) and surrounding environment, and airflow visualization for the intervention activities, are essential to demonstrate that airflow turbulence is minimized.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

SUS (Single Use Systems) and VPHP compatibility: The packaging of single-use components (usually PE/PP plastic bags) may absorb hydrogen peroxide vapor in a VPHP environment. If the amount absorbed is too high, release into the product could cause drug degradation or safety concerns. Confirming that SUS packaging is impermeable to VPHP is therefore a necessary part of validation.

UDAF (Unidirectional Airflow): UDAF above the door ensures that during open-door operations the air flows outward from the higher-cleanliness area rather than inward from outside, protecting the aseptic environment from being compromised.

CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics): Computer simulation used to predict airflow behavior, verifying at the design stage whether the airflow patterns inside and outside the barrier meet sterility protection requirements.

Key Notes

VPHP compatibility of SUS is an easily overlooked detail, but it has been cited as a finding in actual inspections. If your facility uses isolators with SUS components, you must confirm that: (1) the SUS packaging is impermeable to VPHP, or (2) the SUS has been removed from the isolator before the VPHP cycle, or (3) sufficient absorption data demonstrate that the residual level is within a safe range.

Practice Questions

  1. If the SUS packaging used in your isolator is slightly permeable to VPHP, what technical options do you have to manage this risk?
  2. Why must CFD simulation results be confirmed by a physical airflow visualization study (AVS) rather than relying on computer simulation alone?
8.2 General Considerations Regarding Aseptic Interventions

Original Text

  • Quality risk management tools should be employed to define the risk level for each planned intervention, including the intervention detection, mitigations, and controls (e.g., EM, personnel monitoring, sterility samples). Key elements to assess include:
    • Personnel (number and positioning of)
    • Duration of the intervention
    • Complexity of the required actions during the intervention
    • Proximity and handling or manipulation of sterile parts
    • Risks due to potential occluded surfaces
  • All aseptic interventions should be defined in a SOP that defines:
    • Whether the intervention is via glove port, remote manipulator, open door, or other mechanism (open doors are to be avoided whenever possible)
    • Glove checks (for tears, pinholes) and glove sanitization that may be required pre- and post-intervention
    • Procedures to be followed for performance of the intervention to ensure that air flow disruptions are minimized, including if witnessing of the intervention performance is required
    • Tools to be used to protect product-contact components, both direct and indirect, and the required disinfection (pre- and post-intervention) or disposal of those tools
    • Any required line-clearance activities based on identified risks due to the intervention procedure and zone of exposure
    • Disinfection or cleaning and sterilization required post-intervention
    • Documentation requirements for the intervention
    • Any requirement to segregate materials or an appropriate decision-making framework for that decision, for example, quarantine status for a portion of the batch or renumbering of a portion of the batch until review and approvals are gained
  • At the conclusion of the fill, EM samples are collected for direct and indirect product-contact parts which should represent any interventions performed; tools used during interventions should also be considered as sampling sites. All sampling should follow a risk-based approach.
  • SOPs should be demonstrated in an airflow visualization study (AVS) to prove that turbulence is avoided, and that air does not move from an area of lower classification to higher classification when following the correct procedures during such activities as open-door setup in an isolator
  • Each intervention should be qualified for use and included in an appropriately designed aseptic process simulation (APS)
  • Personnel should be trained in the intervention SOP and qualified to perform the intervention

Additional detail on setup, specifically, and interventions, more generally, may be found in industry guidance on aseptic practices (3, 15).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The eight elements of an intervention SOP: This section lists what a complete aseptic intervention SOP must cover. This is not only a compliance requirement but also an action guide for operators before every intervention:

  • Method of intervention (glove port, remote manipulator, open door)
  • Glove inspection and disinfection procedures
  • Operating steps during the intervention (including witnessing requirements)
  • Tool protection and post-use handling
  • Line clearance activities
  • Post-intervention disinfection/sterilization requirements
  • Documentation requirements
  • Material segregation and batch decision framework

Quarantine Status: If a contamination risk that cannot be immediately ruled out remains after an intervention, the relevant part of the batch may need to be placed in quarantine until quality review and approval allow further disposition.

Analogy

Imagine how an emergency-room surgical team handles an unexpected situation: if an extra step has to be added during the operation (equivalent to an intervention), the surgeon cannot decide freely what to do but must follow an established procedure (SOP). After the operation, what happened is recorded (documentation), the impact is assessed (EM results) and, if necessary, the patient is isolated for observation (quarantine). The management logic for aseptic interventions is exactly the same.

Key Notes

The five risk assessment dimensions for interventions: When assessing the risk of each intervention, the QRM tool must consider: personnel (number and positions), duration, complexity of movements, proximity to or contact with sterile parts, and the risk from occluded surfaces.

Occluded Surfaces are a concept worth special attention: an intervention tool or the operator's arm may block the line of sight of EM, so that settle plates or air sampling cannot represent the true contamination situation. This is also why AVS studies need to be designed for each specific intervention.

Every intervention must be covered in the APS: If an intervention is not covered by the APS design, it is regarded by regulators as an "unvalidated activity", no matter how many times it is performed in actual production.

Intervention Risk Scoring

Intervention risk level assessment (conceptual model):

High-risk interventions (strictest control required):
  - Open-door intervention (Open Door)
  - Long duration (>2 minutes)
  - Very close to direct contact parts
  - Multiple personnel involved, complex movements
  - Many occluded surfaces

Medium-risk interventions:
  - Glove port intervention (Glove Port)
  - Short duration
  - Handling indirect contact parts

Low-risk interventions:
  - Remote manipulator (Remote Manipulator)
  - Handling non-contact parts
  - Completed entirely outside the barrier

→ The risk level determines:
   Enhanced EM requirements / batch segregation decisions / APS design complexity

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, customer products may have different intervention needs. For example, high-viscosity products are more likely to clog fill needles and require more frequent corrective interventions. As a CDMO, you must ensure that these product-specific interventions are identified before contract negotiation and that corresponding SOPs and APS designs are in place. Otherwise, discovering a lack of validation support only after commercial production begins will lead to difficulties in batch release or regulatory problems.

Practice Questions

  1. After a filling operator performs an open-door intervention (clearing a jammed vial), what actions should be taken immediately? List them according to the SOP elements in Section 8.2.
  2. If, after an intervention, the EM result near the direct contact parts is positive, what factors should your batch decision framework consider?
  3. Why does every intervention need to be witnessed? What role does this play in the quality system?
8.3 Microbiological Considerations for Filter Changes

Original Text

The sterilizing filter represents a sterile boundary for the fluid pathway. Filter changes should be avoided, when possible, and handled with care when unavoidable. To avoid filter changes, firms will sometimes install more than one filtration manifold in a parallel arrangement, so that switching from one fluid path/filter to another can be accomplished without intervention. Alternatively, installing more than one filter in a series can permit the removal and replacement of the upstream filter with less risk to the downstream sterile barrier (see Section 11.0 for additional discussion on filter configurations).

When filter changes are unavoidable, the system design will influence the requirements for the filter-change activity. Two examples of system designs that represent the extremes of the design considerations include:

  • Aseptic filling lines with the filter outside of the Grade A environment within a stainless-steel (SS) housing
  • Aseptic filling lines that employ presterilized components (e.g., filters, tubing, gaskets, clamps, flush bags) that are aseptically assembled in a Grade A environment

For filling systems that are SIP, when the filter is in a SS housing outside of the Grade A environment, changing the filter-set requires that the sterile fluid path be opened and exposed to a lower-grade environment (e.g., Grade C for isolators and Grade B for RABS filling lines). Opening and exposing the fluid path to a lower-grade environment can lead to microbiological contamination of the product pathway.

Therefore, when configured in this manner, a filter change will necessitate that filling be stopped and the batch be split into two identified portions (e.g., before and after the filter replacement) with separate batch numbers. After removing the original filter, the fluid pathway must be cleaned in place. The new filter is then installed, sterilized in place, and subjected to pre-use integrity testing and flushing before filling can be resumed. To mitigate any risk of microbial contamination of the product, a CIP/SIP process is required (see Section 11.0 for filter placement within the fluid pathway and additional information on PUPSIT).

Configurations that offer improved SA to filters located outside the Grade A environment include gamma-irradiated filters that are connected via intrinsic sterile-connection devices or filters that are introduced through a canister port.

For filling lines employing presterilized components that are aseptically assembled in a Grade A environment, the product transfer is completed by an intrinsic sterile connector or an aseptic connection. In this case, the aseptic connection can be uncoupled and the transfer port closed. Within the Grade A environment, the entire filter-set can be replaced and reinstalled with a replacement presterilized filter-set passed in through a RTP or by using a spare stored in the environment. After reassembly, pre-use integrity

[Text continues on doc p141 / Section 8B — pre-use integrity testing completion of the filter change procedure for presterilized assemblies]

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The Sterilizing Filter as the sterile boundary: In the sterile fluid path, the sterilizing filter is the last safeguard ensuring that the drug solution is sterile when it enters the filling system. Any filter change temporarily "opens" this boundary, so the risk is very high.

Parallel Filtration Manifold: Two parallel filtration sets are installed in advance, so that when one needs to be changed, flow is simply switched to the other without opening the sterile fluid path. This is the best design strategy for avoiding the risk of filter changes.

Series Configuration: Two filters are arranged one after the other. When the upstream filter is changed, the downstream filter still maintains the sterile boundary, which is relatively safe.

Batch Split: When a filter change cannot be avoided, the product before and after the change must be divided into two identified batches, because they have different filtration histories and need to be evaluated separately in quality review.

Filter Change Scenario Comparison

Scenario 1: SS housing, outside Grade A, SIP system

Change procedure:
1. Stop filling
2. Batch split (separate batch numbers before and after)
3. Remove the old filter
4. CIP (clean-in-place of the fluid path)
5. Install the new filter
6. SIP (sterilize-in-place)
7. PUPSIT (pre-use post-sterilization integrity test)
8. Flush
9. Resume filling
Risk: High (fluid path exposed to a lower-grade environment)
---
Scenario 2: Pre-sterilized assembly, aseptic assembly inside Grade A

Change procedure:
1. Disconnect the aseptic connector (adapter closed)
2. Introduce the spare pre-sterilized filter assembly through the RTP
3. Reassemble inside Grade A
4. PUPSIT
5. Resume filling
Risk: Low (completed entirely within the Grade A environment)

Key Notes

PUPSIT (Pre-Use Post-Sterilization Integrity Test): After every filter change, and before filling starts, the newly installed filter must undergo an integrity test to confirm it has no leaks or defects. EU GMP Annex 1 has explicit requirements for PUPSIT. This reflects the principle that sterility assurance comes first: even if the filter is brand new and sterilized, its integrity must still be verified before use.

Gamma-irradiated filter + intrinsically sterile connector: This combination is an improved option for the SS housing design. Intrinsically sterile connections (no manual connection in a cleanroom environment) reduce contamination risk while avoiding the need for CIP/SIP.

Analogy

A sterilizing filter is like the last filter screen at a city water purification plant. If you need to replace this screen, the safest approach is to divert the water to a backup line first (parallel design), rather than cutting off the water, changing the screen and then restoring flow. If a change is unavoidable, you need to: shut off the water, clear the pipe, change the screen, disinfect, test, and only then restore flow. No step can be skipped, or unpurified water could flow directly into customers' pipes. A batch split is like recording that "this cup was filled before the screen change and that one after", for later verification.

Sterility Assurance: first priority
▼
Product CQAs: batch split protects the integrity of product quality evaluation
▼
Commercial flexibility: parallel/pre-sterilized assembly designs improve efficiency

Practical Application

In a CDMO commercial proposal, when a customer asks "What happens if the filter has to be changed midway through a 20,000-vial batch?", you should be able to explain clearly that: (1) this leads to a batch split, (2) CIP/SIP must be performed, (3) PUPSIT must be performed, (4) the whole filter change process may take several hours, during which the product is waiting, and (5) the two batch portions must be reviewed and released separately. The customer needs to factor all of these into planning, scheduling and cost estimates. Pre-sterilized assembly systems have a higher initial cost but can greatly reduce this operational complexity.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does a filter change inevitably lead to a batch split in an SS housing design? Can the filter be changed without splitting the batch? Explain why.
  2. Compare the parallel filtration manifold and series filtration designs. In which scenarios is each more suitable, and what are their limitations?
  3. In a pre-sterilized assembly system, how is PUPSIT performed after a filter change? How does this differ from PUPSIT in an SS housing system?

Section Summary (8.0–8.3)

  • 8.0: Contamination control is the primary objective of aseptic filling. Interventions should be minimized through design, and inherent interventions must be distinguished from corrective interventions and planned for in advance at the design stage.
  • 8.1: Line setup is the operating stage with the highest contamination risk. In a RABS, Grade A is established first and then the parts are installed; in an isolator, the parts are installed first, then the door is closed and VPHP is run to establish Grade A. This sequencing difference is a core exam point.
  • 8.1 (part classification): The three-way classification into direct, indirect and non-contact parts determines the level of protection strategy. Direct contact parts require the strictest protection, and packaging integrity must not be broken until the moment just before installation.
  • 8.1.2: Between-batch setup within a campaign is a high-risk activity, and all setup steps must be included in the APS. Where extensive setup is needed, terminating the campaign and setting up again is sometimes the safer choice.
  • 8.1.3: When SUS are used together with VPHP in an isolator, the VPHP impermeability of the packaging must be confirmed. UDAF and CFD/AVS are essential tools for barrier design and intervention validation.
  • 8.2: Every intervention must have an SOP, be assessed through QRM, be included in the APS, and be backed by personnel training and qualification. EM sampling after an intervention must represent the area affected by the intervention itself.
  • 8.3: The sterilizing filter is the sterile boundary of the fluid path. Designs that avoid filter changes (parallel/series) are preferred. When a change is unavoidable, SS housing systems require batch split + CIP/SIP + PUPSIT; pre-sterilized assembly systems are assembled aseptically inside Grade A, which carries lower risk, but PUPSIT remains a necessary step.
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p141 – p147

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the three response options when a filling needle is damaged, and how a pre-assembled fluid path lowers the risk of replacement
  • Understand the principles for aseptic interventions on broken or blocked primary packaging materials, including the AVS and APS design requirements
  • Distinguish the microbial risk of automated versus manual component transfer, and the criteria for removing each packaging layer
  • Understand the key management points for sorting systems: sterilization, biodecontamination, and residual silicone oil
  • Understand the four categories of mechanical intervention, the risk management principles for each, and when a batch must be stopped
  • Understand the event-driven and time-driven design of environmental monitoring (EM), and the importance of controlling the full life cycle of EM samples
8.4 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Associated with Filling Needle Adjustment, Repair, and Replacement

Original Text

If a liquid filling needle is damaged, there are three options from which to choose:

  • Turn off the needle
  • Repair or adjust the needle
  • Replace the needle

The first option does not require aseptic manipulation, as it can typically be accomplished through the control system and so does not pose any microbiological risk. Regarding repairing or replacing the needle, the general considerations for performing interventions identified in Section 8.2 would apply. The filling needle is one of the most critical locations for an intervention due to its position immediately above the open patient-dose.

When designing the intervention for replacing the needle, whether any portion of the sterile fluid pathway will also be changed at the same time should be considered. A preassembled sterile fluid pathway may be less risky to replace than one component of the pathway alone. In some cases, replacing a single component may risk leaks or drips from improper connections, or it may cause greater environmental exposure to the fluid path, whereas a preassembled pathway may reduce those risks.

In the case of powder filling that makes use of powder dosing-needles, turning off or repairing needles is typically not possible, and full replacement would be required. For liquid needles, repair/replacement is one of the highest risk interventions and should not be undertaken lightly.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Decision among three options for a damaged filling needle:

  • Turn off the needle: done through the control system, with no entry into Grade A and therefore zero microbial risk. This is the preferred option.
  • Repair/Adjust: requires an aseptic intervention that must comply with the general intervention principles in Section 8.2; moderate risk.
  • Replace the needle: one of the highest-risk interventions in liquid filling, because the needle sits directly above the open containers holding the patient dose and exposes the sterile space directly.

A powder dosing needle cannot be turned off or repaired and can only be replaced completely, which makes it harder to manage.

Analogy

Imagine a surgeon who must change the scalpel in the middle of open-chest surgery: swapping a single blade (replacing one component) versus swapping in a whole sterile instrument pack (a pre-assembled fluid path). The latter involves a bigger move, but every connection has been confirmed in advance, which reduces the chance of errors on the spot. The pre-assembled fluid path for a filling needle follows the same logic: assembled and verified beforehand, so the risk is lower when it is replaced during the run.

Key Notes

Key judgment when replacing: when designing the replacement intervention procedure, you must also consider whether part of the sterile fluid path should be replaced together with the needle. Replacing a single component alone may lead to:

  • Improper connections causing leaks or dripping
  • Longer exposure of the fluid path to the environment

Although a pre-assembled path appears to involve "replacing more", overall sterility assurance is actually higher. Decision principle: sterility assurance > operational convenience.

Practice Questions

  1. A filling needle bends but does not break in the middle of production, and your operator suggests adjusting it in place. What preconditions must you confirm before allowing this intervention?
  2. Why is managing a powder filling needle more challenging than managing a liquid filling needle? Explain from the perspective of APS design.
8.5 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Related to Broken or Blocked Primary-Packaging Materials

Original Text

The general considerations for aseptic interventions outlined in Section 8.2 should be followed for the removal of blocked or broken primary-packaging materials. Such interventions are considered corrective interventions that should be included in the AVS and included within an appropriate APS study design. The AVS would be designed to demonstrate that the corrective intervention minimizes airflow disruption and does not have the potential to add contamination. The intervention should be considered for inclusion in the APS design at a frequency representative of the rate of occurrence in routine production.

The intervention should only be performed while using sterilized tools such as forceps. The tools should be placed at any location along the filling line where this intervention is likely to occur.

The intervention should be reduced to the actions necessary to keep the line running, resulting in shorter duration interventions that are generally of lower risk. For example, minimizing actions commonly means that only when debris from a broken container can possibly cause contamination or malfunction of the line should that debris be fully removed. Similarly, actions below the working height should be avoided. For example, should materials fall to the machine base plate, they would commonly remain there until the conclusion of the filling operation unless they posed a risk of malfunction.

An intervention risk assessment should describe each required intervention and its associated risks and define the required controls. The intervention and controls should be included in the CCS (Contamination Control Strategy).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Corrective Intervention: an aseptic manipulation performed during production in response to an unplanned event (such as a broken or blocked container). Unlike a preventive intervention, a corrective intervention has these characteristics:

  • It must be included in advance in the AVS (Airflow Visualization Study) to verify that the intervention does not disturb the airflow
  • It must be included in the APS (Aseptic Process Simulation) and rehearsed at a representative frequency
  • It must be included in the CCS (contamination control strategy) as a formal control measure

Analogy

Think of firefighters in a controlled building-fire drill: the drill must simulate the real frequency and location of fires and cannot rehearse only the "easiest scenario". The same applies to APS design for aseptic filling: the simulation frequency for broken containers must reflect the actual occurrence rate in production, not be a token one-time rehearsal.

Key Notes

The "minimize actions" principle is the key:

  • The shorter the intervention, the lower the risk of microbial contamination
  • Fragments that fall to the bottom of the machine should be left until the end of the batch unless they pose a risk of machine malfunction. This is a deliberate risk-based judgment, not an oversight
  • Movements below working height should be avoided, because aseptic technique is harder to maintain below the working surface and such movements easily disturb the unidirectional airflow

Core logic: every "extra movement" in Grade A is a risk; if it can be avoided, avoid it.

Practical Application

In a CDMO environment, the SOP for handling broken containers should include a list of positions for pre-placed sterile forceps, an APS rehearsal frequency plan (referencing historical breakage rates), and a section on intervention risk assessment in the CCS. During inspections, regulators often ask for confirmation that the APS intervention scenarios adequately represent actual production.

8.6 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Associated with Supply of Components

Original Text

Automated transfer of components to the aseptic filling line is preferred to reduce microbiological risk. An automated system is repeatable, can be biodecontaminated, and can be validated. Depending on the primary-packaging materials used, different automated solutions may be required (e.g., e-beam, depyrogenation tunnel, RTP transfer, no-touch transfer). All interventions in a Grade A environment linked to the automated transfer of materials should be designed and performed taking into account the general rules for aseptic manipulations (see Section 8.2). The supply of components should be included in a representative manner within both the AVS and APS. Transfer technologies are further discussed in Sections 9.0 and 10.0.

Manual transfer of components is only possible in cleanroom conditions where the transfer occurs from a Grade B environment to the Grade A environment. As the components transition through the cleanroom classifications, successive layers of sterilized wrapping are removed. Special attention is required to avoid contamination of the outer surfaces of the inner bag at each transition. The second-to-last bag should be removed, using aseptic techniques under unidirectional airflow, when transferring the materials from Grade B to Grade A. The layers of removed wrapping materials should be prevented from contacting surfaces within the Grade A space. The final bag should only be removed within the Grade A environment.

When using a mousehole, RTP, or other equipment doors for transfers, dynamic airflow pattern studies in the AVS should prove that the transfer of materials to the inside of the barrier does not result in turbulence inside the barrier or result in airborne contamination transfer. In the case of a mousehole or door (such as those that may be opened to restock elastomers), it is important to demonstrate that there is no ingress of air from Grade B into Grade A. In both cases, the addition of components from a bag to a hopper should be executed considering the general rules for aseptic manipulations (see Section 8.2). The transfer and addition of components should be demonstrated in a representative manner and frequency within an appropriately designed APS.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Component transfer technologies (from lowest to highest risk):

  • No-touch transfer: fully automated, lowest risk
  • RTP (Rapid Transfer Port): sealed docking transfer that prevents Grade B air from entering Grade A
  • Depyrogenation tunnel: suitable for heat-resistant materials such as glass vials
  • E-beam: electron-beam sterilization, suitable for plastic containers
  • Manual transfer through a mousehole: highest risk; AVS must demonstrate that no reverse airflow is created

The three main advantages of automated systems: repeatable, biodecontaminated, and validated.

Analogy

The "layer-by-layer bag removal" principle for manually transferred components is like peeling an orange: each time you enter a cleaner area you remove one layer of skin, but you must make sure that peeling does not contaminate the layer underneath. The innermost layer may be opened only in the Grade A environment (the cleanest place). If the innermost layer is opened in Grade B, the "protective outer skin" is effectively brought into the cleanroom and contaminates the surface of the contents.

Key Notes

AVS requirements for mouseholes and RTPs: regulators pay particular attention to this area. When a mousehole or door transfer is used, the AVS must demonstrate that:

  • No turbulence is generated inside the barrier
  • There is no ingress of air from Grade B into Grade A

EU GMP Annex 1 explicitly requires that airflow pattern studies of the transfer process be documented, and that the APS simulate the replenishment process at a representative frequency.

Practice Questions

  1. A CDMO client's product uses siliconized rubber stoppers, and stoppers are currently replenished manually through a mousehole. Would you recommend upgrading to an RTP or an automated system? What data would you need to support this decision?
  2. For manual transfer, what is the rationale for removing the last bag layer only in Grade A? What risk arises if it is removed in Grade B?
8.7 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Associated with Sorting Systems for Components

Original Text

Sorting systems are each independently machined (custom made), so there can be small geometric differences between each sorting system. Characterizing and qualifying each stoppering-set is recommended to define optimal settings, as this will reduce the requirement for fine-tuning during both the LSU (Line Set-Up) and the aseptic filling operation.

Sorting systems should be designed to be handled and assembled by touching only the external surfaces (e.g., outside of the feeder bowl) avoiding any manipulation in the portion that is in contact with components. Sorting systems should be controlled (e.g., using kitting procedures or through the use of ID numbers) to ensure that all required parts are used together consistently. Checks should be performed at the start of a batch or campaign to optimize the setup and adjustment prior to the start of fill. Any fine-tuning after setup should focus on optimization of machine parameters that do not require an aseptic intervention. Any aseptic interventions required should apply the general considerations regarding aseptic interventions (see Section 8.2). The intervention actions associated with initial setup and fine-tuning should be demonstrated through both AVS and APS.

Sorting systems are indirect product-contact parts; consequently, they should be sterilized before use. When transporting and installing the sorting systems, especially the large and often-awkward feed bowls, protective covers are recommended to avoid recontamination after sterilization during LSU (see Section 8.1). In the case of isolators, several approaches have been acceptable to regulators and have been justified through risk assessment and validation. For some facilities, the outermost protective bag (of the sterile sorting bowl) will be removed prior to biodecontamination, but a protective cap will stay in place over the opening of the stopper bowl to maintain the sterility of the interior surfaces until the isolator is biodecontaminated. After the end of aeration an intervention will be performed using a glove, tool, external manipulator, or robot to remove and discard the protective cap. For other facilities, the cap is removed just before or just after the door is closed, but before the biodecontamination is initiated so that the internal surfaces of the sorting bowl are also fully exposed to the biodecontamination. The approach to be taken should be established through risk assessment and included in the CCS (12). The PDA Points to Consider for the Aseptic Processing of Sterile Pharmaceutical Products in Isolators may be referenced for additional approaches and details about the risks (16).

Biodecontamination effectiveness can be affected by any residues that remain on surfaces after cleaning (and sterilization). For sorting systems which are used with siliconized components, special care should be taken to remove any residual silicone oil from surfaces during cleaning before sterilization as it may inhibit effective biodecontamination.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

What makes sorting systems special: sorting systems (such as vibratory bowls and feed bowls) are custom-fabricated items, and there are subtle geometric differences between sets. Therefore:

  • Each stoppering set must be individually characterized and qualified
  • Use a kitting procedure or ID numbers to ensure that matched parts are always used together, so that mixing does not cause performance differences
  • Setup adjustments should be completed before the start of the batch as far as possible, to reduce the need for aseptic interventions during filling

Key principle: setup optimization takes priority over adjustment during production, because adjustment during production = aseptic intervention = risk.

Analogy

Managing protective caps on a sorting system in an isolator is like a racing driver's helmet routine: "put the cap on before entering the car (protect the sterile inner surfaces first), then remove the protective visor once inside the safe enclosed environment (remove the cap after biodecontamination)". Each approach (removal before decontamination vs. after decontamination) has its supporters; the key is to use a risk assessment to justify which is more effective in your facility, and to document it in the CCS.

Key Notes

Residual Silicone Oil: a frequently overlooked risk:

After siliconized stoppers run through a sorting bowl, silicone oil is left on the inner surfaces. Silicone oil is hydrophobic and can:

  • Block vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP) or other biodecontamination agents from contacting the surface
  • Significantly reduce biodecontamination efficacy, so that sporicidal log reduction data fall short of the target

The cleaning step must therefore include confirmation that silicone oil has been removed, and this must be completed before sterilization. This is one of the common FDA 483 observations.

Practice Questions

  1. Your facility uses an isolator, and the current practice for the sorting bowl is to "remove the protective cap before biodecontamination". If an auditor asks for the rationale for this choice, how would you answer? What documents would you need to prepare?
  2. Why is a kitting procedure especially important for sorting systems? What problems could occur if parts from different sets are mixed across batches?
8.8 Microbiological Considerations for Mechanical Interventions

Original Text

Mechanical interventions to repair or replace parts fall into one of four categories:

  1. Sterilized or disinfected mechanical components within the cleanroom environment for which failures have been anticipated
  2. Disinfected mechanical components within the cleanroom environment for which failures have not been anticipated
  3. Mechanical components that are not disinfected due to being occluded (and, therefore, not disinfected during preparation of the line)
  4. Equipment located in enclosed mechanical cabinets, also known as technical areas or gray zones

The microbiological risk of each of these four categories is directly related to the ability to perform the intervention in an aseptic manner, while minimizing airflow disruptions and without risk of compromising the aseptic condition of the equipment, personnel gowning, or the environment. While Categories 2 and 3 are far less frequent, and perhaps entirely unanticipated and rare, they should not be executed without risk assessment (including risk assessment of the means for execution of the intervention), and approval of the risk by the quality unit. If risk is high or not acceptable, then steps should be performed to reduce the risk or to eliminate the intervention. If the activity cannot be eliminated or the risk reduced to an acceptable level, then the activity should not be allowed to be performed.

Category 4 (also subject to risk assessment) should rarely, if ever, be permitted from the cleanroom without discontinuing the batch. Some of the specific risks associated with all four categories are described below.

Category 1: The first category, sterilized or disinfected mechanical components, involves interventions that were anticipated, risk-assessed, and followed the standard practices for interventions, including the performance of the intervention under both AVS and APS. These are standard corrective interventions that must be documented within the batch record and executed by personnel who have been qualified in the performance of that or similar interventions (see Section 8.2 for standard intervention practices).

Category 2: The second category, disinfected mechanical components, can generally be manipulated during aseptic operations. If the specific intervention was not included in a procedure and challenged during AVS and APS a risk-based decision should be made by operations and the quality unit to allow the intervention, stop the aseptic process, and/or to address it as a deviation, which may result in additional investigation, actions, and the potential loss of the portion of the batch that follows the required intervention. For this reason, it is important to have procedures that plan for and address unexpected interventions. Planning for unexpected interventions must include appropriate Quality Assurance involvement in risk assessment and decision-making at the time the mechanical failure occurs. Considerations for improved detection may include additional supervision or oversight and sampling (e.g., risk-based EM samples collected after the conclusion of the fill to represent the surfaces associated with the intervention, sterility samples). Also included in the plans for the unexpected intervention are stringent requirements to isolate and quarantine portions of the batch that are associated with or that follow the performance of the intervention.

Category 3: For equipment in the third category, where a surface is potentially occluded during surface biodecontamination (e.g., a nut or a bolt in a difficult-to-reach area) but there is a known risk of needing access to the surface during interventions in the filling process, the risk should be assessed and the approach for accessing this area should be considered as part of any potential interventions. Some firms may disinfect this area with a sporicidal disinfectant prior to LSU (during open-door phases of the setup) in order to reduce the risk of exposing this occluded surface during any potential interventions. The exposure of this surface, however, and the manual disinfection should be considered as part of the original qualification of the line, and all intended actions should be included in the appropriate AVS and APS. The ability to perform this activity in a manner that is appropriate to prevent microbiological risk should be considered on a case-by-case basis and pre-approved by the quality unit if it is determined that the intervention should proceed.

Category 4: Opening of technical areas of the filling line that are not biodecontaminated or disinfected is not allowed during aseptic processing with one exception. A technical area that is accessed from a service area that is isolated from the cleanroom that the filling line is installed in can be allowed during aseptic processing. Should a repair or replacement require access to an area that is only accessible from the cleanroom, the fill needs to be suspended, and a line clearance should be conducted in the affected zones. Technical measures should be taken to restrict the scope of the impact to the cleanroom and isolator or RABS. Even with these technical measures, such access will require disinfection of the portion of the equipment, isolator, or cleanroom impacted by the opening. Depending on the extent of the exposure to the nondisinfected zone and the possible pressure differentials experienced after the work is complete, the cleanroom may require more than one successive cleaning and disinfection event. Equipment will also need to be recleaned and resterilized prior to restarting. For many products, such an interruption could cause product hold times to be exceeded or would represent such a high sterility-assurance risk that the filling operation is discontinued, and the remaining product is rejected, filled via a re-setup of the line, or reprocessed (if permissible and justified by site SOPs and by product license).

Tutorial Commentary

Analogy

These four categories are like the emergency triage levels in a hospital operating room:

  • Category 1: backup sterile instruments are ready and can be swapped in directly, with a standard procedure
  • Category 2: a tool is needed that has not been prepared in advance, so an urgent meeting must decide whether to continue
  • Category 3: reaching a corner that was missed during disinfection requires case-by-case evaluation
  • Category 4: the operating room wall must be opened to repair piping, so the surgery must be paused and the patient moved out first

Key Notes: Severe Consequences of Category 4

Opening a technical area (Gray Zone) is the most serious interruption event in aseptic filling:

  • Filling must be stopped and line clearance performed
  • The entire affected area must be recleaned and disinfected (possibly several times)
  • Equipment must be recleaned and resterilized
  • Remaining product may be rejected because hold times are exceeded or sterility assurance is at risk

Commercial impact: for biologics with a short shelf life, this means scrapping the entire batch. This is exactly why Category 4 interventions should be eliminated through engineering controls when the filling line is designed: sterility assurance always takes priority over salvaging a batch.

Decision Framework

Mechanical failure occurs
    ↓
Q1: Is the component sterilized/disinfected?
    ↓ YES → Q2: Is the intervention included in advance in the AVS + APS?
               ↓ YES → Category 1: perform the standard intervention procedure
               ↓ NO  → Category 2: immediate QA involvement + risk assessment
    ↓ NO  → Q3: Is the surface occluded?
               ↓ YES → Category 3: case-by-case evaluation + QA pre-approval
               ↓ NO  → Category 4 (technical area): stop the batch

Decision principle:
Sterility assurance > batch salvage > production efficiency

Practice Questions

  1. A belt on a filling machine breaks in the middle of production, and replacing it requires touching a screw that is normally hidden behind a panel and cannot be disinfected during cleaning. Which category is this? What is your next step?
  2. Why must a Category 2 intervention include "segregating the portion of the batch affected by the intervention"? What is the purpose of this segregation?
8.9 Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Manipulations Related to Environmental Monitoring

Original Text

Environmental Monitoring (EM) includes viable particulate-monitoring (e.g., settle plates, volumetric air, swab, and contact plates for surface, gloves, and gowns) and total particulate-monitoring (e.g., particles greater than or equal to 0.5 µm and 5 µm). Risk-based EM should be undertaken for the full duration of critical processing, including LSU (17). Manually manipulated EM techniques or activities taking place in Grade A and B spaces prior to or during the aseptic process are interventions and should follow recommendations associated with intervention design and qualification. New techniques such as biofluorescent particle counting offer a non-invasive method to measure airborne viable particles and should be considered as an alternative to conventional monitoring when seeking a less invasive method.

Total particulate EM sampling should be continuous throughout the entire operation. The EM microbiological sampling plan is both event-driven and time-driven, meaning the EM sampling plan is designed to measure across the full duration of the aseptic operation. Samples, like settle plates and volumetric air samples, are taken for specific intervals throughout the operation (time-driven), whereas other microbiological samples, like contact plates and swabs, are taken to represent the monitoring of specific events (event-driven). Examples of event-driven monitoring include samples collected during setup, aseptic interventions, exit of personnel after shift, end of the batch, and/or line-changeover during a campaign. The sampling sites and critical control points should be justified and included in the CCS.

Personnel represent the greatest risk to microbiological control during aseptic processing. EM is conducted by people; therefore, it follows that people are the greatest risk to both the environment during the sampling activities and to the integrity of EM samples. In addition, the introduction of growth-promoting media into the aseptic environment for the purpose of sampling represents a risk that growth-promoting residues are left behind if sampling sites are not appropriately cleaned after sampling.

Therefore, the design of the viable monitoring program should ensure controls for the full lifecycle of the EM samples (plates and swabs) to ensure the validity of the results, including:

  • Media supplier management
  • Receipt
  • Quality control of incoming media (including identity, general condition and appearance, growth promotion, sterility check, and expiration dating)
  • Handling and storage prior to use
  • Use in aseptic operations:
    • Transport into cleanrooms (and removal of outer wrapping/layers)
    • Sampling aseptic techniques and minimized sample-handling within the cleanroom
    • Closing of plates and swabs to maintain integrity after sampling
    • Cleaning and disinfection after sampling (of gloves and surfaces)
  • Reconciliation, labeling, and chain of custody
  • Transportation to incubators (including any taping, bagging, or wrapping to protect samples)
  • Incubation, reading (with confirmation of results), and subculture (if any)
  • Identification and specification
  • Handling of any discrepancies

Risk assessment tools should be used to define the controls to be put in place for the end-to-end chain of custody for all phases of the plate- or swab-handling process, with specific focus of reducing the following contamination risks during the process:

  • Handling and labeling of media prior to sampling
  • Sample collection by EM sampling personnel
  • Handling, labeling, and transportation following sample collection
  • Laboratory handling for incubation and reading post-monitoring

Detailed procedures, training, and qualification of personnel are essential to ensure that these technique-driven handling procedures (especially during the exposure of the samples in the cleanroom) are well practiced and performed effectively by each person assigned to a role in handling EM samples.

SOPs should be established to define the processes to be followed for atypical events including desiccated plates, cracked plates, dropped plates, nonviable particulate matter on plates, and viable growth (which should be atypical in Grade A and B). These SOPs should include documentation containing example pictures of the impacted plates and details on how to handle atypical plates. A deviation, out-of-limits, or equivalent laboratory investigation should be raised to initiate the examination of any abnormal result. The impacted plates should be retained until completion of the investigation (18).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The dual nature of EM:

Environmental monitoring (EM) is itself a paradox: it is a tool used to verify that the environment is under control, yet the personnel who perform EM and the media themselves are a potential source of contamination of the environment.

Time-driven vs. event-driven:

  • Time-driven: settle plates and volumetric air sampling, collected at time intervals and reflecting the overall trend
  • Event-driven: contact plates and swabs, tied to specific events such as after an intervention, after a personnel shift change, or at the end of a batch

Total particulate monitoring should be performed continuously throughout.

Analogy

Controlling the full life cycle of an EM sample is like the chain of custody for physical evidence in court: from sampling to the verdict (microbial identification), every step must be recorded, and any break may make the result inadmissible. The media supplier, incoming quality control, cold-chain storage, cleanroom handling technique, incubation conditions, and plate-reading method each need an SOP and training records; otherwise, even if the incubation result is normal, it cannot be shown to be trustworthy.

Key Notes

The regulatory view that "the media itself poses a contamination risk":

Settle plates contain growth-promoting media. Once placed in the Grade A environment:

  • If media residue is not cleaned up after sampling, it becomes a nutrient source for subsequent microorganisms
  • The sampling personnel are themselves the greatest contamination risk: an EM operator entering Grade A is itself an intervention and must be designed and qualified like any other intervention

New technology: biofluorescent particle counting can detect viable particles in real time and non-invasively, and is a potential alternative to traditional settle plates. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022) has begun to mention such emerging technologies.

Practical Application

In audits of a CDMO's EM program, the questions auditors most often ask include:

  • Is the growth promotion test of the media performed for every lot?
  • How are dropped settle plates handled? Does the SOP include photographic illustrations?
  • Are the event-driven sampling locations (such as after an intervention) consistent with the CCS?
  • Are the technique qualification records for EM personnel complete?

Any growth in Grade A should immediately trigger a deviation investigation, and the plates should be retained until the investigation is complete.

Practice Questions

  1. While collecting a settle plate, an EM sampler accidentally lets the plate touch a Grade A surface and then continues to finish the sampling. How should this event be recorded and assessed? Is the sampling result still valid?
  2. Why is the act of EM sampling itself regarded as an "intervention"? What does this mean for APS design?

Section Summary (8.4–8.9)

  • Filling needle management (8.4): repair or replacement of a liquid filling needle is one of the highest-risk interventions; a pre-assembled fluid path reduces the risk of replacement; a powder filling needle can only be replaced completely.
  • Handling of broken containers (8.5): all corrective interventions must be included in the AVS and APS and simulated at a representative frequency; follow the "minimize actions" principle, and avoid movements below working height.
  • Component supply (8.6): automated transfer is preferred; manual transfer requires layer-by-layer bag removal, with the last layer removed only in Grade A; mouseholes/RTPs must have AVS airflow verification.
  • Sorting systems (8.7): qualify each stoppering set individually; manage with kitting; residual silicone oil can inhibit biodecontamination and must be completely removed during cleaning.
  • Four categories of mechanical intervention (8.8): Category 1 is performed as standard; Categories 2-3 need immediate QA risk assessment; Category 4 (technical area) in principle requires stopping the batch; sterility assurance always takes priority over salvaging a batch.
  • Environmental monitoring (8.9): EM is both a "monitoring tool" and a "contamination risk"; the sampling plan combines time-driven and event-driven sampling; the full life cycle of the media must be tightly controlled; EM personnel are themselves the greatest source of contamination risk.

→

→
