Containment and decontamination considerations should be included in the design of filtration manifolds so that waste associated with PUPSIT or filter-flush at the beginning of processing is handled in a way that does not risk the employees, the environment, or the outside of any filled containers.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Sterile fluid pathway: the complete piping system that starts at the formulation vessel, passes through the sterilizing filter and extends to the point of fill. Every connection, valve and length of tubing along this path is a potential contamination risk point.

Filterability: not every liquid passes easily through a 0.22 µm sterilizing membrane. Highly viscous products, products containing protein aggregates, and large-molecule products tend to block or blind the membrane. In these cases, redundant paths (parallel filter trains) or in-line prefilters must be designed in.

Analogy

Think of a city water supply line: water plant (formulation vessel) → purification filter (sterilizing filter) → individual households (point of fill). If the source water is turbid (a high-protein product), a single filter will clog quickly, so engineers design two lines in parallel so that one can be cleaned while the other keeps supplying water. This is the design logic of a parallel filter train.

Key Notes

Special obligations for highly potent products: the waste generated by PUPSIT integrity testing or filter flushing must go to a dedicated waste collection system (biocontainment bag, waste system). Without proper design, HPAPI waste could contaminate the environment or personnel; this is not only a GMP issue but also an occupational safety issue. When designing the fluid pathway, the waste flow path is just as important as the normal product flow path.

Practice Questions

  1. If a monoclonal antibody (mAb) begins to aggregate after standing for 2 hours at 37°C, how would this affect the filter design? What design countermeasures would you recommend?
  2. Why does PUPSIT waste need a specially designed waste management system? When should a CDMO discuss this design detail when taking on a highly potent drug?
11.3 Product Transfer Modalities and Influence on System Design

Original Text

The two primary methods to get product from a vessel through the filter-manifold, either to another vessel or directly to the filler, are overpressure and pumping.

Overpressure is provided by the application of a sterile gas (either clean, compressed air or an inert gas such as nitrogen) in the headspace of the pressure vessel. The increase in pressure in the headspace forces the product through the bottom outlet of the vessel and through the transfer lines. The pressure can be controlled to either continuously or intermittently feed the product.

Pumping is the application of a mechanical transfer of the fluid in the transfer line. The pump can be product-contacting (e.g., rotary lobe, centrifugal) or non-product-contacting (e.g., peristaltic). Care must be taken to ensure that, with either transfer mechanism, the pressure and any pulsation of the liquids does not harm the filter membrane or create shear stress on the product that can result in the formation of particulate or harm-filterable suspensions for example.

Configurations for transfer can include presterilized intermediate vessels (also known as surge vessels) in conjunction with a manifold, or the transfer can be made directly to the filler manifold without an intermediate vessel. The filler manifold assists in securing a stable flow of product to the filling pumps and needles by providing a small upstream reservoir or widening of the fluid pathway.

Table 11.3-1🔍 Transfer System Design Influences on Filtration Risks

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Overpressure transfer: sterile gas (compressed air or nitrogen) pressurizes the top of the vessel and pushes the liquid out from the bottom. The advantage is that there is no risk from mechanical contact with the product; the disadvantage is complex pressure control, since unstable pressure directly affects the dosing accuracy of a time-pressure filling system.

Pumping: the liquid is moved by mechanical drive. Peristaltic pumps do not contact the product but produce pulsation; rotary lobe pumps contact the product directly and may generate shear stress that damages protein molecules.

Surge vessel / sterile intermediate vessel: an intermediate holding vessel located downstream of the filter and upstream of the filling manifold. It allows the filtration speed to be controlled independently and greatly reduces the risk of the filter being subjected to pump start-stop shocks.

Analogy

Imagine a kitchen hot water supply: overpressure is like a water tower supplying by gravity (stable, but the pressure depends on the water level); pumping is like an electric booster pump (the flow rate is controllable but pulsating). The surge vessel in between is like the storage tank of a water heater, so that while you shower (filling) you do not have to worry about changes in the tower's water level (filtration speed) affecting the water pressure (fill accuracy). With the surge vessel, the two ends are decoupled and each can be optimized more easily.

Key Notes

Key insight from Table 11.3-1🔍: whether or not a sterile intermediate vessel is present is the watershed in design complexity. Without an intermediate vessel, filtration and filling are coupled, and rate fluctuations at either end affect the other (pressure drop, dosing accuracy). With an intermediate vessel, the two unit operations are decoupled and controlled independently, which greatly reduces risk, but at the cost of more space and more validation. This is a typical engineering trade-off: design complexity in exchange for operational stability.

Practical Application

A CDMO takes on a mAb product with a 200 L batch and an expected fill time of 8 hours, using a time-pressure (TP) filler. Your engineer proposes "overpressure + direct feed to the filling manifold (no intermediate vessel)" to save space. In a long fill, what happens to the pressure on the filtration side as the vessel level falls? How would you modify the design?

11.4 Filter Selection and Influences on System Design

Original Text

The two primary filter types are cartridge filters and capsule filters.

Cartridge filters are filter membranes installed within a filter housing that is part of the equipment. O-rings at the bottom of the filter create the seal with the equipment housing. Cartridge filters can be either sterilized out of place in an autoclave or SIP on a rigid piping system, and then integrity-tested in place (see Section 11.9).

Capsule filters are supplied with a molded-polymer housing that is an integral part of the supplied filter. The housing, which is pressure-rated, is equipped with connectors and test connections that can be clamped directly to existing stainless-steel transfer lines, creating a continuous pathway that can be CIP, SIP, or assembled and autoclaved. The capsule filter is then integrity-tested according to the PUPSIT justification (see Section 11.9). The selection of the type of filter to be used is driven in part by the complexity of connections and complexity of the equipment for the filtration-unit operation. Capsule filters are more highly integrated with the fluid pathway and are considered the filter of choice for SUS.

The materials of construction of the transfer lines, filter, and filter-housing should be evaluated for compatibility with the product to prevent the risk, for example, API or preservative adsorption, oxidation, or exposure to free radicals. When any of these conditions are unavoidable, consideration should be given to the flush quantities required to standardize the product homogeneity (e.g., through binding to available sites). This flush quantity must be proven through validation, and the line length and filter surface area must be tightly controlled and standardized by procedure.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Cartridge filter: the membrane is installed in a metal filter housing that belongs to the equipment and is sealed with O-rings. It can be steam-sterilized in place (SIP), or removed and autoclaved before being refitted. It suits fixed stainless steel piping systems, is durable and has a lower long-term cost.

Capsule filter: the membrane and a polymer shell are formed as one unit and clamped directly onto the tubing. No housing or O-rings are needed, which makes it especially suitable for single-use systems (SUS). With the trend toward SUS in aseptic manufacturing, the capsule filter is the mainstream choice.

Compatibility and adsorption: some APIs (especially small molecules or charged proteins) are adsorbed by the membrane or tubing, so the actual filled concentration is lower than the labeled concentration. The solution is to design a pre-flush quantity (flush quantity): the product itself first occupies the adsorption sites (saturation), so that the product concentration in the actual production meets specification. This flush quantity must be validated and included in the discard calculation.

Key Notes

"The filter of choice for SUS" has an important meaning: the dominance of the capsule filter in SUS is not only a matter of convenience. It means that the entire pathway (transfer line + filter + connectors) can be brought into the aseptic area as a pre-assembled, pre-sterilized system, greatly reducing the number of assembly steps and the contamination risk from human intervention. This is a direct expression of sterility assurance logic.

Formula Thinking

Pre-flush volume validation logic:

Product loss = tubing volume × adsorption coefficient + filter holdup volume

Validation requirements:
  1. Determine the minimum flush quantity → the outlet concentration reaches the target specification
  2. Fix an upper limit on tubing length (too long = more adsorption sites)
  3. Fix the filter area (too large = larger holdup volume)
  4. Write the flush quantity into the SOP; any deviation triggers an investigation

Golden rule of tubing design: the shorter and the narrower the better (provided the flow rate is met)

Practice Questions

  1. A CDMO uses stainless steel piping with a capsule filter to fill an ophthalmic preparation, and finds that the concentration at the start of the first batch is about 8% low and returns to normal later in the fill. What is the most likely cause? How could it be prevented at the design stage?
  2. Why is the capsule filter called "the filter of choice for SUS"? Explain from the perspective of sterility assurance.
11.5 Filter Configuration Alternatives

Original Text

A wide variety of filter configurations are possible. The product attributes will drive the selection of the filter configuration, as will considerations for risk mitigation associated with SA.

One common approach is the installation of a bioburden-reduction filter placed upstream of the sterilizing filter. In some cases, two sterilizing filters can be placed in a series; this ensures that, if the downstream filter fails an integrity test, the upstream filter may be tested for integrity. If the upstream filter passes, then the batch disposition is not compromised.

Another common configuration is the installation of two parallel fluid pathways, each with a sterilizing filter in place. In this redundant parallel configuration, the process would proceed through the first pathway, with pressure being monitored throughout, until a pressure rise is observed across the membrane. When that pressure rise is observed, the fluid pathway is switched to the secondary pathway. This approach is often used when working with products that are likely to block the filter due to particulate or product deposition that blocks the filter's pores (e.g., large molecules, proteinaceous, long filtration times due to large batches or prolonged filling operations).

"Legacy configurations that employ the removal of a prefilter during processing, rather than employing a redundant filtration manifold, should be assessed for compliance; breaking into a transfer line and filtration manifold after integrity-testing presents a significant risk (see Section 11.9)."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three main filter configurations:

  • Series: a bioburden reduction filter plus a sterilizing filter, or two sterilizing filters in series. The benefit of the latter is that if the downstream filter fails its integrity test, the upstream filter can be tested to salvage the batch.
  • Redundant parallel: two flow paths, each with a sterilizing filter. When the first path becomes blocked (rising differential pressure), filling continues on the second path without stopping. Suitable for protein drugs and large-batch products.
  • Prefiltration (bioburden reduction): a prefilter with a larger pore size (0.45 µm) is placed ahead of the sterilizing filter to extend the life of the main filter.

Key Notes

Regulatory risk of legacy configurations: some older facilities remove a blocked prefilter in the middle of production, replace it with a new one and then continue production. The spirit of EU GMP Annex 1 clearly opposes this practice: reopening the line after the integrity test (breaking into the manifold) is equivalent to introducing a new contamination risk. FDA and EU inspectors pay particular attention to such designs during inspections. A CDMO with a similar legacy design should plan an upgrade proactively rather than wait for an inspection to find the problem.

Analogy

Redundant parallel filtration is like a two-lane highway toll station: when the first lane (filter) becomes congested (rising differential pressure), traffic switches immediately to the second lane, and the highway (filling) never has to close. Series double sterilizing filters are like passport control followed by customs: only when both checkpoints are passed is release truly granted, and there is also a safety net: if customs (the downstream filter) fails, passport control (the upstream filter) can still be used to salvage the situation.

Practice Questions

  1. A 500 L protein drug batch has an expected fill time of 10 hours, and there is a history of filters blocking early on several occasions. Which filter configuration would you recommend? Explain your selection logic.
  2. Why is "opening the line to replace the prefilter" after the integrity test considered a significant risk? Explain from the sterility assurance (SA) decision logic.
11.6 Duration of Fill and Impact on Filtration System Layout

Original Text

When considering the configuration for the fluid path and whether to make use of a sterile holding vessel, the duration of the filling process and the likely duration of the filtration process should be taken into account. The duration of the filtration is an important parameter in the initial qualification of the filter membrane and one that will require requalification should the filtration time be changed over the life of the product (26).

Two failure modes are possible if the filling process is prolonged. First, as the bulk product is held during presterilization, the bioburden may replicate in the nonsterile bulk intermediate vessel and, as a result, present a challenge to the sterilizing filter. Second, there is a risk of "grow through" for the filter, where microorganisms on the upstream side of the filter can divide and multiply, grow through the membrane, and breach the intended sterile barrier of the filter membrane.

Consequently, if the filling process is prolonged, thereby prolonging the filtration process, consideration should be given to using a sterile transfer vessel so the filtration can be accomplished more quickly. This approach will require additional space for the placement of the sterile vessel. The presterilized intermediate vessel must be held under positive pressure after sterilization and throughout the filling operation. In addition, the sterile intermediate vessel will require a sterilizing vent-filter during the transfer process, which will also require an integrity test at the conclusion of the filling process.

The sterile hold-time for the bulk must be validated as part of the manufacturing process. Other possible consequences of prolonged filling operations include blocking of the sterilizing filter, as discussed in Section 11.5.

For direct filtration without a bulk intermediate vessel, slow and fast fill-speeds must be validated to ensure that the filtration parameters (e.g., maximum and minimum flow rate, differential pressure) can be maintained while supplying the filler with consistent product flow.

"Aseptic filling operations are expected to have point-of-use filtration, regardless of the filling system design, when permitted by the product and filler attributes (see Section 11.11)."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Two failure modes with extended fill time:

  • Bioburden replication: microorganisms in the non-sterile formulation vessel multiply heavily during a long hold, exceeding the retention capability of the sterilizing filter (the upper limit of its LRV design). This is a risk at the front end of filtration.
  • Grow-through: during a long filtration, microorganisms upstream of the membrane gradually cross the 0.22 µm membrane into the sterile side through cell division. This is a hazard of particular concern in EU Annex 1, and it is why filtration time must be one of the key validated parameters.

Sterile hold time: the maximum time the product can be held in a sterile state after sterilizing filtration; it must be validated through a bioburden challenge study.

Analogy

Grow-through is like a group of ants (microorganisms) placed in front of a fine sand screen (the membrane). If they are only near it briefly, the ants cannot get through; but if they are left in front of the screen for a long time, they keep dividing, multiplying and looking for gaps, and may eventually breed a path that crosses it. This is why the filtration time limit must be validated and locked in, and why the production schedule must not be extended arbitrarily.

Key Notes

Cost and benefit of a sterile intermediate vessel design: complete filtration quickly (filter everything into the sterile vessel first) → both time-related failure modes are eliminated → fill slowly afterwards. The cost: more cleanroom space for the vessel, the vessel itself needs SIP/autoclave validation, and the vent filter on its exhaust also needs PUPSIT and integrity testing. This is a typical engineering decision that trades space and complexity for sterility assurance.

Two-sided requirement for fill rate validation: too slow → filtration time too long (grow-through risk); too fast → differential pressure too high (risk of filter membrane damage). Therefore both the minimum and the maximum rate must be validated, not just one end.

Practice Questions

  1. Your product batch is 300 L, with a historical fill time of about 12 hours. The "maximum filtration time" in the filtration validation report is set at 6 hours. How would you modify the process design to meet this limit without affecting the fill time?
  2. "The sterile intermediate vessel must maintain positive pressure throughout the filling process": what is the purpose of this requirement? If positive pressure is lost, what is the risk?
11.7 Sterilization of the Filter and Filter Train

Original Text

When selecting a sterilizing filter, there are multiple options for ensuring the sterility of the filter and its associated transfer lines. Filters can be gamma-irradiated SU, or they can be sterilized on site, either through an autoclave load or SIP cycles.

For optimal SA, all connections required for the filter should be made prior to the sterilization step, especially on the downstream side; as an alternative, intrinsic sterile connection-devices should be considered to reduce the risk of sterility breaches during assembly. These approaches would require coordination with the filter supplier to ensure that the needed connections can be supplied if the filter will arrive RTU (Ready-to-Use). For on-site filter assembly, there may be more flexibility in the connectors used, as bioburden-controlled assembly can be implemented prior to the sterilization step.

The mechanism of transfer to the line should be considered, as it will determine whether the filtration apparatus requires special packaging, such as double- or triple-bagging for introduction to the filling area, or whether a RTP (Rapid Transfer Port) system or other advanced protective measures will be used (see Section 9.0 and Section 10.0 for the transfer of materials and components).

The method of sterilization should also be evaluated for impact on the product. For example, when using gamma-irradiation, the formation of free radicals may result in the need to reject the first quantity of filtered product as a precautionary measure (see Section 12.0 for information on discard considerations).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Comparison of the three filter sterilization methods:

  • Gamma-irradiated single-use (SU): sterilized by the supplier and supplied ready-to-use (RTU). This is the most convenient, but note that residual free radicals may oxidize the product; normally the initial filtered product must be discarded (initial discard), see Section 12.0.
  • Autoclave: removed and steam-sterilized in an autoclave. Suitable for capsule filters; the whole assembly is autoclaved together, so no SIP line is needed. Flexibility is high, but handling and introduction require double or triple bagging or RTP transfer.
  • Steam-in-place (SIP): the piping is fixed in place, and steam is fed directly into the piping and filter for sterilization. The piping design must support it (drainage, steam inlet, condensate discharge). Suitable for cartridge filters in fixed stainless steel piping.

Pre-sterilization connection: the optimal SA strategy is to complete all connections (especially on the downstream side) before sterilization, to avoid the contamination risk of making connections afterwards. For filter assemblies supplied RTU, coordinate with the supplier to ensure the pre-connected specification meets the site's needs.

Key Notes

The free radical problem with gamma irradiation: polymer materials generate free radicals after gamma irradiation, and these can dissolve into the liquid at the start of product filtration, causing oxidative degradation (particularly harmful to biologics with oxidation-sensitive APIs). Industry practice is to specify that the first X liters of product filtered be discarded; this discard volume must be validated and recorded in the batch record. It directly affects the batch material loss calculation (yield).

The introduction method determines the packaging requirements: if autoclaved components must be brought into the Grade A area manually by personnel, triple bagging is needed, with one layer removed in each environment of different cleanliness level. With an RTP system, a single layer of packaging allows quick introduction, greatly reducing contamination risk and improving efficiency. This is a typical case of equipment investment affecting the SA of the operating process.

Analogy

Filter sterilization and introduction are like the preparation of surgical instruments: autoclaving (SIP) is like the hospital's central sterile supply department handling stainless steel instruments (fixed equipment, done on site); a gamma-irradiated SU is like a disposable sterile surgical pack (open and use, but mind the post-irradiation effects of the material, i.e. free radicals); and double-bag introduction is like the multiple layers of protection on the way from the sterile supply department to the operating table, where one outer bag is removed on entering each cleaner environment.

Practice Questions

  1. Your CDMO is building a new SUS filling line, and the customer requires gamma-irradiated RTU capsule filter assemblies. To avoid the effect of free radicals on the protein drug, how would you plan this in the fluid pathway design and the batch operating SOP?
  2. What effect does the principle of "completing all connections before sterilization" (pre-sterilization connection) have on the engineering design timeline when a CDMO takes on a new product? What items do you need to discuss with the filter supplier in advance?

Section Summary (11.0–11.7)

  • Core logic of design decisions: every design choice in the sterile fluid pathway (filter type, transfer mode, presence of an intermediate vessel, sterilization method) should start from sterility assurance first, with commercial convenience and operational flexibility second.
  • Trade-offs in transfer mode: overpressure is simple, but unstable pressure may affect dosing accuracy; pumping gives controllable flow but carries the risks of shear stress and start-stop shocks; a sterile intermediate vessel decouples filtration from filling and greatly reduces mutual interference, but increases space and validation requirements.
  • Modern trend in filter selection: the capsule filter is the first choice for SUS because it is highly integrated and easy to pre-assemble and pre-sterilize, consistent with the spirit of EU Annex 1; cartridge filters suit long-term, high-capacity facilities with fixed stainless steel piping.
  • Grow-through is a hidden risk: the longer the fill, the longer the filtration time and the greater the chance of microorganisms penetrating the membrane. Filtration time must be a key validated parameter, and exceeding it triggers a deviation investigation.
  • The sterilization method affects product safety: although gamma irradiation is convenient, the free radical issue must be addressed at the design stage through validation of the initial discard volume; completing all connections before sterilization is SA best practice, and RTU and RTP are important tools of modern aseptic manufacturing.
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p175 - p181

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the filtration risk points of each filling technology (RPP, DP, TP, PP), including back-flow, pulsation and pressure drop
  • Understand how manifold design affects sterility assurance, including dead-leg, venting and SIP design requirements
  • Understand the control strategy for non-filterable products (suspensions, cell therapies) and the core concept of "the process is the product"
  • Become familiar with the filtration needs of powder filling systems (VPPF, AF), including compressed air, vacuum, inert gas and dust-extraction filtration
  • Be able to prioritize filtration design options according to the decision hierarchy (sterility assurance > CQAs > commercial flexibility)
11.8 (cont.) Fluid Pathway Design Risk by Liquid Filler Type — Manifold Considerations

Original Text

For rolling DPs, the pump itself may cause some pulsation (depending on design and size), which presents a higher risk to the filter membrane. Increasing the distance between the filter and the pump may dampen this effect.

For RPPs, there is a risk of back-flow through the filter if the volume (e.g., manifold or reservoir) between the pump and the filter is inadequate.

Having a manifold (header) upstream of the filling heads (e.g., filling pumps for RPP or DP, pinch valves in TP filling systems, rotors in PP filling systems) is a common design feature. When the filter is positioned to provide point-of-use filtration, a small dead-leg can be formed between the filter and the end of the manifold. This dead-leg can create a risk when performing such activities as filter-flushing at the beginning of the filling operation. The dead-leg provides some uncertainty about whether the full volume of the waste solution has been expelled from the system.

For RPP and TP filling systems, including a mechanism that vents air from the filling system should be considered. For example, air removal is beneficial at startup, as the manifold first fills, or when there are interventions that introduce air to the system. If the manifold can be positioned below the filling pumps, this positioning may reduce or eliminate the need for a separate venting mechanism, if air can escape through the filling heads.

Design of the manifold should be carefully considered to ensure that it can be appropriately sterilized and assembled in the fluid pathway in an aseptic manner, especially when introducing the manifold through a RTP for assembly. If it is subject to SIP, the manifold represents a widening of the line and a transition to multiple filling systems, so it is imperative to ensure that an adequate mechanism for complete air removal during sterilization is present.

In addition to these considerations for in-line filtration to liquid filling systems, other filters may be in place along the fluid pathway, including:

  • Vessel vent filters (not required for SU bags)
  • Inert-gas point-of-use filters
  • Manifold/filling-head venting system filters (as applicable)

Integrity-testing will be required for each of these additional process filters. That integrity-testing will commonly be performed off-line as these are hydrophobic filters that would commonly be tested with alcohol.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Manifold / dead-leg: A manifold is the piping that distributes a single filtered liquid to multiple filling needles. When a filter is installed at the end of the manifold for "point-of-use filtration", a "dead-leg" can form between the filter and the end of the manifold, i.e. a short section of the fluid path that cannot be flushed completely.

Hazard of a dead-leg: when the filter is flushed, waste liquid in the dead-leg (such as alcohol from integrity testing or flushing water) may not drain completely, leaving residues that dilute the product or introduce impurities.

RPP back-flow risk: During the idle stroke, the RPP piston briefly creates negative pressure. If the volume upstream of the filter is insufficient, liquid may flow backward through the membrane and damage it through reverse pressure.

DP pulsation risk: The output of a rolling diaphragm pump is cyclically pulsatile. If the filter is too close to the pump, repeated pressure waves accelerate membrane fatigue and increase the risk of failure.

Analogy

Think of taking a shower. The showerhead body is the manifold, the water heater is the pump, and the water filter in between is the sterilizing-grade filter. If the filter is installed very close to the showerhead, but the showerhead base has a small bend (a dead-leg), then each time you start flushing, the old water in that bend (possibly cleaning solution left from last time) does not necessarily all flow out.

RPP back-flow is like water in a pipe flowing backward when the pump stops. Without enough buffer volume (such as a storage tank), the reverse flow hits the membrane. DP pulsation is like a heartbeat: without proper damping, regular pressure waves will, over time, give the membrane "heart failure".

Key Notes

Decision hierarchy reminder: Manifold design must first ensure sterility assurance (SA). If a dead-leg causes incomplete flushing, it is not only a product dilution problem but also a potential site for microbial growth, which directly violates the first priority.

SIP design trap: During SIP (steam-in-place), a manifold turns the piping from a single line into a multi-branch structure, and steam must reach the end of every branch. If venting points are poorly designed, some dead zones may never reach sterilization temperature and become cold spots. This is one of the most common causes of SIP validation failure.

Integrity testing of hydrophobic filters: Hydrophobic filters such as vent filters and inert gas filters cannot be tested directly with water-based methods (bubble point / diffusion). They must be wetted with alcohol and tested offline, which is more complicated to perform than testing hydrophilic filters.

Practice Questions

  1. If your filling system uses an RPP with a point-of-use filter and the manifold design creates a significant dead-leg, which design corrections would you take first?
  2. Why is filter pressure drop a particular concern for a TP system that has no sterile receiver?
  3. When a CDMO takes on a new client's product, if the equipment is already fixed and the manifold has a slight dead-leg, how would you quantify and control this risk in process validation?
11.11 Considerations Regarding Products that are Not Filterable

Original Text

Some products cannot be sterile-filtered, for example, some suspension products and cell therapy products where the particle size of the suspension or cells exceeds the porosity rating of the filter. Terminal sterilization should always be the first choice for the preparation of sterile products. However, where neither terminal sterilization nor sterile filtration are possible due to the composition and attributes of the product, a control strategy must be in place.

The product and process control strategy must address the steps taken to ensure the sterility of each ingredient/component of the product, including the potential for filtration of each prior to introduction to the unfilterable component, and to ensure that the procedures used to bring the various ingredients/components together provide the highest possible SA.

Minimizing the length of the fluid pathway and ensuring its integrity after sterilization are essential elements to success for these products. A risk assessment is recommended to support the robustness of the overall control strategy for SA.

"In these cases, the process is the product; that is, the combination of all the sterile inputs provides the assurance of sterility for the final product. Hence, each must be separately assured."

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Non-filterable products: When the active component of a product is itself a "large particle" (for example suspended particles, live cells, viral vectors or lipid nanoparticles), a 0.22 µm sterilizing-grade filter will not only fail to retain bacteria but will also retain the product itself. Filtering the product means destroying it.

Typical examples:

  • Suspension injectables (such as insulin crystal suspensions and vaccine adjuvant suspensions)
  • Cell therapy products (CAR-T, stem cells)
  • Large viral vectors (AAV gene therapy)

"The process is the product": Because the final product can be neither sterilized nor filtered, the only way to guarantee sterility is to ensure that every input material, every process step and every contact surface is sterile. The final sterility equals the sum of all sterile inputs.

Analogy

Traditional injectable manufacturing is like cooking a pot of soup, then passing it through a fine sieve to remove all impurities before bottling. The final filtration is the last safety net.

Cell therapy is different: the "ingredients" in your soup are themselves the precious material you want to keep (live cells), so you cannot use a sieve because it would block all of them. Instead you must make sure that every ingredient is clean from the moment it is purchased, every pot is disinfected, and the entire kitchen is run at cleanroom standard. There is no final safety net; your "kitchen process" itself is the only guarantee.

Key Notes

Application of the decision hierarchy: For non-filterable products, the rule "sterility assurance (SA) always comes first" is challenged the most, because you can rely on neither terminal sterilization nor sterilizing filtration. Here, risk assessment (QRM) is not optional but mandatory. EU GMP Annex 1 explicitly requires a stricter contamination control strategy (CCS) for such products.

Minimize the length of the liquid pathway: The longer the path, the higher the exposure risk, since every connector, valve and length of tubing is a potential contamination point. The design principle is "the shorter the better, the fewer the connections the better".

Assure the sterility of each raw material separately: Every filterable excipient should be filtered before the non-filterable component is added. Once mixed, the product can no longer be filtered, so sterility assurance of each component before mixing is critical.

Practical Application

When a CDMO accepts a cell therapy or gene therapy client, the first point to assess is whether it has adequate isolator or RABS facilities. The sterile pathway requirements for these products are even higher than for conventional small-molecule drugs, and any single point of environmental exposure may cause the batch to be scrapped.

Impact on the CDMO business model: accepting such products means accepting a business with a very high risk of batch loss, so liability for batch failure and risk-sharing terms must be negotiated explicitly in the contract in advance.

11.12 Filtration Associated with Powder Filling

Original Text

Although there is no filtration associated with a product in powder-filling, filtration is associated with:

  • Powder delivery and handling
  • Inerting
  • Drying after cleaning
  • Exhaust and dust collection

For vacuum pressure powder fillers (VPPF), point-of-use filtration is used for the clean compressed air and the vacuum. The filters are installed between the utility source (e.g., vacuum, dosing air, purge air) and the mechanical backplate or the pneumatic rotary joint. (For fillers designed for dosing needles, there is one filter per air or vacuum pathway.) The filter assembly is installed as part of the aseptic setup of the filling system.

For both VPPF and auger fillers (AF), an inert gas or clean compressed air may also be introduced to assist with powder flow within the hopper. For both VPPF and AF, if the product requires protection from oxygen, a filtered inerting-gas is also used during the filling operation.

For AF, no clean compressed air or vacuum is associated with the filling operation; however, filtered clean compressed air is associated with drying the powder pathway after cleaning. If CIP is associated with the bulk-hopper component of the VPPF filler, the bulk hopper would also be subject to drying with filtered clean compressed air. (VPPF dosing-system elements, other than the bulk hopper, are not capable of CIP and, therefore, will not have clean compressed air for system drying.)

All filter usage for VPPF and AF described here make use of a sterilizing-grade hydrophobic filter with a nominal pore size of 0.22 µm. These filters are typically procured as sterile, gamma-irradiated capsule filters, although autoclavable options may also be used. All piping downstream of the filter should be capable of sterilization. All filters should be subject to integrity-testing, and the integrity-test results should be considered in the batch disposition process.

Either filler type may make use of dust collection, which would use HEPA-filtered exhaust at the point of collection. These filters are generally located within a gray space to facilitate change-out of the filter and emptying of the reservoir outside the cleanroom environment; however, cleanroom models do exist. Dust-collection systems may also employ a bag-in–bag-out configuration for potent compounds that require containment. These HEPA filters are intended for containment rather than microbiological control; therefore, the frequency of integrity-testing is at the discretion of the manufacturer based on application, system design (e.g., location of the filter), and risk.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Filtration logic for powder filling: The powder product itself does not need to be filtered, because it is already a sterile solid. However, all gases that contact or affect the powder (compressed air, vacuum, inert gas) must pass through sterilizing-grade filters, because these gases can be carriers of microbial contamination.

VPPF filtration points: Each gas line (dosing air, purge air, vacuum) needs its own 0.22 µm hydrophobic filter, installed between the gas source and the machine backplate or rotary pneumatic connector. A multi-needle VPPF may therefore have dozens of gas filters to manage.

Bag-in / bag-out: In the dust-extraction systems for highly active compounds (highly toxic, highly potent drugs), the filter itself may carry a large amount of drug powder, so changing it exposes operators. A bag-in/bag-out design lets operators change the filter without touching the contaminated filter: the new filter is installed from its bag first, and then the old filter bag is sealed and removed.

Overview of Powder Filling Filter Management

Filter type          Application             Pore size  Integrity test
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
VPPF gas filter     dosing/purge air        0.22 µm    Required (batch record)
VPPF vacuum filter  vacuum pathway          0.22 µm    Required (batch record)
Inert gas filter    N₂ inerting             0.22 µm    Required (batch record)
Cleaning drying air filter  AF/VPPF CIP drying  0.22 µm  Required (batch record)
HEPA dust filter    exhaust/containment     HEPA       Frequency set by manufacturer
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
All filters: sterilizing-grade hydrophobic (gamma-irradiated capsule or autoclavable type)
HEPA filters: mainly for containment, not microbial control; testing frequency is more flexible

Analogy

Gas filtration in powder filling is like the air-conditioning system of an operating room. The scalpel itself is sterile, but if the supply air carries bacteria, the wound can still become infected. The VPPF powder is the "scalpel" (already sterile), while compressed air and vacuum are the "supply air". Without filtration, even sterile powder can be contaminated by the gases during filling.

A HEPA dust-extraction filter is more like the filter on a facility exhaust duct. Its purpose is not to make the air sterile but to keep highly potent powder dust from escaping and harming operators. The purpose differs, so the way it is managed differs.

Key Notes

Integrity testing and batch disposition: The integrity test results of all 0.22 µm gas filters must be considered in batch disposition. This is consistent with the requirements for sterilizing filters in liquid filling; it is a mandatory regulatory requirement and cannot be omitted.

CIP limitation of AF: Only the bulk hopper of a VPPF can be CIP-cleaned; the dosing system components (the metering part) of a VPPF cannot be CIP-cleaned and therefore do not need drying compressed air filters. The AF filling operation itself needs no gas, but gas is needed for drying after cleaning. This difference affects the scope of equipment qualification (OQ/PQ) testing.

Flexibility for HEPA filters: The integrity test frequency of HEPA dust-extraction filters is set by the manufacturer based on risk (location, application, system design). This contrasts clearly with sterilizing filters in aseptic processes (tested every batch) and reflects the two different control purposes, containment vs. sterility.

Practice Questions

  1. A 16-needle VPPF has three gas lines (dosing air, purge air and vacuum) for each filling path. What is the minimum number of 0.22 µm filters this machine needs to manage? How would the integrity tests of these filters be integrated into the batch record?
  2. A client asks to fill an oxygen-sensitive, highly potent anticancer powder using an AF. Describe what additional filtration considerations are needed and how you would assess the need for a bag-in/bag-out design.
  3. The integrity test frequency of HEPA dust-extraction filters is "set by the manufacturer". What criteria do you think should be used to decide this frequency when designing a CDMO SOP?
Table 11.10-1🔍 — Summary Commentary: Fluid Pathway Design Risks of Each Filling Technology

Risk Summary

Table 11.10-1🔍 compares the key design risks of the four main liquid filling technologies side by side and is an important reference for equipment selection and process design. The following is a full explanation of the original table.

Note: For PP, the operational risk column reads "None" because the tubing of a peristaltic pump is a closed system and the liquid is driven by external squeezing of the tubing, so there is no back-flow or pulsation problem. However, the common design requirements for manifolds and venting still apply.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts: Essential Differences Among the Four Technologies

Why does PP (peristaltic pump) have no operational risk? A peristaltic pump moves liquid by squeezing the tubing with external rollers. The liquid path is fully enclosed in the tubing, so back-flow is almost impossible and no damaging pulsation is produced. This is one of the reasons PP is widely used in aseptic filling.

Pressure drop in TP (time-pressure filling): A TP system uses gas pressure to push product out of a pressure vessel. When a filter is installed at the outlet, its resistance (pressure drop) affects filling accuracy, because fill volume is determined by pressure × time. If the pressure drop is unstable (for example as the membrane gradually clogs), the fill volume drifts.

Key Notes: Application of the Decision Hierarchy

When a CDMO selects filling equipment for a new client, Table 11.10-1🔍 is the input for the risk matrix:

  • High-value suspension products → RPP back-flow risk is especially dangerous (suspended particles may lodge in the membrane), so a larger buffer volume design is needed
  • Protein drugs (shear-sensitive) → DP pulsation may damage protein structure, so the buffer distance should be evaluated, or PP/TP used instead
  • Precise small-volume filling (<0.5 mL) → TP pressure drop management is key to dose control and must be built into the process design

All of these risk assessments follow the same decision hierarchy: sterility assurance > CQAs > commercial considerations.

Practical Application

In a CDMO technology transfer assessment, if the client moves a product from one filler technology to another (for example from RPP to TP), Table 11.10-1🔍 can serve as a structured framework for the risk assessment:

  1. Identify the new risks introduced by the new technology (such as the TP pressure drop problem)
  2. Confirm that the manifold and venting design need to be revalidated
  3. Assess whether the existing integrity testing scheme is sufficient to cover the new design

This assessment should be documented explicitly in the Technical Transfer Agreement and should trigger re-execution of equipment qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ).

Section Summary (11.8–11.12)

  • Filter location and manifold design: Point-of-use filters give the best sterility protection, but poor design creates dead-legs that compromise flushing; the SIP design of the manifold must ensure that every branch has enough venting points to avoid cold spots.
  • Differences in operational risk among technologies: RPP has a back-flow risk (needs sufficient buffer volume), DP has a pulsation risk (keep the filter at a distance), TP requires pressure drop management, and PP has no particular operational risk. These differences directly affect equipment selection and process validation strategy.
  • Core philosophy for non-filterable products: When neither terminal sterilization nor sterilizing filtration is available, "the process is the product". Every input component must be assured sterile individually, the liquid pathway must be minimized, and risk assessment (QRM) is mandatory to support the control strategy.
  • Gas filtration in powder filling: Although the powder itself does not need filtration, all gases that contact the powder (compressed air, vacuum, inert gas) require 0.22 µm sterilizing-grade hydrophobic filtration, and integrity test results must be included in batch disposition; HEPA dust-extraction filters serve containment rather than sterility, and their test frequency is determined by the manufacturer based on risk.
  • The decision hierarchy runs through the whole section: Whether it is dead-leg risk, the control strategy for non-filterable products, or integrity testing requirements for powder filters, all design and validation decisions are governed by the highest criterion of "sterility assurance > product CQAs > commercial flexibility".

Learning Objectives

  • Understand discard decisions when filling nested components: a single unit vs. the whole tub
  • Know the common causes of fill inaccuracy at the end of a batch (end of fill) and how to handle them
  • Compare the relative risk of the four liquid filling technologies across the different types of discard event
  • Understand the complete end-of-operation procedure for aseptic filling (EM, reconciliation, residual liquid, hazardous-product WIP, line clearance, documentation)
