12.5

Discard Strategies Associated with Conclusion of Fill

Causes of Fill Inaccuracy at the End of a Batch and Discard Strategy

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p181

At the end of the aseptic fill-unit operation, as bulk product volume decreases, fillers can encounter a loss of fill accuracy. This may be due to:

  • Low levels in the filling manifold / intermediate vessel
  • Foam or air introduced while the final volume of product is pumped or pressurized through the filter or transferred from the bulk vessel
  • Loss of homogeneity due to loss of recirculation or mixing capability from low volumes, especially for suspension products

Fillers may receive automated signals from the manifold or intermediate vessel to start and stop transfer from the bulk vessel. When the alarm is triggered due to lack of available bulk (low or low-low-level alarm), the filler is directed to begin shut down or initiate line clearance or empty mode. For high-value products, the shutdown may occur in stages — individual filling paths shut down progressively.

The same technology used to permit refilling during priming can also be employed at end of fill. End-of-fill procedures must be included in the validation of the process.

Commentary

Core Concept: Why Is the End of a Batch Prone to Inaccuracy?

End of fill is the most vulnerable period of the whole batch. There are three main causes of inaccuracy:

  • Insufficient liquid level: the level in the manifold or intermediate vessel is too low, so the pump cannot draw enough liquid
  • Foaming/air entrainment: as the last of the liquid passes through the filter, air bubbles enter the filling path
  • Loss of uniformity: at very low volumes, circulation and mixing of a suspension are inadequate, particles settle, and content becomes non-uniform

Everyday Analogy: The Last of the Hand Soap

When a bottle of hand soap is nearly empty, each press delivers a different amount, and sometimes air comes out with it. A filling machine faces exactly the same problem: when there is not enough liquid, dosing accuracy is lost.

Key Point: For high-value products, shut down in stages

For high-value products (such as biologics or rare APIs), do not stop the whole line at once. Instead, close the filling paths one by one (progressive shutdown) so that each pump uses up as much of the remaining liquid as possible and product recovery is maximized. This serves Priority 3 (business flexibility), but only on condition that it does not compromise Priority 1, sterility assurance.

CDMO Application Questions

Does your SOP clearly define the trigger conditions for end of fill (the low-level alarm set point)? Is there a separate procedure for the end of fill of suspensions (such as insulin crystal formulations)? Is end-of-fill included within the scope of process validation?

12.6

Discard Strategies Associated with Nested Components

Discard Decisions for Nested Components: a Single Unit vs. the Whole Tub

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p181-182

Filling syringes nested in tubs poses discard challenges when dose-control performance fails on an individual filling-needle position. Discarding the affected doses is the minimum action required. Two approaches:

  1. Discard individual syringes from a failing pump/needle — significantly more complicated; requires robotic verification (reject marking/tracking or physical segregation) or four-eyes principle (independent verification step)
  2. Discard the full tub — more conservative and simpler from standpoint of quality system and documentation

Note: Some filling technologies do not easily permit deactivation of a single filling station; especially true in nested configurations. Reset of entire line may be more appropriate should a fault occur in a single filling station.

Filling lines that permit return of units for re-dosing or which employ re-stoppering technology can reduce the number of discards.

Commentary

Core Concept: The Discard Dilemma for Nested Components

Nested syringes in tubs are the dominant packaging format for prefilled syringes. A tub usually holds several dozen syringes that share one sterile barrier (the tub lid). When one filling needle starts to dose out of control, the question arises:

  • Option A: discard only the affected units. Precise and saves product, but requires robotic verification or a second-person check (four-eyes principle), and the documentation is more complex
  • Option B: discard the whole tub. Conservative and costly, but places the least burden on the quality system and the documentation is clear

Under Priority 1 (sterility assurance), Option B is the safest default choice.

Everyday Analogy: A Bad Egg in the Carton

A carton holds 12 eggs and you suspect one of them is cracked. You can: (A) check each egg carefully and throw away only that one; or (B) return the whole carton. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, (A) requires robotic or two-person verification and a huge amount of documentation; (B) is wasteful but the least error-prone.

Key Point: Not all equipment supports single-station shutdown

Some nested filling equipment is designed so that a single filling station cannot be taken out of service independently; once one station fails, the only option is to reset the whole line. This means that discarding a whole tub is more common than you might expect. This capability should be assessed when selecting equipment, and the validation program must cover the procedure for handling a "single-station shutdown".

Questions to Consider

Suppose your product is an expensive monoclonal antibody (mAb) filled in nested PFS, and the filling needle at station 3 triggers a low-weight alarm. Before deciding whether to discard a single unit or the whole tub, what information do you need to confirm? (Hint: equipment capability, traceability, quality system requirements)

12.6-1

Table 12.6-1🔍: Common Discard Events & Liquid Filling Technology Risk Matrix

Common Discard Events and Relative Risk Comparison by Liquid Filling Technology

Original Text — Notes on Table 12.6-1🔍

The table below compares risk levels across four liquid filling technologies for five common discard event categories. Risk levels are highly variable depending on selected materials and system design. Minimizing distances always results in lower risk.

Technologies compared:

  • PP — Peristaltic Pump
  • RPP — Rotary Piston Pump
  • TP — Time Pressure
  • DP — Diaphragm Pump
Commentary

How to Read This Table

Each row represents one type of discard risk scenario; each column represents one filling technology. Risk levels are color-coded: High risk Medium risk Low risk Design-dependent.

The key point: no single technology is low risk in every respect. When selecting a technology, you must carry out a risk matrix analysis against your product characteristics (suspension? high oxygen sensitivity? long product-contact path?).

Risk Matrix Decision Framework

Discard risk assessment = f(technology type, material compatibility, tubing length, presence of a feedback mechanism)

Key principles:
  - Shorter tubing → lower risk (applies to oxidation, adsorption, uniformity)
  - Feedback mechanism present → lower dose control risk
  - Intervention outside the isolator → lower sterility discard risk

Notes: Risk levels are highly variable depending on selected materials and system design. Minimizing distances always results in lower risk.

Table Summary: PP has the highest overall risk; RPP has the highest intervention risk

The peristaltic pump (PP) is high risk for adsorption, oxidation and suspension uniformity, because tubing length is its greatest weakness. The rotary piston pump (RPP) carries the highest risk for interventions, because the intervention point is usually inside the filling isolator. Shortening the product-contact path is the common rule for reducing risk with every technology.

12.7

Miscellaneous Discard Strategies while Operating

Discards in Other Operations: Sensors and Reject Stations

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p183

Rejections may occur for other reasons not directly related to filler operation:

  • Raised stopper/plunger placement detection
  • Missing stopper/plunger
  • Fallen components
  • Bad crimp seals/closures (at capper)

These sensors and rejection stations should be integrated into the filling conveyance system and tested during qualification.

Commentary

Core Concept: Rejects Not Caused by the Filler Itself

The rejections discussed in this section are not dosing problems but container/closure integrity problems. Any one of these defects can compromise sterility assurance (Priority 1) or patient safety (Priority 2):

  • Stopper raised too high → possible leakage and contamination
  • Missing stopper → sterile barrier failure
  • Fallen component → contamination risk; traceability needed
  • Poor crimp → closure integrity failure

Key Point: Sensors must be included in validation

These sensors and reject stations must be tested during equipment qualification, including confirmation of sensor sensitivity, physical verification of the reject position, and integration with the batch record. If a sensor itself fails qualification testing, every reject decision that relies on it carries compliance risk.

CDMO Application Questions

On your filling line, does the SOP for "fallen components" clearly define the traceback scope? When a component falls, how many containers before and after must be traced? Is there an automatic marking mechanism, or does it rely on manual judgment?

13.0

Considerations for the End of the Aseptic Fill Unit Operation

Overall Considerations at the End of the Aseptic Filling Unit Operation

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p183-184

After completion of filling, elements to consider for orderly completion:

  • For single-batch production: entire line disassembled for cleaning and sterilization after batch
  • For campaign production: more limited interventions before resuming for next batch

Activities and sequence for end of aseptic fill-unit operation:

  • Completion of EM (Environmental Monitoring)
  • Handling of remaining unused containers and closures
  • Collecting, off-line labeling and accounting for batch samples
  • Handling of residual product
  • Washing in place of containment barrier (for hazardous/potent products)
  • Line clearance activities
  • Close-out of documentation (rejects, line losses, samples, finished goods)
  • Assessing equipment batch reports and audit trails
Commentary

Core Concept: Single Batch vs. Continuous Batches (Campaign)

The intensity of end-of-batch operations depends on the production mode:

  • Single-batch production: after the batch, the whole line is disassembled, cleaned and sterilized, and the next batch starts from zero. This is the most thorough approach but has the highest time cost.
  • Continuous batches (campaign): the same product is produced in several consecutive batches, with minimal intervention between batches, mainly handling samples, waste and documentation, without full line disassembly. Risk management focuses on preventing cross-contamination.

Everyday Analogy: Closing a Restaurant vs. Turning a Table

Single-batch production is like closing a restaurant for the night: dishes are washed, the area is cleared and prep starts all over again. Campaign production is like turning a table quickly: clear the plates, restock, and the next guests sit down right away. The two call for completely different depths of cleaning.

The Eight End-of-Batch Steps (the order is critical)

Sequence of steps (must not be rearranged):
  1. Complete environmental monitoring (EM) sampling
  2. Handle unused containers and closures
  3. Collect and label batch samples
  4. Handle residual product
  5. Hazardous-product WIP (if applicable)
  6. Line clearance
  7. Close out documentation (reconciliation, verification)
  8. Review equipment batch reports and audit trails
13.1

Completion of Environmental Monitoring at End of Aseptic Fill

Completing Environmental Monitoring at the End of the Batch

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p184

EM (total particle and viable sampling) must continue until all filled containers are fully closed, sealed, and have exited the filling line. In campaign production, EM must continue through changeover activities.

Surface EM is typically conducted at end of aseptic fill for critical product-contact surfaces (filling needles, feed bowls in sorting systems). These samples should be collected before significant disassembly activities. However, some stoppers must be removed from sorting systems before sampling bowl — requires careful sequencing preplanned in SOPs for each specific filling-line design.

If used media plates have accumulated within the barrier, they need to be removed and reconciled for laboratory submission. Exit monitoring for cleanroom personnel conducted when personnel leave the environment.

Commentary

Core Concept: Defining the End Point of EM

EM sampling time points are often misunderstood. The correct definition is:

  • Air particle + viable air sampling: must continue until all containers are fully closed and have left the filling line
  • Surface sampling: should be completed before major disassembly, especially of the filling needles and feed bowl
  • Campaign production: EM must extend through the changeover and must not be interrupted

Key Point: The EM sampling sequence must be planned in advance in the SOP

On some filling lines, certain stoppers must be removed before the feed bowl can be sampled. This creates a conflict: removing the stoppers is itself an intervention. The solution is to plan in advance, in the SOP, an EM sampling sequence specific to each filling line, so that sampling does not contaminate the surfaces to be tested and disassembly does not overwrite microbiological evidence.

CDMO Application Questions

Does the SOP for your filling lines define a separate EM sampling sequence diagram for each line (Line A, B, C...)? If a single generic SOP is currently shared, this is a compliance risk that needs to be improved.

13.2

Handling of Unused Containers and Closures at End of Aseptic Fill

Handling Unused Containers and Closure Components at the End of the Batch

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p184-185

Unused containers can often be emptied by conveying to end of line. Closures/components removed from sorters and hoppers (may require vacuum cleaners or specialty tools). Care must be taken to ensure complete line clearance to avoid mix-up. EM sequencing imperative.

Consideration should also be given to serialization — the process of assigning a unique serial number to each saleable product unit. If serialization identity is conferred at point-of-fill, the serialization system should be subjected to orderly shutdown. Empty containers conveyed down the line should not be assigned serial numbers.

Commentary

Core Concept: The Logic of Clearing Unused Containers

After the batch, all empty containers on the filling line must be removed to prevent mix-up. The main methods are:

  • Empty vials/syringes: conveyed to the end of the line and removed together
  • Small components such as stoppers and caps: removed from the sorter and hopper, which may require a vacuum cleaner

All activities must be coordinated with the EM sampling sequence and must not disturb surfaces that have already been sampled.

Key Point: Conflict between serialization and empty containers

If serialization (assigning unique serial numbers) takes place at the point of fill, you must make sure the serialization system has been properly shut down when empty containers pass through during line clearance. Otherwise the empty containers will be assigned serial numbers and enter the traceability system, causing serious reconciliation confusion later. The shutdown procedure for the serialization system must itself be included in an SOP and validated.

13.3

Handling of Batch Samples at End of Aseptic Fill

Collecting, Labeling and Delivering Batch Samples

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p185

Any batch samples (filled containers, bulk samples) remaining within the line need to be submitted to laboratory with appropriate labels. Samples with sensitivity (temperature, light) may have been stored in local controlled environments. At end of aseptic fill: ensure all samples are collected, accounted for, and submitted. Batch samples included in reconciliation section of batch record.

Commentary

Core Concept: Sample management is part of closing the accounting loop

Batch samples are not just "retention samples"; they are part of batch reconciliation. The batch record must document the number of samples taken, whether they are correctly labeled, whether any temperature- or light-sensitive samples need special storage, and the time and record of delivery to the laboratory. Any sample that cannot be reconciled can lead to problems at batch review.

Everyday Analogy: The Bank Cash Count

It is like the bank cash count before the daily close: every banknote (every sample) must be accounted for, with no unexplained loss. Delivering batch samples to the laboratory is this "cash count" step.

13.4

Handling of Residual Product at End of Aseptic Fill

Handling Residual Product and Yield Calculation

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p185-186

A small amount of residual product will remain in bulk vessels, transfer lines, filtration apparatus, and filler at conclusion of batch. Batch record should include methodology for calculating this waste for accountability and yield purposes.

Considerations for handling residual product:

  • Running filler up to point of dry-cycling to purge fill lines before disconnection while rejecting final containers
  • Breaking connections, draining liquid product through low points or evacuating powder product
  • Controlling potential for drips (or powder) and controlling excess product

If product is potent or toxic: additional controls such as flushing parts to avoid drips or sending excess product to waste treatment (chemical or heat inactivation).

Commentary

Core Concept: Residual liquid is a legitimate loss in the material balance

After every fill, product inevitably remains in the following locations:

  • the bottom of the bulk vessel
  • transfer lines
  • filtration assemblies
  • the filling machine head

This residue is an engineering limitation and cannot be avoided, but it must be recorded in the batch record using a systematic calculation method as the basis for yield calculation. Excessive residual liquid can be a signal of an engineering or operational problem.

Everyday Analogy: The Bottom of the Shampoo Bottle

When the shampoo is almost gone, a little remains at the bottom, and adding water to use it up is common sense. Residual liquid in pharmaceutical manufacturing is the same physical limitation. The difference is that it must be recorded and calculated precisely, and, depending on product characteristics, a decision made on whether to recover it, discard it, or render it harmless.

Key Point: Toxic/highly potent products require special disposal procedures

For highly toxic or highly potent products (such as cytotoxics or OEB 4/5 compounds), residual liquid and rinse liquid must be directed to a waste treatment system (chemical inactivation or heat treatment) and must not be discharged directly. These procedures must have dedicated SOPs and be incorporated into the occupational exposure protection program.

Questions to Consider

In your current batch records, is the residual liquid calculated as a fixed constant (a fixed loss percentage) or measured for each batch? Which approach is more convincing at batch review? If residual liquid suddenly increases between batches, what engineering signal does that represent?

13.5

End of Aseptic Fill for Potent or Hazardous Products

End-of-Operation Procedures for Highly Potent or Hazardous Product Filling: WIP and Decontamination

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p186-187

After processing potent or hazardous products, a wash-in-place (WIP) cycle must be performed before the containment barrier can be opened. WIP may be used to:

  • Knock down aerosols or dust
  • Dilute active ingredients
  • Flush active ingredients to drain or waste treatment
  • Inactivate the active ingredient (where water/chemical agents/temperature capable of inactivation)

WIP is performed using automated spray balls and/or spray wands through glove ports. Takes place within the zone where product exposure is possible (from below HEPA filters down to air returns). HEPA filters cannot be wetted — care must be taken.

For biologically active materials (Biosafety Level rated), WIP inactivation process (liquid and/or gas) must be sufficiently rigorous. VPHP (Vaporized Hydrogen Peroxide) has been successfully used for inactivation of biohazardous materials.

Note: Filling lines for potent/hazardous products often employ separate external container washing unit operation. May occur in-line immediately after capping or as off-line process. When working with nested containers, common to denest containers for adequate coverage of all external surfaces — but nests themselves must also be treated or disposed of.

Commentary

Core Concept: WIP (wash-in-place) is a mandatory step before opening the door

Wash-in-Place (WIP) is a required step for hazardous-product filling isolators after the batch and before the door is opened. Its purpose is to reduce operator exposure risk. WIP has four main functions:

  • Settle aerosols and dust
  • Dilute the concentration of the active ingredient
  • Flush the active ingredient into the wastewater treatment system
  • Chemical or thermal inactivation (depending on the characteristics of the active ingredient)

Key Point: HEPA filters must not get wet

The WIP spray range runs from below the HEPA filter to the return air grille. Once HEPA filter media is wetted, its structure is damaged, filtration efficiency drops sharply, and it is difficult to dry. The design and installation position of the spray ball must ensure that the spray does not reach the HEPA filter. This detail must be confirmed at equipment acceptance.

VPHP vs. Liquid WIP: Comparison of Biohazard Decontamination

Decontamination options for biosafety level (BSL) materials:

Liquid WIP:
  Advantages: fast, low cost, widely available equipment
  Applicable to: chemical drugs, biological materials that can be inactivated in liquid
  Limitations: insufficient effect on spores or highly resistant microorganisms

VPHP (vaporized hydrogen peroxide):
  Advantages: strong penetration, no residue (breaks down into water and oxygen)
  Applicable to: BSL-rated biological materials, broad-spectrum inactivation
  Limitations: longer cycle time, requires a VPHP generator

CDMO Application Questions

If you take on ADCs (antibody-drug conjugates) or highly potent cytotoxic products in the future, is your filling isolator already equipped with a WIP system? Has spray ball coverage been validated? Does the wastewater destination meet environmental regulations? Is there a separate SOP for denesting nested containers?

13.6

Line Clearance at End of Aseptic Fill

Line Clearance: the Key Control Against Mix-ups

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p187

Line clearance = inspection of line to ensure no product, containers, or components were missed during clearing.

Purposes:

  • Preventing mix-up of materials batch to batch
  • Ensuring all samples are captured and accounted for
  • Ensuring all rejects are captured and accounted for

Line clearance may be performed more than once. Operators often conduct initial clearance to ensure all batch-related materials are captured, then formal line-clearance check activity with independent double-check by Quality Assurance.

Commentary

Core Concept: The three purposes of line clearance

Line clearance is not just "cleaning up"; it is an accountability check that ensures:

  • Materials from different batches are not mixed together (preventing mix-ups = Priority 2, patient safety)
  • All samples have been fully recovered and none has been left on the line
  • All rejects have been accounted for and cannot flow into saleable stock

Everyday Analogy: Collecting Exam Papers at School

When an invigilator collects exam papers, they do not just stack the papers. They confirm that every seat has handed in a paper (equivalent to all containers being cleared), that no papers have been mixed into another class (equivalent to mix-up prevention), and after collection an assistant checks again (equivalent to independent double verification by QA).

Key Point: Two-stage clearance + QA double verification

The standard practice is two rounds of verification:

  1. Preliminary clearance by the operator: ensures all material has been removed
  2. Independent QA re-check: the formal line clearance verification, which must be recorded in the batch record

A single round (the operator checking their own work) is insufficient from a regulatory standpoint. QA involvement and independence are key.

13.7

Close-Out of Documentation at End of Aseptic Fill

Closing Out Batch Documentation: Reconciliation and the Use of ERP Systems

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p187-188

Master batch record should capture: usage quantities, usage statistics, percentage yield, and reconciliation. Many item types to record: inventoried materials, rejects and line losses, samples, labels, packaging materials, finished goods.

When requirement is for inventory control or business/process optimization, an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) System may be used in place of master batch record. Most important reason to collect and record data: account for all materials to prevent mix-up.

Commentary

Core Concept: Checklist of reconciliation items

Closing out the batch record requires reconciliation of all of the following items:

  • Raw materials and packaging materials issued and used
  • Rejects and line losses
  • Number of samples taken
  • Label usage (including destroyed labels)
  • Packaging materials
  • Quantity of finished goods

Input = finished goods + rejects + samples + residue + line losses. Any deviation outside the acceptable range must be investigated.

Yield Calculation Formula

Batch Yield:

  Theoretical yield = quantity charged / unit volume

  Actual yield (%) = (quantity of finished goods / theoretical yield) × 100%

  Material balance:
  Quantity charged = acceptable units + samples + rejects + residual liquid + line losses

  Acceptable yield range: upper and lower limits must be predefined in the master batch record
  Outside the range → a deviation investigation must be initiated

Key Point: ERP cannot replace the regulatory function of the batch record

An ERP system (such as SAP) can support inventory management and business optimization, but from a GMP regulatory perspective, the batch record is the primary document required by regulation and ERP is only a supporting tool. If a company chooses to use ERP as its primary recording tool, it must ensure compliance with 21 CFR Part 11 (electronic records/electronic signatures).

13.8

Assessment of Batch Reports and Audit Trails at End of Aseptic Fill

Reviewing Equipment Batch Reports and Audit Trails

Original Text — PDA Guide No.1 p188-189

Batch record review includes printouts or electronic records from:

  • Washers, tunnels, autoclaves, ovens
  • CIP/SIP systems
  • Biodecontamination units (hydrogen peroxide)
  • Fillers
  • Lyophilizers
  • Cappers
  • Exterior vial washers
  • Terminal sterilizers
  • Packaging equipment (including serialization system)

Also reviewed: EM (total particulate, temperature, relative-humidity monitoring), utility monitoring through building automation systems, isolator control systems, EM systems.

Not only process parameters but also alarms and alarm acknowledgement. Audit trails evaluated to demonstrate:

  • No inappropriate adjustments were made
  • All personnel interacting with system were qualified and permitted
Commentary

Core Concept: Equipment checklist for batch record review

Batch record review for a complete aseptic filling batch covers the entire chain of equipment, from container handling through to final packaging:

  • Vial washer, depyrogenation tunnel, autoclave, dry heat oven
  • CIP (clean-in-place) / SIP (sterilize-in-place) systems
  • Biodecontamination system (H₂O₂)
  • Filler, lyophilizer, capper, vial exterior washer, terminal sterilizer
  • Packaging equipment (including serialization system)

Key Point: Alarms + alarm acknowledgment = the core of the audit trail

Modern regulatory inspections (FDA, EMA) place heavy emphasis on alarm records in the audit trail. The review focus is not only whether process parameters are within range, but also whether:

  • Alarms were appropriately acknowledged
  • Any inappropriate parameter changes were made
  • All operators were qualified and authorized

If the audit trail shows unauthorized parameter adjustments, batch release can face serious challenge even if the final product appears to conform.

Audit Trail Review Framework

An audit trail review should confirm three things:

  1. Integrity
     - Are all process steps recorded?
     - Are there no data deletions or gaps?

  2. Compliance
     - Are all parameters within specification?
     - Were all alarms appropriately acknowledged and dispositioned?

  3. Authorization
     - Does each operator user ID have an authorization record?
     - Are there no unauthorized data changes?

  → Any item not met = potential deviation requiring investigation

CDMO Application Questions

In your current batch review process, is there a separate audit trail review step? Does the filler electronic batch record (eBR) comply with 21 CFR Part 11? When QA reviews alarm acknowledgment records, are there clear acceptance criteria (which alarms can be acknowledged and production continued, and which must trigger a deviation)?

Section Summary

Discard Strategy Key Points (Sections 12.5-12.7)

  • Three main causes of inaccuracy at the end of a batch: insufficient liquid level, air bubble entrainment, loss of suspension uniformity
  • Two options for discarding nested containers: discard single units (requires robotic/two-person verification) vs. discard the whole tub (conservative but simple)
  • The four filling technologies have different risk emphases: PP long tubing = high adsorption/oxidation risk; RPP intervention inside the isolator = high sterility risk
  • Shortening the product-contact path is the common rule for reducing risk with every technology
  • Sensors and reject stations must be included in equipment qualification testing

End-of-Batch Operations Key Points (Sections 13.0-13.8)

  • The eight steps have a strict order; EM sampling comes first and must not be disturbed by disassembly
  • The serialization system shutdown procedure must ensure empty containers are not assigned serial numbers
  • The residual liquid calculation method must be recorded in the batch record to support the material balance
  • Hazardous-product WIP is a mandatory step before opening the door; HEPA filters must not get wet
  • Line clearance requires two rounds: preliminary by the operator + independent QA re-check
  • Audit trail review focus: alarm acknowledgment records + exclusion of unauthorized operations

Decision Hierarchy Reinforcement

1. Sterility assurance: the bottom line for every discard decision; EM must not be interrupted
2. Product CQAs: uniformity, assay and leachables all affect patient safety
3. Business flexibility: staged shutdown for high-value products; minimal intervention in campaign production
13

Section 13: APS / Media Fill

p189-p195

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p189 - p195

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the core role of the barrier system in aseptic filling: complete separation of operators from the product
  • Distinguish the design principles and level of control of the three system types: isolator, cRABS (closed restricted access barrier system) and oRABS (open restricted access barrier system)
  • Master the comparison table in Table 14.2-1🔍 and the regulatory significance of each attribute, along with CDMO selection considerations
  • Apply the decision hierarchy of sterility assurance > product CQA > commercial flexibility to weigh the risks and benefits of barrier selection
  • Understand how aseptic process simulation (APS) requirements differ across barrier types
14.0 Filling System and Environmental Considerations — Overview

Original Text

Aseptic processing is expected to take place in a manner that separates personnel from the process, which is commonly accomplished by providing a barrier to attain separation. A barrier is a physical partition that separates the aseptic processing area (Grade A) from the background environment, protecting it from the environment and the people working in it.

Further, most regulatory authorities consider standard aseptic cleanrooms, those that do not include controlled separation of operators and product filling, legacy systems that require improvements. Risk assessments and risk mitigations to continue operations until full barrier-technology upgrades are in place are recommended to be undertaken in consultation with the appropriate regulatory partners.

For additional detail beyond what this section provides on the design of cleanrooms, isolators and RABS, see the following references:

  • ISO 14644 Cleanrooms and Associated Controlled Environments
  • ISO 13408-6 Aseptic Processing of Healthcare Products Part 6 – Isolator Systems
  • PDA Technical Report No. 34: Design and Validation of Isolator Systems for the Manufacturing and Testing of Health Care Products
  • PDA Points to Consider for the Aseptic Processing of Sterile Pharmaceutical Products in Isolators
  • PDA Points to Consider No. 12 Restricted Access Barrier Systems (RABS)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Barrier: A structure that physically separates the Grade A aseptic filling area from the external environment (including operators). It is the foundational design principle of modern aseptic filling.

Legacy System: A traditional design with no barrier, in which operators work directly in an open cleanroom. Regulators explicitly regard it as an outdated system that needs to be improved.

Grade A: The highest cleanliness grade for aseptic operations. It requires non-viable particles ≥0.5 µm ≤3,520 particles/m³ (at rest) and practically no viable particles.

Analogy

Think of a surgical operation in an operating room: the surgeon cannot touch the patient's open wound with bare hands, but must wear gloves and a sterile gown and work in a strictly disinfected environment.

The barrier system in aseptic filling is like the "isolation measures" of an operating room: people always work outside the barrier and the product is protected inside it, and this physical separation is the first line of defense for sterility assurance.

A legacy cleanroom is like an "operating room without surgical gowns": the rules are strict, but the risk of close personnel contact remains, and regulators have clearly called for upgrades.

Key Notes

Clear regulatory position: "Most regulatory authorities" classify cleanrooms without barriers as legacy systems that need to be upgraded. This is not just a recommendation but a clear direction backed by regulatory pressure.

Strategy during the interim: Until the barrier technology upgrade is completed, risk assessments and mitigation measures should be discussed with the regulators; the upgrade plan cannot be postponed indefinitely.

Reminder on the decision hierarchy: Sterility assurance always comes first. The barrier system exists to prioritize protection of sterility, not operator convenience.

Practice Questions

  1. Which barrier system does your facility currently use? If it still uses a conventional cleanroom (no barrier), what is the next step in the upgrade path?
  2. Why do regulators place particular emphasis on "separating personnel from the filling process"? Which contamination risks can a barrier system effectively control?
  3. What are the core overlaps between the requirements of PDA TR34 and EU GMP Annex 1 for barrier systems?
14.1 Types of Barrier Systems for Aseptic Operations

Original Text

The two barrier systems primarily used by the pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industry that provide the required separation between operators and aseptic operations in Grade A environments are:

  • Isolators
  • Restricted Access Barrier Systems (RABS)

Isolators are either fully closed or partially open to allow the ingress and egress of components and finished goods; they are characterized largely by their ability to withstand automated biodecontamination cycles usually with a vapor phase, gaseous, or aerosolized agents (e.g., hydrogen peroxide). In contrast, RABS provide a rigid-wall enclosure that cannot always be fully sealed. RABS are disinfected mainly with liquid disinfectants and/or sporicides applied to surfaces, though some closed RABS can support automated biodecontamination (e.g., using hydrogen peroxide in vapor phase) with or without the same treatment for the surrounding cleanroom environment.

Both isolators and RABS may provide access to the enclosed equipment and process through glove ports and make use of RTPs (Rapid Transfer Ports) to introduce equipment, components, monitoring, and cleanroom supplies. Likewise, the sterile fluid pathway may be introduced through a transfer port or intrinsic sterile connection device at the barrier boundary. See Section 9.0 and Section 10.0 for more information on various transfer mechanisms, their operations, and controls. See Section 11.0 for more information on sterile fluid pathways.

Both isolators and RABS have doors; however, how and when they are used differs. For the isolator, the door is opened only at the beginning of the setup and, again, at the end of the aseptic fill-unit operation or, if multiple batches can be manufactured, at the end of the campaign. After the initial setup and cleaning are performed, the isolator is closed and biodecontaminated before use.

RABS, on the other hand, must be fully disinfected prior to setup, and any further opening of the RABS doors, including setup, constitutes an intervention. Any ingress or egress after disinfection must be protected by overhead unidirectional airflow that covers the region of the open door to prevent contamination of the Grade A environment. Consequently, intense design activities should be undertaken to minimize the number and types of open-door interventions that will be required within a RABS. The intent is to limit open-door interventions to the absolute minimum (see Section 8.2). Highly detailed procedures must govern those open-door interventions (and indeed all interventions) due to the potential disruption of the unidirectional airflow and the proximity of the operator to the critical aseptic zone. See Section 8.0, PDA Points to Consider No.1: Aseptic Processing (Revised 2023) and PDA Points to Consider No 12: Restricted Access Barrier Systems (2025) for additional details on critical interventions and for working within RABS, respectively.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Isolator: A closed barrier that can withstand automated biodecontamination cycles, usually using vaporized hydrogen peroxide (VHP). Doors are opened only at the start of setup and at the end of the batch, and remain fully closed in between.

RABS (restricted access barrier system): A rigid-wall enclosure whose surfaces are disinfected mainly with liquid disinfectants/sporicides. It is less tightly closed than an isolator, and any door opening constitutes an intervention.

Glove Port: A glove-sleeve assembly fixed to the barrier wall that lets operators work inside the barrier without breaching its integrity.

RTP (rapid transfer port): A dedicated transfer device that allows materials (parts, monitoring equipment, consumables) to enter and leave the barrier without exposing the Grade A environment.

Biodecontamination: Removal of microorganisms from an enclosed space at a sterilization level using chemical agents (such as VHP). Unlike ordinary disinfection, it achieves a higher level of microbial kill.

Analogy

Isolator vs. RABS = Space Station vs. Cleanroom Surgical Tent

An isolator is like a space station: a fully sealed, self-contained environment in which people work through fixed glove ports, and materials must pass through an airlock. It is thoroughly sterilized with VHP before start-up and, once in use, its doors are not opened. It offers the highest assurance but is the most expensive to build.

A RABS is like a surgical tent inside a cleanroom: it provides a physical barrier and downward airflow protection, but the tent itself is not completely sealed. Every door opening is a risk event that needs unidirectional airflow coverage, and the SOPs must be extremely detailed.

In short: an isolator is "active defense" and a RABS is "enhanced passive defense". The regulatory trend clearly favors isolators.

Key Notes

Opening a RABS door = an intervention: This is a key regulatory concept. Once a RABS has been disinfected, any door opening (including during the setup phase) must be recorded as an intervention and controlled by strict SOPs. This directly affects APS (aseptic process simulation) design: the APS must simulate all anticipated types of intervention.

Prevention by design: The document stresses minimizing the number and types of RABS door-opening interventions at the design stage. This reflects the principle that engineering prevention beats after-the-fact remediation: design the intervention risk out rather than compensate for it with SOPs.

Unidirectional airflow protection: When a RABS door is opened, overhead unidirectional airflow (UDF) must cover the opening area. This is the last line of defense for the Grade A environment.

Practical Application

CDMO selection considerations: When a client requires a higher level of sterility assurance (such as RNA vaccines or highly sensitive biologics), an isolator is the only choice. For small batches with frequent product changeovers (such as early clinical phases), a cRABS offers better cleaning flexibility. An oRABS is usually an upgrade transition option for older facilities.

Link to APS design: The barrier type directly determines the scope of the APS. With a RABS, the APS must include all anticipated door-opening intervention scenarios. With an isolator, the APS focuses on VHP biodecontamination validation and glove port integrity.

EU GMP Annex 1 (2022) position: It clearly prefers isolators and requires manufacturers using a RABS or a conventional cleanroom to provide an adequate risk-assessment justification.

Practice Questions

  1. What is the fundamental difference between isolators and RABS in biodecontamination methods? How does each affect APS design?
  2. Why must door openings in a RABS be treated as interventions? What regulatory risks arise if they are not recorded?
  3. A CDMO takes on both Phase 1 clinical and commercial batches. How should it choose its barrier technology? Explain your decision logic.
14.2 Design Considerations for the Integration of the Filling System with the Environment

Original Text

RABS have historically been designed in two configurations—open (oRABS) and closed (cRABS)—although engineering innovations have often blurred the lines between them as each design has improved to enhance controls and operation.

Traditionally, oRABS use HEPA-filtered unidirectional airflow flowing down through the process, within the barrier, before the air is returned to the cleanroom low-wall returns for recirculation. Thus, the enclosure is neither sealed to the equipment nor to the cleanroom. The oRABS have been commonly employed as an effective improvement to conventional cleanrooms previously without barriers.

The cRABS, in contrast, is a positive-pressure system that provides a process enclosure with integrated HEPA-filtered fan units that provide filtered unidirectional airflow down through the process with integrated low-level returns within the equipment base. One common use for cRABS is the handling of potent products. Both oRABS and cRABS are placed within a Grade B (or better) environment as the interior of the barrier may be exposed to the external environment during processing which, in the case of oRABS, is an incomplete barrier. There are many variations of RABS that can borrow features from isolators to improve the capabilities of any specific barrier.

Regardless of the type of barrier employed, airflow visualization studies (i.e., smoke studies) must be performed as part of the equipment qualification. In addition, CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) can be of great help during the design phase to understand airflow within and around the barrier and to confirm that, by design, the airflow is unidirectional with minimal turbulence and minimal potential to introduce contamination at all equipment and product surfaces. As stated in Section 8.2, open-door interventions performed on RABS during the aseptic process, where product or product contact surfaces are exposed, presents a high level of risk to sterile product and should be avoided.

The type of barrier selected, whether isolator, oRABS, or cRABS, will drive very different design decisions and cleanroom operating principles. Depending on which barrier design is selected, specific design elements that should be considered include:

  • Room conditions
  • Room and equipment finish
  • Air handling (room and equipment)
  • Transfer mechanisms for materials:
    • Equipment format parts
    • Sterile fluid pathway (e.g., tubing, sterilizing filters and PUPSIT connections, needles, fill pumps)
    • Supporting equipment and consumables (e.g., forceps, sterile wipes, environmental monitoring equipment, contact and settle plates)
    • Primary packaging materials (e.g., containers, closures)
    • Product and associated vessels
  • Use of cleaning, disinfection (or biodecontamination for closed systems), and SIP

Table 14.2-1🔍 provides a comparison of the key design features and control attributes for isolators, cRABS, and oRABS. In all cases, the company's CCS (Contamination Control Strategy) should identify the controls needed and the monitoring for both the isolator and its surrounding environment.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

oRABS (open RABS): Air is recirculated back to the cleanroom through low-level wall returns, and the barrier is not sealed from either the equipment or the cleanroom. It needs a Grade B background environment. It is the most common first step in upgrading a conventional cleanroom.

cRABS (closed RABS): A positive-pressure system with built-in HEPA-filtered fans and low-level returns, in which air circulates within the barrier instead of flowing into the cleanroom. It is more tightly closed than an oRABS and also needs a Grade B background environment. It is suitable for handling highly potent products (high OEB).

Airflow Visualization Study (smoke study): Uses smoke particles to verify whether the airflow inside the barrier is truly unidirectional, with no eddies or reverse flow. It is a required part of equipment qualification.

CFD (computational fluid dynamics): Computer simulation of airflow behavior at the design stage to predict potential problems. It intervenes earlier than physical smoke testing and saves later modification costs.

CCS (contamination control strategy): The overall contamination control framework required by EU GMP Annex 1, which defines the controls and environmental monitoring requirements for each barrier type.

Analogy

oRABS vs. cRABS = Open-Top Tent vs. Sealed Inflatable Tent

An oRABS is like a tent with walls on four sides but an opening at the top: air enters through the HEPA filters above, flows across the work area and returns to the cleanroom through the low wall openings. If the external environment (the Grade B cleanroom) has a problem, it could in theory affect the inside of the barrier.

A cRABS is like a fully sealed inflatable tent with its own internal air circulation: air recirculates inside the tent and does not depend on airflow from the external cleanroom. However, unlike an isolator, the tent itself cannot withstand VHP biodecontamination (unless specially designed).

A smoke study = lighting a stick of smoke inside the tent to see whether it flows in the designed direction and whether it swirls or flows backward.

Key Notes

Key difference in background environment requirements: The background of an isolator can be as low as Grade C (open type) or Grade D (closed type), whereas a RABS (open or closed) must operate in a Grade B environment. This directly affects the construction and operating cost of the cleanroom.

Note on potent products: A cRABS is particularly suitable for filling potent products because the positive-pressure closed system can provide operator protection. Exhaust filtration must still be evaluated: an isolator can contain its exhaust completely, whereas a RABS usually cannot.

Transfer mechanisms are the core design challenge: Whichever barrier is chosen, the movement of materials in and out (parts, sterile fluid pathways, container closures, consumables) requires carefully designed transfer mechanisms. This is where barrier integrity is most easily compromised.

The CCS must cover both inside and outside the barrier: The CCS does not govern only the Grade A environment inside the barrier; it must also cover the monitoring and control of the background environment (Grade B/C/D). Controls inside and outside the barrier form one complete system.

Design Decision Framework

Selection decision matrix:

          Isolator     cRABS        oRABS
Background  Grade C/D   Grade B      Grade B
Biodecon.   VHP (auto)  Design-dependent   Liquid disinfectant
Operator protection  Highest      High           Medium
Build cost   Highest        Medium           Lowest
Changeover flexibility  Low          Medium           High
APS complexity  Medium          High           Highest
Regulatory preference  Best        Next           Lowest

Decision principles:
1. High sterility assurance requirement → isolator
2. Highly potent products → cRABS or isolator
3. Many products in small batches → evaluate cRABS cleaning flexibility
4. Upgrading an older facility → oRABS as a starting point

Practice Questions

  1. What is the fundamental difference between oRABS and cRABS in airflow design? Why do both have the same background environment requirement?
  2. Why should CFD simulation be done before the smoke study at the design stage? Can one replace the other?
  3. For a facility using an oRABS, how should the CCS ensure that contamination control of the background environment (Grade B) is sufficient to support barrier integrity?
Table 14.2-1🔍: Comparison of Control and Design Elements for Isolators and Restricted Access Barrier Systems (RABS)🔍

Original Text

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts: Reading the Table

Table 14.2-1🔍 is the most important reference tool in this chapter and compares five categories of attributes:

  • Barrier Design Intent: All three system types protect the product; only isolators and cRABS can also provide operator protection (containment), whereas an oRABS cannot.
  • Control Elements: Isolators have the strongest ability to control temperature, humidity and differential pressure independently; an oRABS can hardly control them independently of the background environment.
  • Qualification Elements: APS is mandatory for all three system types. Airflow visualization studies must in every case include door-opening scenarios, but an oRABS requires the most scenarios to be simulated (setup, interventions, recovery).
  • Maintenance/Periodic Testing: Glove port integrity testing is required for all three system types; the enclosure leak test is mandatory only for isolators, depends on the design for a cRABS, and is not applicable to an oRABS.
  • Design Elements: For isolators, material selection, piping penetration design and exhaust filtration are all subject to the strictest requirements.

Key Notes: Key Differences in the Table

Differences in background grade drive cleanroom construction cost:

  • Isolator (closed): background needs only Grade D → lowest cleanroom construction cost
  • Isolator (open): background needs Grade C
  • RABS (open or closed): background must be Grade B → highest cleanroom cost

This means that although the isolator equipment itself is the most expensive, its lower background requirement can make its overall TCO (total cost of ownership) the lowest in long-term, high-volume production.

Operator safety implications of exhaust filtration: Exhaust filtration is mandatory for isolators, making them suitable for highly potent (OEB 4/5) products. An oRABS cannot provide it at all, and for a cRABS it depends on the design. This is the decisive factor in selecting a system for filling hazardous products.

Piping Transiting Grades: Because the isolator background is Grade C, the design of piping passing from Grade A to Grade C is "Critical"; with a RABS the background is Grade B, so the difference in grades crossed is smaller and the design challenge is relatively lower.

APS Requirements by Barrier Type

Isolator APS focus:
  - Simulate the first fill after VHP biodecontamination
  - Glove port operation scenarios (interventions)
  - Door-opening setup and recovery scenarios
  - Continuous simulation between batches/campaigns

cRABS APS focus:
  - All anticipated door-opening intervention scenarios
  - Verification of Disinfection Position coverage
  - Equipment movement after gas-phase biodecontamination (Jog Feature)

oRABS APS focus:
  - Three categories of scenarios: setup, all interventions, recovery
  - The largest number of simulated door-opening interventions
  - Verification of environmental recovery after each intervention
  - Confirmation of the status of the cleanroom (Grade B)

Common requirements:
  - APS = Yes (mandatory for all three types)
  - Glove port integrity test = Yes (required for all three types)
  - Airflow visualization study = Yes (required for all three types)

Practical Application

Barrier selection process when a CDMO procures a new filling line:

  1. Confirm the product portfolio: Does it include highly potent/toxic products? If so, an isolator or cRABS (with exhaust filtration) is needed.
  2. Confirm the batch pattern: Single long-term commercial product? An isolator gives the best TCO. Many products in small batches? A cRABS offers greater cleaning flexibility.
  3. Assess the existing cleanroom grade: If a Grade B background already exists, a RABS can be fitted immediately; if a new build is needed, the lower background requirement of an isolator can save construction cost.
  4. Assess the regulatory markets: If the target markets include the EU, Annex 1 prefers isolators and a sound justification for using a RABS is needed.
  5. APS planning: After the barrier is selected, plan the list of interventions the APS will cover, ensuring that all high-risk operations are simulated and validated.

Practice Questions

  1. From Table 14.2-1🔍, identify the three attributes with the greatest difference between an isolator and an oRABS, and explain why these differences matter most for sterility assurance.
  2. Why can an oRABS not provide operator protection (containment)? What does this mean for a CDMO filling highly potent cytotoxic drugs (such as certain anticancer drugs)?
  3. What role does the "Jog Feature" play in the disinfection of cRABS and oRABS? Without it, what dead-spot risks would arise in disinfection?
  4. What is the significance of performing the isolator enclosure leak test before biodecontamination? If there is a leak, is VHP decontamination still effective?

Section Summary

  • Barriers are the foundation of aseptic filling: Physically separating personnel from the product is a core requirement of modern aseptic manufacturing, and regulators have clearly required that all legacy systems without barriers be upgraded.
  • Technology tiers of the three barrier types: Isolator > cRABS (closed RABS) > oRABS (open RABS). The level of sterility assurance decreases in that order, while flexibility and initial cost increase in that order.
  • Background environment requirements drive overall TCO: The isolator (closed) background needs only Grade D, giving the lowest long-term cleanroom operating cost; a RABS background must be Grade B, the strictest cleanroom requirement.
  • Every door opening in a RABS = an intervention: It must be controlled by SOPs, protected by airflow, documented, and simulated in the APS. This is the central challenge of RABS operational management.
  • APS is mandatory for all three barrier types: The scope of simulation varies by barrier type: an oRABS must cover the most door-opening intervention scenarios, while an isolator focuses on biodecontamination validation and glove port integrity.
  • The CCS must be planned as a whole: The contamination control strategy (CCS) must cover both the inside of the barrier (Grade A) and the background environment, which together form an interdependent control system.
  • The decision hierarchy always applies: Sterility assurance > product CQA > commercial flexibility. Every decision on barrier selection and APS design must give sterility assurance the highest priority.
