Section 14-15: Powder & Auger

p196-p205

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p196 - p205

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the types of utilities needed for aseptic operations, their design requirements, and the principles of risk control
  • Master the core principles of, and differences between, the two mainstream powder filling systems: the Vacuum Pressure Powder Filler (VPPF) and the Auger Filler (AF)
  • Be able to evaluate which filling technology suits a given product based on its characteristics, dose range, and container type
  • Understand VPPF dose design, sterility assurance challenges, setup complexity, and lifecycle cost considerations
14.0 - Utility Considerations for Aseptic Operations

Original Text

15.0 Utility Considerations for Aseptic Operations

Numerous utilities other than HVAC, light, and electricity may be required to support an aseptic filling operation. In general, utilities should not be present in the cleanroom, unless it is unavoidable, and they have been integrated into the design of the equipment and cleanroom. Consideration should always be given to the integrity of the containment of any utility that is not sanitary, where leakage would be considered a contaminant. If utilities are required to be present, care should be taken to minimize the impact of the utilities on the environment and process.

The required utilities may include:

  • Clean compressed air
  • Vacuum, especially for rolling DPs and vacuum powder fillers
  • Exhaust, venting, and/or dust collection
  • Other compressed gases (e.g., nitrogen)
  • Water for injection or purified water
  • CIP solutions (supply and return)
  • Clean steam and condensate for SIP
  • Heating and cooling transfer fluids (e.g., cooling water)
  • Hydraulics

Of these, the direct-product-contact utilities and those that come in contact with direct-product-contact equipment (e.g., CIP, SIP, nitrogen) are the most critical. The ASME standard BPE-2024 (Revision of ASME BPE-2022): Bioprocessing Equipment and EU GMP Annex 1: Manufacture of Sterile Medicinal Products provide design and operational considerations for their piping design and installation, respectively. Some considerations for the installation and supply of utilities are among the elements addressed in Table 14.3-1, such as:

  • Design of piping transiting grades
  • Materials of construction
  • Surface finish
  • Sanitary piping standards
  • Geometry, routing, and slope
  • Gas-tightness connections required for isolators

The materials of construction and surface finish should be suitable to a cleanroom environment, including being nonadsorptive, low particulate-shedding, and able to withstand exposure to disinfectants of the exposed surfaces on a routine basis. Piping should make use of sanitary connections (to reduce crevices) or welded connections (preferred). Routing should be designed to minimize pressure drops or line constrictions, by limiting the number of bends, while also entering the Grade A environment in a position that minimizes disruption to airflow. Slope should be considered to ensure that piping is free-draining.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Utilities: In an aseptic filling environment, "utilities" means more than water and electricity. It refers to every engineered system that supports the operation of the filling machine, including sterile air, vacuum, nitrogen, CIP solutions, and SIP steam.

Direct-product-contact utilities: Utilities such as nitrogen overlay and CIP/SIP steam have a direct impact on product sterility assurance, so they are the highest-priority items for control.

Material requirements: Nonadsorptive, low particulate-shedding, and resistant to disinfectants. These three points are the common baseline of EU GMP Annex 1 and ASME BPE.

Analogy

Imagine the aseptic filling area as a kitchen inside an operating room: every water pipe, air line, and cable must be clean to "surgical grade." A leaking water pipe in an ordinary kitchen just means a wet floor. A leaking line in an operating room could contaminate the surgical field directly, and the consequences are completely different.

This is why the guide requires that any line that does not need to enter the aseptic area should stay out of it. For those that must enter, connections should be sanitary or welded, never ordinary threaded fittings.

Key Notes

Order of priority in design: Utility design should follow a decision hierarchy: sterility assurance > product CQAs > commercial considerations. A leaking CIP line is not a "maintenance issue" but a "contamination risk event" that can lead to batch rejection.

Welded preferred: Sanitary connections can be used, but in sensitive isolator areas welded joints better withstand thermal expansion and contraction and are less likely to loosen. The guide explicitly recommends them.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does the guide say utilities should "in principle not enter the aseptic area"? List two risk control measures for cases where they must enter.
  2. Is nitrogen overlay a "direct-product-contact utility"? Why? What is its impact on sterility assurance?
14.1 - Operational Considerations for Utilities

Original Text

15.1 Operational Considerations for Utilities Supplied to Aseptic Filling Systems

Operational considerations for supplied utilities include:

  • Point-of-use filtration
  • Capability of cleaning and disinfection of supply lines
  • Sampling for routine monitoring

The use of clean compressed air, other compressed gases, exhaust, and dust collection may require sterile filtration (nominal pore size <0.22 µm). The placement of the filters should be carefully considered to ensure appropriate access for integrity-testing and replacement. Ideally, these operations should take place away from the Grade A environment to reduce the risk of contamination in the critical zone. In some cases (e.g., exhaust and dust collection), placement within a gray space entirely outside of all cleanroom areas will enable the safe exchange of filters without the risk of product contamination. The mechanisms by which the ducts and piping lead to the filters, however, must be kept clean and sanitary; this should be included in the design and assessed regularly.

Similarly, most supplied utilities will require some ability to collect samples at the point of use. The position of the sampling ports should be carefully designed to provide access without disrupting the Grade A space, while also ensuring that the samples will represent the quality of the utility as it is delivered to the process.

Water always brings the risk of microbiological proliferation. While it may be a risk-mitigating measure to have CIP/SIP capability for a filler, to avoid the need for aseptic assembly, the presence of the associated utilities within the cleanroom remains a significant risk to be managed. Frequent checking to ensure that points of use are not leaking and are in good repair are warranted. The thermal expansion and contraction of piping that occurs during cycles or disinfection of these systems should also be considered as it may result in a loosening of connectors as they expand and contract with the heating and cooling. Therefore, the verification of tightness of the sanitary connectors should be part of routine system-status checks. Welded connections should be sought in sensitive zones of the cleanroom to reduce this risk.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Point-of-use filtration: A filter installed at the "last step" before the utility enters the process, usually a sterilizing-grade membrane of ≤0.22 µm. It is the final barrier against microorganisms being introduced by the utility.

Sampling ports: They should be located where they represent the quality "actually delivered to the process", and the act of sampling must not disturb the Grade A environment. This is a classic design conflict between operability and representativeness that must be resolved at the engineering design stage.

Analogy

Choosing the location of a utility filter is like choosing the location of a kitchen range hood filter: you want it where it is easy to replace, not hidden deep inside the wall. Aseptic filling follows the same logic: a filter change is an intervention, and the farther the intervention point is from Grade A, the lower the contamination risk.

Changing the filter outside the gray space = changing the exhaust filter outside the kitchen, with no effect at all on what is happening in the operating room.

Key Notes

Thermal expansion is a hidden risk: CIP/SIP cycles involve hot steam and cooling, so lines repeatedly expand and contract, and sanitary clamps may gradually loosen. Loosening does not necessarily cause an immediate leak, but it creates a crevice where microorganisms can grow. The routine system-status check must therefore include checking clamp torque, not relying on visual inspection alone.

Water is the biggest microbial risk: Even Water for Injection (WFI), if it stagnates in a dead leg, can form biofilm within hours. This is why WFI loops must be kept circulating at a temperature ≥ 70°C.

Practice Questions

  1. If you were an engineer at a CDMO, which factors would you prioritize when deciding where to install the sterilizing filter on a compressed air line?
  2. At which level of the CCS should the risk of thermal expansion loosening connections be controlled (prevention / detection / response)?
15.0 - Filling Systems for Powder Filling: Overview

Original Text

16.0 Filling Systems for Powder Filling

Parts 1, 2, and 3 of the PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No.1: Aseptic Filling, Engineering and Operation have addressed both liquid-filling technologies and general topics concerning aseptic-filling operations. Part 4 focuses on the aseptic filling of powders.

16.1 Common Elements Between Aseptic Powder and Liquid Filling

To properly consider the requirements for the aseptic filling of powders, many of the general topics already addressed also apply to powders, as listed in Table 16.1-1.

In the case of sterile powder-filling, there are two main technologies available: AF systems (Auger Filler) and VPPF (Vacuum Pressure Powder Filler). These systems are different from both technology and complexity standpoints.

  • The AF is based on the concept of mechanical movement of the powder; in some systems, transfer may be facilitated by vibration.
  • The VPPF enables filling through the mechanical flow of powder by means of vacuum and air pressure. It is a volumetric filler at its core, where a correctly sized chamber is filled with powder (using vacuum) and dispensed. The VPPF does not require vacuum or pressurized air for the dosing mechanism itself, but relies on the mechanical transfer of the powder in the dosing disc.

Both methods are strongly influenced by the characteristics of the sterile powder to be filled. In some cases, this influence is such that only one of the two technologies is suitable for a specific type of sterile powder or fill-weight range. There are many filling system characteristics to keep in mind when choosing the filling system that best matches each product's needs.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The two systems for powder filling:

  • AF, Auger Filler: Uses the mechanical force of a rotating screw to move the powder, with no vacuum or air pressure needed. Think of a kitchen meat grinder, which moves material by turning a screw.
  • VPPF, Vacuum Pressure Powder Filler: Uses vacuum to draw powder into a dosing chamber, then pushes it out into the container with dry air. Think of a syringe: draw in, then push out.

The core difference between the two technologies is mechanical force vs. air pressure/vacuum, and this determines their respective strengths and limitations.

Analogy

Choosing a powder filling technology is like choosing a kitchen tool:

  • AF (auger) = pasta extruder: It extrudes by mechanical rotation and suits sticky or fibrous materials. It is easy to clean and can also be cleaned in place (CIP).
  • VPPF (vacuum pressure) = measuring spoon + air blast: Vacuum first compacts the powder into a "slug", which air pressure then blows into the vial. It suits free-flowing crystalline powders, but format changes are costly.

No kitchen tool suits every ingredient, and the same is true of powder filling: the technology choice must start with understanding "the personality of your powder."

Key Notes

Powder filling is not a simplified version of liquid filling: This chapter stresses that powder filling borrows heavily from the general practices of liquid filling (such as aseptic interventions, component introduction, and container closure), but the physical properties of the powder itself (flowability, static charge, particle size distribution, moisture content) affect filling accuracy and equipment selection far more than they do for liquids.

The importance of cross-references: The 15 related sections listed in Table 16.1-1 remind us that powder filling is not an isolated unit operation but is embedded in the whole aseptic manufacturing system. Poor design in any one area affects final sterility assurance.

Practice Questions

  1. Why does powder filling need to cite so many subsections of Section 8, "Microbiological Considerations for Aseptic Interventions"? What characteristic of powder filling does this show?
  2. In a CDMO commercial setting, if a client has three powder products at once, how would you begin evaluating whether to choose AF or VPPF?
15.1 - VPPF Technology: Design & Operation

Original Text

16.2 Aseptic Filling Technologies: Vacuum Pressure Powder Filling (VPPF)

Powder is loaded in the upper feeding-hopper, then moved to the lower hopper, which feeds the dosing disc. The dosing disc is fitted with radial chambers housing the dosing pistons. The powder is drawn into the dosing chamber or port from the lower hopper, via constant vacuum, and densified into a slug during disc rotation. In its lowest position, above the container opening, the disc discharges the powder into the container by means of dry sterile air. After dosing, the chamber that discharged the powder is cleaned by sterile air jets, with dust control applied to exhaust any residual powder.

The filling dose is governed by:

  • The overall volume (the dosing cylinder depth and cylinder diameter)
  • The vacuum negative-pressure (which compacts the powder)
  • The number of doses delivered into the same container

As the dosing disc rotates, the vacuum and pressure are transferred to the dosing disc via a mechanical backplate and/or rotary pneumatic joint. This mechanism on the rear side of the dosing disc provides the vacuum and pressure to each dosing chamber at the relevant position.

16.2.1 VPPF: Design Configurations

There are alternative designs to the standard configuration that include:

  • Dosing drum: Essentially a dosing wheel with two lanes, feeding two containers at the same time. Likely to have twenty-four cavities (twelve per lane), versus twelve in a standard dosing disc.
  • Filling needles: The dosing needle draws powder from a reservoir positioned below the needle. The needle is mounted vertically and may be moved vertically, enabling it to dispense powder just above or into the opening of the container.

There are some filler designs that permit assembly of the dosing wheels, connections to the hopper, and utility connections on a single plate — a super plate or chassis — in a Grade C environment. This super plate permits the entire assembly to be sterilized in an assembled state. The assembled plate can then be brought to the aseptic zone, where it takes only one or two aseptic connections to install the filler. This approach requires specialized trolleys and continuous unidirectional Grade A zoning from the autoclave unload section to the line.

16.2.2 VPPF: Setup

VPPF is a high-precision dosing system. Accuracy of dosing is mainly impacted by the physical characteristics of the powder and the environment. If the powder particle-size varies, agitation in the dosing hopper(s) is an essential means of ensuring consistent powder flow. The following factors can all affect flow characteristics and accuracy over time:

  • Particle-size distribution
  • Powder moisture content
  • Humidity and temperature of the environment
  • Airflow

Each dosing chamber has a dosing filter (e.g., sintered stainless steel, nylon), and it is essential to ensure that there is no plugging of the filters over the course of the filling operation. Statistical weight-check is a must for all filling operations; however, an in-line 100% weighing system is a highly recommended upgrade. Some filler models offer automatic dosing chamber adjustments to address trends in weights.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The three factors that determine VPPF dose:

  • Chamber volume (bore diameter × bore depth) = the physical volume limit
  • Vacuum pressure = determines the compaction density of the powder (the higher the density, the more mass fits in the same volume)
  • Number of dosing strokes (how many times the same container is filled) = allows flexible dose adjustment, but each additional stroke is an extra opportunity for intervention

These three variables constrain one another, and if any of them is affected by the environment (for example, humidity affecting powder flowability), the final fill weight will be affected.

Analogy

Super Plate = the powder version of an F1 pit-stop tire change strategy: The traditional approach brings each part into the aseptic area individually and assembles them one by one, so every contact step is a contamination opportunity. The Super Plate approach is: "Assemble and sterilize all the parts in a clean area first, then move the whole system in at once and make only the last two connections." This greatly reduces the number and complexity of aseptic interventions.

Formula

Factors affecting VPPF dose:

Fill Weight ≈ f(chamber volume, vacuum pressure, powder density, temperature and humidity)

Typical precision range: ~2% to 5% RSD
(depending on fill dose and powder characteristics)

If a trend is detected → the dosing piston length is adjusted automatically
(feedback control from a 100% in-line weighing system)

Key Notes

Clogging of the dosing filter is one of the biggest operational risks of VPPF: Each chamber contains a sintered stainless steel or nylon filter. Once it clogs, vacuum can no longer draw powder in properly, and the fill weight of that chamber will be low or the chamber will fail to fill at all. The choice of filter material (pore size, air permeability) needs to be optimized for each product at the feasibility study stage.

Environmental conditions are CPPs: Temperature, humidity, and airflow in the filling room are critical process parameters (CPPs) for VPPF because they directly affect powder flowability and therefore filling accuracy. This must be included in the validation design.

Practice Questions

  1. A new product has a fill weight target of 500 mg, but the powder density is strongly affected by temperature and humidity. Which weight control system would you recommend procuring first (statistical sampling vs. 100% weighing)? What is your rationale?
  2. The main benefit of the Super Plate design is fewer aseptic interventions, but what are its prerequisites (which facility support is needed)?
15.2 - VPPF Container Compatibility & Sterility Assurance

Original Text

16.2.4 VPPF: Filling Container Compatibility

VPPF systems can be used with a variety of container types, depending on the selected filler design. Table 16.2.4-1🔍 depicts typical containers and their applicability to the various VPPF system designs.

*Bag shape is specifically designed to configure the bag mouth to be suitable to the chosen technology.

When working with nested components (such as syringes or cartridges), VPPF fillers are adapted to either provide robotics (e.g., XY table) to dose from a dosing needle to each position within the nest, or to de-nest the components, fill them, and then re-nest the components. Care should be taken with the approach for the IPC weight check, as these approaches may restrict the ability to perform 100% net-weight capabilities.

16.2.5 VPPF Sterility Assurance (Microbial and Total Particles)

The dosing disc transports the powder slugs at approximately 10–20 rpm from the powder hopper to the point of product delivery. The dosing disc is shrouded from the aseptic environment as it rotates by a dust collector, which prevents stray powder from escaping to the environment. At the point of dosing, there is a small (1–2 mm) gap between the filler and the mouth of the container. This gap accommodates container dimension variation and enables weigh cells to register tare and gross weight.

VPPF does not permit CIP/SIP except for the bulk-feed portion of the filler. The dosing disc, drum, and needle are cleaned and sterilized off-line and require aseptic assembly within a downflow booth. For isolators, mounting can be performed after external biodecontamination of packages (e.g., VHP surface biodecontamination) or after aseptic transfer through an alpha-beta port.

During the assembly and setup phases, EM (Environmental Monitoring) must be conducted. Regulatory expectations require constant monitoring for both viable and total particulate. Due to the nature of powder, particulate may interfere with monitoring, requiring positioning of probes at a height above typical working height for liquid filling. Firms should defend and document the location of the probes. If powder has an inhibitory effect on media, special EM materials must be used.

Microbiological plates must be positioned at the critical points. As powder fillers tend to be wider than liquid fillers, the ergonomics for microbiological plate placement should be verified as part of the initial qualification. Monitoring positions should be included as part of the filler design (e.g., during mock-up).

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Flexibility of the dosing needle design: The container compatibility table shows that the dosing needle is the only one of the three VPPF designs that can fill cartridges, syringes, and ampoules. For a CDMO, the dosing needle design offers the greatest container flexibility and is a priority consideration for a multi-product platform.

The sterility assurance challenge: VPPF cannot be CIP/SIP: This is the most important sterility assurance limitation of VPPF. The dosing disc, dosing drum, and dosing needle must be cleaned and sterilized offline and then assembled into the equipment aseptically. Every assembly step is a potential contamination opportunity, and must be described in detail in the SOP and included in APS validation.

Analogy

Aseptic assembly of VPPF is like the instrument table in surgery: A surgeon does not wash the scalpel personally. The scrub nurse sterilizes the instruments in the sterile processing room, then passes them one by one to the operating table using aseptic technique. The same applies to the VPPF dosing disc: it must be assembled with aseptic technique inside the downflow booth (the equivalent of the operating table), and every contact point must comply with aseptic practice.

This is why VPPF setup is so complex: aseptic technique training for operators is critical.

Key Notes

Powder interfering with environmental monitoring is a challenge specific to VPPF: During powder filling, airborne dust particles can trigger false-positive alarms on the particle counter. The monitoring probe must be positioned higher than in liquid filling, and this decision must be clearly explained and defended and documented in the validation report. This is not a step that "can be omitted" but a documentation obligation explicitly required by regulation.

The 1-2 mm gap is a necessary design feature: This small gap may seem trivial, but it exists to accommodate container dimensional tolerances and the operation of the weighing cell. For sterility assurance, this gap means the filling point is technically "open", so the filling area must maintain continuous Grade A unidirectional airflow protection.

Practice Questions

  1. If a client's product is an inhaler, which VPPF design would you recommend? Why?
  2. The environmental monitoring (EM) probe position for powder filling must be "higher than liquid filling." Explain the scientific logic behind this, and describe how you would verify that this decision is justified in the APS.
15.3 - VPPF: Efficiency, Costs & System Complexity

Original Text

16.2.6 VPPF Efficiency and Impact on Risk

VPPF speed (containers per minute) is quite fast and can be increased with a filler that employs multiple dosing lanes and fill heads for larger doses. The use of multiple fill heads will require additional aseptic interventions during setup.

16.2.7 VPPF Costs: Initial and Ongoing

If multiple fill-weights are required, VPPF encounters additional costs for different formats and discs. Lifecycle costs for VPPF consumables include filters and O-rings for the filter and pistons. Other wear parts are those typical of any filling machine (e.g., bushings, bearings, seals). VPPF uses clean compressed air and vacuum, supplied via house utilities or through localized generation.

The mechanical backplate and/or pneumatic rotary joint behind the dosing disc may be a point of friction during rotation. Over time, this rotational mechanism may need replacement, generally after multiple millions of cycles.

16.2.8 VPPF System Complexity: Setup, Handling, and Changeover

VPPFs are systems with high complexity during the setup phase. Setup can be lengthy, but by implementing ergonomic features and installation aids, the setup could potentially be reduced.

Assembly activities for the hoppers can be performed in a Grade C area with subsequent sterilization. For the dosing discs, drum, and needle, the parts are typically sterilized and then aseptically assembled in a downflow booth to install O-rings and pistons (unless working with a super plate design where assembly precedes sterilization).

There may be rare cases where a dosing disc chamber plugs or a screen is breached during an operation. Changing the dosing disc during the operation is not recommended as this is a significant intervention. Changing the dosing disc would require:

  • Availability of a second, sterilized disc within the cleanroom or isolator
  • Clearance of the line
  • Performance of the intervention (with all required EM samples)
  • Restandardization of fill weights

Risk assessments for this operation should be performed and mitigation actions considered (e.g., reducing batch duration, optimizing powder and airflow characteristics). Testing during filling system feasibility should ideally uncover such a risk before registration.

At the time of changeover, all product-contact pieces (e.g., hoppers, discs, feed pipes) must be manually disassembled prior to cleaning. After cleaning, there are two options:

  • Sterilize the pieces in an autoclave, then assemble in the aseptic area
  • Use the super plate concept (assemble in Grade C, sterilize in autoclave assembled, then transport to the line for mounting)

Once setup is complete, system handling (governed by procedures) is quite easy. Modern systems are provided with 100% weight checks and with automatic adjustment of the dosing-piston lengths to maintain weight(s) within specified limits.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

VPPF is "complex to set up, simple to run": This is an important characteristic of the VPPF system. The setup stage is highly complex (aseptic assembly is required), but once setup is complete and the run has started, modern systems can automatically adjust the dosing piston length and maintain fill weight accuracy through 100% weighing feedback, so very little operator intervention is needed.

Total cost of ownership (TCO) considerations: The main sources of ongoing VPPF cost are filters, O-rings, and pistons (consumables), plus format parts for each different dose. The rotary pneumatic union needs replacing after millions of cycles, which is an easily overlooked long-term maintenance cost.

Formula

VPPF TCO cost components:

Initial capital expenditure (CapEx):
  Equipment itself + format parts (one set per dose strength)
  + Super Plate transfer cart (if applicable)

Ongoing operating costs (OpEx):
  - Consumables: filters, O-rings, pistons
  - Utilities: compressed air + vacuum
  - Maintenance: bearings, belts, seals
  - Long term: rotary pneumatic union (after millions of cycles)

Format change costs:
  Each new fill weight = a new set of dosing discs / format parts
  → hidden cost accumulation for a CDMO multi-product platform

Key Notes

A clogged dosing chamber is not something you can fix by simply "stopping and swapping a disc": Changing the dosing disc is a major aseptic intervention. A second sterilized dosing disc must be on standby inside the cleanroom/isolator, the fill weight must be re-standardized after the change, and all EM samples must be taken throughout the process. This means preventing clogging is far more important than responding to it: filter selection and powder flowability should be tested with the target product at the feasibility study stage.

More filling heads = higher speed + greater setup risk: This is a classic trade-off between efficiency and sterility assurance. Each additional filling head adds another set of dosing components that must be assembled aseptically. The decision hierarchy requires confirming the feasibility of sterility assurance first, and only then considering speed requirements.

Practical Application

Suppose you are the engineering director at a CDMO. A client wants powder filling capability added to the existing liquid filling line, and the product has three different fill weights (50 mg, 200 mg, 500 mg). Based on this section:

  • VPPF needs a set of format parts for each fill weight → capital investment for three sets of dosing discs
  • Each format changeover requires a full aseptic disassembly and reassembly → assess whether a Super Plate is feasible
  • If the 50 mg low-dose product is toxic → for VPPF, confirm the feasibility of an offline cleaning approach (see §16.2.12)
  • Conclusion: VPPF suits a product portfolio with a wide range of fill weights but infrequent format changeovers

Section Summary

  • Utility design principles: Keep utilities out of the aseptic area where possible. For those that must enter, prefer welded connections and periodically verify connection integrity. Direct-product-contact utilities (nitrogen, CIP/SIP) are the highest-risk control focus and should be designed to EU GMP Annex 1 and ASME BPE.
  • The two powder filling technologies: AF (auger, mechanical transport, CIP/SIP capable) vs. VPPF (vacuum pressure, volumetric dosing, offline sterilization followed by aseptic assembly). The choice is determined jointly by the product's powder characteristics, dose range, and SA requirements, and neither is absolutely better.
  • Core features of VPPF: Dose is determined by chamber volume + vacuum pressure + number of dosing strokes; environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, airflow) are CPPs; clogging of the dosing filter is the main operational risk; the inability to CIP/SIP is the biggest sterility assurance challenge; setup is complex but operation is highly automated.
  • Decision hierarchy reaffirmed: All technology choices and operational designs must be evaluated in the order sterility assurance (SA) > product CQAs > commercial benefit. The question of whether production "can continue" when a dosing disc is clogged must be answered from an SA perspective, not under capacity pressure.

Section 16: Vacuum Powder

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p205 - p210

Learning Objectives for This Chapter

  • Understand how the vacuum pressure powder filler (VPPF) works, including the complete fill cycle of dosing disc, vacuum pick-up and pneumatic discharge
  • Evaluate the setup complexity challenges of the VPPF and how the super plate concept reduces aseptic intervention risk
  • Analyze VPPF efficiency, cost, CIP/SIP limitations and maintenance needs, and make a meaningful comparison with the auger filler (AF)
  • Understand the differences between the VPPF and AF for highly potent products, container compatibility and sterility assurance, and apply the decision hierarchy to equipment selection

Section Structure
