Section 17-19: Powder Func & Dose

p210-p221

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p210 – p221

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the seven product characteristics that influence the choice of powder filling technology, and the conditions under which VPPF and AF are each suited.
  • Understand how the bulk powder transfer method affects filler design, and the key points for controlling content uniformity.
  • Explain the discard strategy and risk control methods for each stage of powder filling (startup / filling / dose control / end of fill / other).
  • Apply the decision hierarchy (sterility assurance > product CQAs > commercial flexibility) to day-to-day operating decisions in powder filling.

Section Structure

17.0 Product Characteristics Compatibility 17.1 Influence of Product Attributes 18.0 Effect of Powder Transfer 19.0 Discard Strategies Overview 19.1 Startup & Priming 19.2 Filling & Interventions 19.3 Dose Control 19.4 Conclusion of Fill 19.5 Other Rejection Considerations
17.0 Product Characteristics Compatibility for Vacuum Pressure Powder Filler and Auger Powder Filler Technologies

Original Text

With all powder filling, the attributes of the powder influence the powder-handling and flow characteristics, which will drive the selection of the technology. The attributes to be considered include:

  • Density (tap and bulk)
  • Particle size
  • Porosity and particle surface area
  • Angle of repose (flowability)
  • Friction effects and temperature sensitivity
  • Electrostatic charge
  • Hygroscopicity

Section 17.1 explores powder attributes and their influence on the selection and design of a powder filling system.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

The seven physical properties of powder: These seven attributes do not act independently; together they shape how the powder behaves in the filler. Density determines the volume filled per dose, flowability (angle of repose, the angle a powder pile forms with the horizontal) determines whether the powder moves smoothly, and electrostatic charge directly affects dose accuracy and whether powder clings to the container neck.

Technology selection logic: Powder attributes do not necessarily determine which machine can be used, but they often determine which machine is more cost-effective and more stable.

Analogy

Choosing a filling technology is like choosing a cooking tool: liquids can be measured with a measuring cup, but powders (flour, sugar, salt) each behave differently. Flour clumps easily (hygroscopic), salt flows freely (free-flowing), and sugar builds up static. A cook picks the tool to suit the ingredient, and a powder filling engineer applies the same logic.

Practice Questions

  1. If your product is a highly hygroscopic powder, which technology, VPPF or AF, places stricter demands on environmental control, and why?
  2. When a filling engineer faces a product with severe electrostatic charge, which design feature of the filling system should be confirmed first?
17.1 Influence of Product Attributes on Selected Powder Filling Technology

Original Text

During product and process development, the attributes of the powder should be tested to confirm its handling characteristics and to establish the critical process parameters and machine setup (e.g., mesh sizing and material for VPPF or auger selection for AF) that will be required for successful filling. While the powder characteristics may not limit the selection of the filling technology, the restrictions on certain process parameters, such as speed of filling, may make one technology more favorable than another. Often, equipment suppliers can perform this testing for the company if the equipment is not available within the development department to confirm the appropriate equipment settings.

The selection of the container and its neck size are more critical for powder filling than for liquid filling. The centering of the container is essential to the delivery of the powder to the container. The size of the neck opening will impact the quantity of powder that can be dosed with each rotation for VPPF. For both VPPF and AF, a small neck opening may affect the speed at which the machine can be operated. The neck opening does not necessarily impact the selection of the specific filling technology, although with very small neck openings, such as ampoules, there may be some practical limits for each technology.

Table 17.1-1🔍 evaluates the attributes of the product, one aspect at a time, with each filling technology. In reality, however, the powder has aspects of each attribute simultaneously, and the best technology will be the most suitable compromise for all characteristics. In practice, it is not always possible to determine the appropriate technology from a list of attributes; often, testing the powder with the selected technologies is the best way to determine handling and behavior. Finally, cost, flexibility, fill speed, containment considerations, and availability of the technology within the factory may also be deciding factors.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Key insight: attributes do not decide the technology, but they decide cost and stability. The guide states clearly that powder attributes usually do not "exclude" a technology; they make one of them "more advantageous" in a given situation. This means a CDMO should evaluate product attributes, equipment availability, required filling speed, and containment/toxicity considerations together before making the final decision.

Container neck size: In powder filling, neck size is more critical than in liquid filling. A neck that is too small limits the amount per fill (VPPF) or the filling speed (both technologies). Ampoules, because of their very narrow necks, may impose practical limits on both technologies.

Key Notes

Electrostatic charge vs hygroscopicity: the two most common root causes of filling failure:

  • VPPF electrostatic risk: Static charge interferes with the formation and release of the vacuum plug, causing inaccurate doses, and powder may cling to the container neck and compromise the seal.
  • AF frictional heat risk: The auger generates more friction than VPPF, which is a potential problem for thermosensitive products (for example, powder pre-filled before lyophilization).
  • Common to both: Highly hygroscopic products require strict relative humidity control in both cases; the difference is that VPPF also needs control of the humidity of the compressed air or nitrogen.

Analogy

Choosing between VPPF and AF is like choosing how to portion seasonings in a restaurant: VPPF is like a measuring cup that uses vacuum to hold a fixed volume (precise, but demanding on powder compressibility), while AF is like a screw feeder that controls the amount by the number of rotations (flexible, but generates frictional heat). The best method depends on whether you are portioning salt (free-flowing) or corn starch (prone to clumping).

Formula

VPPF single-fill range:
  Maximum single dose ≈ 1 cc (about 1 mL volume)
  Minimum effective single dose ≈ 0.050 cc

AF strategy for large doses:
  Multiple rotations × amount filled per rotation = target dose
  The number of rotations can be adjusted dynamically as density changes

Priority consideration for toxic/potent products:
  AF (supports CIP/SIP) > VPPF (requires offline cleaning, increasing exposure risk)

Practice Questions

  1. A new product powder has high electrostatic charge and is temperature sensitive. Setting other factors aside, what are the risks of VPPF and AF respectively? How would you evaluate them?
  2. When a CDMO evaluates filling technology for a highly potent powder product, why does the CIP/SIP capability of AF reflect "first priority in the decision hierarchy"?
18.0 Effect of Powder Transfer on Technology Selection

Original Text

Powder transfer from the bulk source to the powder filler will influence the filler design. There are several types of bulk containers that can be used for drug product, including bags and kegs. Typically, bags or kegs are loaded and connected manually; therefore, when considering machine speed, the rate of replenishment and duration of reconnection should also be considered.

Split valve connections will require that the hopper receiving the product from the bag or keg be placed in the Grade A environment to maintain the connection in an aseptic state. Intrinsic sterile connection devices may permit the charge-point to be located in a lower grade. During disconnection, either connector type might have exposed product on the surfaces, so containment should be considered for highly potent or toxic products. A risk analysis should be performed to determine the microbiological and containment needs for the product.

Powder transfer can be accomplished by gravity or with augmented feeding, such as vibratory feeders or positive displacement with compressed air. There are practical limitations for gravity-fed powders with regard to the distance that can be traversed. With augmented feed systems the distances can be extended, but it is still best to keep the distance as short as possible. In some factories, the manufacturing process and facility layout may dictate the position and distance that the bulk powder needs to travel, which will mandate feeder augmentation.

Minimization of the transfer distances will also help to ensure that segregation of powders (i.e., separation of powders by particle size, possibly resulting in the separation of one molecule from another within the transfer) does not occur. The filler designs incorporate mixers, which also help to ensure homogeneity of the powders at the point of fill. Homogeneity and content uniformity are important measures that will be tested during the process validation and as part of routine batch Quality Control.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three ways powder transfer affects design:

  • Connection point classification (grade): A split valve must be connected in a grade A environment, whereas a device with an intrinsic sterile connection may allow the connection to be made in a lower grade, which directly affects facility layout cost.
  • Transfer distance: The longer the distance, the higher the risk of powder segregation and the harder it is to assure blend uniformity (content uniformity). The best design is to "let the powder take the shortest path".
  • Replenishment rate: The frequency and duration of keg/bag changes affect overall line throughput and must be factored in when evaluating filling speed.

Key Notes

Powder segregation is the biggest hidden enemy of content uniformity: When a powder blend is transferred through piping, particles of different sizes separate under gravity, vibration, or air flow. Larger particles settle outward and fine powder gathers toward the center, ultimately giving each container a different proportion of active ingredient. This directly affects the patient dose and is a CQA-level issue. The mixer built into the filler is the last line of defense.

Analogy

Powder segregation is like shaking a box of cereal: the large flakes rise to the top and the fine crumbs sink to the bottom. If you always scoop from the bottom, every bowl tastes different (a different composition). The mixer in a powder filling system is the mechanism that "re-mixes" the powder, but the most fundamental solution is to let the powder take the shortest path, reducing its chances of being "shaken".

Practical Application

When a CDMO takes on a new powder filling project, the facility layout assessment should cover: (1) the placement of the source keg/bag and its vertical distance from the filler hopper, (2) the cleanroom grade required by the connection device type (split valve or sterile connector), and (3) the effect of batch size on replenishment frequency (more frequent replenishment = higher risk of stoppages = more discards). These three points directly affect project quotation and the risk matrix.

19.0 Discard Strategies for Aseptic Filling of Powders: Overview

Original Text

The selection of a filling technology and its specific system design can influence the discard strategies that are employed for such line events as startup, priming, line stoppages, interventions, and end of the aseptic fill-unit operation. Products that are very expensive or limited in availability will be impacted disproportionately by systems that have high discard requirements. Therefore, careful consideration of the system design and the integration of the filling technology with the filling enclosure or isolator is warranted.

VPPF and AF are selected based on the attributes of the powder to be filled, the required fill weight, and the opening of the container. Both VPPF and AF will encounter some need to reject containers during the process. In many cases, the cause of rejection is the same for both technologies. The various points within the process at which rejection might occur are included in Sections 19.1–19.5.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Discard strategy is a hidden cost in a CDMO quotation: For high-value drugs (such as orphan drugs and biologics) or products with scarce raw materials, the cost of each discarded container can range from hundreds to tens of thousands of US dollars. The expected discard rate must be quantified at the design review stage and treated as one of the factors in technology selection. This is a "commercial and flexibility" tier consideration, but one that affects CQAs.

Key Notes

Section 19.0 emphasizes that how the filling system is integrated with the isolator/RABS directly determines the amount discarded. This is not simply an equipment issue; it results from co-designing the facility, equipment, and process. In a CMO quotation, the "discard rate" is a key indicator for quantifying risk and is directly tied to batch size and drug cost.

19.1 Discard Strategies at Startup and Priming

Original Text

During powder-filler setup, standardizing the dose and priming the filler are necessary actions; however, both of these actions can result in rejections. Taking the following steps during setup may help avoid rejections or minimize their number during the priming and dose-standardization steps:

  • Adjust the conveyance mechanism to ensure the proper centering of the container under the dosing station
  • Ensure that the correct distance of the dose delivery system from the container is established
  • Adjust the agitator type (should be part of system design) and speed to ensure homogeneous delivery of the powder for powder blends

Startup rejection may also occur as a consequence of the risk that the initial product has been degraded due to exposure to conditions that would adversely impact the product. To avoid or minimize rejections, an inert gas overlay (for products that are oxygen-sensitive) should be established and any product that was exposed to air during the priming should be eliminated.

For VPPF, during setup, the piston depth may be set with a fixture or gauge which will expedite the process of establishing the weight within the specified range. As standardizing the dose is undertaken, the piston is adjusted to change the volume of the dosing chamber. Typically, a progressive increase in the depth of piston-movement occurs to adjust the dose. For some piston and filter designs, the potential exists for powder to be retained between the piston-filter OD and the dosing-chamber ID, which may create difficulties in reducing piston depth.

For AF, the dose is adjusted by changing the number of rotations of the auger. Some fillers are equipped with a 100% net-weight filling, which will minimize priming rejects due to an underfilled or inaccurate dose.

During process validation, careful evaluation of content uniformity (for powder blends) and fill accuracy should be performed. Once established, the process parameters that deliver these CQAs should be carefully defined in SOPs and batch records.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Two root causes of startup/priming rejects:

  • Machine not yet stable (dose not standardized): VPPF sets the dose volume by adjusting the piston depth, while AF does so by adjusting the number of rotations. Both need several filling cycles to reach stable output.
  • Degraded product: If an oxygen-sensitive product is exposed to air during startup, it must be discarded even if the weight is correct. The nitrogen overlay must be established before filling begins.

Key Notes

Mechanical trap in VPPF piston depth adjustment: If powder becomes lodged between the piston filter OD and the dosing-chamber ID, it may become difficult to shorten the piston stroke (reduce the dose). This is a design detail to confirm when selecting VPPF equipment; a good design avoids such powder-trapping spaces.

Strategic value of 100% net-weight filling: A filler equipped with 100% net-weight measurement can greatly reduce startup discards, which is especially important for high-cost products. This is a feature worth the extra investment at equipment purchase.

Practice Questions

  1. Suppose your product is an oxygen-sensitive antibiotic powder. In the SOP, before which step should the nitrogen overlay be established? Does this differ between the VPPF and AF operating sequences?
  2. Why is evaluating content uniformity during process validation more critical for a powder blend than for a single-component powder?
19.2 Discard Strategies at Filling and Interventions

Original Text

Changes in powder attributes during the run could also result in dosing inaccuracies due to changes in the dynamics of flow, for example, the powder becoming gummy or sticky due to environmental conditions, the presence of an undissipated electrostatic charge, or an increase in density due to an increase in fines, particularly at the end of bulk containers.

Modern filling lines are equipped with adequate environmental controls (i.e., humidity, temperature, deionization technology), making environmental and electrostatic failure modes less likely. However, care should be taken to ensure that the filling system operation does not increase the temperature of the powder (e.g., due to friction forces).

Electrostatic build-up may not be associated with the powder or filler itself but is often due to dry conditions and the conveyance of glassware. Electrostatics, if left undissipated, can affect dust on the container neck and closure surfaces, can affect the environment, and can affect the weigh-cell accuracy.

For powder-density changes on VPPF, once cavity sizes are set, an increase in density will require a reduction in dose size (which may be automatic on some models). During setup, the potential exists for powder to be retained between the piston-filter OD and the dosing chamber ID, which may create difficulties in reducing piston depth with some piston–filter designs. For AF, changes in product density may require an adjustment to the number of rotations of the auger to adjust the fill weight (may be an automatic function with some models).

As with liquid filling, during powder-filling operations, interruptions in the filling operation that result in stoppage on the line (e.g., gaps in component supply, interventions, breaks) or other unforeseen events (e.g., particle excursion, loss of temperature in the tunnel resulting in an equipment stoppage, jams or collisions at the capper) may result in rejections.

When interventions occur during powder-filling, the powder, or the powder-filler itself is not generally impacted detrimentally. If the intervention requires an open door, such as might occur within a RABS, consideration should be given to ensuring that the environment surrounding the RABS is also well-controlled to avoid any powder characteristic changes. If the product requires inert gas overlay (e.g., nitrogen), the overlay must be maintained through any intervention or stoppage, or it will require rejection of containers and filled unsealed units that have potentially been exposed to air.

With some systems, an automated clearance mode is available that will stop the infeed to the filler and reject all containers within the conveyor system in front of the filler. With legacy systems, the rejection may be entirely manual, and care must be taken to perform the intervention, picking up each rejected container with a sterile tool and following appropriate aseptic techniques, while taking care not to cause any spills.

If there are filled, fully sealed containers within the line's clearance zone, the decision to reject or keep those containers must be based on an appropriate risk assessment and documented in intervention SOPs at the site.

For oxygen-sensitive products, an inert gas overlay (e.g., nitrogen) may need to be established to purge air from the headspace of the container. When analyzing container headspace at the conclusion of filling, containers with too much oxygen in the headspace may need to be rejected. Any failure in the inert-gas headspace controls during the filling operation (e.g., when the filler is shut down) will result in rejections during the processing.

If there is powder at the neck of the container during filling (e.g., due to inaccurate fill-targeting into the container opening or uncontrolled electrostatic charge), the powder may cause a poor seal around the elastomer, which can result in an ingress of oxygen during the shelf life of the product. Powder at the necks of containers may be difficult to observe during initial visual inspection due to the crimp seal. Therefore, additional controls should be put in place for targeting delivery of the powder to the container-opening during setup, and electrostatic control should be part of the standard environmental controls. The filling process should be verified intermittently to ensure continued dust control at the neck. Headspace analysis may be used for nitrogen-flooded containers to ensure that the closure is integral, thereby demonstrating an effective seal between elastomer and neck without interference due to the presence of powder.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Three main triggers of discards during filling:

  • Dynamic changes in powder properties: Fines increase toward the end of the batch, so density rises and VPPF/AF doses run heavy. Modern equipment can compensate automatically, but older equipment requires manual intervention.
  • Electrostatic build-up: Static charge not only affects dose accuracy but also makes powder cling to the container neck and stopper, disrupting the elastomer seal and allowing oxygen ingress during long-term storage. This is a hidden CQA failure risk that may be completely invisible on visual inspection.
  • Line stoppages: An interruption of the nitrogen overlay = all exposed containers must be discarded. This is the highest-priority control point for oxygen-sensitive products during interventions.

Key Notes

Powder at the neck is a hidden threat to sterility assurance: Powder caught at the neck means the stopper/elastomer cannot seat fully against the glass, so oxygen enters over time and the drug degrades. This is almost invisible by eye after capping. Headspace oxygen analysis is the only way to verify seal integrity. Decision hierarchy: sterility assurance is #1, and this situation falls into that category.

Automated clearance mode vs manual clearance: Automated clearance in modern equipment reduces the time personnel spend intervening in the grade A environment, directly lowering sterility risk. When purchasing equipment, automated clearance should be listed as a specification requirement, especially for products with frequent interventions.

Practice Questions

  1. During the filling of a batch of antibiotic powder, the filler stops for 20 minutes for an external reason. How should your SOP define which containers are kept and which are discarded? What documentation is needed to support this?
  2. If nitrogen headspace analysis shows high oxygen levels in some containers, but visual inspection shows no powder at the neck, how would you trace the root cause?
19.3 Discard Strategies at Dose Control

Original Text

For net-weight fillers, rejection should be automatic and demonstrated during the qualification of the equipment to determine that the correct containers have been rejected. As with liquid filling, if the weight-check function is statistical (intermittent), the segregation and rejection will need to occur beginning at the last confirmed correct-weight check (see Section 5.0).

One of the key reasons that dosing becomes inaccurate for VPPF is blinding of the screen, which affects both powder compression and powder expulsion. Another, less-frequent reason could be screen breakage. (Screens should be changed as part of routine preventive maintenance and inspected regularly after cleaning to verify screen integrity.) Either condition can result in rejections during the run due to inaccurate dosing.

AF primarily encounters dosing inaccuracies when the conditions of the powder change during the run. Both the VPPF and AF are available with net-weight models that enable automatic adjustments to keep the weights within preset weight limits throughout the run. For some AF fillers, the weight adjustment may be capable of occurring dynamically for each dose, whereas the VPPF will react to a trend in weights over several cycles.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

A VPPF-specific dose accuracy risk: screen blinding. VPPF uses vacuum to draw powder against a screen to form the dose plug. If the screen is blinded by fine powder, the powder cannot be compressed or ejected correctly, causing inaccurate doses. The screen is a critical consumable in VPPF; it must be included in the preventive maintenance (PM) program and its integrity confirmed after each cleaning.

Dynamic weight adjustment in AF: An advanced AF can adjust the number of rotations for the next dose immediately after each dose based on the net-weight result, responding much faster than VPPF (which needs a trend over several cycles to trigger an adjustment).

Key Notes

Statistical IPC vs 100% net-weight measurement: the key difference in discard scope: When statistical (intermittent) sampling finds overweight or underweight containers, discard must reach back to the "last measurement point confirmed to be acceptable", which may cause many acceptable units to be discarded along with them. 100% net-weight measurement can precisely identify and automatically reject individual problem containers, greatly reducing losses. For high-value powder products, the price premium for 100% net-weight equipment is often recovered with the first batch.

Practice Questions

  1. When should the VPPF screen be replaced? Which post-cleaning checks can prevent sudden discards during filling?
  2. If your filler uses statistical IPC (one measurement every 10 units) and, after filling 500 containers, you find that the 480th container is out of weight specification, what range must you discard?
19.4 Discard Strategies at Conclusion of Fill

Original Text

At the end of the filling process, as powder levels start to drop in the hopper, dosing may become inconsistent. Proper hopper design is essential to minimize residual powder waste and to maintain filling accuracy for as long as possible. It is important during development of the filling process parameters that the level at which this occurs is noted and defined (measurable). Shutting down when this level is reached must become a normal part of the operation and must be defined in the site SOPs or batch record.

For net-weight fillers, there may be an option to continue to fill until the rejection level becomes too high to be practicable and compliant. The company must establish procedures to handle the end of fill consistently to ensure that only good-quality containers are produced (see Section 13.0).

Table 19.4-1🔍 summarizes common discard events and the specific risks represented by primary powder-filling technologies.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Hopper end-of-fill effect: As the amount of powder in the hopper decreases, the weight pressure of the powder bed falls, which affects both VPPF vacuum filling and AF screw back-pressure, so the dose begins to become unstable. "Defining a measurable shutdown level" is a required output of process development and must be recorded in the batch record.

Differences between VPPF and AF in end-of-fill waste: VPPF generates very little waste for small-dose filling (the hopper can be emptied to a very small amount); AF needs a certain back-pressure to deliver accurately, so the hopper must retain more residual powder, and AF therefore discards relatively more powder at the end of fill.

Key Notes

Key takeaway from Table 19.4-1🔍: The main risk for VPPF lies in the screen (blinding/breakage), whereas at the end of fill AF may leave more residual powder and waste because of insufficient back-pressure. For high-cost drugs, the estimated powder discard per batch should be calculated during equipment evaluation and included in the TCO (total cost of ownership) analysis.

Practical Application

How to confirm the shutdown level at end of fill in process validation: across the three validation batches, record how the dose coefficient of variation (CV%) changes once the hopper reaches a given level, find the critical point at which CV% begins to exceed the specification, define that level as the mandatory shutdown level, and write it into the SOP. This is the key data that makes the batch record "speak".

19.5 Other Rejection Considerations

Original Text

Rejections along the filling line may occur for other reasons that may not be directly related to the operation of the filler, for example:

  • Raised stopper or plunger placement detection
  • Missing stopper or plunger
  • Fallen components
  • Bad crimp seals or closures (at capper)

These sensors and rejection stations should be integrated into the filling conveyance system and tested during qualification to ensure that detection and rejection timing is appropriately integrated.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Line-integrated rejections: These rejections are unrelated to the filler itself and are triggered by sensors at downstream stations, for example abnormal stopper position or poor crimping. These sensors must be verified during equipment qualification: when a known defective container passes, the system must detect it 100% of the time and reject it to the correct location (with correct timing).

Key Notes

"Bad crimp seals" are the last line of defense for seal integrity: A container with a bad crimp, even if the powder was filled perfectly, indicates that the container closure system (CCS) has failed. This is the final critical control point for sterility assurance. 100% visual inspection after crimping or an in-line vision system, together with periodic destructive testing (crimp pull-off force), is the standard qualification strategy.

Practice Questions

  1. In filling line qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ), how do you verify that the rejection timing of the "bad crimp detection sensor" is correct? What is an acceptable detection rate?
  2. A container is flagged by a sensor as having a "raised stopper", but looks normal on visual inspection. How should you handle it, and where should this decision be documented?

Section Summary (Sec 17-19)

  • Sec 17.0-17.1: The physical properties of the powder (the seven factors, including density, flowability, electrostatic charge, and hygroscopicity) together determine the best compromise in filling technology selection; Table 17.1-1🔍 is a systematic tool for a comprehensive VPPF vs AF comparison. Powder testing with actual equipment is an indispensable verification step beyond theoretical analysis.
  • Sec 18.0: The connection method for bulk powder transfer (bag/keg transfer) affects the cleanroom grade required; the longer the transfer distance, the higher the segregation risk; content uniformity is the core measurement for process validation and QC batch release.
  • Sec 19.1-19.5: Discard triggers in powder filling span five stages: startup / filling / dose control / end of fill / other line events. 100% net-weight measurement and automated clearance mode are the key features of modern equipment for reducing discards; static control and nitrogen headspace protection are the two-fold defense for oxygen-sensitive products; the decision hierarchy runs through the whole section: sterility assurance always comes first.
21

Section 21: Case Studies

p225-p267

PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p225 - p246

Learning Objectives

  • Understand how product characteristics (viscosity, oxygen sensitivity, shear sensitivity, foaming tendency) translate directly into filling equipment design requirements
  • Grasp the design differences and decision logic between small volume parenterals (Case 1: prefilled syringe) and large volume parenterals (Case 2: liquid in a bottle)
  • Learn how to use a structured requirements matrix to systematically compare the suitability of four filling technologies: PP, RPP, TP and DP
  • Understand how production scale (batch size, campaign strategy, IPC selection) affects filling line design and annual output estimates
21.1 Case 1: Small Volume Parenteral — Liquid in a Syringe

Original Text

Specifications for Case 1 are detailed below:

  • Product: monoclonal antibody
  • Filling Volume: 0.5 mL
  • Container / Closure System: prefilled syringe (PFS); 1 mL long
  • Dosing System: to be determined

21.1.1 Case 1: Product Characteristics

Table 21.1.1-1🔍 provides details on product characteristic considerations. Refer to Section 1.0 and Section 4.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Product Characteristics Drive Design Decisions

Case 1 has three key design drivers:

  • Oxygen-sensitive: Inert gas (nitrogen) must be introduced at the filling and closing station to protect product quality. This directly affects the station design of the filling machine.
  • Shear-sensitive: The protein structure of a monoclonal antibody (mAb) is fragile, and high shear forces can denature it, so the rotary piston pump (RPP) is ruled out immediately.
  • Foaming tendency: The filling profile (acceleration and stop control) must be carefully designed, and a diving needle should be used to prevent foam contamination.

Note: Although this product is not highly potent, the vendor proactively chose an isolator, with the rationale of "increasing sterility assurance". This is a textbook example of decision hierarchy #1, sterility assurance, taking priority over commercial considerations.

Analogy

Imagine cooking a soup that foams easily (soy milk, for example). You cannot bring it to a rolling boil; you have to heat it gently, pour it in along the edge of the pot, and avoid over-stirring. Filling a monoclonal antibody follows the same principle: the descent speed of the filling needle, the starting fill position and the stop profile all have to be controlled as carefully as a chef would, to avoid foaming and protein damage.

Practice Questions

  1. Why did the vendor still choose an isolator rather than RABS for a product that is "not highly potent"? Which design priority does this decision reflect?
  2. If different shear-sensitive mAbs are to be filled on the same line in the future, is a rotary piston pump viable? Explain your reasoning.
21.1.2 Case 1: Container–Closure Characteristics

Original Text

Table 21.1.2-1🔍 provides details on container-closure characteristic considerations. Refer to Section 1.0, Section 6.0 and Section 7.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Design Details of the Nested Prefilled System

Case 1 uses nested prefilled syringes, and every design detail affects a specific subsystem of the filling machine:

  • Nest specification (160 syringes per tray): Directly determines the number of filling heads (fill lanes) and the X/Y motion requirements.
  • Tub height (97 mm): Affects the design of the lid and liner removal station, and can even determine whether a robotic arm is needed.
  • Container closure integrity (CCI): Must be confirmed during development to ensure that a sterile seal is maintained throughout the entire transport chain (including cold storage).

The headspace maintenance requirement directly raises a design question: is 100% in-line headspace inspection needed? This will affect the filling rate and equipment selection.

Key Point — The Importance of Supplier Drawing Numbers

The table frequently cites "Supplier Name, Drawing #XXX", and this is not mere formality. Each drawing number represents precise dimensional tolerances that directly affect the design of the sorting bowl, the tracks and the stoppering (plunger insertion) station. A CDMO needs to lock down this information early; changing the supplier or specification later may require the entire filling machine to be retrofitted.

Practice Questions

  1. If the vendor decides to switch to a 200-syringe nest, what impact would this have on the filling machine design?
  2. What is the basis for the judgment that "bubble size is not important"? Under what circumstances would bubble size become a critical design parameter?
21.1.3 Case 1: Specific Filling Requirements — Headspace & Deaeration

Original Text

Table 21.1.3-1🔍 provides guidance on specific filling requirement considerations. Refer to Section 2.0 and Section 7.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Design Logic for the Timing of Nitrogen Gassing

For the application of inert gas (nitrogen), the design principle is "the later, the better":

  • Gassing during closing: This is the choice made in this case. Nitrogen is introduced into the headspace at the moment of stopper insertion, displacing the last of the air, which is the most direct approach.
  • Gassing before or during filling: Suitable for products that are extremely oxygen-sensitive (such as certain liposomes), but it adds equipment complexity and nitrogen consumption.

The combined design of "evacuating before filling, then gassing with nitrogen" (as in this case) is the most common industry solution for oxygen-sensitive syringes.

Key Point — Forward-Looking Design for Future Flexibility

The text specifically notes: "If plastic syringes with silicone-free stoppers are used in the future, the vacuum short vent tube may become important." This reflects the consistent philosophy of the whole Guide: design for today's requirements while leaving room for future upgrades, so that equipment limitations do not later cost you product variety.

Practice Questions

  1. If the same line is to fill an "extremely" oxygen-sensitive product (<0.1% O₂) in the future, is the current "gassing during closing only" design sufficient? What additional stations would be needed?
21.1.4 Case 1: Multi-container / Multi-volume / Multi-product Flexibility

Original Text

Table 21.1.4-1🔍 provides guidance regarding multi-container/multi-volume/multi-product filling requirements. Refer to Section 1.0, Section 2.0 and Section 5.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — A Flexible Mindset for CDMO Platform Design

For a CDMO, a filling line designed for a single product makes almost no commercial sense. Case 1 demonstrates systematic thinking about a "multi-product platform design":

  • Container flexibility: From glass syringes to plastic syringes to cartridges, each change may require new static elimination devices, vacuum stoppering capability or sensor filling.
  • Fill volume flexibility: From 0.2 mL (lower-end capability) to 3 mL, a 15-fold volume range, which not every pump type can handle gracefully.
  • Filling technology flexibility: Whether the same machine base can accommodate different pump types (for example, RPP and PP side by side) must be decided at the initial design stage; adding them afterwards is almost equivalent to rebuilding.

Analogy

It is like designing a restaurant kitchen: you only make pasta today, but you already know that sushi and grilled meat will be added in three years. If you reserve space for gas lines, exhaust ducts and refrigerated zones from the start, future expansion only requires installing equipment; if you do not, walls have to be torn down and rebuilt at ten times the original cost. The same applies to CDMO filling line design.

Practice Questions

  1. If 0.2 mL of mAb is to be filled on this line in the future, which filling technology is most suitable? Why might DP (rolling diaphragm pump) be ruled out?
  2. When changing from "nested glass syringes" to "plastic syringes", which two main capabilities need to be added to the design?
21.1.5 Case 1: Anticipated Batch Sizes and Operating Practices

Original Text

Table 21.1.5-1🔍 outlines typical batch parameters to consider. Refer to Section 1.0 and Section 5.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Formulas and Calculations — Framework for Estimating Annual Output

Available hours per year = 365 days × 24 h × equipment efficiency (70-80%)
           ≈ 365 × 24 × 0.75 = 6,570 hours

Filling time per batch = batch fill quantity ÷ filling rate
Campaign changeover = 32 hours
Batch-to-batch changeover = 4 hours

Example with a 1 mL fill, 10-lane filler:
100 L batch = 100,000 syringes
If filling rate = 400 syringes/min → approx. 4.2 hours/batch

5-batch campaign = 5 × 4.2 h filling
           + 4 h × 4 batch-to-batch changeovers
           + 32 h campaign changeover
           ≈ 85 hours / campaign

The annual output estimate must integrate all of the above parameters, and a change in any single assumption (such as yield, line efficiency or changeover time) will significantly affect the number of batches per year.

Key Point — Trade-off Between 100% IPC and Statistical IPC

The Guide states clearly that if a nested filler is to perform 100% IPC (weighing every syringe), the filling rate drops from "hundreds per minute" to "hundreds per hour", a difference of more than 100 times. However, for a high-value mAb product, the product loss avoided by 100% IPC may outweigh the opportunity cost of the lost speed. The decision is essentially product CQA (drug product integrity) vs. commercial efficiency, decision hierarchy #2 vs. #3.

Practice Questions

  1. If a peristaltic pump (PP) is selected and a 500 L batch (2.5 million syringes) is run, why does hose wear become a key consideration? How would you mitigate this problem in the design?
  2. What mainly delivers "85% line efficiency": equipment automation or operator skill? What is the Guide's view?
21.1.6 Case 1: Comparison of Requirements to Filling System Capabilities

Original Text

Now that some of the preliminary design requirements for the product and its intended packaging have been defined, the requirements can be compared to the filling-system capabilities and attributes as described in Section 2.0. Comparison of the filling system-capabilities to the product needs, for this example, leads to the following evaluative matrix.

"Based on the above chart, the product characteristics make PP, TP, and DP the leading candidates as shear-sensitivity of the product may preclude RPP. PP, TP, and DP are well-matched. Decision-making may come down to whether smaller volume fills will be required in the future (ruling out DP, which is at the lower end of its capability at around 0.2 mL), or whether single-use (SU) technology (favoring PP and DP) or CIP/SIP are preferred (favoring TP and DP). If the foaming with the product is severe and SU technology is the desire, then PP will be the strongest contender, as long as the number of cycles between tubing changeout is managed."

21.1.7 Other Design Elements for Consideration

There are a number of other design decisions that will impact the layout and operation of the filling line, such as:

  • Operator Interface with the line (Section 8.0)
  • Supply of Components (Section 9.0 and Section 10.0)
  • Product Filtration, including location of filters, required number of filter elements, integrity testing pre- and post-filling (Section 11.0)
  • Filling Environment and Utilities (Section 14.0 and Section 15.0)

Generally, these decisions should be made as part of the filling-line specification process as they may affect costs and can influence placement of equipment; however, these are generally less of a direct impact on the selection of the filling technology itself.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Practical Application of the Matrix Decision Method

The most important lesson of this section is "how to use a requirements matrix to make a filling technology decision". The Guide's concluding logic is:

  1. RPP is excluded first: Shear sensitivity is a non-negotiable red line, which eliminates it immediately.
  2. DP is conditionally excluded: If the 0.2 mL small dose is a required future need, DP is at the lower limit of its capability and the risk is higher.
  3. The final contest between PP and TP:
    • If SU fluid path + severe foaming are preferred → PP is optimal
    • If CIP/SIP + precise fill stability are preferred → TP is optimal
    • DP is also competitive as an SU alternative, but its volume flexibility is weaker

This is the decision hierarchy in practice: sterility assurance (SA) drives the choice of an isolator; product CQA (shear sensitivity) drives the exclusion of RPP; and commercial flexibility (SU vs. CIP/SIP) determines the final choice among PP / TP / DP.

Analogy

It is like choosing a main kitchen knife: first rule out the knife types that do not suit the ingredients (a boning knife is not suitable for slicing thinly, for example); then, among the remaining candidates, make the final decision based on your habits (Japanese or Western style, how often you replace it). The logic for choosing a filling pump is exactly the same: first use product CQA to eliminate incompatible options, then use commercial requirements to make the final comparison.

Practice Questions

  1. In this case PP, TP and DP were finally selected as candidates. If you were the CDMO's technical director, which would you choose? Give your reasons from the perspective of wear and SU cost for "5-batch campaigns × 500 L batches".
  2. What impact does the limitation that "sensor filling is incompatible with nested fillers" have on the plan to add cartridges in the future?
21.2 Case 2: Large Volume Parenteral — Liquid in a Bottle

Original Text

Specifications for Case 2 are detailed below:

  • Product: blood-plasma protein product
  • Filling Volume: 250 mL
  • Container / Closure System: Bottle 250 mL
  • Dosing System: to be determined

21.2.1 Case 2: Product Characteristics

Table 21.2.1-1🔍 provides details on product characteristic considerations. Refer to Section 1.0, Section 3.0 and Section 4.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Key Differences Between Case 1 and Case 2

Case 2 differs from Case 1 in two decisive structural ways:

  • Container type: The change from nested prefilled syringes (PFS) to conventional bulk bottles requires a glass bottle washer plus a depyrogenation tunnel, so the whole container supply logic is completely different.
  • Fill volume: Jumping from 0.5 mL to 250 mL is a 500-fold scale-up. This affects not only pump selection (higher flow rates are needed) but also the fill profile design and needle diameter.
  • Environment choice not yet decided: Case 1 clearly chose an isolator, whereas Case 2 is still evaluating isolator vs. RABS. This is the point at which a commercial decision (cost considerations) enters the design process, but only on the premise that both can meet sterility assurance requirements.

Similarities: also oxygen-sensitive, also shear-sensitive and also prone to foaming, as plasma proteins and mAbs share many physicochemical behaviors.

Key Point — The Design Significance of a Viscosity of 25 mPa-s

The viscosity of Case 2 (25 mPa-s) is much higher than that of the water-like liquid in Case 1 (1-2 mPa-s), but the Guide states clearly that it is "not high enough to limit the choice of technology". Typically, filling technology is only significantly affected when viscosity exceeds 100-200 mPa-s (for example, when a heating system or special pump type is needed). This teaches us that viscosity is a continuous variable in design screening, not an on/off switch.

Practice Questions

  1. The fill volume in Case 2 is 500 times that of Case 1, but the filling rate does not need to be 500 times higher. Why? In what respects does large volume filling actually make the design "simpler"?
  2. Why has the filling environment (isolator vs. RABS) not yet been decided for Case 2, while Case 1 has already settled on an isolator? What design logic does this difference illustrate?
21.2.2–21.2.3 Case 2: Container–Closure Characteristics & Specific Filling Requirements

Original Text

21.2.2 Case 2: Container–Closure Characteristics

Table 21.2.2-1🔍 provides details on container-closure characteristic considerations.

21.2.3 Case 2: Specific Filling Requirements

Table 21.2.3-1🔍 provides guidance on specific filling requirement considerations. See Section 2.0 and Section 7.0 for additional information.

Tutorial Commentary

Core Concepts — Differences in Container Supply Between Bulk and Nested Lines

Case 2 uses conventional bulk glass bottles, with no tub/nest system. This means:

  • An in-line washer and a depyrogenation tunnel are needed, and the equipment occupies a larger footprint.
  • Roundness control of the glass bottles is critical: bottles with poor roundness easily jam or topple on the conveyor, affecting line efficiency.
  • The crimping specification (32 mm flip seal, 13 mm aluminum skirt length) directly determines the crimping pressure settings and the acceptance criteria for in-line visual inspection.

The headspace oxygen specification (<4% O₂) is a concrete CQA target, and the equipment design must ensure that this target is achieved consistently.

Key Point — Choosing Between Mechanical Stoppering and Vacuum Stoppering

Case 2 uses mechanical stopper insertion because the neck of the 250 mL bottle is large enough (32 mm) that vacuum assistance is mechanically unnecessary. However, the text requires a development report demonstrating that the stopper will not pop off under pressure after insertion, which is a concrete expression of quality risk management (QRM) in the closing operation. By comparison, the syringe in Case 1 uses vent tube stoppering because the syringe barrel is narrow: vacuum is unnecessary, but the vent tube helps to release air.

Analogy

Imagine bottling wine: a large 250 mL bottle (Case 2) can simply be capped mechanically, with the cork pressed firmly in by mechanical force; but a slender syringe (Case 1) is like fitting a cap onto a needle barrel, where space is tight and a vent tube is needed to let the air escape so the stopper can seat properly. Container geometry determines the closing method.

Practice Questions

  1. The headspace specification for Case 2 is <4% O₂. If you were the equipment acceptance engineer, which tests would you design to demonstrate that this specification can be achieved consistently?
  2. Case 2 does not require cold storage design, but Case 1 does. How does this difference affect the design of the facility layout (the link between the cleanroom and warehousing)?

Section 21A Summary

  • The structured requirements matrix is the core tool: Through a five-step framework of "product characteristics → container closure → filling requirements → batch scale → technology comparison", the Guide systematically converts product knowledge into equipment design decisions.
  • The decision hierarchy runs through every case: Sterility assurance (SA) drove the decision to choose an isolator in Case 1 (even though the product is not highly potent); product CQA (shear sensitivity) excluded RPP; and commercial requirements (SU vs. CIP/SIP) determined the final pump type.
  • Where Case 1 and Case 2 diverge in design: Container format (nested vs. bulk), fill volume (0.5 mL vs. 250 mL), stoppering method (vent tube vs. mechanical) and filling environment choice (decided vs. under evaluation) show how different product formats lead to very different equipment design paths.
  • Forward-looking flexibility is a CDMO's lifeline: From flexible planning for multiple volumes, containers and products to the scalability of filling technology, the Guide repeatedly stresses that decisions made without considering the future at initial design will be paid for many times over later.
  • The practical meaning of specific operating metrics: 98% yield, 85% line efficiency, 70-80% equipment efficiency and a 32-hour campaign changeover: these numbers are not slogans. They are the basis of the annual output calculation and the underlying assumptions behind a CDMO's delivery commitments to its customers.
PDA Manufacturing Technology Guide No. 1 | doc p247 - p267

Learning Objectives

  • Understand how the requirements of a multi-container / multi-volume / multi-product filling line are translated into equipment design specifications
  • Grasp the relationship between batch size, campaign length and the durability of the filling technology
  • Be able to use a Capability Comparison Matrix to select the most suitable filling technology
  • Build a calculation mindset for line efficiency, facility efficiency and annual output targets
21.2.4 Case 2: Requirements for Multi-container / Multi-volume / Multi-product Filling

Original Text

Table 21.2.4-1🔍 provides guidance regarding multi-container/multi-volume/multi-product filling requirements. Refer to Section 1.0 and Section 2.0 for additional information.

Table 21.2.4-1🔍 Case 2: Requirements for Multi-container/Multi-volume/Multi-product Filling

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Change Parts: Mechanical components on the filling line that must be exchanged when the container format changes, including feed screws, star wheels and walking beams. Each container format requires its own set of change parts.

IL / R / H glass classification: IL = molded glass infusion bottle, R = tubing vial, H = tubing injection bottle. The three types differ in weight, diameter tolerance and neck/shoulder dimensions, so mixing them requires the change parts to be revalidated.

Line Footprint: The physical space required by the whole line. In this case, bulk containers are used (requiring a washer plus a depyrogenation tunnel), so the footprint is much larger than that of a line using RTU pre-washed containers.

Analogy

Imagine a restaurant serving both 50 mL concentrated soups and 500 mL large bowls: the pots, portioning equipment and tray sizes are all different. If the restaurant did not design a "pot-changing system" at the outset, every menu change would mean a major kitchen rebuild. The change parts design in this case is the equivalent of preparing matching cookware for every menu size in advance.

Key Notes

Reminder on the decision hierarchy: Filling technology flexibility is a "business flexibility" requirement (third priority), but if it is not built into the initial design, adding a new filling technology later may require revalidation of the entire filling line, at a cost far higher than planning ahead.
Therefore: before the design is locked, confirm whether the product pipeline for the next 5 years will need different filling technologies.

Practice Questions

  1. If a tubing vial (R type) is added later, which change parts must be redesigned? Why would the tolerance difference between molded glass and tubing glass affect filling line speed?
  2. This case chose bulk container washing rather than RTU. What are the respective impacts on facility footprint and validation workload?
21.2.5 Case 2: Anticipated Batch Sizes and Operating Practices

Original Text

Table 21.2.5-1🔍 outlines typical batch parameters to consider. Refer to Section 1.0, Section 3.0, and Section 4.0 for additional information.

Table 21.2.5-1🔍 Case 2: Anticipated Batch Sizes and Operating Practices

Operating Criteria (and their influence on batch throughput)

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Campaign Strategy: Multiple batches are filled consecutively, with only a minor changeover between batches rather than a full changeover each time. The advantage is a substantial reduction in downtime; the cost is a longer accumulation of aseptic risk, which is why an isolator is preferred over RABS.

Rate-Limiting Step: In this case the depyrogenation tunnel is the bottleneck. Even if the number of filling heads is increased, overall line speed cannot improve, because the tunnel conveyor speed is the key limit. This is the classic "weakest stave of the barrel" effect.

Efficiency Calculation Framework

Available hours per year = 365 days × 16 hr/day × (5/7 days/week)
           ≈ 4,160 hours/year

Less downtime (Facility Efficiency 75%):
Available production time ≈ 4,160 × 0.75 = 3,120 hours

Line efficiency 85% → actual filling time ≈ 3,120 × 0.85
           ≈ 2,652 hours/year

Yield 98% → effective output = filled quantity × 0.98

Practical takeaway: every 1% improvement in line efficiency
is equivalent to about 26 additional hours of effective filling time per year.

Key Notes

EM management during a campaign is critical: EM samples must be completed at the end of each batch, but the EM materials must be staged inside the isolator/RABS before the filling line starts up, or transferred in via RTP. This is a detail of the operating plan, yet it is an important part of the APS design.

The filling path strategy determines whether a 4-hour batch changeover is feasible: If CIP/SIP is used, confirm that the CIP/SIP cycle time is < 4 hours (including all documentation and integrity testing); if this is not feasible, a single-use pathway should be adopted early in the design.

21.2.6 Case 2: Comparison of Requirements to Filling System Capabilities

Original Text

Now that some of the preliminary design requirements for the product and its intended packaging have been defined, the requirements can be compared to the filling system capabilities and attributes as described in Section 2.0. Comparison of the filling system capabilities to the product needs for this example leads to the following evaluative matrix in Table 21.2.6-1. Refer to Section 2.0 and Section 4.0 for additional information.

Table 21.2.6-1🔍 Case 2: Comparison of Requirements to Filling System Capabilities

Legend: filled circle = available or acceptable | empty/noted = not available or not acceptable

Based on the above chart, the product characteristics make PP and TP the leading candidates, as planned fill volumes and shear-sensitivity of the product may preclude RPP (both volume and shear) and DP (volume alone).

PP and TP are well-matched. Decision-making may come down to whether SU technology (favoring PP) or CIP/SIP (favoring TP) are preferred. That decision may be driven by the changeover time with each, as the modest batch sizes will result in frequent changeover of the fluid pathway within the campaigns. If the foaming with the product is severe and SU technology is the desire, then PP will be the strongest contender if the cost of SU is not prohibitive based on the planned number of batches.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

How to use the capability comparison matrix: The matrix is not meant to find the "perfect technology"; it is a systematic way to eliminate options that do not meet the requirements. In this case:

  • RPP is eliminated - at large volumes (250-500 mL) pump size is limited, and the shear risk to the protein is unacceptable
  • DP is eliminated - likewise limited by the large volume
  • PP vs TP - the outcome depends on a preference for SU versus a preference for CIP/SIP, which is settled by a business decision

Decision hierarchy: sterility assurance > product CQAs (shear sensitivity) > business flexibility (SU cost)

Analogy

The matrix is like choosing cookware for a restaurant: you have four kinds of cooking equipment (PP/RPP/TP/DP), but the menu (large-volume protein filling) places clear requirements on the cookware. Not every piece of cookware can handle a large batch, and not every one is gentle enough for the ingredients. The matrix scores them item by item, and in the end two options tie for first place; the final choice depends on your kitchen cleaning strategy (dishwasher vs disposable containers).

Key Notes

Deciding factors for PP vs TP:

  • If the product foams heavily and SU is preferred → choose PP (but calculate SU cost × number of batches per year)
  • If the changeover time is tight (4-hour interval between batches) and CIP/SIP can be completed within that time → choose TP
  • If the campaign spans 5 days and wear is a risk → the tubing wear of PP requires a more rigorous monitoring plan

This is the central lesson of the guide: there is no single correct answer, only the best choice based on data.

Practice Questions

  1. If you are a technology transfer engineer at a CDMO and the client's drug substance batch cost is extremely high ($2M per batch), what does 100% IPC mean for PP? How does this factor influence the choice between PP and TP?
  2. If a campaign lasts as long as 5 days, how is PP tubing wear reflected in the APS? How should the monitoring plan be designed?
21.2.7 Case 2: Other Design Elements for Consideration

Original Text

There are a number of other design decisions that will impact the layout and operation of the filling line, such as:

  • Operator Interface with the line (Section 8.0)
  • Supply of Components (Section 9.0 and Section 10.0)
  • Product Filtration, including location of filters, required number of filter elements, integrity-testing pre- and post-filling (Section 11.0)
  • Filling Environment and Utilities (Section 14.0 and Section 15.0)

Generally, these decisions should be made as part of the filling-line specification process as they may affect costs and can influence placement of equipment; however, these are generally less of a direct impact on the selection of the filling technology itself.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Notes

This section closes out Case 2 and reminds readers that once the filling technology has been selected, a series of "peripheral design decisions" still remain, including the operator interface, component supply, filter locations and integrity testing, and utilities.

Although these decisions do not directly determine the filling technology, they affect equipment footprint, CAPEX, operating risk and, ultimately, the content of the URS (User Requirements Specification). It is advisable to start discussing these peripheral designs immediately after the filling technology is confirmed.

Key Concepts

Priority order of design decisions:

  1. Filling technology selection - the core of this case study (21.2.1-21.2.6)
  2. Peripheral system design - covered in this section (operator interface, component supply, filtration, utilities)
  3. Space layout and cost estimation - carried out after the first two are complete

This sequence ensures that the most important decisions (sterility assurance > CQAs) are made first and the design then proceeds layer by layer, avoiding a situation where layout or cost forces the technology selection.

Tutorial Commentary

Key Concepts

Nature of the vendor resources section: Section 22 consists of paid advertisements included at the end of the PDA technical guide, and PDA explicitly states that it does "not represent endorsement or preference." For the reader, the practical value of this section is to learn which major equipment suppliers are on the market today and which technology directions each emphasizes.

It is worth noting that these four vendors (Bausch+Ströbel, groninger, IMA, OPTIMA) are all leading European manufacturers of aseptic filling equipment, reflecting Europe's dominance in high-end pharmaceutical machinery.

Key Notes - Technology Trend Observations

The core proposition of GENEX (Bausch+Ströbel): "Gloveless Aseptic Production." The glove port has traditionally been one of the greatest contamination risk points in RABS/isolators (see the intervention management requirements of EU GMP Annex 1). Replacing manual interventions with robotic automation is the core trend for the next generation of aseptic filling lines.

The "Single Rejection" concept of IMA Detecta: After a conventional vision system detects a defect, it may reject an entire batch or multiple units; Single Rejection means the robot precisely removes only the single defective unit, greatly improving yield. This echoes the importance of 100% IPC for high-value products discussed in Section 5 of this guide.

Analogy

These vendor advertisements are like the vendor directory at the back of a car magazine: not a review, but a quick way to grasp the market landscape. When you later write an RFQ (request for quotation) or URS (User Requirements Specification), these vendor names are your first-round inquiry list.

Section 21B Summary

  • Multi-container/multi-format design (21.2.4): At the start of the design, all container formats, the change parts list, and the possibility of adding different glass types (IL/R/H) in future must be locked down; otherwise any new format added later will require revalidation.
  • Batch parameters and campaign (21.2.5): The depyrogenation tunnel is the rate-limiting bottleneck for large containers; the campaign strategy favors the use of isolators; the 4-hour changeover between batches must cover all tasks (CIP/SIP, integrity testing, EM reconciliation, documentation).
  • Three-layer efficiency structure: Line Efficiency (85% target) × Facility Efficiency (70-80%) × Yield (98%) together determine actual annual output; every percentage point requires significant investment to improve.
  • Technology selection conclusion (21.2.6): RPP and DP are excluded because of large volume/protein shear issues; PP and TP tie as the best options, and the final choice depends on a preference for SU (PP) or for CIP/SIP (TP), determined jointly by the campaign changeover time and SU cost.
  • The decision hierarchy always holds: Sterility Assurance > Product CQAs > Business Flexibility. In this case, the campaign drives the isolator selection (sterility assurance first), shear sensitivity excludes RPP (CQA first), and SU vs CIP/SIP is the commercial decision considered last.
